issues.title: It's official: creatives are using AI daily, but most aren't making extra money from it
issues.summary: Envato's second annual survey of more than 1,000 creatives finds that AI use has become routine, even if they don't always tell the client. But whether they're using it well remains an open question....
issues.author: Tom May
issues.content_html:
Envato's second annual survey of more than 1,000 creatives finds that AI use has become routine, even if they don't always tell the client. But whether they're using it well remains an open question.

This time last year, many creatives were rushing to adopt AI tools, but nervously. Twelve months later, things have changed a lot. That's according to Beyond the Hype: The State of AI in Creative Work, the second annual report from Envato, the creative asset and AI toolkit owned by Shutterstock.

Based on a survey of 1,033 creatives across 103 countries and territories, the report reveals what creatives are actually doing with AI. And two big things immediately grabbed my attention. Firstly, more than half of AI users have used it on key client work without telling their client. And secondly, while AI may save you time, most creatives aren't seeing that turn into actual money.

To unpack these findings and more, I spoke to Hichame Assi, president of Shutterstock, which includes Envato.

Why ask?

Envato first ran the survey in 2025, and Hichame says the reason was simple. The public conversation about AI didn't match what he was seeing from the working creatives who use Envato. "At face value, the narrative was all hype or doom," he recalls. "Yet in our community, creatives were quietly working AI into client jobs." So last year, Envato asked creatives how they were using it.

One finding from that first survey stayed with Hichame in particular. "Almost half were using AI every day, but only about a third felt really prepared for it. That gap felt worth keeping an eye on, so we came back to see what had changed."

So what has changed in the last 12 months? Well, quite a lot actually. For a start, today 87% of creatives use AI at work at least occasionally, and 58% use it every day.

"AI is now part of the daily routine for most creatives," says Hichame. "Daily use rose from 49% to 58%, and agentic tools, which we didn't even ask about last year, are now used regularly by more than a third of AI users. At the same time, active avoidance has grown from 3% to 8%, so not everyone is on board yet."

But while most creatives are using AI to help them in their work, that doesn't mean that AI is doing their work, at least not all of it.

The survey split people's creative work into six stages, from research and admin to editing. At five of the six stages, "directing [AI] closely" was the most common approach. The percentage of creatives who let AI work "with little input" never went above 11%, and at some stages, it dropped to 4%. As for generating assets, only 7% took a hands-off approach.

The fall of the prompt

For Hichame, the biggest surprise in this year's data concerned the skill that, only a year ago, everyone seemed to agree was essential: prompting.

"Last year, our respondents named prompting as a skills gap and predicted 'prompt engineer' as a new job," he recalls. "This year, though, creatives ranked it last of eight factors, at 19%." Taste and judgement came first, at 53%. Craft came second, at 49%, followed by the strength of the idea, at 39%.

So what's going on? Perhaps this is just a sign that models have got much better at understanding natural language and visual references. Consequently, the time when precise prompts were all-important is long gone.

"The tools are going to keep getting easier and more accessible, so knowing how to use them won't be what sets creatives apart," says Jessica Walsh, founder of New York studio &Walsh and one of the experts interviewed for the report. What will, in her view, is "being able to recognise great work when you see it [which is] not something you can prompt, or learn overnight."

A lack of rules

One thing that surprised me personally is that nearly six in 10 creatives who work in teams say they have no written AI policy. Even in organisations of 250 or more people, four in 10 say they've been given nothing in writing. As Hichame puts it: "The tools moved fast, and the rules didn't. Most are working it out as they go." Which brings us to a thorny question: should creatives disclose whether they've used AI in their work?

In practice, it seems, this has become a matter of personal judgement. More than half of AI users (53%) have used it on key client work without telling the client, and most don't see that as a problem. Only 7% felt uncomfortable staying quiet.

Hichame notes, though, that when there are rules in place, "creatives are more open with clients, with 47% always disclosing AI use, compared with 38% where there's no policy." Age can play a part, too: while only 40% of creatives always tell clients when they've used AI, that rises to 53% among those aged 50 and over.

What humans are for

One of the most commonly cited concerns about AI is that its output is bland and lacks soul. Yet when creatives discard AI-generated concepts, that's rarely the real reason. According to the report, one third (34%) do so because the concepts missed the brief or vision, and a similar number (32%) do so because of errors or low quality, such as garbled logos or glitchy video. Only 5% drop them because they lack feeling or soul.

What's just as interesting is what creatives keep. "The typical creative generates three to five AI concepts and keeps about two," notes Hichame. "Three in four keep half or fewer of their concepts." That, as he sees it, shows how important human creativity remains in the creative process. "Quality control is where humans make the difference," he says. "Knowing what the brief needs, seeing where an output falls short and choosing what makes the cut are judgement calls.

"Generating 10 options is easy," he adds. "Knowing which one is right is the skill, and it's one that creatives build over years."

Where's the money?

Here's another interesting question the report poses: is AI making creatives richer? The answer is: mostly not, or at least not yet.

"Half of creatives who use AI say it makes them faster," says Hichame. "But of those, only one in four report any financial upside. Another one in five earn about the same for less effort. For the rest, they gain time, not money."

This isn't, though, because people are cutting their rates: quite the reverse. "Of the freelancers and agency owners we asked, 40% raised their rates this year and only 6% cut them," he says. More to the point, more than a quarter of AI users (28%) now offer services they couldn't before, and 26% of those whose rates moved credited new services.

The conclusion in Hichame's mind is clear. "Getting better results from AI is the skill creatives most want to learn, at 45%, while creative direction sits near the bottom at 18%," he notes. Yet in the survey, the creatives who have raised their rates credited speed, reputation and creative direction ahead of AI skills. "This suggests people are chasing the skill the market isn't paying for, and ignoring the ones it is."

His advice? "Take the hours AI gives back and put them where clients pay," he says. "That means turning work around faster, investing in your own name and point of view, so your work is recognisable as yours, and sharpening your direction. Because three in four creatives already discard at least half of what AI produces, and that judgement is what sets you apart."

issues.title: Why GTA 6 is the year's biggest campaign for a brand that refuses to sell ad space
issues.summary: Rockstar won't take a penny for product placement, yet half the world's brands are currently trying to look like Vice City. On the eve of launch, here's why I think GTA 6 matters to any creative profe...
issues.author: Katy Cowan
issues.content_html:
Rockstar won't take a penny for product placement, yet half the world's brands are currently trying to look like Vice City. On the eve of launch, here's why I think GTA 6 matters to any creative professional.

I'm an enthusiastic gamer. But I skipped Grand Theft Auto V entirely. I just couldn't join the 230 million people who've snapped up a copy since it came out 13 years ago, because I couldn't play as a woman.

Tomorrow, that changes. GTA 6 unlocks at midnight. One of the lead characters, Lucia Caminos, will be waiting for me. And I've cleared my diary for the next week.

If you don't game, you might think that's a bit pathetic. Fair enough. But if you're an art director, illustrator or marketer who's seen those pink-and-orange sunsets flood your feeds lately and wondered what all the fuss is about – it's only a video game, surely? Well, no it isn't. Not really.

Not to be dramatic, GTA 6 marks one of the biggest cultural moments in a century. And that's hugely rewarding, especially for someone who grew up in an era when we still did things together.

A collective phenomenon

Alas, there isn't much left that everyone experiences together, all at once. We stream different shows on different nights and scroll different feeds. It's not like the good old days when we'd wait for our favourite programmes on one of four TV channels or get the bus to Hanley's Fezzy Park to see the latest blockbuster (and hope we bumped into Mark from the year above). GTA is one of the few exceptions. It's a single date that tens of millions of people have been anticipating for years.

The numbers are daft, too. The second trailer was watched 475 million times in a day. When Rockstar premiered a 27-minute preview on Netflix in August, it drew 31.1 million views in four days and topped the film chart in 87 of the 93 countries Netflix tracks. Strauss Zelnick, chief executive of Rockstar's parent company Take-Two, described that premiere as "one of the hors d'oeuvres". Now we're all hungry for the main course.

Analysts estimate 15.88 million digital pre-orders, worth around $1.54bn. So yeah, it's big. But the numbers aren't why I think creatives should be sitting up and paying attention.

Not for sale

As you can imagine, the most wanted media space on the planet right now is a billboard inside Vice City. Yet you can't buy it.

Zelnick has ruled out product placement and brand deals altogether, on the grounds that "all the brands are made up". So you'll not spot any real fizzy drinks or real trainers. Just the usual Patriot Beer, Sessanta Nove and hundreds of other parodies written and designed entirely in-house.

Naturally, the brands have done their thing anyway. Hyundai, BMW and Burger King are among those dressing their social posts in GTA's sunset palette. Perhaps they're hoping to enjoy some of that Vice City glow, too.

Paint, print and fashion

I've just spent a week in Miami Beach, and it was fun to walk around the city GTA 6 is based on. I spotted the ads for the game everywhere. I especially loved seeing street kiosks carrying ads for the game's fake brands, double entendres and all. A clever bit of marketing, and my friends at Creative Bloq agree.

In Williamsburg, Brooklyn, there's a vast mural of Jason and Lucia, hand-painted by Colossal Media – the New York sign painters who've worked with Rockstar since San Andreas in 2004.

Then there's the press. The first on-record interviews about the game didn't go to a gaming site – they went to Dazed, which put Jason and Lucia on the cover of its autumn 'New Idols' issue and dressed them in Vice City's fictional fashion labels. Just brilliant.

And in Wynwood, Miami's street art district, 10 new murals have gone up from artists including FAILE, Lady AIKO, Queen Andrea and DENIAL, alongside a deal that gives Miami-Dade residents free entry to the Wynwood Walls Museum through 2028. Rockstar says more than 50 real street artists painted the walls inside the game, too. And no generative AI was used.

What's in it for the rest of us?

OK, so most of us creatives will never have the luxury of a billion-dollar budget or 13 years for a project. But take away that scale and you're left with something pretty old-fashioned.

Rockstar just concentrated on building its virtual Vice City and everything you might find in it, from parody brands and radio stations to murals made especially for the game. When you think about it, the advertising came naturally. The campaign existed before anything appeared in the real world.

It also said very little. There was a year of silence between trailers, and the studio has barely given an interview. There's a lot of mystery around it all, and that's done Rockstar no harm.

And it even said no to the brand deals and easy money. It's quite impressive to see this kind of restraint at play. But Rockstar can afford to hold back. Analysts at Newzoo estimate the game could make between $3.3bn and $5.2bn in its first week alone. Does it really need anything more than that? Particularly with Take-Two forecasting record sales of more than $8bn (around £6bn) for its financial year?

And yes, I'm here for the violence

I've got to admit: this is still Grand Theft Auto. It's violent and crude, and the conversation around it remains overwhelmingly male. None of which is putting me off.

I'm a girl who loves the scene in 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood' when Brad Pitt throws a can of dog food into the face of an intruder. I roared "yessss" at the screen. I enjoy a bit of violent vengeance, yet I know the difference between reality and fun.

So does my nephew, who's now old enough to play it too. (I'd better get practising my shooting skills.) That might be the part I'm looking forward to the most: being part of something with family and friends. Comparing notes and being social rather than passively watching telly (which I find boring).

Can GTA 6 live up to all the hype? Will it be worth the 13-year wait for a female protagonist? Given Rockstar's track record, I know it will.

Most importantly, I love how a game got the whole world's attention at the same time, and it did it with a bit of paint, parody and a refusal to sell out. That alone is worth a week off work, sitting in my pyjamas and enjoying the ride. Lucia and I have plans. See you on the other side.

issues.title: 'It's going to be scary': a week on from Adobe MAX 2026, creatives get honest about the future
issues.summary: I left this year's Adobe MAX Sneaks feeling a bit wary. So I asked creatives what scares them most about their work, listened to what two of Adobe's most senior people had to say, and ended up facing...
issues.author: Katy Cowan
issues.content_html:
I left this year's Adobe MAX Sneaks feeling a bit wary. So I asked creatives what scares them most about their work, listened to what two of Adobe's most senior people had to say, and ended up facing a few of my own fears.

If you're familiar with Adobe's Sneaks, you'll know they've earned legendary status at Adobe MAX over the years. It's an hour or two when the people who build the experimental tools get up and show them off to a live audience, livestreamed to millions of creatives worldwide. A nerve-racking experience, I'm sure... Not just because the whole world is watching, but because anything could go wrong.

Usually, there are loud whoops and almost cult-like, frenzied excitement as Adobe proudly reveals its latest innovations. Not so much this year, from where I was sitting, or indeed the last. Certainly not as much since Adobe started to introduce AI into its suite; maybe the audience was just too stunned to applaud.

For more than a decade, I watched from my desk in Manchester in the middle of the night, scribbling down notes for readers who wanted to know what was coming next. How their working lives were about to get easier thanks to the software they'd spent ages learning. This year, I was right there in the room in Miami Beach, as an editor, sitting with the other British journalists. Terry Crews was hosting, dressed head to toe in a bright pink suit with shiny blue shoes and pink socks. And much like anyone who watched, I'm still processing it.

So what did Sneaks show us?

The tools come straight out of Adobe Labs, and none of them is guaranteed to ship, although some do. And yeah, AI played a leading role. Of course it did. The future is here.

As always, I'm pretty nuanced about these things. It's not so black-and-white. If Adobe can empower creatives to skip the mundane stuff and focus on their creativity, then brilliant. If it can open the playing field to those who previously didn't have the means to create, then I'm all for it. The computer, after all, opened the gates to so many more people back in the 1990s, and the internet welcomed even more.

But there are multiple fine lines. Where AI might be useful in one corner, it feels unwelcome in another.

Ten projects took to the stage. Some were very much welcome, and those were the ones that got the whoops. Project Rinse Repeat copies edits you've made in one area of an image to another, while keeping everything editable in Photoshop.

Project Link Up lets you drag design elements into a scene and sit back and watch their perspective, scale and style adapt to fit, landing as editable vector artwork. Project Deep Brush, my personal favourite, understands an image's shape, colour and lighting, so you can quite literally paint light into a scene. All clever, time-saving stuff.

Others were not so welcome. Project Screen Test lets you build a fictional character's look, voice and personality, and then chat to them. I mean, it was incredible, sure. But is it really necessary? Project Live Set changes a subject, a set or a camera move while the video is still playing.

Project Sight Span turns a single image into a 3D-style space that feels like you can step into it and walk around, framing shots that were never taken in real life. And then Project Sound Bender lets you describe a sound and pick it clean out of a finished mix. Mind-blowing, but I'm not sure the audience was happy.

As I sat there, looking around at my startled fellow attendees, I finally realised how fast things are moving. Casting, set design, location scouting, sound editing... whole corners of the industry flashed past in a few minutes each. I've been using AI tools for three or four years now. I'm an adopter, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But sitting there in that big conference hall, I felt a bit sick rather than excited.

So, still in Miami, I did what I always do in these situations. I asked you.

What keeps you up at night

I posted a simple question on LinkedIn: what are you most scared of in your work right now? More than a dozen replied, and their thoughts offered some brilliant insight.

For some, yes, the fear is real. "I used to have three to five projects monthly, and this year I had three to five in the year," says illustrator and lettering artist Ana Moreno Chávez. Tom Grattan, managing director and co-owner of consultancy EXP, has been meeting graduates who see a bleak future while watching "an Instagram feed of Adobe MAX attendees celebrating what feels like an accelerating decline of an industry".

Then there's what clients now expect. "I'm not afraid of the tools," says motion designer Oleksandr Merkulov. "I'm worried about clients getting used to 'fast and fine' and losing patience for that one extra round that makes the work 'good'." Designers Kieron Lewis and Bijesh Amatya see it too: people reaching for AI, as Kieron puts it, like "a takeaway because it's quicker and more convenient".

Elsewhere, others raised concerns about what we might lose if things get easy. "When the first attempt already looks finished, we lose the friction that turns a good idea into a great one," says Isabella Wordsworth, a designer at D&P in London. "Experimentation is becoming a luxury... It sits at the core of our industry." Francesca Oddenino, co-founder of Vicine, says her best work "is always born out of discomfort". Web developer Tom Harrison feels "very little pride making things this way".

Of course, juniors kept coming up. They're "being replaced by AI, but who do they train to become seniors?" asks brand designer Sophie O'Connor. A senior creative at a fast-growing start-up, who asked to remain anonymous, told me everyone at her company uses AI, and she misses the grunt work. "That's where I cut my teeth," she says, and she's scared for newcomers who won't get it. And she can't say any of this publicly. "I feel ashamed in a way, using it so much."

And then there's the even bigger elephant. "I'm scared of jumping on the 'bandwagon' and playing my role in the demise of my own role. And at the same time shunning AI and playing my role in the demise of my own role," says UX and UI designer Andrew Areoff.

Designer Bart Fish was the most forthright: "I am very concerned about how creatives are embracing this technology, even as it steals from them and threatens to replace them. I'm concerned that creatives think adoption will provide job security, even as they train the models and are asked to create systems intended to displace them."

Putting all this to Adobe

As it happens, I got the chance to sit down with two of Adobe's most senior people at MAX the day before Sneaks, and many of these same fears were swimming around my head. In fairness, much of what you told me you're scared of isn't Adobe's doing alone. And naturally, it's their job to be optimistic. But neither brushed my worries aside, which I really appreciated.

Karen Robinson is Adobe's vice president and associate general counsel, and she spends much of her time talking to lawmakers in the UK, EU, US and Australia. I asked whether the backlash from creatives in 2024, when the government floated its opt-out proposal for AI training, was justified. "I mean, yes, of course it was," she says. "You have people who are worried about what their livelihood is going to be like."

But two years on, she believes there's a reason for "some level of confidence". Artists are still earning a living, she argues, and "the sky did not fall". (Ana, with her three to five projects a year, might disagree.)

What was really interesting was her view that the fear itself has changed. Because what Adobe is hearing from creatives, she explains, is "candidly now less about the training and more about the output, because ultimately... AI-generated output is the thing that will compete directly with artists and creatives". She goes on: "And so what we're hearing is: we don't want to be pushed out of a market that our own art has created. So we want to talk about style protection. If I am an artist and I have a demonstrable style, I should be able to protect that." Right now, she says, you can't.

It's why she reckons licensing alone won't save any of us. She tells me about asking an illustrator Adobe works with how much licensing money would make it acceptable to be pushed out of the market by AI copies of her style. The answer? There isn't enough. "They want to control their art... If you're an artist and you make a very particular type of art, and now somebody comes, knocks off your style and starts putting it on aprons and oven mitts, that's not what you want," she says. "And so that requires protection on the output side that does not currently exist."

Essentially, we're in the Wild West again. The geeky lawyer in her (her words) also offers some perspective. When cameras arrived, photographs weren't eligible for copyright, because the machine supposedly did all the work. It took a series of court cases to recognise that the photographer (the human) was making creative decisions about subject, lighting and angle. And plenty of painters never picked up a camera at all. There will always be room, she says, for artists who don't want AI anywhere near their work.

She was candid about trust, too. The row over Adobe's terms of use in 2024 taught the company it had to communicate better. "In a time of uncertainty, companies aren't going to get the benefit of the doubt," she says. "And I don't mean that as a negative... It is our responsibility to clearly articulate what we're doing."

Eric Snowden, senior vice president of Adobe Design, is another optimist. He's also been a retoucher for 20 years, and he doesn't believe Photoshop is going anywhere. How do I know? I asked him outright with a cheeky chuckle: if AI can do pretty much anything, will anyone still need Adobe's tools? Will we even be using Photoshop in three years? "When I generate an image, I'm still editing every single one in Photoshop," he says. "I'm doing high-end retouching, I'm doing frequency separation, I'm doing all these things, like traditional Photoshop, and you'd be surprised at how much they still need that."

Without that human precision? "They come out looking good, and I think especially to an untrained eye they look good. But at the level our customers care about the details of these images, they do not look good enough."

He's not pretending these next few years will be painless, though. "Things are going to change. It's going to be scary... But there are some really bright spots, where we're also incredibly empowered to do things we've never been able to do before," he says. "Lean into that."

Scared? Yes. And still here

So, should we be scared? I think we're in a period of adjustment. A lull phase. A temporary era of people struggling, perhaps, before more work comes out of this revolution, not less.

But perhaps I'm deluded. Maybe I'm hoping optimism will overcome my fear. Fear for the juniors coming up behind us. Fear for my own career. And fear for the industry I've spent nearly two decades championing.

It's like being on a train with a party on board. Everyone's enjoying the champagne and the party food, knowing the track might run off into a deep chasm at any point. But we can't get off.

Much like you study the faces of the cabin crew on a bumpy, final descent, I realise I'd been studying Adobe's own people, looking for reassurance. Are we going to be OK? I kept thinking. What I got was honesty. Karen didn't tell me the fear was unjustified. And Eric didn't tell me it would be fine. "It's going to be scary," he said, with a smile. And then he told me to lean into it.

issues.title: Meet the strange and wonderful creatures of María Valeria Pazos' Anima Mundi
issues.summary: From crowned horses to fish covered in eyes, the Mexican artist brings together philosophy, poetry and generative technology to create a fantastical world. Gold leaf glows across María Valeria Pazos's...
issues.author: Ayla Angelos
issues.content_html:
From crowned horses to fish covered in eyes, the Mexican artist brings together philosophy, poetry and generative technology to create a fantastical world.

Gold leaf glows across María Valeria Pazos's images like candlelight on a chapel wall; fish drift through moonlight skies speckled with tiny eyes; a horse carries a procession of sun-faced saints on its back; and spiky-haired figures in dotted dresses stand among hens and herons. Her pieces nod to folk art, illuminated manuscripts and the hushed black-and-white photography of handmade sculpture – creating a world where every object seems to be watching you.

María lives in Mexico City and works between philosophy, poetry, visual art, sensory theatre, generative technology and imagination. "From a very young age, the imagination was a territory where I could find possibilities different from those my body was experiencing," she says. "Imagination allowed me to believe that reality could be otherwise, that there were other ways of inhabiting the world. And that possibility gave me hope."

For more than 10 years she devoted herself to sensory theatre, building rooms where "scents, textures, sounds and imagination could reorganise our perception of reality." She studied philosophy at UNAM and is now completing a PhD in Philosophy of Science on embodied imagination.

The theatre years still shape how her pictures feel, so much so that she wants an image to suggest a "temperature, a scent, a texture or a bodily sensation" – and you can certainly sense it in the warm honey of the gold, the cool blue of patterned fish and the frosty paper wings of a fox balanced on stilt-thin legs.

When it's not the theatre and sensory experiences driving her work, María will turn to language – in which a poem becomes a scene, a scene then becomes a character. A character grows into a small audiovisual story. She uses image and video generation models as one instrument among several others, alongside drawings, collages, and material references, and these tools have allowed her to realise universes she has carried in notebooks and poems for more than 25 years. "Artificial intelligence expands my possibilities for experimentation, while aesthetic decisions emerge from a continuous relationship between my imagination, my sensibility and the materials I work with."

Anima Mundi, her ever-growing project, runs on a method borrowed from the Surrealists. "Sometimes I take the head of one creature, the body of another, the limbs of an animal, the texture of a flower or the atmosphere of a dream," she says. "I mix and transform them, then observe what happens." She calls it a visual cut-up, and each new creature seems to belong to a family tree – a bird-legged fish, a lion-faced figure and a crowned horse all share the same eyes and the same dotted skin, for instance.

Gold has also become a recurring character for María, arriving after she found a text she wrote 15 years ago, full of golden beings, golden threads, and a woman immersed in a golden sea. "I had no conscious memory of writing these images, yet somehow, my unconscious had led me back to them," she says. "It fascinates me how certain images continue to live within us, quietly finding their way back into our creative worlds."

Of how she hopes her audience responds to her work, María has a wish – that they, too, can meet their own dreams. "I often imagine an image as a kind of Big Bang, an origami. Or a strand of DNA," she says. "I like to think that each image contains a sleeping universe, waiting for someone to encounter it and allow it to unfold within them."

issues.title: Carsten Höller’s Monumental Slides Bring Play to Mexico City
issues.summary: Four towering, functional slides connect different parts of Antara, where Sordo Madaleno’s latest expansion brings architecture, contemporary art, and public space together
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
Leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City. Four monumental slides by artist Carsten Höller are the centerpiece of a major expansion at Antara, a mixed-use development designed by architecture firm Sordo Madaleno. The interactive installations bring an unexpected element of play to a destination that combines retail, hospitality, workplaces, and contemporary art.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

Titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date. The four spiraling structures range from 39 to 125 feet in height, with lengths extending from approximately 102 to 295 feet. Rather than functioning as standalone sculptures, they are integrated into the architecture, connecting different parts of the development while giving visitors a new way to move between them.

The slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area. Their arrangement transforms what might otherwise be separate destinations into a shared experience, bringing people from different parts of the complex together in an unexpected way.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

“People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants, and from an art center are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” Höller explains. “They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and fear.”

The installation is part of the latest chapter for Antara, which opened in 2006 on a former industrial site in Mexico City’s Colonia Granada neighborhood. Developed by SOMA and designed by Sordo Madaleno, the original project introduced an open-air retail concept that has since evolved into a larger destination for shopping, dining, and cultural programming.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

Twenty years later, the expansion places greater emphasis on the spaces between buildings and the ways visitors move through them. A new 26,000-square-foot public garden, landscaped pathways, and stepped terraces connect the development’s different components, creating places to gather beyond its commercial spaces.

Art plays a central role in that approach. SOMA’s nonprofit contemporary art foundation, Arte Abierto, will open a new location within Antara, Arte Abierto Polanco, in December 2026. Alongside Höller’s installation, the venue will present Now What (2026), an exhibition by Danish artist collective Superflex that examines the relationship between built environments and natural forces. Combining architecture, sculpture, and text, the exhibition explores how human systems of design and organization influence our relationship with the surrounding world.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

For SOMA president Javier Sordo Madaleno De Haro, the investment in publicly accessible space is fundamental to the development’s long-term value. “I’ve realized that the most valuable thing is not the capital gain of a building itself, but the value it brings to its surroundings,” he says. “Art and public space are how we create that value.”

The expansion also introduces more than 80 new retail brands and concepts, bringing Antara’s total to 260. A forthcoming 43-story tower will house Rosewood Mexico City, with 163 guest rooms and suites, restaurants, a spa, and an outdoor pool deck, along with office space for international companies.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

Yet the most distinctive addition may be the one that challenges how people typically navigate a building. By incorporating Höller’s slides directly into the architecture, Sordo Madaleno and SOMA have made art part of the development’s circulation, turning movement between spaces into an experience in its own right.

The new public spaces and gardens are now open, while Mexico City Slides and the Superflex exhibition are scheduled to open in December. Access to the slides will be free, offering visitors a decidedly unconventional way to experience the evolving development.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

issues.title: OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali
issues.summary: Designed by OMA, Potato Head's Good Times General Store brings Balinese craftsmanship, circular design, and interactive workshops to the traditional retail experience
issues.author: Murrye Bernard
issues.content_html:
What if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the new Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA, Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

The architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” says Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

Reclaimed and locally sourced materials bring natural variations in color, texture, and form. Instead of concealing these irregularities, the designers embraced them, letting the materials guide the assembly and detailing.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

Inside, the store unfolds across five interconnected bays, guiding visitors from finished products toward the processes behind their creation. The first showcases souvenirs and lifestyle objects by Indonesian craftspeople, while the second presents the Potato Head Collection, an apparel line inspired by Bali. The third introduces Wasted by Potato Head, a collaboration with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homewares.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

In the final two bays, visitors move from browsing to making. A working natural dye studio transforms food and plant waste into pigments used in workshops exploring dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Beyond it, The Workshop features a wall of shredded HDPE plastic recovered from waste collectors across Bali and Java. The colorful fragments become part of the architecture, making the material’s previous life visible, while the surrounding space is dedicated to experimentation.

“While the first three bays focus on products and the stories behind them, the final two bays prioritize participation, inviting visitors to engage directly with materials and processes,” Gianotten explains.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

The store also connects to Desa Potato Head’s broader sustainability initiatives, including its Waste Lab and Follow the Waste Tour, which demonstrate how discarded materials can be recovered, processed, and transformed into new objects. For OMA, the project extends ideas explored in N*thing is Possible, a 2022 exhibition in Singapore examining the potential of zero-waste hospitality.

“Circularity therefore becomes something experiential rather than abstract,” says Gianotten.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

Designing around reclaimed resources required flexibility, especially around material consistency and availability. Rather than forcing materials into predetermined specifications, the team adapted the design to their natural characteristics and limitations.

“We discovered that circularity goes beyond material selection,” Herkarisma explains. “It is about rethinking how we design, build, operate, and engage people in the process of giving new value to resources that would otherwise be discarded.”

Photography by Sharon Angelia

At the Good Times General Store, the act of making is as visible as the finished product. By placing workshops alongside retail displays and allowing reclaimed materials to shape the architecture, OMA and Potato Head offer a model of shopping that encourages visitors to look more closely at what they consume—and what might otherwise be thrown away.

issues.title: The Best Tech Gifts for Design Enthusiasts
issues.summary: Thoughtfully designed technology that brings something unexpected to everyday life
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
Technology has become so thoroughly integrated into our lives that it’s easy to overlook the design behind it. But look beyond the specifications, and you’ll find plenty of objects worth paying attention to: a clock that uses light and sound to mark the passing hours, a digital frame that resembles a printed photograph, and a cassette-playing boombox that brings back the pleasure of physical controls.

For this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do. Some embrace the past, others experiment with new technology, and a few make the everyday business of charging, organizing, and staying connected a little more enjoyable.

Photography courtesy of MoMA Design Store

SB214OS Bluetooth Boombox by Studebaker

The boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters. Studebaker’s retro-inspired design brings the 1980s into the present with Bluetooth connectivity, a CD player, USB playback, and a cassette deck that can even record music. A rechargeable battery and built-in carrying handle make it easy to take the nostalgia wherever the party goes.

The SB214OS Bluetooth Boombox is available at store.moma.org for $250.

Photography courtesy of Polaroid

Mod Instant Camera by Polaroid

Polaroid’s Mod puts creative controls directly on the camera, inviting experimentation without the distraction of a smartphone screen. Dedicated physical controls make it easy to explore effects like double exposures, light painting, motion freeze, and split-shot compositions. It’s a refreshingly hands-on approach to photography that encourages a little spontaneity and plenty of happy accidents.

The Polaroid Mod Instant Camera is available at polaroid.com for $169.99.

Photography courtesy of Therabody

CryoTherm Palm by Therabody

Therabody takes a different approach to workout recovery with a device designed to fit between your hands. To help manage body heat during workouts, the handheld device uses temperature-controlled surfaces to cool both palms simultaneously, with additional heat and contrast therapy settings. Compact and cordless, it provides an alternative to ice baths and other more cumbersome temperature-based recovery equipment.

The CryoTherm Palm is available at therabody.com for $399.99.

Photography courtesy of Balmuda

The Clock by Balmuda

Inspired by traditional pocket watches, Balmuda’s The Clock reimagines how we experience time through light, sound, and movement. Its carved aluminum body houses 75 LEDs that create an animated display, while built-in speakers play ambient soundscapes designed for focus, relaxation, and sleep. With customizable alarms, app connectivity, and USB-C charging, it’s a thoughtful alternative to the conventional bedside clock.

The Clock is available at us.balmuda.com for $499 in Silver and $519 in Champagne.

Photography courtesy of Bang & Olufsen

Beoplay H100 Headphones by Bang & Olufsen

Bang & Olufsen’s Beoplay H100 headphones are undeniably a splurge, but they’re designed with longevity in mind. The Danish brand developed the H100 with replaceable components, including the ear cushions, headband, and batteries. The custom titanium drivers, soft leather detailing, and rich color options give them a distinctly luxurious feel, while advanced noise cancellation and immersive sound make the listening experience just as considered as the design. It’s an investment piece for someone who appreciates exceptional craftsmanship as much as great audio.

The Beoplay H100 Headphones are available at bang-olufsen.com for $2,200.

Photography courtesy of Warby Parker

Intelligent Eyewear by Warby Parker

Smart glasses are getting a stylish update thanks to Warby Parker’s collaboration with Google and Samsung. Available in three of the brand’s familiar silhouettes, the lightweight frames incorporate a camera, open-ear speakers, and Gemini AI for hands-free photography, calls, navigation, and more. Subtly translucent temples offer a glimpse of the technology inside without compromising the classic eyewear design. With prescription, nonprescription, reading, and sunglass options, they’re a surprisingly versatile gift.

Intelligent Eyewear is available for preorder at warbyparker.com, starting at $395.

Photography courtesy of Flowtica

Flowtica Scribe AI Recording Pen by Flowtica

What looks like an ordinary ballpoint pen has a few technological tricks up its sleeve. The Flowtica Scribe combines a functional writing instrument with an AI-powered voice recorder, allowing users to capture conversations while taking notes on paper the old-fashioned way. A companion app can transcribe recordings and turn them into summaries and action items, bringing digital convenience to a familiar analog tool. An optional vegan leather charging case gives the device a place to rest between meetings.

The Flowtica Scribe is available at flowtica.ai for $159.

Photography courtesy of Bellroy

Tech Kit by Bellroy

Anyone who’s ever untangled a mess of charging cables at the bottom of a bag will appreciate Bellroy’s thoughtfully designed Tech Kit. The small organizer opens flat to reveal a series of mesh pockets and elastic loops that keep chargers, cables, earbuds, and other tech essentials neatly in place. Its structured shape makes everything easy to see and access, while the streamlined exterior, made from recycled woven fabric, slips neatly into a backpack or carry-on. It’s a simple solution to one of travel’s most persistent little annoyances.

The Tech Kit is available at bellroy.com for $59–$69, depending on color.

Photography courtesy of Amazon

Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition by Amazon

Amazon’s latest Kindle redesign brings a more refined look and feel to the familiar e-reader. The Paperwhite Signature Edition pairs a sleek aluminum body with a 7-inch, glare-free display, adjustable warm lighting, and double-tap page turning. Waterproof construction and wireless charging make it an easy travel companion, while two finishes, Graphite and Seaglass Green, offer a choice between classic and colorful.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is available at amazon.com for $250.

Photography courtesy of Daily Objects

Surge Foldaway 3-in-1 Wireless Charger by DailyObjects

Who says charging stations have to be boring? DailyObjects’ Surge Foldaway turns an everyday tech essential into a sculptural desktop accessory. Its adjustable design accommodates an iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods simultaneously, consolidating three charging spots into one tidy footprint. The bold Cosmic Orange finish adds a welcome pop of color, giving the accessory a presence even when the devices are elsewhere.

The Surge Foldaway 3-in-1 Wireless Charger is available at dailyobjects.us for $175.

Photography courtesy of ModRetro

Chromatic by ModRetro

A love letter to handheld gaming, ModRetro’s Chromatic brings the original Game Boy experience into the present with a few thoughtful upgrades. Its magnesium-alloy body houses a custom, pixel-perfect display designed to play original Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges. The colorful finishes include four translucent options that expose the internal hardware, turning the console’s components into part of its visual identity.

The Chromatic + Tetris Bundle is available at modretro.com starting at $199.

Photography courtesy of Shark

CryoGlow Plus LED Face Mask by Shark

Shark’s CryoGlow Plus combines two skincare technologies in a single wearable device: LED light therapy and under-eye cooling. Red, blue, and infrared lights power several treatment modes, while adjustable cooling pads help refresh tired eyes. The upgraded design offers improved LED coverage around the eyes and mouth, and the soft Pastel Berry finish makes this wearable gadget surprisingly stylish.

The CryoGlow Plus LED Face Mask is available at sharkninja.com for $379.99.

Photography courtesy of Mudita

Mudita Kompakt by Mudita

In a market crowded with phones competing for attention, the Mudita Kompakt is designed to demand less of it. Its minimalist design centers on a 4.3-inch E Ink display, favoring a restrained interface over colorful notifications and app-heavy screens. Essential features like calling, messaging, offline maps, and a camera remain, while a dedicated offline switch offers a physical way to disconnect.

The Mudita Kompakt is available at mudita.com for $399.

Photography courtesy of Birdfy

Feeder Wood by Birdfy

Who says smart technology has to look high-tech? Birdfy’s Feeder Wood combines the charm of a traditional wooden birdhouse with a built-in camera, letting bird lovers watch their feathered visitors up close. Made from FSC-certified wood, the solar-powered feeder captures 1080p video. Its companion app can identify more than 6,000 bird species, bringing a layer of digital discovery to an otherwise familiar backyard ritual.

The Feeder Wood is available at birdfy.com for $189.99.

Photography courtesy of Wallie

Wallie 10 Digital Photo Frame by Wallie

Wallie’s approach to the digital photo frame starts with a simple idea: make the screen look less like a screen. Its 10-inch color E Ink display gives photographs the appearance of printed images, while real wood construction and a choice of four finishes help it blend into a gallery wall or shelf arrangement. Rounded or square corners offer further customization, and a rechargeable battery eliminates the need for a visible power cord. Photos can be updated remotely through an app.

The Wallie 10 is available at shop.wallieframe.com for $299.

Photography courtesy of Eve

Eve Flare Portable Smart LED Lamp by Eve

With its simple spherical form, Eve Flare looks more like an illuminated object than a conventional lamp. The rechargeable, water-resistant light offers millions of customizable colors, with app and voice controls for setting the mood indoors or outside. Its wireless charging base and portable design mean it can move effortlessly from a bedside table to the patio, adding a little atmosphere wherever it lands.

The Eve Flare Portable Smart LED Lamp is available at apple.com for $99.95.

Photography courtesy of Best Buy

Retro Mechanical Keyboard N Edition by 8BitDo

8BitDo borrows the visual language of the original Nintendo Entertainment System for a mechanical keyboard that feels straight out of the 1980s. Chunky gray keys, red accents, and tactile mechanical switches establish the retro aesthetic, while an included joystick and two oversized programmable buttons bring arcade-style controls to the desktop. Bluetooth and wireless connectivity keep the throwback design compatible with contemporary setups.

The 8BitDo Retro Mechanical Keyboard N Edition is available at bestbuy.com for $79.99.

Photography courtesy of Orbitkey

Nest v2 by Orbitkey

Even the most organized desk tends to accumulate charging cables, adapters, and other small tech accessories. Orbitkey’s Nest v2 gives them a designated home in a compact storage box with adjustable dividers and a fabric-lined interior. The removable leather-covered lid doubles as a valet tray and 15W wireless charger, keeping everyday essentials within reach while concealing the clutter underneath.

The Nest v2 is available at orbitkey.com for $125.

issues.title: Lindye Galloway Brings Intimacy to a 10,000-Square-Foot Home
issues.summary: In Dana Point, California, the interior designer uses natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings to create a warm, inviting family residence
issues.author: Leo Lei
issues.content_html:
At 10,000 square feet, a home can easily feel more expansive than inviting. For a new residence in Dana Point, California, interior designer Lindye Galloway approached that challenge through a careful balance of natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings. The goal was to create a home that felt as warm and comfortable as it was refined, with a relaxed atmosphere suited to everyday family life.

Photography by Grace Combs

Galloway drew inspiration from the architecture and natural surroundings, aiming to create a timeless home. The interiors are organized around texture and natural materials in a soft, understated palette. Warm woods, soft neutrals, and natural stone run through the rooms alongside linen, wool, and mohair.

Photography by Grace Combs

Tactile upholstery and darker accents contrast with the lighter woods and stone, adding depth and dimension to each room. Furniture was selected for comfort and sculptural appeal, with clean lines and soft, organic forms, giving rooms a relaxed, lived-in quality.

Photography by Grace Combs

The attention to detail extends to the home’s fixtures and finishes. Hardware from Rocky Mountain Hardware and Nanz is complemented by mirrors from Claude Home and Croft House, while lighting comes from Ravenhill, Atelier de Troupe, and Roll & Hill.

Photography by Grace Combs

The kitchen, primary bathroom, and living room carry the same combination of wood, stone, and natural fibers. Beyond the main rooms, the property includes a separate guest house with its own bedroom and an indoor-outdoor living area. Galloway extended the same material palette to these spaces, creating continuity throughout the property.

Photography by Grace Combs

Rather than relying on dramatic gestures, Galloway lets the interplay of materials, textures, and forms define the interiors. It’s an approach that brings warmth and intimacy to a home of considerable scale.

Photography by Grace Combs

issues.title: Seaweed earplug among grant-winning Design Museum prototypes
issues.summary: A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed, two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants. UK-based studios Searo Labs, WeCanMake, Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their "cutting-edge" environmental […] The post Seaweed
issues.author: Anna Skrebels
issues.content_html:
A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed, two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants.

UK-based studios Searo Labs, WeCanMake, Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their "cutting-edge" environmental prototypes.

Described as the "world's first seaweed-based single-use earplug", SearoSoft by Cambridge-based Searo Labs is a fully biodegradable and renewable alternative to single-use earplugs.

According to SearoSoft, the soft, mouldable earplugs are made without microplastics or chemicals and designed to hydrate the ear canal, unlike plastic-based products, which can be drying.

Once discarded, they are biodegradable in water or soil after 30 days. As seaweed is a regenerative crop, SearoSoft explained that there is no need for land, freshwater or fertilisers, making the process simple and more sustainable.

Among the other prototypes is a building material project by Sussex-based Local Works Studio. The initiative, named Ferment, will repurpose agricultural waste into an insulating material fit for retrofitting buildings.

Local Works Studio aims to develop an accessible product for farms via what it calls a "harvest-to-house system", where farmers can produce the insulation themselves using their existing infrastructure, skills and machinery.

Bristol-based studio WeCanMake's winning prototype, Neighbourhood Factory Futures, is a homegrown timber kit-of-parts system designed to be used for constructing low-rise apartment buildings.

With the Design Museum's grant, the studio plans to create a neighbourhood factory model, allowing local communities to build and maintain their own homes.

WeCanMake explained it created the system as part of a wider movement aiming to make the UK a "nation of growers, producers and makers" while using reusable materials that store, rather than emit, carbon.

Prototyping PhytoFloc by social enterprise SY Ecofit in collaboration with Phyona and Studio Bio is a zero-waste project that, similarly to Local Works Studio, aims to develop plant-based insulation for building construction.

The project uses biowaste created as a byproduct of phytomining, where former industrial land is rejuvenated by plants that extract pollutants from the soil.

The project intends to recognise the value of post-industrial soils while creating a locally made, low-carbon material.

The grants are part of the Design Museum's Future Observatory program, which is run in partnership with the Arts and Humanities Research Council. The winning projects were amongst 140 prototypes that were submitted to the scheme.

The museum explained that at a time when supply chains are under pressure, the Future Observatory aims to support designers' practical research to drive the green transition.

"The climate crisis demands rapid change, and we believe that design is critically important if we are to meet that challenge," said Design Museum director Tim Marlow.

"The presence of Future Observatory allows us an extraordinary opportunity to get involved with practitioners and problem-solvers and have a direct impact on the development of new technologies at the frontier of current design thinking."

The four projects will be funded from November 2026 until July 2027. Afterwards, the prototypes will be tested and begin the commercialisation process.

issues.title: Programa software tracks everything from product dimensions to material quantities
issues.summary: Studio operations software Programa has redesigned its programme to rethink how interior design studios operate, giving practices more flexibility and freeing up their time. According to Programa, beautiful interiors are built on "hundreds of decisions", which take long periods of time to decide upon and update across multiple spreadsheets. Each decision brings specification details, quantities, [
issues.author: Dezeen staff
issues.content_html:
Studio operations software Programa has redesigned its programme to rethink how interior design studios operate, giving practices more flexibility and freeing up their time.

According to Programa, beautiful interiors are built on "hundreds of decisions", which take long periods of time to decide upon and update across multiple spreadsheets.

Each decision brings specification details, quantities, pricing and revisions that studios must keep updated as a project develops.

These include minute, precise details such as dimensions, materials, finishes, technical requirements, and component quantities.

Programa's redesigned programme keeps a record of each item used in an interior project, from furniture and lighting to hardware and finishes, and optimises their organisation based on how the project runs.

The company explained that increased AI use is making convincing images "easier to generate than ever", yet clients often run into logistical issues when using this alone.

For example, the AI model doesn't take into account whether a wardrobe or sofa fits through the door, suits the needs of the people living there, or whether the overall design takes full advantage of a space's natural light.

With Programa, the designer can smoothly make these judgements using the software's organisation of specifications, cost, quantities and overall project coordination.

The company explained that if a designer updates a product’s shared specification once, the change appears in the Programa schedules that include it, while quantities can be individually allocated by room.

For Austin Carrier of Californian design studio, Hommeboys Interiors, this is particularly helpful.

"We use schedules for everything from lighting and hardware to plumbing fixtures and furniture, indoor and outdoor," Carrier explained.

"For furniture, we can break down every room, then the pieces within that room, and give clients several options to reject or accept," he added.

As a result, the software aims to cut the "gruelling amount of work" updating schedules, preparing presentations, and communicating with suppliers. It also reduces repeated data entry, freeing up time.

The platform is defined as an "alternative to spreadsheets", which often have to be made from scratch and reformatted for different presentations.

"The issue with the spreadsheet is that it's like a blank cell," added Los Angeles-based designer Paul Chan. "You can put anything in there – it doesn't carry from one project to another."

"With Programa, I can take a format from one project and move it into the next," Chan continued. "There's consistency between each project."

Specifically, the Programa Schedule function details the items' code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.

It offers a streamlined place to reference drawings, get client approval and work with contractors to meet on-site deadlines.

The company explained that one of its platform's main benefits is that it can be used from early product decision-making through to final delivery.

Here, the studio manages the specification and controls what is shared, whereas the clients review selections and provide approvals. Collaborators also receive the information relevant to their work.

"Once we get all of the information in there, we can send it out in one email to all of our vendors, and then they are able to get us pricing back very easily," added Tana Nesbitt-Hayes of Studio 8 Architect.

"If we're exceeding our budget in one area, we can tailor it back. It's always up-to-date."

"We share our Programa Schedules with the millworkers and the engineers," she added. "They can see the refrigerator we're going to put in, and they can make the panels to fit."

Programa offers a free trial for all studios. To learn more, visit its website.

The Bubbly lamp comprises a statuesque […] The post Bubbly lamp by Canalside
issues.author: Alice Laycock
issues.content_html:
A table lamp comprising a plastic base topped with five magnetically attached glowing orbs is among the products recently published on our Showroom section.

Bubbly lamp by Canalside Studio

Magnetic connector points are placed inside the five globe-like bulbs that light this table lamp by Hong Kong-based Canalside Studio.

The Bubbly lamp comprises a statuesque base with five bulbs attached, which can be removed and positioned around a room – including attached to metal surfaces – to spread out its ambient glow.

Other products published last week include a tile collection by Ceramiche Keope, acoustic pods by Actiu and an outdoor rug range by Rima Dain.

Read on to find out about some of our latest products:

Grace Lithos tiles by Ceramiche Keope

Grace Lithos tiles by Ceramiche Keope are intended to mimic the striated appearance of natural Villeneuve quartzite quarried in Italy.

As well as being striped with differently coloured striations, the tiles feature the stone's abundance of mineral inclusions and the glinting mica microcrystals that it is studded with.

Find out more about Grace Lithos

Blueroots marble by Antolini

Amber and white veining streaks across the surface of Italian stone company Antolini's aptly-named Blueroots marble.

The slabs can be used in kitchens and bathrooms as interior cladding or to create furnishings, imbuing interiors with visually stimulating surfaces.

Find out more about Blueroots

Qyos acoustic pods by Actiu

Office furniture brand Actiu has evolved its Qyos acoustic pods, expanding on its configuration options and capacity for personalisation.

issues.title: CLB Architects creates ADU in Wyoming with rock-climbing wall
issues.summary: US studio CLB Architects has completed an accessory dwelling unit called Wiley, which features an outdoor climbing wall and compact living quarters for an empty-nester couple. The post CLB Architects creates ADU in Wyoming with rock-climbing wall appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Jenna McKnight
issues.content_html:
US studio CLB Architects has completed an accessory dwelling unit called Wiley, which features an outdoor climbing wall and compact living quarters for an empty-nester couple.

The small building stands on a one-acre site in Wilson, Wyoming, located just beyond the popular ski town of Jackson. The site is dotted with mature trees and sits along the west bank of the Snake River.

Before the project's inception, the clients had lived on the property for 25 years – in a modest, 1960s house they had renovated – and had raised their son there.

As their son neared graduation from high school, the couple decided to build an ADU on the property and make it their full-time residence, while renting out the main residence.

Drawings and photography

    Drawings and photography

    "The new house would allow them to remain on the land they had known for decades, while experiencing it in a new way – closer to nature, with stronger connections to light, views and outdoor living," said Jackson-based CLB Architects.

    The house also represents a way to accommodate a growing need for housing while preserving the natural landscape.

    "In our region, there’s a clear need for this housing type, which is economical, compact and responsive to place," said CLB Architects partner Eric Logan.

    A primary challenge for the design team was to ensure the house “met the couple’s programmatic and budget constraints” within a very compact footprint. Per country regulations, the new house could not exceed 1,000 square feet (92.9 square metres).

    The architects conceived a simple, rectangular volume that rises two levels and is topped with a gabled roof. The house was carefully sited so it would feel separate from the main residence.

    "Siting the building toward the back of the parcel and introducing new landscaping and tree plantings created a soft buffer between the two dwellings," the architect said.

    The team carved out portions of the exterior to form inset terraces, along with a climbing wall that is used by the couple’s son while home from college. On the east-facing elevation, a boxy protrusion forms a balcony.

    Both inside and out, the team opted for materials that were durable, cost-efficient and complemented the building’s form. Dark corrugated metal clads most of the building, while tight-knot cedar was used for inset areas to provide “warmth and depth”.

    The ground level contains a spacious garage for vehicles and outdoor gear. The upper level holds two bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms, all of which are organised around a central living area.

    “Locating the main living spaces on the second floor allows the interiors to engage the tree canopy while maximising natural light, offering a more intimate relationship with the landscape,” the team said.

    Read:

    CLB Architects wraps Caju House in Wyoming in weathering steel

    The living area opens onto a west-facing deck, which acts as an “outdoor living room” for much of the year. Large, sliding glass doors diminish the boundary between inside and out and usher in breezes during summer months.

    The clients, both of whom have deep experience in design and construction fields, poured themselves into the project. The husband served as the general contractor and engaged local tradespeople to help out.

    "A true labor of love, the couple built much of the house themselves, working on the construction every evening and on weekends," the team said, noting the project was completed in about nine months.

    The project offers ideas for how communities in the Mountain West can accommodate growth while preserving the natural landscape.

    “With rising land values and the need to accommodate more residents, homes like this – that are compact, efficient, and contextual – can provide more housing while preserving open space,” the team said.

    "As local communities grapple with growth, projects like this suggest one path forward."

    Other ADUs in America include a small, cedar-clad dwelling in California’s wine country by Schwartz and Architecture, and a compact, metal-clad building in Austin by North Arrow Studio that resembles a birdhouse.

    Project credits:

    Architecture and interior design: CLB Architects
    Architecture and interior design team: Eric Logan (partner), Darcey Prichard (partner), Sarah Kennedy (principal), Paige Hobson (project manager), Stephanie Wright (project coordinator)
    Contractor: Dembergh Construction, Mike Prichard (partner)
    Structural engineer: Tectonic Design
    MEP Engineer: Jim Bob Schell
    Landscape: Agrostis and The Tree and Landscape Company
    Lighting: Helius Architectural Lighting
    Owners: Darcey and Mike Prichard

issues.title: The joy of reading The Power Broker with strangers at 3 AM.
issues.summary: No one is well served by listening to pedants, but I think I’ve found an exception. This past weekend, I was a reader at The Power Broker Marathon, where 400+ volunteers took turns reading the entirety of Robert Caro’s magisterial
issues.author: James Folta
issues.content_html:
Screenshot

" />

No one is well served by listening to pedants, but I think I’ve found an exception.

This past weekend, I was a reader at The Power Broker Marathon, where 400+ volunteers took turns reading the entirety of Robert Caro’s magisterial book, in ten minute chunks, over the course of 66 hours. The event’s organizers found their readers through an open call. A startling number of my friends and family forwarded the sign up form to me. It asked, among other things, when you would be available to read. I selected “Afternoon,” “Evening,” and after a pause, “Morning” too. I’m an early riser with a young son, after all, so I didn’t foresee any issues.

A few weeks later I got my assigned time: 3:10 AM on Sunday. Technically, a morning slot. But I’m more of a fan of Robert Caro than I am of sleeping in. I confirmed.

I’m a devoted reader of Caro, and I’ve taken up the Bob beat on Lit Hub too, where I’ve covered fellow Caro-heads, his posts on Instagram, and the 50th anniversary of The Power Broker, Caro’s 1162 page book about Robert Moses and his transformative tenure as New York City Parks Commissioner, during which he built miles and acres of highways, roads, bridges, and parks, at the expense of low-income families, farmers, and other less powerful New Yorkers. It’s a great book.

So much to say, I had no trouble popping up with my 1:15 AM alarm and heading out into the cold to read. I traveled northwest across Brooklyn towards the harbor, where the marathon was 50-hours or more old, having stretched from Thursday, through Friday, Saturday, and now into Sunday. I guessed that the story was probably well into the mayoralty of Robert Wagner at that point. I walked by a few giggly couples, walking in the other direction and on a different timeline, enjoying the end of their late Saturday, and soon found myself at Judgy Baby.

Judgy Baby is an industrial warehouse space in the shadow of Moses’s Gowanus Parkway; the event was organized by Brad Vogel, their director of special projects. Vogel told The New York Groove that the idea for the marathon came out of a Power Broker reading group he ran last year.

“Instead of people saying ‘no that’s ridiculous,’” he said, “people were actually excited.”

I’d seen the set-up inside Judgy Baby on social media, later covered glossily in places like The Times: a banner, a microphone, and a podium with a copy of the book. In pictures of the marathon’s opening, the stage was filled with luminaries like Caro’s editor, the voice of the NY subway system, and a number of current government officials. Power Broker fans are everywhere, like some kind of nerd Illuminati.

None of those big names were in attendance when I arrived at 2:00 AM, but I was happy to see a small and dedicated crew of volunteers, readers, and fans. The big warehouse was much livelier than I’d anticipated; a few people were curled up napping, but the majority were awake: hanging out, chatting, grabbing a quick meal. At least one person was engrossed in a novel. There was coffee, and wine, and a pile of commemorative t-shirts. I took a cup of coffee and a small.

A volunteer checked me in and oriented me. When it was my time, a volunteer would point out where the last reader had left off, and then step back on stage when my ten minutes were up, when I would need to find a natural place to stop. He stressed that this might not be the end of a full sentence, so I might need to find a comma to pause on. Caro is long winded, I was warned, but little did this volunteer know that I was hoping for one of Caro’s famous lists to be in my section (though the most famous one, inspired by Homer, had already long passed.)

I was also asked to read slowly, if I could. The readers before me had been over-eager, and the marathon was ahead of schedule. Caro really does get people excited.

I still had about an hour until my slot, so I found a seat in a back pew (appropriately devotional seating) and listened. In the book, the Tavern on the Green controversy was just coming to a head, one of the rare moments when Moses was personally exposed to public scrutiny. One by one, each reader was replaced by a guiding volunteer, with hearty applause at each transition. Unlike a typical reading, there was no introduction of each new reader (though all our names were in a program, in a tiny font). We were each anonymous, a succession of Vestal priestesses keeping the flame of this project warm.

One reader took the slowdown command very literally, and read his section with long and deliberate pauses between each word. There was some delirious laughter at the careful pacing, and he ended with a round of appreciative cheers and applause.

At 2:50 AM, I was shown to a chair next to the stage. To my right was the on-deck reader, with her own copy of the book to follow along. When she was brought on stage, I took her seat and her warm-up Power Broker. I forgot how small the typeface was in this book, and immediately started feeling like a panicked sixth grader again, skimming ahead and trying to count paragraphs. We were in chapter 43, “Late Arrival”, with the press finally starting to get wise to Moses and his vast, unelected power. Over 1,000 pages in, Moses was nearing the end of his public life.

And then I was up and on stage, following the volunteer’s finger. “Robert Moses still ran the show,” my section began. I stumbled once or twice—“daises” briefly looked like “daisies,” and I read “Rockefeller 3d” as “three d” until I corrected to “the third.” But I was delighted to find a list in my three pages, a comma-laced sentence detailing all the elements that were a part of Moses’s plan for Lincoln Center.

When my time was up, I rejoined the crowd for a few more pages, and then tiptoed into the green room to gather my things. I talked with a few of the volunteer organizers, and compared notes on how the reading went, when we had first finished the book, and which of Moses’s highways confounded us the most in our daily lives. The bleary but bright-eyed energy reminded me of other big efforts I’d been a part of, like the City Marathon or the WGA Writers Strike. Everyone was stretched, but proud. We were doing something, together, and no one would risk letting the rest down. No wonder we were speeding through the book ahead of schedule.

I took a longer walk home, since my train was skipping stops, and passed under the Gowanus Expressway, feeling the crumbling yet still powerful hand of Moses’s ghost on my shoulder.

The feeling of history’s living nearness is why this book is catnip for New Yorkers. It’s a way for us to navel gaze, to talk about how much we love our big, beautiful, messy town, and to gush about how exceptional it is, that even its flaws are so grand to be worth a thousand pages of beautiful prose. But it’s also a way into our other favorite topic of conversation: which trains are delayed, why, and how it’s ruining our day. As one volunteer put it, reading The Power Broker in New York feels like running into an ex—every corner you turn, there Moses is again, standing in your way.

It was nice to be home at 4:30 AM, and nice to know that the Marathon was still marching along. The next day—or rather, later the same morning—I pulled up the livestream on my phone to catch the last sections of the book.

Clocking in to read the last page was Robert A. Caro himself, there on pre-recorded video, the final volunteer reader. Watching the livestream on my phone, I misheard the penultimate line, swapping “he” for “we”: “Couldn’t people see what we had done?”

I teared up a little—from sleep deprivation as much as anything else—to hear it in Caro’s thick, New York accent.
