issues.author: The Editors
issues.content_html:
Americans are getting ready to celebrate Thanksgiving, the middle entry in the Halloween-Thanksgiving-Winter holidays trifecta. Plate up with some table talk about the origins of the holiday, the reason we eat turkey, and what really makes people so sleepy after the annual meal. Extra fixings: all stories contain free links to the supporting academic research on JSTOR. Happy Thanksgiving!

How Thanksgiving took shape

Quakers Against Thanksgiving

Livia Gershon November 24, 2025 In colonial America, government “thanksgivings” blurred faith and politics. For Quakers, rejecting them was an act of religious conviction.

Why the Pilgrims Were Actually Able to Survive

Peter C. Mancall November 28, 2019 If you were reading Bradford's version of events, you might think that the survival of the Pilgrims' settlements was often in danger.

Thanksgiving Has Been Reinvented Many Times

Matthew Wills November 1, 2019 From colonial times to the nineteenth century, Thanksgiving was very different from the holiday we know now.

The Modern Invention of Thanksgiving

Livia Gershon November 26, 2014 Thanksgiving as we know it was deliberately invented in the nineteenth century.

Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade: A History in Pictures

The Editors November 12, 2021 In 1927, the parade replaced live animals with helium balloons designed by puppeteer Tony Sarg.

Indigenous histories and living traditions

Translating Corn

Matthew Wills November 22, 2023 To most of the world, “corn” is “maize,” a word that comes from the Taíno mahizwas. Not for British colonists in North America, though.

Returning Corn, Beans, and Squash to Native American Farms

Christina Gish Hill November 24, 2020 Returning the “three sisters” to Native American farms nourishes people, land, and cultures.

How (Not) to Teach Kids about Native Cultures

Livia Gershon November 23, 2020 Even well-intentioned books for children can romanticize (or demonize) Native Americans. But better materials exist.

From turkey to tofu

Let’s Talk Turkey

Matthew Wills November 26, 2014 First of all, why the name "turkey?"

The Great American Turkey

Livia Gershon November 27, 2024 The turkey was semi-domesticated and kept in pens in the American Southwest some 2,000 years ago—but not for the reason you think.

Seven Things You Might Not Know About Cranberries

Matthew Wills November 21, 2018 They're red, tart, and mostly eaten at Thanksgiving. Love them or hate them, here are seven things you might not have known about the humble cranberry.

Vegetarian Thanksgiving Dates Back to the 1900s

Lina Zeldovich November 25, 2019 Tofu Turkey was created in 1990, but some Americans celebrated Thanksgiving with veggie dishes over a century ago.

The Real Joy of Mock Food

Livia Gershon November 8, 2019 "Wow, this really kind of tastes like turkey.”

Beyond the meal

Thanksgiving Is a Feast of Things Forgotten

Sarah McColl November 22, 2016 Thanksgiving is a feast so complex and semiotically dense that things are very often forgotten and rarely go according to plan.

What Does Thanksgiving Look Like in Prison?

Morgan Godvin November 23, 2021 Our American Prison Newspapers collection provides a peek at Thanksgiving celebrations in prisons throughout the decades.

Why Does Eating Food Make You Sleepy?

James MacDonald November 25, 2015 Your turkey is not to blame.

Synesthetic Adjectives Will Make You Eat Your Words

Chi Luu November 23, 2016 Fragrant. Sweet. Tangy. Certain synesthetic adjectives actually trigger cognitive simulations of eating.

It’s Time to Reinvent Food Waste!

Lori Miller Kase November 13, 2018 Startups worldwide convert refuse into energy, biomaterials, and more food.

A moment of gratitude

Eight Poems of Gratitude

The Editors November 23, 2020 Let us pause now and give thanks.

issues.title: The Great American Beer Wars
issues.summary: In the late nineteenth century, rival breweries slashed prices in a ruthless fight to dominate America's booming beer industry. The post The Great American Beer Wars appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: Matthew Wills
issues.content_html:
Since wet grains ferment naturally in the presence of airborne yeasts, various forms of beer were likely discovered by multiple agriculturalists across the early farming regions of the world. The earliest archeological evidence of fermentation dates back 13,000 years. For thousands of years, beer was an artisanal product made at home, one that was sometimes safer to drink than the local water. Then the Industrial Revolution transformed beer into a mass-produced beverage.

German immigrants were largely responsible for bringing beer culture to the US. Anheuser-Busch, Pabst, Schlitz, Coors, and Yuengling, for instance, were all founded by German Americans. These giants of the industry today (minus Schlitz) emerged victorious from the wild and foamy “beer wars” of the late nineteenth century.

In one locally notorious case, a construction worker’s rented room collapsed from all the hoarded cheap beer he was storing against an inevitable price increase.

Historian Braden Neihart explores that ferocious competition in a case study of Rock Island, Illinois.

“Brewers fought constantly for market share on multiple fronts, through price dropping and undercutting each other with little concern for the immediate fallout. The end goal was survival, and the casualties along the way were the cost of sustaining business.”

In 1886, Rock Island’s three major local breweries produced a total of 80,000 barrels of beer. This was enough, Neihart figures, for an astonishing 800 beers per resident annually. Because this was well-above-average, the brewers were clearly finding additional markets in nearby towns like Moline as well as in Bettendorf and Davenport across the Mississippi in Iowa.

“Brewers operated within a fiercely capitalist market, restrained by few rules and characterized by high risk,” writes Neihart, noting that the competition was both homegrown and from big beer cities like Peoria, Chicago, and Milwaukee.

Locally, the Rock Island Brewing Company (RIBC) ended up buying its competitors, Atlantic Brewery, City Brewery, Rock Island Brewery, and Junge’s Bottling Works, by 1894. But then, in early 1895, Milwaukee-based Schlitz Brewing Company started rolling its barrels into town. On the road to becoming the nation’s largest beer producer, Schlitz dropped the price of its barrels from $6 to $4. The RIBC was forced to follow suit, though the price was ruinous for the company. The RIBC counterattacked with an advertising campaign to “Sustain Home Industry” and support local unions, which helped it weather the onslaught.

More to Explore

“Brewed with Blood”: The Coors Beercott of the 1970s

H.M.A. Leow June 12, 2026 An unusual coalition transformed a labor dispute into one of the longest-running consumer protests in US history.

Drinkers, on the other hand, celebrated; in one locally notorious case, a construction worker’s rented room collapsed from all the hoarded cheap beer he was storing against an inevitable price increase.

Another strategy was to challenge a competitor’s ingredients and hence impugn their purity. German immigrant brewers came with the tradition of the centuries-old Reinheitsgebot “purity order.” This stated that “beer” was to be made from water, barley, and hops. As a form of time-honored branding, this meant that if you added anything else, you could be called out for faking it.

Challenging the purity of ingredients still goes on, as Neihart notes. Anheuser-Busch spent $30 million during the 2019 Super Bowl boasting that its Bud Light was made from rice while Molson Coors’ products, Miller Lite and Coors Lite, were made from corn syrup. Molson Coors subsequently took Anheuser-Busch to court. The Court of Appeals, which hopefully didn’t have to do a taste test, said the companies were free to list each other’s ingredients.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

But back to the turn-of-the-twentieth-century strife and competition. It all came to a sudden end with the onset of Prohibition in January 1920. The Eighteenth Amendment to the Constitution prohibited the “manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors.” The law crippled America’s robust beer industry and culture. Local brewers like the RIBC were driven out of business, but large factory producers had the wherewithal to pivot to legal “near-beers” and “soft drinks.”

The re-legalization of beer in 1933 left the field to the beer factories that had survived the dry years. Local beer-making didn’t really recover until the 1970s, when craft beer and the microbrewery movement began. These were in many ways a protest against the bland quaffs sold by the major players. More recent years have seen the rise of “nanobrewers”—very small operations producing beer for sale—because, like all those millennia ago, you can still brew beer at home.

issues.title: A world of wealth: 12 of the richest people who ever lived
issues.summary: How do you weigh Genghis Khan’s empire against Elon Musk’s shares? Meet 12 people from world history whose fortunes reveal just how many ways there are to be rich
issues.author: Jonny Wilkes
issues.content_html:
When it comes to sifting through history’s uber-wealthy and deciding exactly who was rolling in the biggest pile of cash, a myriad of issues arise. One that stymies historians and economists is how to go about adjusting values across different epochs and different, even defunct, currencies.

Then there’s how to distinguish between personal wealth (essentially, how much money a person has stuffed under their mattress) and the worth of holdings, whether that is in assets, land or glittering treasures. This is especially tricky with sovereign leaders: their domain might bring in spectacular wealth, but that does not necessarily make it their money.

Is it possible to compare Elon Musk – who, in June 2026, made history when a rise in his shares temporarily made him the world’s first trillionaire – with Genghis Khan, who built a colossal empire filled with lucrative resources and industries?

Identifying the richest people in history, therefore, is fraught with difficulty and open to infinite interpretation. Regardless, there's no doubting that these rulers, businessmen and bankers all had the deepest of deep pockets.

Amenhotep III (Unknown–c1353 BC)

Egyptian pharaoh whose wealth is estimated in the trillions of US dollars, though his personal fortune is unknown.

The pharaohs of ancient Egypt were, to put it mildly, not embarrassed about flaunting their wealth. Standing tall above them all as the wealthiest was Amenhotep III of the 18th Dynasty, during the 14th century BC.

His reign witnessed a golden age both for Egyptian culture and political power. Diplomats and leaders from other nations would write to Amenhotep simply to ask him for gifts of gold, such was his reputation. There is no knowing the value of his domain, or personal fortune, but suffice to say that it ran into the trillions, and since he was deified as a god, all of Egypt’s glory was indeed his.

Marcus Licinius Crassus (c115 BC–53 BC)

Roman statesman and general worth approximately 200 million sesterces, according to Pliny the Elder.

While Marcus Licinius Crassus reached the top of Roman politics as one-third of the First Triumvirate, he is better known as “the richest man in Rome”.

As a general, he prospered thanks to proscriptions (the confiscation of property belonging to enemies of the state) and as a businessman, he was a ruthless estate agent and bought up many of the houses in Rome. One of his tricks was to set up his own fire brigade and offer to put out any houses that caught ablaze when the owners promised to sell it to him for slashed prices.

Crassus’s wealth is hard to gauge in modern terms, although Pliny the Elder claimed he had 200 million sesterces, which equated to the entire annual budget of the Roman Republic. Such was his reputation for lucre that a rumour spread after his death in 53 BC that his enemies had poured molten gold down his throat.

Augustus (63 BC–AD 14)

Roman emperor worth approximately US$4.6 trillion, based on his estimated share of the imperial economy.

Calculating the personal wealth of a historical ruler is enough to give historians and economists alike a headache, but the sums attached to Augustus are truly head-spinning.

Not only did he oversee the finances of a mighty empire, but, after defeating Mark Antony and Cleopatra, he took ownership over Egypt. To be clear, the land of the pharaohs did not just become part of the Roman world – it was a personal province of Augustus. Estimates about what this did to his wealth suggest that he owned one-fifth of the imperial economy, which has been translated into a modern-day value of $4.6 trillion (almost £3.5 trillion).

Wu Zetian (AD 624–705)

Empress of China who ruled an economy valued at approximately US$16 trillion.

On top of being the only female emperor in China’s history, Wu Zetian may well hold the title as the richest woman of all time.

Having ruled the Tang Dynasty alongside her husband and in the name of her sons for decades, in AD 690 she proclaimed her own Zhou Dynasty and acted as sole sovereign for 15 years. Under her efficient and brutal leadership, the empire expanded and the economy flourished with the tea and silk trades to western nations. In fact, while she was empress, China accounted for around 23 per cent of the global GDP, which has been estimated to be at the $16 trillion (almost £12 trillion) mark. For context, the richest woman today – Alice Walton, the heiress of Walmart – has a fortune 120 times smaller.

William the Conqueror (c1028–1087)

King of England worth approximately US$230 billion.

After seizing the English throne in 1066, the conquering Duke of Normandy set about confiscating vast swathes of land and bringing the resources of the country under his personal control. For the next 20 years, revenue poured in through rents, taxation and plundered treasures, and William the Conqueror protected his position and his purse with new castles, most famously the White Tower, the central fortification of the Tower of London.

Not content with accumulating wealth for himself alone, he also handed out huge sums to his allies. One relative, Alan Rufus, received such extravagant rewards for his military service in the Norman Conquest that his fortune ballooned to around $194 billion (almost £145 billion), just off the pace of William’s $230 billion (£170 billion).

Mansa Musa (c1280–c1337)

Ruler of the Mali Empire worth approximately US$400 billion, by a speculative estimate.

A name that crops up on every list of the historical rich is Mansa Musa.

In the first half of the 14th century, he presided over the pinnacle of the Mali Empire, a vast realm in West Africa rich in gold and salt, and strategically placed for trade routes. Mansa Musa is often credited as the richest person in history due to his dragon-sitting-on-a-treasure-sized piles of gold, with his mines supplying the Islamic world. Most famously, when he embarked on a hajj to Mecca in 1324, he travelled with 60,000 people and long caravans of slaves, dressed in Persian silk, each carrying gold bars.

According to accounts of his fabulous parades in Cairo, Mansa Musa handed out so much gold that it caused a major devaluation of the precious metal and a currency crisis that lasted years. A conservative estimate of his adjusted wealth is $400 billion (almost £300 billion), although many historians refuse to give a figure at all, instead claiming his wealth was beyond calculation.

Jakob Fugger (1459–1525)

German merchant and banker worth up to US$400 billion.

As the man behind the scenes and pulling the purse strings of medieval politics, Jakob Fugger was far wealthier than emperors, kings and popes.

Born in 1459 into a successful merchant family, he possessed a canny head for business and bookkeeping, shifting from Italian textiles to a more diverse portfolio. Most lucratively, he engaged in silver and copper mining, and tried his hand as a banker. Offering loans to the rich and powerful made him even richer and more powerful, with every deal negotiated bringing in assets and compounding wealth. He funded military campaigns, loaned to the Vatican and acted as chief financier of the Habsburgs, securing the position of Holy Roman Emperors.

On his death in 1525, he left a fortune of 2 million guilders; in today’s money Fugger the Rich may have been worth as much as $400 billion (£300 billion).

Heshen (1750–1799)

Chinese imperial official worth up to US$270 billion.

Heshen has been described as the most corrupt official in Chinese history.

As a favourite of the Qianlong Emperor in the 18th century, he gained control over ministerial posts and imperial revenue, which allowed him to steal funds and take bribes on an almost-industrial scale. At the same time, he built his own commercial empire of banks and pawnshops. During a revolt in 1796, he made sure the military campaign to put it down was prolonged so that he could pocket money being allocated to the army. It all came crashing down with the death of the emperor in 1799, with Heshen arrested and forced to put himself to death. His property was seized, valued at 1.1 billion taels of silver, or possibly as much as $270 billion (£200 billion) in today’s money.

Andrew Carnegie (1835–1919)

Scottish-American steel industrialist worth over US$300 billion before his major charitable gifts.

Andrew Carnegie made his fortune with steel.

Born to a poor family in Scotland and immigrating to the United States as a child, he built a career at the Pennsylvania Railroad Company before setting up the first steel plants in the country in the 1870s. By the time he sold Carnegie Steel in 1901, it was worth around two per cent of the entire US gross domestic product (GDP). While that fortune – adjusted to over $300 billion (£225 billion) – earns his place on this list, Carnegie did not die in 1919 as one of history’s wealthiest people. After retiring, he dedicated his life to philanthropic pursuits and gave way most of his money, espousing the mantra: “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.”

John D Rockefeller (1839–1937)

American oil industrialist worth well over US$300 billion.

The Rockefeller name is a bulwark of American business: throughout the 20th century, it became synonymous with wealth and success, thanks to its patriarchal figurehead. John D Rockefeller founded Standard Oil Company in 1870, correctly predicting the potential impact of oil on the modern world, and under his leadership, the company grew so powerful that it refined more than 90 per cent of all the oil in the United States. He held the monopoly on what was quickly becoming one of the most precious resources, accruing a fortune worth well over $300 billion (almost £225 billion) today.

In 1916, he was recognised as the first American to hit the magic ten figures to become a billionaire.

Henry Ford (1863–1947)

American automobile industrialist worth up to US$200 billion.

Henry Ford forever changed the world of the 20th century by making the automobile available to the mass market and revolutionising industrial practices through the introduction of assembly line production.

His Ford Motor Company, founded in 1903, unveiled the Model T and sold 15 million of them around the world over the next two decades (no car sold more until the Volkswagen Beetle). Needless to say, this made Ford a fabulous fortune. He joined the billionaire club in the 1920s, only a few years after John D Rockefeller, and by the time of this death in 1947 he had the equivalent of up to $200 billion (£150 billion) today. And, of course, Ford's company is still going strong.

Osman Ali Khan (1886–1967)

Nizam of Hyderabad worth upwards of US$200 billion.

Here’s how rich Osman Ali Khan was: he used the Jacob Diamond – a 184-carat masterpiece and one of the largest diamonds in the world – as a paperweight. During his 37-year reign as nizam (ruler) of the Indian state of Hyderabad (1911-48), he built his monumental wealth by issuing his own currency and controlling the world’s primary diamond mines, including where the Jacob and Koh-i-Noor were unearthed.

His private treasury was reportedly bursting with gold, silver and precious jewels, which would be worth upwards of $200 billion (almost £150 billion) today. No wonder the cover of a 1937 issue of Time magazine described him as “the richest man in the world”.

issues.title: The Odyssey has a "bizarre" sequel, but it's been forgotten for a good reason
issues.summary: The hero of Homer’s epic poem didn’t just relax when he finally got back to Ithaca. Instead, Odysseus soon set out to sea again
issues.author: Serafina Kenny
issues.content_html:
The Odyssey is a long book, but it doesn’t cover the whole story of its hero. As well the Iliad, which shows us Odysseus as one of Agamemnon’s most trusted commanders at Troy, there was a sequel called the Telegony. This covered what Odysseus did once he returned from his travels, although sadly its full text has been lost.

You might think that, after being away from home for decades, Odysseus would have wanted to stay put for a while. Not at all, says says Dr Daisy Dunn, classicist and author, speaking on the HistoryExtra podcast. “[In the Telegony], he decides that he can’t just sit still. After all that travelling, he can’t just be done with it, so he continues on his travels,”

  • Read more | Is The Odyssey based on a true story? The movie's historical accuracy explained

The Telegony involves yet more years spent away from home and yet another two families for Odysseus, before concluding with his untimely end.

The Epic Cycle in the literature of ancient Greece

To understand how the Telegony came to be written, it helps to understand that it was part of the Epic Cycle, a collection of narrative poems that told the story of the Trojan war.

“The whole idea with this Epic Cycle is that [its poem] are prequels and sequels to the Iliad and the Odyssey,” Dunn says. Furthermore, there is debate among scholars about whether the Odyssey and the Iliad themselves should be included in the Cycle.

It’s also not clear if the various poems were originally intended to be one cohesive collection of stories. Instead, they may have originated separately, and then been edited and tidied up so that there were no overlaps.

  • Read more | Did the Trojan War really happen? Here's why even Odyssey experts can't agree

They all probably come from the oral tradition, meaning they weren’t written by one person and were instead told verbally with variation each time. Despite this, the poems have been attributed to various people – most notably a group conveniently called the Cyclic Poets – over the years.

The Telegony was often attributed to Cinaethon of Sparta in antiquity, whereas another source says it was stolen from the polymath Musaeus by Eugammon of Cyrene. This makes it hard to date, since Cinaethon was writing in the eighth century BC and Eugammon was around in the sixth century BC.

Words that didn’t endure

This much we do know about the Epic Cycle: unlike the Odyssey and the Iliad, any records of the content of the Epic Cycle poems have been mostly lost. However, we know about their existence through summaries of their plots from other ancient sources, although these have vague provenances.

The most notable is Venetus A, a manuscript from the 10th century AD that is one of the most famous sources of the full text of the Iliad. Although it was produced up to 1,800 years after Eugammon was around, it is also one of the best records we have of the Epic Cycle, because its preface contains summaries of their stories. These summaries are taken from a longer work called Chrestomathy by Proclus, a figure scholars struggle to identify definitively because his name is shared by a fifth-century philosopher and earlier grammarians.

Whoever wrote down the plot, the Telegony picks up on after the Odyssey ends. It tells of a further voyage Odysseus makes to a place called Thesprotia. It moves on to tell the story of his son, Telegonus. Some scholars think these may in fact have been two different epics, but others think the story starring Odysseus may have just been a chapter called the Thesprotis within a wider poem.

Odysseus leaves home. Again

The Telegony opens with Odysseus finally at home in Ithaca with his wife, Penelope, and their son, Telemachus. He is burying all of the men who had been competing to marry Penelope while he was believed dead, those he killed at the end of the Odyssey.

Unhappy to just sit put at home, Odysseus sets off for further travels on the mainland of Greece, ostensibly to make sacrifices at the behest of a prophet we encounter in the Odyssey.

But true to form, he soon gets distracted in Thesprotia, where he meets another queen, called Callidice. They get married and have a son, Polypoetes, before Odysseus fights with the Thesprotians in a war with a neighbouring kingdom.

We don’t know how long Odysseus stays in Thesprotia, but it’s long enough for Callidice to die and for Polypoetes to become old enough to inherit the kingdom. Odysseus leaves Polypoetes to rule Thesprotia and returns to Ithaca.

An epic soap opera

The Telegony says that Odysseus fathered a son called Telegonus by the sorceress Circe when, as recounted in the Odyssey, he lived with her in Aeaea for a year.

In the second part of the Telegony, Telegonus sets off to try to find his father. For protection, Circe gives him a spear that has been tipped with the poison barb of a stingray.

He doesn’t know his father is in Ithaca, but meets him by accident when a storm forces him to land on the island. Telegonus is really hungry, so he starts stealing cattle that belong to Odysseus, who comes to fight off the stranger trying to take his property.

  • Read more | Was Telemachus a real person? The history behind The Odyssey character explained

“There’s a proper tussle between Odysseus and the Ithacans, and this new stranger,” Dunn says. Telegonus stabs Odysseus with his stingray barb, fulfilling a prophecy in the Odyssey that says death will come for Odysseus “out of the sea”. It’s only as Odysseus lies dying that the two recognise each other.

“Quite bizarre, but it doesn't end there,” Dunn says. Accompanied by Penelope and Telemachus, Telegonus brings the corpse of Odysseus back home to Aeaea to bury him. At which point, Circe makes them all immortal.

“And then, even more bizarre, Penelope decides to marry Telegonus and Telemachus, her son, marries Circe,” Dunn says.

Certainly, a strange epilogue to one of history's greatest stories.

issues.title: Hungary's freedom fight: how one nation's resistance to Soviet tyranny changed history forever
issues.summary: Seventy years ago, Hungarians incensed by repression rose up against the country’s communist regime – and were brutally crushed. Martyn Rady reveals how the memory of 1956 rehabilitated the nation’s reputation, and is still used today as a political weapon
issues.content_html:
The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was not a media event. The surviving photographs of its course and suppression by Soviet tanks are mostly grainy, and the few snatches of film are frustratingly short. But one photograph stands out: a portrait of a girl in a padded jacket and fur cap holding a sub-machine gun. Taken in Budapest by the Danish photographer Vagn Hansen on 1 November 1956, a week after the outbreak of the uprising, it was first published in the Danish magazine Billed Bladet and reproduced across the world. It became the face of resistance to Soviet tyranny.

Hansen was not the only journalist to take an image of the girl, but it was not until the late 2000s that her identity was confirmed as Erika Széles, a catering apprentice just 15 years old at the time. Erika did not live long enough to see her face in the international press. By the time the photo appeared in Billed Bladet on 13 November, she had been dead for a week – killed in a shoot-out with Soviet troops after she’d gone to rescue a wounded companion. A square in Budapest is now named in her honour.

The portrait of Erika does not just commemorate courage. It stands, too, for Hungary’s rehabilitation and for the way in which the 1956 revolution altered perceptions of the country.

Rewriting history

Hungary’s story in the first half of the 20th century makes for a bad one. It fought on the ‘wrong’ side in both world wars and, in 1920, was the first modern European power to pass antisemitic legislation. Its native fascist movement, the Arrow Cross, had in 1944–45 been no less genocidal than its Nazi counterpart, slaughtering tens of thousands of Jews, many of whom they shot on Budapest’s Danube embankment.

With the Soviet takeover after 1945, Hungary’s new communist rulers became the most slavish of Stalin’s acolytes, brutally imposing a rigid ideology with the help of a sadistic secret police force. Possibly as many as one-tenth of its people were hauled before the courts on political grounds or on charges of economic ‘sabotage’. Purges, show trials, torture and internment without trial were parts of everyday life. When, in his 1949 novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, George Orwell described the future as a “boot stamping on a human face”, he could have been writing about postwar Hungary.

The 1956 revolution redeemed the country. Not only did its people prove that they were not Stalinist stooges, they also demonstrated and fought in the streets. Up to 3,000 were killed in battles in Budapest and other Hungarian cities. The revolutionaries took on a Soviet army of 200,000 men and 5,000 tanks equipped with only light arms and petrol bombs. Their bravery inspired another portrait, this time an artist’s generic impression: the ‘Hungarian Freedom Fighter’, chosen by Time magazine as its 1956 ‘Man of the Year’.

In the wake of the revolution’s violent suppression, refugees flooded out. Over several months, 200,000 Hungarians fled to the west, some 20,000 of whom came to the UK. Most of the refugees were less than 40 years old, and many belonged to the professions. Altogether, about 20 per cent of Hungarians who had received a post-secondary-school education migrated to the west, including about half of the faculty and students of the Sopron School of Forestry, which relocated en masse to the University of British Columbia in Canada.

Young and versatile, some of the refugees went on to become world-leading scientists, academics and literary figures. Others would use the skills that they had already mastered in the service of their new homelands. Chef Lajos Permayer set up the Louis patisserie on Heath Street in Hampstead, north London. And after several years in the sporting wilderness, legendary footballer Ferenc Puskás moved to Spain in 1958 and signed for Real Madrid. Almost universally, the refugees proved themselves ‘good citizens’ whose example did much to eclipse the more disagreeable features of Hungary’s recent past.

Reputational damage

Hungary’s rehabilitation came at the cost of Soviet communism’s reputation. Throughout western Europe, communist parties suffered a haemorrhaging of membership. The aggressive defence of the Soviet military intervention by the Italian, French and British Communist Party leaders disillusioned the rank and file; roughly a third of their members now drifted off to join the mainstream socialist movement or fringe Trotskyite groups. Many eventually embraced the democratic alternative of Euro-Communism and the ideal of a communism freed from Soviet oversight.

Among those leaving the Communist Party of Great Britain was the journalist Peter Fryer, who wrote for the Daily Worker (later renamed the Morning Star) and went to Budapest in 1956 to report on the revolution. Fryer was outraged by the Daily Worker’s editorial decision to call the Hungarian uprising a “counter-revolution”, and by the continued spiking of his articles. One of his pieces, which the Daily Worker did not print, gave this account of the revolution’s origins: “After 11 years the incessant mistakes of the communist leaders, the brutality of the State Security Police, the widespread bureaucracy and mismanagement, the bungling, the arbitrary methods and the lies have led to total collapse. This was… the upsurge of a whole people… against a police dictatorship dressed up as a Socialist society.”

Fryer’s assessment was shrewd, but the bungling also went right to the top of the Soviet bloc. Ultimately, it was the Soviet leadership that misjudged events and made Hungary ripe for revolution.

  • Read more | Why did the Soviet Union adopt the hammer and sickle, and how did it become a symbol of communist revolution?

With Stalin’s death in March 1953, the collective Soviet leadership – headed first by Georgy Malenkov then, after 1955, by Nikita Khrushchev – began the dismantling of the old dictator’s legacy. The gulags started to open, consumer goods became available, and economic priorities shifted from heavy industry to light manufacturing and housebuilding. Soviet cities such as Moscow and Kyiv suddenly brightened up, with restaurants opening to cater to a smart clientele, food stores offering more than just bottled vegetables, even a scattering of teddy boys dressed in what they took to be western fashions.

The Soviet leadership intended that the ‘New Course’, as it was known, would be adopted by the satellites – and that meant that the old guard who had dominated the Hungarian Communist Party would have to give way. Power there had been concentrated in the hands of Mátyás Rákosi, who was simultaneously prime minister and head of the Communist Party, known after 1948 as the Hungarian Workers’ Party. An engaging personality with fluent English and a distinctive Yul Brynner profile, Rákosi was also vicious and manipulative.

Summoned to Moscow in June 1953 to meet Soviet party bosses, Rákosi bore the full brunt of their criticism. Everything he had done had been wrong, Khrushchev explained, from backing heavy industry to orchestrating purges and show trials. The other Soviet leaders chimed in, accusing Rákosi of bossiness, abuse of power, and disregarding legal process.

Rákosi did what was expected of a good communist. He admitted his mistakes and agreed to give up the office of prime minister, while retaining leadership of the party. His successor as prime minister was the veteran communist Imre Nagy. The Soviet leadership trusted Nagy, who had long reported on his colleagues to the Soviet secret police, but they had underestimated Rákosi. When Nagy did as he thought the Soviet leadership wanted by relaxing controls over society and easing up on industrialisation, Rákosi mobilised the party against him, accusing Nagy of “splintering revisionism”. In the contest between the two communist leaders, Hungarian writers and intellectuals lined up behind Nagy but the Soviet leadership reluctantly backed Rákosi as a flawed but more reliable communist. The Kremlin was worried in particular that Nagy’s talk of political pluralism and of broadening decision-making could only weaken communist control in Hungary.

Nagy’s fall was swift. At Moscow’s direction, the 70-strong Central Committee of the Hungarian Workers’ Party denounced him in March 1955 for “party-damaging, anti-Marxist, opportunistic and right-leaning tendencies”. Nagy was progressively stripped of his offices and, at the end of the year, expelled from the party altogether.

Winter of discontent

In November 1955, a new theatre production opened in Budapest: Shakespeare’s Richard III. It was a sell-out, attracting theatregoers who easily read the politics of the day into “the winter of our discontent” and the villainy of the king. That show was typical of the way that arts and culture began to define Hungarian politics. Theatres, poetry readings and discussion groups increasingly provided forums for the coded criticism of communist policies and of Rákosi’s leadership.

But Moscow was giving mixed messages. In February 1956, at the Twentieth Congress of the Soviet Communist Party, Khrushchev denounced Stalin and the brutality and incompetence of his rule. Supposedly secret, the speech was soon leaked and gave hope to reformers throughout the Soviet bloc. Amid conditions verging on civil war, the communist party in Poland broke free of Moscow’s control, appointing Władysław Gomułka as leader despite Khrushchev’s disapproval of him. (Significant, enduring democratic reforms would, however, have to wait until 1989).

  • Read more | Churchill vs Stalin: did this one speech cause the Cold War?

In Hungary, meanwhile, pressure grew for a political amnesty and pardon. These rumblings culminated in the ceremonial reburial of one of Rákosi’s victims, László Rajk – a communist mass-murderer as odious as Rákosi himself, but hanged on bogus charges in 1949 – which attracted as many as 200,000 onlookers. Student halls of residence and university classrooms became centres of political discussion; one academic debate on freedom of the press drew an audience of no fewer than 7,000.

Visiting Hungary in July 1956, the senior Soviet politician Anastas Mikoyan found only chaos. He reported back to Moscow in alarm:

“Day after day the comrades are further losing their grip on power. A parallel centre is forming from enemy elements operating actively, decisively and self-confidently. The press and radio are not under Central Committee control any more… In this dangerous situation, the party leadership practically exists in a state of prostration.”

There was only one thing for it: jettison Rákosi. But the Soviet decision in July 1956 to appoint another communist dinosaur, Ernő Gerő, as Rákosi’s successor and party boss showed the limits of the Kremlin’s thinking. Communists tend to believe that they have the masses on their side. When they find that they do not, they panic – history is not turning out as it should. On 23 October, a student demonstration to show solidarity with the reformers in Poland turned violent when the security police shot at the crowd. The demonstrators responded by seizing weapons and pulling down the massive statue of Stalin that loomed over the city centre. As the fighting intensified, with revolutionaries taking on Soviet tanks, Gerő rang up Moscow to ask for military help.

Moscow was uncertain what to do. The leadership was divided between hardliners who favoured armed intervention and pragmatists – led by Khrushchev – who hoped for a political solution. In the event, Gerő was dismissed, Nagy was brought back as prime minister and the party leadership was given to the moderate János Kádár. On 28 October, the Soviet commander Marshal Georgy Zhukov ordered all Soviet troops in Hungary to return to barracks.

It looked as if the revolution had won, but Nagy was not in control of events. The Hungarian leadership earnestly debated how to repair broken windows and rewrite history textbooks in schools, while simultaneously giving way to increasingly radical demands from the streets – for the removal of all Soviet troops from Hungary, for a multiparty democracy with free elections, even for breaking Hungary’s military alliance with the Soviet Union. Meanwhile, revolutionaries slaughtered several hundred Workers’ Party officials and shot captured secret policemen.

It was the murder of communists, “our people”, that forced Khrushchev’s hand. On top of this, as Khrushchev explained to his colleagues in Moscow, the progress of the revolution in Hungary made it likely that a ‘capitalist’ restoration was imminent, which could only diminish Soviet prestige. So, on 31 October, Khrushchev gave the order for a full-scale military invasion. What followed was a textbook operation. Over several days, Soviet troops and tanks began covert manoeuvres which effectively sealed off Budapest and other cities. Then, on 4 November, with Budapest encircled, the assault commenced with armoured columns punching their way into the capital along the main highways. The countdown to Erika Széles’s murder had begun.

János Kádár became Moscow’s man in post-revolutionary Hungary. He saw to the prosecution and judicial murder of the leading revolutionaries – including Imre Nagy, latterly the figurehead of the revolution, who was hanged in 1958.

Signs of progress

Kádár ruled Hungary for the next 32 years. His regime was mostly benign: there was censorship, but an underground press flourished. Dissidents were harassed but seldom jailed. The shops were full. Coming to Budapest as a postgrad student in the late seventies, I was surprised and relieved to find that my local ABC had as great a variety of food on offer as the West Hampstead International supermarket (now a Sainsbury’s) where I had shopped in London.

Political debate was allowed, but discussion of 1956 was off limits; the revolution was euphemistically referred to as ‘the events’. My landlord in Budapest, an old conservative, blamed the west for not coming to Hungary’s aid. “We won’t go onto the streets again,” he would say with a shrug of his shoulders.

In fact, Hungarians did not need to return to the streets. Once Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev had let the communist bosses of the satellites know that they could not expect Moscow to intervene on their behalf, the game was up.

In June 1989, Hungary’s communist leaders ceded to popular demands for the ceremonial reburial of Imre Nagy, giving him a state funeral in front of 300,000 mourners. Over the following few months, they peacefully surrendered power in return for immunity from criminal prosecution and their pension entitlements.

Contested memory

After 1989, memory of 1956 became one of the symbols around which Hungarians built a new democratic nation. As one of its first acts, the new Hungarian parliament made 23 October an official holiday, while Plot 301 – where the communist leaders had ordered the burial in unmarked graves of Nagy and other murdered revolutionaries – was made into a site of national mourning.

Even so, memory of 1956 is still contested by left and right. For the left, the revolution was a fight for democracy, civil liberties and the rights of the individual. For the right, it was, above all, a struggle against tyranny of all types. Viktor Orbán, the long-serving rightwing prime minister of Hungary (in power 1998–2002 and 2010–2026), likened his country’s fight against the Soviet Union to his own battle against the ‘tyrannical’ rule of Brussels and the European Union.

  • Read more | This secret speech gave people heart attacks: when Khrushchev denounced Stalin

Orbán and his political party, Fidesz, have a bad reputation – and deservedly so. Accused of harassing migrants with razor-wire fences and tear gas, closing down opposition media, gerrymandering elections and undermining the judiciary, Orbán and his lackeys seemed little different from the tyrants they claimed to despise. Indeed, Orbán happily lined up with fellow authoritarians – not only Vladimir Putin (“a fair partner”) but also Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan (“one of my personal friends”) and President Ilham Aliyev of Azerbaijan (“a model state… stable, predictable and successful”).

On top of this, Orbán’s stooges plundered the state to make themselves Hungary’s richest men, unashamedly advertising their wealth with private jets and castles. Kickbacks, single-bidder contracts and smears, often loaded with a dose of antisemitism, made what had been a functioning democracy into a kleptocracy.

Since Fidesz was roundly defeated in the parliamentary election of April 2026, the photogenic Péter Magyar has been Hungary’s new prime minister. A former Fidesz stalwart who broke with Orbán as recently as 2024, Magyar heads up an umbrella party with little ideological glue. In Magyar’s rhetoric, 1956 is a key plank – one that he invokes in the name of national unity, of making a clean break with the recent past, and of reorient ing Hungarian policy away from Moscow. Even so, after Orbán’s tenure, Hungary’s reputation as one of Europe’s bad boys is close to where it was before 1956. Péter Magyar has work to do.

Martyn Rady was a student in Hungary in the late 1970s, and is now Masaryk professor emeritus of central European history at University College London. His next book, Eastern Europe: A New History, will be published by Allen Lane in 2027

This article was first published in the December 2026 issue of HistoryExtra Magazine

issues.title: GLP-1 drugs linked to reduced alcohol use and healthier eating in real-world study
issues.summary: Tracking 135 patients across Spain for nearly a year, researchers found that routine treatment with drugs like semaglutide and dulaglutide coincided with lower self-reported alcohol intake and better dietary adherence.
issues.author: Eric W. Dolan
issues.content_html:
Adults taking popular diabetes and weight-loss medications tended to cut back on alcohol and stick more closely to healthy diets over nearly a year of routine medical care, according to a new study published in Addictive Behaviors. Patients also reported feeling calm and peaceful more often, although broad measures of overall mental health and long-term physical activity did not show meaningful changes. The findings add real-world clinical evidence to growing scientific interest in how metabolic drugs might relate to everyday habits beyond blood sugar and weight control.

Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, a class of medications that includes drugs such as semaglutide and dulaglutide, mimic a natural hormone released in the gut after eating. By binding to specialized proteins called receptors on cells in the pancreas, stomach, and brain, these drugs stimulate insulin release, slow digestion, and promote feelings of fullness. Doctors prescribe them widely to lower blood sugar in people with type 2 diabetes and to support weight loss in people with obesity.

Receptors for this hormone are not limited to regions that manage hunger and digestion. They also appear in the mesolimbic system, a network of deep brain structures that processes pleasure, motivation, and reward by releasing the chemical messenger dopamine. Animal experiments indicate that activating these receptors dampens dopamine surges triggered by addictive substances and reduces alcohol-seeking behavior.

Human studies have begun testing whether similar patterns emerge in medical patients. In people diagnosed with alcohol use disorder, a 2025 randomized clinical trial found that nine weeks of low-dose semaglutide lowered weekly alcohol cravings and reduced the amount of alcohol participants drank in a laboratory test compared with a placebo. Outside of controlled trials, a 2026 survey of a nationally representative U.S. sample indicated that roughly 44 percent of drinkers who started a GLP-1 medication recalled cutting back on alcohol during their first three months of treatment.

Whereas controlled clinical trials have focused largely on people seeking treatment for alcohol use disorder, most observational studies of everyday diabetes and obesity patients have relied on backward-looking medical record reviews or one-time surveys asking people to recall past habits. Less is known about how drinking, diet, exercise, and mood evolve together when tracked forward in time during routine metabolic care. Earlier work on the same patient dataset, reported in a 2026 study by several of the same authors, showed that 44 weeks of GLP-1 therapy improved body weight, blood sugar, physical functioning, and overall quality of life, while an overall mental health summary score did not show a statistically significant change.

To examine day-to-day habits and specific emotional states in closer detail, study lead author José Seijas-Amigo and his colleagues reanalyzed data from that Spanish clinical cohort, known as the SEVERAL study. Seijas-Amigo is head of the Clinical Trials Unit for Cardiology and Intensive Cardiac Care in the Department of Cardiology at the University Clinical Hospital of Santiago de Compostela, and is affiliated with the Foundation Health Research Institute of Santiago de Compostela and the University of Santiago de Compostela in Spain. Because the original project was designed primarily to evaluate metabolic health and drug safety rather than drinking or behavioral changes, the researchers framed this follow-up investigation as an exploratory, hypothesis-generating analysis.

“Addiction remains a major public health challenge, and pharmacological treatment options are still limited for many substance use disorders,” Seijas-Amigo told PsyPost. “This creates an important need to explore new therapeutic approaches, particularly medications that are already widely used for other conditions.”

“Growing evidence suggests that GLP-1 receptor agonists may influence not only metabolic regulation but also biological pathways involved in reward and addictive behaviors,” he added. “Although this was a post hoc observational analysis, we wanted to contribute real-world evidence to help determine whether these early signals deserve further investigation in dedicated clinical trials.”

The study followed 135 adults with both obesity and type 2 diabetes across multiple healthcare centers in Spain as they started or stepped up treatment with a GLP-1 medication as part of routine care. Participants had an average age of about 62 years, slightly more than half were men, and their average body mass index was 36.2, well above the threshold of 30 used to define obesity. Most patients had additional cardiovascular risk factors such as high blood pressure or abnormal cholesterol levels.

“I would like to highlight the collaborative work behind the SEVERAL project, particularly the contribution of primary care pharmacists, and the importance of multidisciplinary research connecting cardiology, metabolic medicine, and addiction specialists,” Seijas-Amigo noted. “This is also an approach we aim to promote through the Cardiology Clinical Trials Unit in Santiago de Compostela, which I lead.”

Doctors prescribed medications according to standard clinical judgment rather than random assignment. Roughly 35 percent of patients received dulaglutide, 31 percent took oral semaglutide, 30 percent used injectable semaglutide, and about 4 percent took liraglutide or exenatide. Over the 44-week study period, 43 percent of participants experienced an adverse drug reaction, with digestive issues such as nausea accounting for more than four-fifths of those cases. Among the 58 patients who experienced an adverse reaction, four stopped treatment permanently.

Clinicians assessed lifestyle habits at the start of the study and again at weeks 4, 12, and 44. Participants reported their typical daily alcohol intake in standard drink units, with one unit defined in Spain as 10 grams of pure alcohol, or roughly one small glass of wine or beer. Responses were grouped into three categories: zero to one drink per day, two drinks per day, or more than two drinks per day.

At those same visits, patients answered yes-or-no questions about whether they were following dietary recommendations and whether they were engaging in regular physical activity. At the beginning of treatment and at week 44, participants also completed two standardized health questionnaires that measure overall mental well-being, anxiety and depression, and specific emotional experiences over recent weeks, such as feeling calm and peaceful, feeling downhearted, or accomplishing less in daily tasks because of emotional difficulties.

Even before starting treatment, drinking levels in this group were generally low. Among the 130 patients with complete alcohol records, 87.7 percent already fell into the lowest category of zero to one standard drink per day, while 6.9 percent reported two drinks per day and 5.4 percent reported more than two.

Over 44 weeks of therapy, self-reported drinking shifted downward across those categories. By the final visit, 96.2 percent of participants were in the zero-to-one drink group, 3.8 percent reported two drinks per day, and none reported drinking more than two units daily.

Adherence to dietary advice also rose over the course of treatment. At the initial visit, 47.7 percent of participants reported following their recommended diet, a share that climbed to 66.7 percent at week 4 and settled at 63.2 percent at week 44. That improvement held steady when the researchers used statistical techniques to account for missing follow-up answers.

Physical activity followed a different trajectory. The proportion of patients reporting regular exercise climbed from 43.9 percent at the start to 56.1 percent at week 12, before slipping back to 50.4 percent by week 44. Comparing the start of the study with week 44, that long-term difference in physical activity was not statistically significant, a finding that remained unchanged after accounting for missing follow-up data.

“What I found particularly interesting was that not all lifestyle behaviors changed in the same way,” Seijas-Amigo observed. “We observed a shift toward lower categories of alcohol consumption and improved dietary adherence, but these changes were not accompanied by sustained improvements in physical activity.”

“This suggests that changes in health-related behaviors during GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy may be more complex than a general improvement in lifestyle,” he continued. “It raises interesting questions about whether different behavioral pathways are involved, although our study was not designed to investigate the underlying mechanisms.”

Broad assessments of mental health showed little overall movement over the 44 weeks. Changes in the general mental health summary score, which averaged 50.3 at baseline and 52.2 at week 44, were not statistically significant, and a separate rating of anxiety and depression problems also did not reach statistical significance.

When the researchers looked individually at specific mood questions in exploratory checks, one item stood out. The share of patients who reported feeling calm and peaceful all or most of the time rose from 51.9 percent at the beginning of treatment to 69.2 percent at week 44. Downward shifts in daily limitations from emotional problems were much more tentative: a drop in accomplishing less than desired sat right on the statistical borderline, and a reduction in working with less attention than usual fell slightly short and was not statistically significant.

Reports of feeling downhearted and blue, meanwhile, barely budged over the 44 weeks and were nowhere near statistically significant. Because the team tested multiple emotional items without statistical adjustments for repeated testing, the authors note that the increase in calmness could reflect a chance finding and should be read cautiously.

“I was also interested in the changes observed in certain aspects of emotional well-being, but these findings were exploratory and did not translate into statistically significant improvements in overall mental health measures,” Seijas-Amigo noted.

The downward shift in drinking aligns with a randomized placebo-controlled trial of adults with alcohol use disorder and obesity, which found that weekly semaglutide reduced heavy drinking days. That trial evaluated addiction patients rather than routine drinking categories in people with type 2 diabetes, yet both studies point toward lower alcohol intake during treatment. A similar pattern emerged in a health-registry study of patients with alcohol use disorder, which linked semaglutide and liraglutide to fewer alcohol-related hospitalizations rather than tracking self-reported drinking in people with diabetes and obesity.

In interpreting their results, the authors suggest several overlapping possibilities for why eating habits, drinking, and feelings of calmness shifted during therapy. Losing weight and gaining better control over blood sugar might boost how patients feel about their health and reinforce healthier routines. The researchers also propose that GLP-1 signaling in brain regions tied to appetite, stress, and reward could make rich foods and alcoholic beverages less enticing, though they caution that their study did not measure brain activity, cravings, or impulsivity directly.

Even with growing interest in how metabolic therapies might relate to behavior, Seijas-Amigo emphasized that everyday habits remain foundational. “For the general public, the most important message is that maintaining a healthy diet and avoiding alcohol consumption remain essential strategies for improving long-term health,” he said. “From a health perspective, drinking less is generally better, and not drinking alcohol is the safest option. Medications may eventually provide additional benefits, but they should never be viewed as a substitute for healthy lifestyle choices.”

There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Because this was an observational study without an untreated comparison group, it cannot establish that the medications caused the behavioral changes. Regular checkups with healthcare providers, routine lifestyle advice, weight loss itself, or even digestive side effects like nausea could lead patients to eat differently and turn down alcoholic drinks.

In addition, nearly nine out of ten participants already drank one standard unit or less per day before starting the medication, leaving only 16 patients in the higher drinking brackets. Grouping zero drinks and one daily drink into a single category meant the questionnaire could not detect whether light drinkers quit altogether or cut back slightly, and no clinical screening tools for problem drinking were used. The findings also come from older adults managing obesity and type 2 diabetes in Spain, meaning they may not apply to younger people or to individuals seeking treatment for alcohol addiction.

Because of those baseline and measurement limits, Seijas-Amigo cautioned that “we cannot determine how much alcohol individuals actually reduced or whether these changes translated into meaningful long-term health benefits.”

“The changes we observed were encouraging, but their practical significance should be interpreted carefully,” he added. “I would consider these findings an interesting clinical signal rather than evidence of a large therapeutic effect. Their main value is helping identify questions that should be tested in larger, controlled clinical trials.”

“The most important misconception to avoid is that our study demonstrates that GLP-1 receptor agonists can treat alcohol addiction. It does not,” Seijas-Amigo stressed. “I believe these findings support further research, but they should not encourage people to use GLP-1 medications specifically to reduce alcohol consumption outside established medical indications. Promising biological hypotheses must ultimately be confirmed by well-designed randomized clinical trials.”

Future studies built specifically to track alcohol use and mental health will be needed to test whether these everyday behavioral shifts hold up under stricter conditions. Controlled trials that use detailed drinking logs, validated craving scales, and biological markers of alcohol intake could help clarify whether GLP-1 therapies directly alter reward-driven habits or work mainly through broader improvements in physical health.

“My main goal is to help move this field from promising observational findings to rigorous randomized clinical trials that can establish whether GLP-1-based therapies have a meaningful role in treating addictive disorders,” Seijas-Amigo explained. “I believe the priority now is to conduct well-designed clinical trials with clinically meaningful outcomes, such as sustained abstinence, relapse prevention, and long-term safety. These studies should be encouraged regardless of whether they are led by pharmaceutical companies, hospitals, or universities. Ultimately, what matters is generating robust, independent, and reproducible evidence that can determine whether these therapies offer real benefits to patients.”

Researchers are also beginning to look at related drugs such as tirzepatide, a newer diabetes and weight-loss medication that targets both GLP-1 receptors and a second gut hormone receptor involved in metabolism and appetite. Preclinical work, including a laboratory study in rodents that examined controlled drinking and brain reward signaling rather than self-reported alcohol intake in adult clinical patients, similarly linked tirzepatide to lower alcohol consumption, and scientists are exploring whether such medications might affect other addictive behaviors like smoking.

“In fact, I previously developed a research proposal to investigate tirzepatide as a potential aid for smoking cessation in patients with cardiovascular disease,” Seijas-Amigo added. “Although the project did not ultimately receive funding, it reflects my interest in exploring the intersection between cardiovascular health, addiction, and pharmacological innovation.”

“Finally, addiction remains highly stigmatized, sometimes even within healthcare,” Seijas-Amigo said. “We need greater recognition of addiction specialists and multidisciplinary treatment teams, better access to evidence-based pharmacological and psychological therapies, and more clinical research. People with substance use disorders deserve the same scientific attention and quality of care as patients with any other medical condition.”

The study, “Alcohol consumption, lifestyle behaviors, and emotional well-being during GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy: a post hoc analysis of the several study,” was authored by José Seijas-Amigo, Ángel Salgado-Barreira, Rosana Castelo-Dominguez, María Teresa Pérez-Álvarez, Belén Ponce-Piñón, Marlén Fernández-Silva, Marta Rodríguez-Barreiro, Mercedes Pereira-Pía, Jose Manuel Iglesias-Moreno, Mar Gago-García, Raquel Montáns-García, Agustina Fernandez-Perez, Dolores Fraga-Gayoso, Montse Fernandez-Montenegro, Beatriz Riveiro-Barciela, Natalia Rilla-Villar, Begoña Cardeso-Paredes, Marta Ribeiro-Ferreiro, Diego Rodriguez-Penas, Alberto Cordero, Moisés Rodríguez-Mañero, José R. González-Juanatey, and Several Investigators.

issues.title: Heavy cannabis use linked to mild psychotic symptoms and depressive thoughts
issues.summary: Frequent cannabis use is closely linked to higher rates of mild hallucinations, paranoia, and depressive symptoms, particularly among individuals who begin using the drug heavily at a young age.
issues.author: Karina Petrova
issues.content_html:
Frequent cannabis consumption is associated with a higher rate of mild hallucinations, unusual thoughts, and depressive symptoms compared to occasional use or abstinence. Starting cannabis at a younger age also correlates with an increase in these subclinical symptoms. The findings were published in the Journal of Psychiatric Research.

Psychotic-like experiences are phenomena that resemble the symptoms of psychotic disorders like schizophrenia but occur at a much lower intensity. They can include mild paranoia, hearing occasional whispers, or holding highly unusual beliefs. These experiences do not mean a person has a psychiatric disorder.

About seven to thirteen percent of the general population report having these mild perceptual experiences at some point. While often harmless, these subclinical symptoms can sometimes act as early warning signs for future mental health conditions.

In psychiatric terminology, symptoms fall into distinct categories. Positive symptoms refer to the addition of abnormal experiences, such as hallucinations or delusions. Negative symptoms refer to a loss of typical emotional responses, such as a lack of motivation, social withdrawal, or a flattened affect. Depressive symptoms involve persistent sadness and low energy.

University of Turin psychiatrist Valerio Ricci and his colleagues noticed a gap in the existing scientific literature regarding these symptoms. Past investigations often focused exclusively on healthy community volunteers or individuals already diagnosed with severe psychotic disorders.

The researchers wanted to study people who fell somewhere in the middle. They focused on individuals receiving psychiatric care for non-psychotic issues, such as anxiety or mood disorders. This group carries some underlying mental health vulnerability but does not have schizophrenia.

The research team recruited 150 adults between the ages of 18 and 40 from psychiatric clinics in Italy. They excluded anyone with a current or past psychotic disorder. They also excluded anyone with an immediate family member who had a psychotic disorder.

Participants were divided into three groups based on their daily habits. The heavy use group consisted of 43 individuals who consumed cannabis five or more days a week. The occasional use group included 47 individuals who used cannabis one to four times a month.

The difference in consumption volume between the active user groups was massive. The heavy users consumed an average of 2.8 grams of cannabis daily. In contrast, the occasional users consumed an average of 3.2 grams over the course of an entire month.

The groups also favored different methods of consumption. The heavy users predominantly preferred smoking cannabis. The occasional users were more likely to use vaporizers.

The remaining 60 participants were a control group with no history of cannabis use. To ensure accuracy, the researchers verified the participants’ self-reported drug habits with urine toxicology screenings. They also gathered data on the participants’ use of tobacco, alcohol, and prescription medications.

The primary measurement tool was the Community Assessment of Psychic Experiences scale. Participants rated how often they experienced various positive, negative, and depressive symptoms.

To evaluate life skills, clinicians used the Global Assessment of Functioning and Clinical Global Impression rating scales. These standardized instruments evaluate a person’s overall psychological, social, and occupational well-being.

The heavy cannabis users reported substantially higher scores for positive symptoms than the other two groups. Positive symptoms in this context can include feeling as if other people are reading your mind or feeling inexplicably detached from your own body.

The heavy users also reported elevated levels of depressive symptoms. The occasional users scored lower than the heavy users in both categories but reported more symptoms than the non-users. The frequency of cannabis consumption correlated strongly with the severity of these specific experiences.

The age at which participants first started using cannabis also played a role. Individuals who began using cannabis before the age of 16.4 years showed elevated symptom scores compared to those who started later. A longer overall duration of cannabis use followed a similar pattern.

The human brain contains an endocannabinoid system, which is a network of cellular receptors involved in regulating mood, memory, and perception. During adolescence, this system undergoes rapid development and reorganization. Introducing external cannabinoids during this sensitive window might alter regular neurological development.

The researchers found no statistically significant differences among the three groups regarding negative symptoms. Avolition and emotional flatness remained relatively consistent regardless of how much cannabis a person consumed. The researchers noted that standard symptom questionnaires might not be sensitive enough to capture subtle deficits in motivation.

Daily functioning was noticeably lower in the heavy use group. These individuals scored worse on clinical assessments of overall well-being and daily living compared to the other participants. Occasional users did not show similar drops in daily functioning.

The data also revealed a specific connection between cannabis and tobacco. Heavy cannabis users who also smoked tobacco daily reported higher positive symptom scores than heavy cannabis users who used tobacco less frequently.

Tobacco smoking can accelerate the body’s absorption of tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, the primary psychoactive compound in cannabis. Both substances activate reward pathways in the brain. Their combined use might amplify neurological signals beyond the effect of either drug alone.

While tobacco showed an interaction with cannabis use, other substances did not demonstrate the same pattern. The researchers accounted for alcohol, stimulants, and hallucinogens in their statistical models, but these substances did not independently predict the severity of the psychotic-like experiences.

The observational design of the research limits how the results can be interpreted. The investigators evaluated the participants at a single point in time. This prevents them from establishing cause and effect.

It is entirely possible that individuals experiencing mild hallucinations or depressive thoughts turn to cannabis for relief. This self-medication theory remains a valid alternative explanation for the correlation. People with underlying mental health vulnerabilities might use the drug to cope with their symptoms.

The study also relied on self-reported surveys. Participants may have misremembered the exact timeline or frequency of their past drug use. Additionally, some participants had a history of taking other prescription mental health medications, which could influence their symptom reporting.

The researchers did not measure the concentration of specific chemical compounds in the cannabis products used by the participants. High-potency cannabis products are known to carry different risks than those with lower levels of THC.

Future investigations would benefit from tracking individuals over several years to observe how these symptoms evolve. Incorporating chemical analysis of the specific cannabis strains consumed could also clarify how different botanical compounds affect the human brain.

The study, “Cannabis use patterns and psychotic-like experiences: a cross-sectional study of heavy users, occasional users, and non-users,” was authored by Valerio Ricci, Alessandro Sarni, Lorenzo Remondino, Marialuigia Barresi, Domenico De Berardis, Clara Cavallotto, Andrea Di Cesare, Vassilis Martiadis, Giovanni Martinotti, and Giuseppe Maina.
