The closing of your message is the final thing the recipient The post How Do You Write Formal Email Sign-Offs That Leave a Lasting Impress
issues.author: Daily Writing Tips
issues.content_html:
Crafting a digital message takes effort, and most people focus all their energy on the subject line and the main body. They meticulously choose their opening hook and structure their arguments to sound persuasive. Yet, right at the very end, they drop the ball. The closing of your message is the final thing the recipient reads, and it leaves a lingering taste.

A strong email closing is just as important as a good subject line. Proper grammar, precise capitalization, and correct punctuation in an email sign-off leave a polished and highly competent impression. If you fail to stick the landing, your entire message might feel sloppy or rushed. Learning how to properly conclude your messages is a vital skill for anyone looking to build strong business relationships.

Why Is a Proper Sign-Off Crucial for Your Professional Correspondence?

A well-crafted closing carries significant psychological and professional impact. It acts as the final handshake in a virtual environment. When you communicate in the workplace, every single detail contributes to your personal brand and credibility. Crafting a high-quality, professional email establishes a firm standard for corporate communication.

Establishing the Tone of the Relationship

The sign-off dictates the tone of the relationship moving forward. In a world where inboxes are flooded daily, taking the time to format a polite and grammatically flawless goodbye makes you stand out as a careful and considerate professional. Your choice of words reveals exactly how you perceive your professional dynamic:

  • Overly casual closings: These risk appearing disrespectful to new clients or senior leadership.
  • Highly archaic closings: These can make you seem cold or unapproachable to a close colleague.
  • Properly balanced closings: These demonstrate a high attention to detail and respect for the person on the receiving end of the screen.

What Are the Strict Grammar and Punctuation Rules for Email Closings?

Many professionals rely on autocorrect or simply copy what they see others doing, which leads to widespread grammatical errors in email sign-offs. There are strict rules governing how you format the end of your message.

Mastering the Sentence Case Rule

The first major rule concerns capitalization. In standard English writing, only the first word of a sign-off phrase should be capitalized. This rule is called sentence case, and it applies universally to email closings. For example, you must write “Best regards,” with a lowercase “r.” Writing “Best Regards,” with a capital “r” is a grammatical error. You treat the sign-off as a single, continuous phrase where only the initial letter of the very first word earns capitalization.

Applying the Terminal Comma

The second critical rule involves punctuation. You must place a terminal comma immediately after the sign-off phrase and before your name. This comma serves as a natural pause, signaling that your name is about to follow. Omitting this comma creates a run-on effect that looks highly unprofessional. Your signature block should always follow a clear vertical structure consisting of the sign-off phrase, the comma, a line break, and then your name.

Which Formal Email Sign-Offs Are Best for Different Contexts?

Selecting the right closing phrase depends entirely on the context of your conversation. You need to read the room and adjust your language based on the recipient and the nature of the correspondence.

When Should You Use Traditional Closings Like “Sincerely” or “Yours Faithfully”?

Traditional closings carry a sense of formality and historical weight. You should rely on these phrases when writing to highly formal institutions, legal entities, or government officials. They are safe, reliable choices when you are applying for a job or reaching out to a corporate executive for the first time.

Here are the most common traditional closings and their appropriate contexts:

  • Yours faithfully: This is a standard convention in British English when the email begins with a generic greeting like “Dear Sir/Madam.”
  • Sincerely: American English relies heavily on this closing for both known and unknown recipients in formal settings.
  • Respectfully: This is best used when addressing government officials, military personnel, or high-ranking executives.

How Do You Navigate Modern Business Closings Like “Best Regards” or “Kind Regards”?

For most day-to-day corporate emails, traditional closings can feel far too stiff. Modern business environments favor a careful balance of professionalism and warmth. These sign-offs are incredibly versatile and work well when communicating with vendors, active clients, or colleagues in different departments.

Consider these modern standards for your daily correspondence:

  • Best regards: This remains the absolute gold standard for daily corporate emails.
  • Kind regards: This offers a slightly more formal tone while remaining highly versatile.
  • Warm regards: This phrase is completely acceptable if you want to convey a friendlier, more approachable tone.

What Are the Common Grammatical Mistakes to Avoid in Sign-Offs?

Even seasoned professionals make frequent errors at the end of their emails. You must avoid these specific pitfalls to maintain a polished image. Always spell out your words completely to maintain a dignified tone.

  1. Over-capitalization: Writing “Warm Regards,” violates standard sentence case rules.
  2. Omitting the terminal comma: Writing “Best regards” followed immediately by your name on the next line is incorrect punctuation.
  3. Using informal abbreviations: Signing off with “Thx,” “Rgds,” or “Cheers” is highly inappropriate for formal business communications because it suggests you are too rushed to type a full word.

How Can You Summarize Your Professional Email Sign-Off Strategy?

Your sign-off is the final opportunity to reinforce your competence and professionalism before the recipient closes the window. By applying strict grammar rules and carefully matching your tone to the situation, you guarantee that your digital correspondence creates a lasting and positive impression. The correct tone combined with flawless execution shows that you are a serious professional who respects both your own brand and your recipient’s time.

Remember the core highlights of email closing etiquette. You must only capitalize the first letter of the sign-off phrase, and you must always use a comma immediately before your name. Whether you choose the traditional weight of a phrase like “Sincerely,” or the modern warmth of “Best regards,” adhering to these structural rules ensures your message is always well-received.

Do you want to master every aspect of professional writing? Subscribe to the dailywritingtips.com newsletter today for more in-depth grammar guides, vocabulary lessons, and communication strategies delivered straight to your inbox. Share this article with your colleagues and network to help improve workplace communication and ensure everyone on your team leaves a brilliant impression in every single email they send.

issues.title: The Learning-Visibility Loop: How AI Should Participate in Education
issues.summary: Generic AI is built to hand over answers. The bigger opportunity in education is to make the learning itself visible, for students and for the instructors teaching them. A finished assignment doesn’t show how it was made. It shows what a student turned in, but not how they read the prompt, where they got stuck, […] The post The Learning-Visibility Loop: How AI Should Participate in Education appea
issues.author: Grammarly
issues.content_html:
Generic AI is built to hand over answers. The bigger opportunity in education is to make the learning itself visible, for students and for the instructors teaching them.

A finished assignment doesn’t show how it was made. It shows what a student turned in, but not how they read the prompt, where they got stuck, which misconceptions surfaced, or what finally helped them move forward. Those moments are where learning actually happens, and they disappear the moment the work is submitted.

AI has widened that gap. The process is even harder to see now, and students, reaching for whatever tool is closest, get generic help that was never built for learning. Retention, integrity, and faculty workload were already compounding pressures on academic leaders. AI is adding to the pressure.

Why AI in higher education makes learning harder to see clearly

The instinct for many in education is to ask whether students used AI. We think the more useful question is, “Can educators tell that students are learning?” Visibility has become a greater challenge since the introduction of AI in education; instructors see the final submission but not the work that led up to it. The learning process itself has become opaque, even to the people responsible for teaching it.

A loop that makes learning visible

There’s a better way to work when AI is in the mix, one that turns that lost process back into something an instructor can see and act on. We call it the learning-visibility loop. Each turn of a student’s work informs the instructor’s next move, and each move shapes stronger work, so every round leaves both sides further along than the last. Here’s how it comes together.

A student works through a problem with an AI agent, a tool that holds a back-and-forth and works alongside them, guiding them rather than handing over the answer. That interaction leaves an honest record of how the student got there. The instructor reads that record, sees where the class is getting stuck, and shapes the next assignment around it. The student works again, now on ground the last round helped shape.

Each turn feeds the next. Instead of ending with a single graded assignment, every round gives an instructor something to act on, and every new assignment is shaped by what students actually struggled with. The loop moves teaching from what happened to what to do next.

One design choice holds the whole thing together: The agent guides the student rather than generating the work. An agent that hands over answers leaves no record of how the student got there. An agent that asks questions and pushes for revision creates that record, because the back-and-forth is itself the trace of how the student worked through the problem. That is what makes the help genuinely educational, and it keeps the instructor’s signal honest. The two sides are one system, and each makes the other stronger.

What faculty told us

The loop is informed by first-party research led by Yolanda Wiggins, a senior researcher at Superhuman: 12 in-depth interviews with US higher education professionals, from professors and adjuncts to academic and technology leaders. The findings are qualitative and directional. The student side draws on separate, prior research with students.

Two things came through clearly.

1. Faculty want to see how learning happens

Again and again, instructors said they wanted to understand where students were struggling and what they could do differently as teachers.

“We have no idea what prompts they used. Most of this is very opaque to me.” — a CIO who also teaches graduate courses

“We need to know what’s in their heads, not what AI can write.” — an MBA program director

“You’re gonna have to give me all of your prompts, and show me the dialogue.” — a social-psychology professor

Some instructors are already rebuilding this visibility by hand, redesigning assignments at real cost to their time. That effort is the clearest sign of the gap.

2. Students want to show their work

This second finding comes from separate, prior qualitative research with undergraduate and graduate students, who documented their real coursework and tool use. Students reached for AI when they were stuck, to interpret a prompt, get started, or check their work, not to do the assignment for them, and they valued tools that supported their thinking while keeping the work their own. Many are already opting into Grammarly Authorship, which documents how a piece of writing actually came together. The desire for greater visibility runs in both directions.

“You can’t just outsource your homework to AI. You can tell, it just creates AI slop. When students instead use it as a tutor or study buddy, we see much better work.” — an MIS professor

What keeps the loop honest

The loop only works if a few things stay true.

First, humans do the work and own the decisions. Students remain the authors of their own learning, so the agent guides while the thinking and the work stay theirs. Instructors stay the decision-makers, so insight informs a teaching decision without ever making one. As one MBA program director put it, “I will never use AI to grade.” We design for exactly that: the instructor stays the decision-maker, and the tools inform decisions rather than make them.

Second, the student-side agent must be built to support learning. When it’s built well, it does four things:

Third, the instructor-side report has to lead with what to do next. It answers three questions a busy instructor rarely has time to answer alone:

The point is to turn otherwise invisible patterns into a teaching decision, while grading, intervention, and course design remain firmly in human hands. Imagine a report that shows most of the class opened with a one-sided thesis, and that once the agent pushed back, the majority revised toward a stronger argument while a smaller group stayed stuck. That gap is the signal, and it points to exactly what to teach next.

What the loop collects, and what it leaves alone

Because the loop is based on how students learn, it collects only what helps teaching: the work process and class-level patterns, not personal or non-academic data. Students should know what’s captured, see what’s inferred, and be able to contest it. And the institution should stay in control of its own data.

Why higher education needs AI built for learning

Generic AI is getting very good at generating answers. Education needs something different: learning support that leaves an instructor with something to teach. That’s a fundamentally different product problem, and general-purpose assistants weren’t designed to solve it.

This is what it looks like when AI is built for education rather than pointed at it. It keeps students doing the doing, gives faculty a path forward instead of more to police, and gives institutions something they can actually measure: whether learning is happening. It complements an institution’s approach to AI rather than competing with it. And it’s built the way the best campus AI is being built right now: with institutions, not just for them.

Keeping learning visible

When an answer is always a click away, the work worth protecting is the learning. The learning-visibility loop is how we think AI can protect it: by keeping students in the work, keeping instructors in the decisions, and making the learning itself visible to both.

Grammarly is now part of Superhuman , and this is the model we’re building toward with Superhuman Go , alongside the institutions putting it into practice. The best campus AI isn’t handed down from a vendor; it’s shaped by the educators who know what learning should look like and built on a foundation higher ed already trusts.

issues.summary: Instructors want to trust the work students hand in. Students want credit for the work they actually did. Since Grammarly Authorship launched in beta in Google […] The post Grammarly Authorship Is Now Available in Blac
issues.author: Grammarly
issues.content_html:
Instructors want to trust the work students hand in. Students want credit for the work they actually did. As AI use in the classroom becomes routine, both are getting harder, and that’s exactly where writing transparency earns its place.

Grammarly Authorship was built to close that gap.

Since Grammarly Authorship launched in beta in Google Docs in October 2024, it has expanded to Grammarly Docs, Microsoft Word, and Word Online, so students can show their writing process wherever they write. It now recognizes AI-generated content both pasted in and generated from within a document, including Copilot in Word and Gemini in Google Docs.

Students have generated more than 5 million Authorship reports to date.

The results show up on campus. After introducing Authorship across its English department, Rowan-Cabarrus Community College reduced academic integrity violations from 27 to 1, a 96% drop, in a single semester.

Authorship delivers value on its own. It goes further when it’s built into the systems an institution already runs. After integrating with Canvas LMS in September 2025, Grammarly Authorship now integrates with Blackboard, giving institutions a scalable way to make student writing transparent while students keep writing in the tools they prefer to use.

What is Grammarly Authorship?

Grammarly Authorship automatically categorizes the sources of text in a document, whether it’s in Google Docs, Microsoft Word, Word Online, or Grammarly Docs. It gives quick signals and detailed reports showing where writing came from: human-typed, AI-generated, copied, or rephrased with Grammarly’s generative AI.

Unlike traditional detection tools, Authorship is built on transparency and attribution, with student consent. Students can show their authentic writing process, and instructors can spend their time guiding rather than second-guessing it with unclear data.

Authorship’s new Blackboard integration

Instructors can require Authorship reports directly within Blackboard assignments. Here’s how it works:

1. Instructor setup

While creating an assignment, instructors simply switch on the new Enable Grammarly Authorship option in the Originality Report section of their Blackboard assignment settings.

2. Students keep writing where they always do

In the tools they already use (Microsoft Word, Word Online, Google Docs, or Grammarly Docs), students can turn on Authorship tracking with a single click and view their Authorship report at any time. It attributes their text sources automatically when they use a gen AI tool or paste from a third-party source. Because Authorship is student-first, students can see their own writing process data but can’t alter it before sharing, which builds two-way visibility into how the work was made.

3. Sharing to Blackboard is easy with a share link

When they’re ready to submit, students select Anyone with the link in their Authorship report access settings.

4. Quick attachment through normal submission workflow

Students attach the Authorship report to their normal Blackboard submission by submitting their report’s share link alongside their assignment document.

5. Instructor insights at scale

Instructors gain a class-level view of the Authorship report and can open any individual student’s full writing process replay when they want to dig in. That makes it easy to focus on outliers while trusting that every submission includes transparent attribution.

Why this matters

Educators want writing to be something students genuinely work through, and institutions need a way to trust in that work as AI use becomes routine. Students want that too: Many are actively looking for ways to use AI they can stand behind .

Here’s what the Blackboard integration gives each group:

  • Students get a low-effort way to show their writing process and get credit for their own thinking, whether or not they used AI, plus protection from false accusations. Over time, attributing their sources builds the AI-literacy habits that matter well beyond any single assignment.
  • I nstructors get assignment-level control with the ability to require students to submit an Authorship report with their assignment. Authorship is visible in Blackboard through a single class view, meaning instructors don’t have to open reports one by one. It also allows them to drill into any student’s process when a conversation is warranted. That gives back hours during grading and turns integrity checks into teaching moments rather than investigations.
  • Institutions get a consistent, scalable way to maintain academic trust across departments, built on tools faculty and students already use, so adoption doesn’t hinge on changing anyone’s habits, plus a defensible answer when leadership asks how AI is being handled.

The Blackboard Authorship integration is now available for Grammarly for Education customers on any institution-wide plan that uses Blackboard. Administrators can install the LTI in a few steps using the setup guide .

We’re glad to partner with Anthology and our school and university customers to make writing transparency a reality for the AI era.

To learn more or get started, visit Grammarly for Education .

Voice dictation promised to fix this. But native phone dictation just gives you a raw transcript, […] The post Say It, Then Send It with Speech to Text appeared first on
issues.author: Grammarly
issues.content_html:
Writing on your phone is still, somehow, a chore. Between a cramped keyboard, autocorrect that guesses wrong, and the mental load of trying to stay focused while on the move, sending a polished message takes longer than it should.

Voice dictation promised to fix this. But native phone dictation just gives you a raw transcript, full of filler words, false starts, and missing punctuation. Cleaning up your text is just as much work as if you’d typed it manually.

That’s what speech-to-text in the Grammarly Keyboard is built to solve. The Grammarly’ Keyboard now lets you dictate directly into any app and delivers clean, polished text without the cleanup.

Dictate anywhere, get polished text.

Speech-to-text is built directly into the Grammarly Keyboard. Tap the mic icon, speak naturally, and Grammarly returns clean, send-ready text—right in the app you’re using.

Grammarly’s speech-to-text handles a wide range of languages, accents, and speaking cadences. Instead of producing a raw transcript, Grammarly cuts filler words, removes spots where you corrected yourself verbally, and fixes grammar, all while preserving your tone and intent.

If you want to take your dictated text further, Grammarly’s AI assistant is available in the same keyboard. You can switch between speaking and typing at any point, or edit your dictated text with the same Grammarly Keyboard across all your apps.

Built for wherever and however you use your phone

Grammarly’s speech-to-text is for anyone who writes a lot on mobile—knowledge workers drafting between meetings, students capturing ideas mid-walk, or anyone tired of fighting a tiny keyboard.

Grammarly’s mic is designed to cut background noise while also keeping you in control of what is recorded. The mic only activates when you tap it. While it’s on, you’ll see a clear signal in the keyboard, plus the iOS orange indicator light at the top of your screen. After your audio is processed into text, it’s deleted. It isn’t stored, linked to your account, or used to train any models. All that’s left is your polished message, ready to send.

Get started

Speech-to-text lives inside the Grammarly Keyboard. Once it’s set as your default keyboard, the mic is available in any app.

  • Download and install Grammarly for iOS : If you haven’t done so already, download the Grammarly Keyboard from the App Store. Setup takes under a minute.
  • Set Grammarly as your keyboard: Go to Settings → General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Add New Keyboard, then select Grammarly. Enable full access when prompted. This allows the keyboard to work across all your apps.
  • Tap the mic and start speaking: Open any app, tap into a text field, and you’ll see the Grammarly Keyboard. Hit the mic icon, say what you want to write, then stop. Clean, ready-to-send text appears right where your cursor is.

issues.title: A University of Florida Professor Stopped Fighting AI in His Classroom: A Peer-Reviewed Study Followed
issues.summary: When Dr. Brian Harfe first noticed that AI tools could answer his essay prompts better than most of his students, he did not panic. He redesigned the assignment. That decision, made in a large-enrollment course at the University of Florida, has since become the subject of a peer-reviewed study published in TechTrends in 2026. What […] The post A University of Florida Professor Stopped Fighting AI
issues.author: Grammarly
issues.content_html:
When Dr. Brian Harfe first noticed that AI tools could answer his essay prompts better than most of his students, he did not panic. He redesigned the assignment.

That decision, made in a large-enrollment course at the University of Florida, has since become the subject of a peer-reviewed study published in TechTrends in 2026. What started as one professor’s practical response to a fast-moving problem is now a data-backed framework for how institutions can approach AI in student writing.

The problem with how we have been measuring AI use

Most institutions trying to get a handle on student AI use have landed on two approaches: surveys and AI detectors. Both fall short in predictable ways.

Self-reported survey data is shaped by what students think their instructors want to hear. Students who see AI use as acceptable tend to over-report it; those who fear academic penalties tend to under-report it. Even honest responses run into a memory problem. Few students can accurately reconstruct how much of a final draft came from a chatbot versus their own editing across multiple writing sessions.

AI detectors have a different problem. They work probabilistically, assessing whether text is likely to be AI-generated rather than confirming whether it actually is. None currently achieve 100% accuracy, and most do not tell you how much of a document is AI-generated or which parts. Just a verdict on the whole, which treats writing as a product rather than a process.

Institutions are left with plenty of anxiety about student AI use and very little reliable data about what students are actually doing.

A different approach to the assignment itself

Dr. Harfe’s response was not to add surveillance. It was to change what the assignment asked students to do.

In his University of Florida course titled “Can We Design Better Humans? Should We?”, he redesigned the final essay around AI rather than removing it. Students were required to begin with a fully AI-generated draft, then revise it to reflect their own views on human cloning and genetic engineering. The final submission had to represent the student’s perspective. How much of the AI draft they kept, changed, or discarded was up to them.

That design did something the traditional essay could not: It removed the incentive to hide AI use. Students were not penalized for leaning on the draft or rewarded for avoiding it. The question shifted from whether they used AI to what they actually did with it.

To track that objectively, Dr. Harfe used Grammarly Authorship, a writing transparency tool that tracks the origin of text. Unlike AI detectors, Authorship does not deal in probability. It records provenance, identifying whether each word was typed by a human, copied from an AI tool, or pulled from another source.

Students submitted their Authorship reports alongside their essays, and Dr. Harfe could use the tool’s replay feature to watch how each submission evolved from AI draft to finished product.

What 310 essays revealed

The resulting dataset, 310 essays from students across seven colleges and more than 100 declared majors, is the foundation of the study, Quantitative Analysis of Generative AI Text Usage and Identification of Factors Influencing Text Choice, that Harfe co-authored with Aaron Thomas of the University of Florida’s Information Technology department. It is among the first studies to track student AI use at the word level across a large, diverse undergraduate cohort.

Three findings stand out.

  1. Engagement shows up in the data. Students who wrote more of their own text took significantly longer to complete the assignment. The correlation was strong and consistent. Time-on-task tracked closely with how much students actually revised, which suggests that when an assignment is built to require genuine engagement, the data reflects it.
  2. Discipline influences editing behavior. STEM students produced more human-generated text than non-STEM students, even though both groups were equally likely to agree with the AI draft’s position on the topic. Subject-matter familiarity alone does not explain the gap. It’s an open question that the researchers have flagged for further study.
  3. Academic standing predicted revision depth. Students who performed above their semester- and major-matched peers revised AI-generated text more extensively. The pattern held across every discipline in the dataset. The tendency to push back on a draft appears to reflect broader academic habits more than discipline-specific knowledge.

On average, students kept about 76% of the AI-generated draft in their final submissions. The roughly 5% who genuinely disagreed with the AI’s position edited far more heavily, which reinforces the assignment’s central logic: Students who have something to say added more of their own writing.

The graph below shows that students with higher academic standing revised AI-generated text more extensively, across every major in the dataset. Each dot represents one student.

Figure reproduced from Harfe & Thomas (2026), “Quantitative Analysis of Generative AI Text Usage and Identification of Factors Influencing Text Choice,” TechTrends. [https://doi.org/10.1007/s11528-026-01182-5] Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

What this means for instructors and institutions

Dr. Harfe’s course is not a template to be copied wholesale. The topic, the student population, and the tool were all choices made in a specific context. But the logic underneath them travels.

Building AI into an assignment rather than designing around it changes the dynamic for students and instructors alike. It is no longer a game of cat and mouse, and instead focuses on the reflection of AI use across the writing process. That’s a more productive conversation, and it’s one that traditional essay design cannot reliably start.

Word-level transparency makes that conversation possible to have with data behind it. Where AI detectors deliver verdicts, Authorship delivers a record. That distinction matters for instructors trying to understand what is happening in their courses and for administrators building AI policies that need to hold up over time.

One of the more persistent worries in higher ed right now is that students will simply hand their thinking over to AI entirely. The data here pushes back on that harder than a usage statistic can. Students in Harfe’s course had explicit, written permission to submit a 100% AI-generated essay and receive full credit. The assignment instructions stated that directly. The only additional requirement was a reflection essay explaining their choices. Despite that, only two of 310 students made no edits to the AI draft. The rest engaged. The students who engaged most deeply were also the strongest academic performers. They did not just happen to engage; they chose to, even though they had every reason not to.

That is worth sitting with. It does not resolve every concern about AI in academic writing, but it does suggest that assignment design has more leverage than most institutions have given it credit for.

“It’s really important to show students what AI can be used for: the good, the bad, the ugly, and then let them make decisions on when and how they should use it in their future lives. Grammarly Authorship is a tool that facilitates that process for faculty in a more collaborative way with students.”

— Dr. Brian Harfe, Professor and Associate Provost, University of Florida

The peer-reviewed study “Quantitative Analysis of Generative AI Text Usage and Identification of Factors Influencing Text Choice” was published in TechTrends in April 2026. Read the full study.

issues.title: Frontier's GoWild All You Can Fly pass is back with no blackout dates and earlier booking
issues.summary: Frontier Airlines has released its latest GoWild All You Can Fly pass and it's better than before, with no blackout dates and an earlier booking window.
issues.author: Eric Rosen
issues.content_html:
It's here! Frontier Airlines is now offering its GoWild All You Can Fly Pass for 2027, letting travelers take to the skies at a deep discount for an entire year (and potentially longer).

Here are all the details.

GoWild All You Can Fly Pass pricing

For a limited time, flyers can purchase a GoWild Pass good through 2027 for just $399. Members of the airline's Discount Den can score the pass for $349.

While that's not quite as good as some offers we've seen in past years (but better than some in other years), it can add up to significant savings if you fly the airline a lot. You must be a Frontier Miles member to purchase one.

Keep in mind that passholders pay $0.01 in airfare plus applicable taxes, fees and charges at the time of booking, so the pass gets you out of the regular airfare, but you're still on the hook for taxes and fees as well as other charges for things like optional seat selection and bags. While taxes on domestic legs are low, international ones can incur $60-$110 each way, depending on the destination.

Sneak peek: Frontier's new first-class seats are finally on sale, set for March debut

Multiple passholders can book travel at the same time, but you can't mix and match passholders with non-passholders on the same reservation.

Likewise, different types of fares can be combined each way on itineraries as long as all passengers hold a valid GoWild Pass at the time of booking and the primary passenger holds a Discount Den membership if Discount Den fares are selected.

Autorenewal

One other big caveat: GoWild passes autorenew, so if you want to cancel when your current pass expires, you'll need to contact the airline to do so. Your renewal date will be stated in your confirmation email when purchasing the pass.

Where can you fly?

The GoWild Pass is valid for flights to over 100 destinations across Frontier's route network, including both domestic gateways and international cities in Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. The airline's route network changes frequently, though, so stay on top of it to make sure your route will be in service when it's time to book.

Travel dates

Travel begins after purchase (meaning as soon as today) and is available through Dec. 31, 2027, meaning potentially over a full year of flying.

There are no blackout dates, like we've seen in some past instances, but on peak dates, you can expect to pay $59-$199 extra per segment.

Peak dates for 2027 include:

  • Jan. 1-3, 14, 15, 18
  • Feb. 11-2, 15
  • Mar. 12-14, 19-21, 26-29
  • Apr. 2-4
  • May 27-28, 31
  • July 1-5
  • Sept. 2-3, 6
  • Oct. 7-8, 11
  • Nov. 23-24, 27-29
  • Dec. 18-24, 26-31

The booking window

Here's the kicker: Standard bookings for eligible GoWild fares begin a day before departure for domestic flights and 10 days before departure for international flights. If your return flight is outside that window, then you'll have to try to make an additional booking when the window opens for that flight.

If you do want to book more in advance than that, however, you can pay an additional charge to do so, though this can vary based on the date and the route.

Also keep in mind that just because a seat is open on the flight you want does not mean it's eligible for a GoWild booking.

Earning miles

You can earn Frontier Miles on the purchase of the pass as well as any extras, like seat assignments, bag fees or priority boarding that you purchase.

Elite status

If you hold elite status with Frontier, you are still eligible for your benefits, including free seats and bags, so that can be a great way to save on optional fees that non-elites have to pay.

Bottom line

All-you-can-fly airline passes are a rarity these days and come with lots of limitations. Frontier Airlines' GoWild All You Can Fly Pass is no exception.

Still, if you fly the airline a lot, have flexibility (and a bit of spontaneity) in your plans and don't need a ton of extra amenities like preferred seats or checked bags, these fares can be a good way to save a bit on flights you'd be taking anyway ... or perhaps some fun last-minute fares you wouldn't be able to take advantage of otherwise.

issues.title: Select Capital One business cardholders can rebook disrupted flights for free
issues.summary: Select Capital One business cardholders can rebook qualifying canceled or delayed flights on any airline for free through January 2027.
issues.author: Becky Pokora
issues.content_html:
When you're traveling for work, a canceled flight is more than a hassle. It can mean missing an important meeting or paying up for a last-minute fare.

Through the end of January 2027, Capital One is giving select business cardholders a new way to manage flight disruptions. Eligible flights booked through Capital One Business Travel will automatically include free rebooking on another airline after a qualifying cancellation or delay, with Capital One covering the new ticket up to $5,000 per traveler.

How Capital One's complimentary flight rebooking works

When travelers book flights through Capital One Business Travel, Capital One will monitor eligible itineraries beginning 24 hours before departure. If the flight is canceled or delayed by at least three hours, the traveler will receive a notification and gain access to a self-service rebooking tool.

The benefit covers several types of disruptions, including:

  • Adverse weather conditions
  • Airport operational issues
  • Air traffic control issues

Last week's ground stop, which backed flights up for days, is a good example of when this benefit could be a huge help.

And unlike traditional airline rebooking, which may be limited to flights operated by the original carrier or its partners, Capital One's tool allows eligible travelers to select a replacement flight on another airline, with the new ticket covered up to $5,000 per traveler.

The flexibility to jump to a competing airline is the standout feature. When one carrier is sold out, another airline may still have space. Re-routing through a different connecting airport can also be strategic to avoid weather issues altogether.

Replacement flights must depart on the same or following day, serve the original destination or a nearby airport and be booked in the same (or lower) fare class. Despite these terms, this will still give travelers far more flexibility than handling things independently.

Travelers can also contact a live agent for 24/7 support.

Which Capital One business cardholders are eligible?

Capital One Business Travel is available to cardholders with several Capital One business cards, including the following:

  • Capital One Venture X Business
  • Capital One Spark Cash
  • Capital One Spark Cash Plus
  • Capital One Spark Cash Select
  • Capital One Spark Classic for Business
  • Capital One Spark Miles for Business (closed to new applicants)
  • Capital One Spark Miles Select for Business (closed to new applicants)
  • Capital One Spark Pro (closed to new applicants)
  • Capital One Spark Classic Miles for Business (closed to new applicants)

Holding one of these cards does not guarantee the free add-on. To check, log in to Capital One Business Travel. If the complimentary rebooking feature is available to you, it will be automatically added to your eligible flight at checkout.

The Venture X Business is particularly relevant for frequent flyers because it earns 5 miles per dollar spent on flights booked through Capital One Business Travel. Plus, it comes with a $300 annual credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel.

New applicants can potentially get even more value from Capital One Business Travel through the card's current welcome offer, which includes up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 travel credit after meeting two spending thresholds:

  • Earn 150,000 bonus miles after spending $40,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening.
  • Earn an additional 150,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 Capital One Business Travel credit (to use in the first cardholder year) after spending $120,000 total on purchases in the first four months from account opening.

The information for the Capital One Spark Classic for Business, Capital One Spark Miles for Business, Capital One Spark Miles Select for Business, Capital One Spark Pro and Capital One Spark Classic Miles for Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Capital One Venture X Business review: High earning rates and premium perks for businesses

What to know before relying on the benefit

This is useful protection, but it comes with restrictions. The original ticket must be booked through Capital One Business Travel, and the disruption must meet the three-hour threshold within 24 hours of departure.

It's also temporary. The complimentary is available for eligible bookings made through the end of January 2027, while supplies last. Capital One hasn't published a final eligible departure date.

Still, this could be valuable for business travelers with time-sensitive trips. It can also eliminate business travel bottlenecks, such as waiting for a manager to approve a costly replacement ticket.

Related: Getting a refund for a canceled or delayed flight

Trip delay coverage still matters

Capital One's new feature will help you with rebooking options, but it won't cover the other costs of getting stranded.

For example, if you're rebooked on a flight the following day, you may need to pay for a hotel, meals or transportation. That's where eligible credit card trip delay coverage could help.

Trip delay insurance covers unexpected costs related to qualifying delays, such as accommodations, meals or transportation while waiting out your delay.

That gap can be especially important during weather or air traffic control disruptions, when airlines generally do not pay for stranded travelers' hotels or meals.

Not every eligible card includes trip delay coverage, though. The Venture X Business covers up to $500 per ticket for meals and lodging when a trip is delayed six hours or more or requires an overnight stay.* Cash-back cards like the Spark Cash don't include it. Check your card's benefits guide before you travel.

Related: Flight delayed? 4 things to do to get trip delay reimbursement from your credit card

Bottom line

Capital One's complimentary flight disruption rebooking could be a valuable perk for business travelers facing cancellations or lengthy delays, particularly when another airline can get them to their destination sooner.

And it costs you nothing extra when booking on Capital One Business Travel.

The promotion is available to select Capital One customers for a limited time, so check whether the benefit appears at checkout before relying on it for an upcoming trip.

*For Capital One products listed on this page, some of the benefits may be provided by Visa® or Mastercard® and may vary by product. See the respective Guide to Benefits for details, as terms and exclusions apply.

issues.title: See if you’re eligible for a welcome offer as high as 100,000 points on the Amex Gold
issues.summary: The Amex Gold Card is one of the best travel rewards cards for dining and groceries. Here are the details of the welcome offer you can earn if you apply now.
issues.author: Augusta Stone and Olivia Mittak
issues.content_html:
The American Express® Gold Card is a favorite among TPG staffers thanks to its strong earning rates on dining and purchases at U.S. supermarkets.

This card also offers several food-focused statement credits that can help offset its $325 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Apply now for the American Express Gold Card: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in your first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Let's take a look at why you should consider adding the Amex Gold to your wallet.

American Express Gold welcome offer

New Amex Gold applicants can find out their offer and see if they're eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases within the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.

While not everyone will be targeted for the Amex Gold's top welcome offer of 100,000 points, it's the highest welcome offer we've ever seen on the card. Previously, the highest number of points you could earn on this card was 60,000 points (offer no longer available).

What is the Amex Gold's welcome offer worth?

This offer is worth up to $2,000, based on TPG's November 2026 valuations. To get the most value from your welcome bonus, you'll want to take advantage of Amex's 20 transfer partners, including standout options like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and ANA Mileage Club.

TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak previously saved thousands by transferring 60,000 points to Air Canada Aeroplan to book a lie-flat United Polaris business-class seat from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Frankfurt International Airport (FRA), plus $59 in taxes and fees.

Related: The best time to apply for these popular American Express cards based on offer history

Should you apply for the Amex Gold Card?

The American Express Gold Card is particularly appealing for travelers who spend heavily on dining and groceries and want to earn transferable points. Its statement credits can also help justify the annual fee if they align with purchases you'd make anyway.

The Amex Gold's bonus-earning categories include:

  • 5 points per dollar spent on prepaid hotels booked through amextravel.com and the Amex Travel App™
  • 4 points per dollar spent on dining at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent)
  • 4 points per dollar spent at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent)
  • 3 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through amextravel.com and the Amex Travel App
  • 2 points per dollar spent on prepaid car rentals booked through amextravel.com and the Amex Travel App
  • 2 points per dollar spent on cruises booked through amextravel.com
  • 1 point per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases

You can maximize your rewards by booking aspirational business-class tickets or picturesque stays at island resorts for far less than their cash equivalent.

Beyond earning points, the Amex Gold offers several statement credits:

  • Up to $10 a month (up to $120 a year) in dining statement credits at participating merchants, including Buffalo Wild Wings, Five Guys, Grubhub, The Cheesecake Factory and Wonder*.
  • Up to $10 in Uber Cash monthly (up to $120 a year) for Uber Eats and Uber rides in the U.S. (You must add the Amex Gold Card to the Uber app to receive the Uber Cash benefit, and you can redeem with any Amex card.)
  • Up to $50 in semiannual Resy statement credits (up to $100 a year). To use them, dine at a participating Resy restaurant in the U.S. and pay your bill with the Amex Gold Card.*
  • Up to $7 a month (up to $84 annually) in Dunkin' statement credits. Use your Amex Gold Card when paying at U.S. Dunkin' locations.*

In addition to the statement credits, cardmembers also receive Hertz Five Star status, which provides vehicle upgrades (when available) and bonus points. Registration in Hertz Gold+ is required.*

*Enrollment required

Related: 5 under-the-radar ways to maximize the Amex Gold's dining credits

Bottom line

The Amex Gold's combination of strong dining and grocery earning rates, transferable Membership Rewards points and food-focused statement credits makes it a compelling option for frequent travelers.

Amex Membership Rewards points are highly valuable, and there are many great redemption options. If you fully use all of the card's ongoing statement credits, you can get up to $424 in value each year, which easily covers the $325 annual fee.

TPG staffers continue to carry the Amex Gold year after year. If you regularly spend at restaurants and U.S. supermarkets and can take advantage of the card's ongoing benefits, the Amex Gold could be worth keeping in your wallet long after you've earned its welcome bonus.

issues.title: New offers on Atmos Rewards credit cards: Earn up to 90,000 points, companion fares and more
issues.summary: Atmos Rewards credit cards offer big bonuses for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines travelers looking to earn points to redeem for award flights.
issues.author: Augusta Stone
issues.content_html:
Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines, allowing members to earn and redeem points across both carriers. Atmos Rewards points can be used for flights on Alaska and Hawaiian, as well as a range of partner airlines, making it easier to turn everyday spending and travel into award trips around the world.

The program offers three cobranded credit cards: one business and two personal cards.

With strong welcome offers currently available on all three cards, now is a good time to consider applying if you regularly fly Alaska or Hawaiian.

Let's dig deeper into the bonuses available right now and whether they're worth applying for.

Atmos Rewards Summit Visa Infinite credit card

The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card features a valuable welcome bonus, useful earning rates and a solid suite of benefits.

Welcome offer: Earn 80,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,680 when you include the value of the 25,000-point Global Companion Award. While not the absolute top offer we've seen in the card's history, the current lower minimum spend requirement can still make it a great time to apply.

Annual fee: $395

Earning rates:

  • 3 points per dollar spent on eligible Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases, eligible dining and foreign transaction purchases
  • 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases

Key benefits:

  • 10,000 status points every year upon account anniversary, plus 1 status point for every $2 spent on the card
  • A 10% rewards bonus on all points earned if you have an eligible Bank of America account
  • A free checked bag on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines for the cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation (when you pay for your flight with your card)
  • No foreign transaction fees
  • Priority boarding on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines for the cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation (when you pay for your flight with your card)
  • Two Alaska Lounge and two Wi-Fi passes each calendar quarter
  • Up to $120 in statement credits for TSA PreCheck or Global Entry every four years

Why we like it: This welcome offer includes a Global Companion Award, which knocks up to 25,000 points off a companion's award ticket when you book two award seats on Alaska, Hawaiian or a partner airline (including Oneworld members)in any class. The card also offers an ongoing 25,000-point Global Companion Award after each card anniversary.

Cardholders can also earn a 100,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $60,000 or more in a card anniversary year.

For frequent international travelers, earning 3 points per dollar spent on foreign transaction purchases is a major advantage and can help quickly accrue Atmos Rewards points. Matt Moffitt, TPG's contributing editor for credit cards, is based in Spain and uses this card for most of his everyday spending there since those purchases are charged in euros.

To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Rewards Summit.

Apply here: Atmos Rewards Summit

Atmos Rewards Ascent Visa Signature credit card

Semifrequent Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flyers who want an affordable annual fee are the target audience for the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card a mid-tier option with its own useful perks.

Welcome offer: Earn 70,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $2,500 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

TPG's valuations place this offer at $1,120, plus the value of the Companion Fare. Like the Summit, this is a strong offer compared to the card's history considering its relatively easy spending requirements, but not the highest we've ever seen.

Annual fee: $95

Earning rates:

  • 3 points per dollar spent on eligible Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases
  • 2 points per dollar spent on eligible gas, electric vehicle charging stations, cable, streaming services and local transit (including ride-hailing services)
  • 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases

Key benefits:

  • A 10% rewards bonus on all points earned if you have an eligible Bank of America account
  • A free checked bag on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines for the cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation (when you pay for your flight with your card)
  • Ability to earn an annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $6,000 on purchases within the prior card anniversary year
  • No foreign transaction fees
  • Preferred boarding on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines for the cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation (when you pay for your flight with your card)

Why we like it: The Ascent offers a lower-cost way to earn Atmos Rewards points while receiving practical airline benefits. For travelers who fly Alaska or Hawaiian a few times each year, the free checked-bag benefit and preferred boarding could help justify the $95 annual fee.

The welcome offer also includes a Companion Fare, which can provide additional value for travelers who regularly fly with someone else.

To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Rewards Ascent.

Apply here: Atmos Rewards Ascent

Atmos Rewards Visa Signature Business Card

Small-business owners who fly Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines regularly the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card is worth considering. It underwent a refresh in Nov. 2026 and now offers new earning opportunities, additional travel perks and a flat annual fee that covers employee cards at no additional cost.

Welcome offer: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

The points in this bonus are worth $1,440, per TPG's valuations. Unlike the personal cards, this represents the highest points offer we've ever seen on the card.

Annual fee: $195 per company (with free employee cards)

Earning rates:

  • 10 points per dollar spent on qualifying flights booked on the Atmos for Business website
  • 3 points per dollar spent on other eligible Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases
  • 2 points per dollar spent on dining
  • 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases

Key benefits:

  • Four Alaska Lounge passes per calendar year, issued quarterly to the primary cardholder
  • Up to $120 in statement credits for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fees every four years
  • One status point for every $3 spent on eligible purchases, with no annual cap, for the primary cardholder
  • A free checked bag on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines for the cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation (when you pay for your flight with your card)
  • Preferred boarding on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines for the cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation (when you pay for your flight with your card)
  • Waived change fees for same-day confirmed flight changes (excluding Saver fares)
  • 20% back on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines inflight purchases when you pay with your card
  • A 10% rewards bonus on all points earned if you have an eligible Bank of America business account
  • No foreign transaction fees

The refreshed card no longer includes the annual $99 Companion Fare or the $100 Alaska Lounge+ membership discount. Existing cardholders will retain their current benefits and won't automatically transition to the new version.

Why we like it: The 10-point earning rate is a standout benefit for businesses that frequently fly Alaska or Hawaiian Airlines, representing a 16% return on eligible flights booked through Atmos for Business based on TPG's November 2026 valuations.

Free employee cards extend perks like checked bags and preferred boarding to more travelers, while four annual lounge passes and waived same-day change fees add value for the primary cardholder. Together, these benefits make the card particularly appealing to businesses that frequently fly Alaska or Hawaiian.

To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Rewards Business.

Apply here: Atmos Rewards Visa Signature Business

Bottom line

The Atmos Rewards cards are offering bonuses that allow new cardholders to add a haul of points to their accounts.

  • The Summit suits frequent flyers who value premium perks and a faster path to status.
  • The Ascent is ideal for casual Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines travelers who value free bags and a lower annual fee.
  • The Business is a specialized choice but one that pays major dividends for loyal Atmos customers.

If you're ready to maximize this program and collect Atmos Rewards points, earning one of these offers is an excellent way to start.

Apply here: Atmos Rewards Summit Visa Infinite credit card
Apply here: Atmos Rewards Ascent Visa Signature credit card
Apply here: Atmos Rewards Visa Signature Business

issues.content_html:
Unlike most surviving Cham towers that crown dramatic hilltops, Binh Lam Tower rises almost unexpectedly from the flat, verdant plains of a quiet lowland village.

Constructed around the late tenth to early eleventh century, this 20-meter brick sanctuary serves as a vital architectural bridge, catching the art form mid-evolution between the delicate, lyrical features of the My Son A1 style and the grand, spear-like forms of classic Binh Dinh towers.

Its weathered facade features slender vertical pilasters, mini-temple false doors, and faint relief carvings of the mythical bird-god Garuda. Beyond its standing brickwork, Binh Lam hides deep subterranean secrets: archaeological digs uncovered vast foundations of a once-extensive religious complex, alongside stone Nagas and relief sculptures.

Furthermore, the tower once formed the eastern heart of ancient Thi Nai Citadel, positioned along river channels leading to the historical port—making this lowland monument a crucial physical anchor to Champa's lost naval and architectural empire.

issues.content_html:
The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, located in Cincinnati along the banks of the Ohio River makes a solemn statement about the lives that were lived enslaved in the early history of the United States, and the many heroic men and women who played important roles in the Underground Railroad movement, which helped to bring an end to African slavery in the United States. Referred to as a "museum of conscience", The Freedom Center is dedicated to exploring the struggle to abolish human enslavement. During the era when the Underground Railroad was active, Cincinnati was a major gateway across the Ohio River where freedom seekers escaped from southern slave states to the northern states or Canada, making the Center's location rather significant.

Having opened its doors in 2004, the Freedom Center uses immersive exhibits across multiple floors to convey an account that is simultaneously rich in the cultural traditions of the enslaved, as well as steeped in the violence and tragedies that were endured. The histories are told through a combination of permanent and traveling exhibits that utilize storytelling, film, artwork, hands-on activities and more.

Perhaps one of the most impressive and prominent displays at the center is an authentic, 19th-century reconstructed slave pen that was obtained from a farm in Kentucky. It stands as America's only remaining, pristinely preserved slave pen and stands as a stark reminder of the atrocious conditions that were endured.

The pen, originally built somewhere around 1830 by a wealthy Kentucky farmer, runaway slave catcher, and slave trader, was used as a holding facility for captured and purchased enslaved men, women and children. It was discovered, quite by accident in 1998 when a farmer, who was preparing to demolish an old barn on his property, discovered that the barn had been built up around this old pen, thus protecting and preserving (and hiding) the slave pen for more than 100 years.

During its unfortunate years of use, enslaved people would be kept in the pen, often for months, until the slave trader accumulated a large enough "stock" to march them further south to be sold. These forced marches would often cover upwards of 750 miles. Conditions in these pens would be brutal, offering no sanitation, lighting or warmth. As many as 65 enslaved people would often be housed in this small pen. Also very moving is the memorial room dedicated to the Transatlantic Slave Trade, as well as the Freedom's Eternal Flame Terrace which overlooks the Ohio River and the city skyline.

The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center is a beautiful and meaningful tribute to the human right for freedom, and to the brave men, women and children who stood up to the inhuman treatment of themselves and of others; and to those who continue to fight for the cause of freedom through out the world today.

issues.content_html:
Above the village of Kalnik in northern Croatia, the walls of Veliki Kalnik Castle rise from a jagged rocky ridge. Built across several levels, the medieval stronghold follows the natural contours of the rock, making its surviving towers and walls appear to grow out of the mountain.

First documented in 1243, the castle is best known for a story involving King Béla IV of Hungary and Croatia. According to local legend, the king took refuge here during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century. As the siege dragged on and supplies dwindled, villagers kept the defenders fed with plums.

The grateful king is said to have rewarded his rescuers with noble status. They became known as the kalnički šljivari—the “plum nobles of Kalnik.” This tale remains part of the region’s identity, connecting an imposing fortress with an unexpectedly humble fruit.

The ruins visible today developed over centuries. Their towers, fragments of walls, and elevated viewpoints reveal how the builders used the steep terrain as part of the castle’s defenses. From the heights, the view opens across the villages, fields, and wooded hills below.

issues.title: The Crucified Tongkonan of Tolu Deri in North Toraja Regency, Indonesia
issues.summary: In the highland villages of North Toraja, the skyline is dominated by tongkonan —traditional ancestral houses with sweeping, boat-shaped saddle roofs that loom dramatically over the landscape. issues.content_html:
In the highland villages of North Toraja, the skyline is dominated by tongkonan—traditional ancestral houses with sweeping, boat-shaped saddle roofs that loom dramatically over the landscape. For centuries, these wooden structures have served as the spiritual and social anchor for Torajan clans, decorated strictly according to Aluk Todolo ("the way of the ancestors"), the indigenous animist belief system. Their facades are traditionally adorned with carved geometric patterns (pa'ssura'), water buffalo horns (kabongo'), and sculpted wooden heads (katik) symbolizing wealth, status, and protection.

However, in the small hamlet of Tolu Deri, just north of Rantepao, one particular tongkonan stands out as a striking, visually arresting symbol of modern Torajan syncretism. Mounted directly onto the front gabled peak of the structure—occupying the exact position traditionally reserved for ancestral motifs—is a massive wooden crucifix bearing a carved figure of Jesus Christ.

While the majority of the Torajan population converted to Christianity (predominantly Dutch Reformed Protestantism and Catholicism) during the 20th century, the integration of Christian motifs into traditional architecture usually remains subtle, such as small carved crosses on support beams or church roofs built in the tongkonan shape. Seeing a full-scale, dramatic crucifix physically fused into the facade of a traditional house—standing directly above the customary buffalo head and skull mountings—is exceptionally rare.

This unique blending of iconographies visually captures the lived reality of Toraja today: a culture where deeply rooted Christian faith does not replace ancestral traditions, but rather sits alongside them in a harmonious, visually striking synthesis.

issues.title: Capture One adds wired tethering for the Hasselblad X2D II 100C
issues.summary: The feature follows July’s native Raw support and requires X2D II 100C firmware 1.4.15.7 and Capture One 16.9.1.
issues.author: Dale Baskin
issues.content_html:
The feature follows July’s native Raw support and requires X2D II 100C firmware 1.4.15.7 and Capture One 16.9.1.

Hasselblad has released firmware version 1.4.15.7 for the X2D II 100C, adding support for wired tethered shooting in Capture One. Tethering is available in Capture One 16.9.1 for desktop and Capture One Mobile 4.3.0. This marks the second stage of a partnership the two companies announced in July.

What the update adds

With the camera connected via USB, each 100MP frame appears in Capture One at full resolution as soon as it’s captured, so focus and exposure can be checked while it is still live. Capture One’s full editing toolset is available while shooting, and adjustments applied to the first frame carry over to subsequent captures.

“You pick up your camera, you plug in, and it just works,” said Capture One chief executive Rafael Orta.

This release only adds tethered shooting for the X2D II 100C. The X2D 100C and CFV 100C digital back, which gained native Raw support in Capture One in July, weren’t included in today’s announcement.

A complicated history

Historically, Hasselblad support had been missing from Capture One, a result of the old rivalry between Hasselblad and Phase One, Capture One’s former parent company, which competed for the same medium format customers.

That changed in July, when Capture One added native support for Hasselblad’s .3FR Raw files in version 16.8.3, covering the X2D II 100C, X2D 100C and CFV 100C, along with dedicated lens profiles for XCD lenses. At the time, the companies said tethering would follow later in 2026.

Bronius Rudnickas, Hasselblad’s global marketing manager, said tethering was one of the top requests from photographers after the collaboration was announced.

Availability

Firmware 1.4.15.7 for the X2D II 100C is available now for download from Hasselblad. Tethering support is available in Capture One 16.9.1 and Capture One Mobile 4.3.0. Capture One is also offering Hasselblad camera owners a 90-day trial of the software.

issues.title: National Geographic reveals its Pictures of the Year 2026, from spawning moray eels to a Greenland shark under the ice
issues.summary: Chosen from more than a million images, this year’s 25 selections range from a six-month solarigraph over an ancient Peruvian observatory to a camera trap on a Kenyan riverbank.
issues.author: Dale Baskin
issues.content_html:
Chosen from more than a million images, this year’s 25 selections range from a six-month solarigraph over an ancient Peruvian observatory to a camera trap on a Kenyan riverbank.

If there’s one name that’s synonymous with great photography, it’s National Geographic, which has just announced its Pictures of the Year for 2026.

National Geographic’s editors sifted through more than a million images captured by its photographers to arrive at the 25 that make up this year’s selection. That ratio alone says a lot about what it takes for a photo to make the cut. But in National Geographic’s tradition, these aren’t just great images; the publication emphasizes that they reflect the patience and dedication its photographers bring to its visual storytelling.

This year’s selections cover a wide spectrum, from the first-ever images of eels spawning in the wild, to a climber suspended from a sea cliff in Spain moments after a total solar eclipse, to Kiliii Yüyan’s encounter with a Greenland shark in the sub-freezing waters near Kulusuk in East Greenland.

Many of the images are as notable for how they were made as for what’s in them. Diego López Calvín used solarigraphy, a single continuous exposure lasting six months, to trace the sun’s path between the solstices over Peru’s ancient Chankillo observatory. Will Burrard-Lucas hid a camera trap on a remote riverbank in Kenya’s Masai Mara, and Prakash Matada mounted a fisheye lens on a telescoping pole to photograph a troop of endangered golden langurs at close range.

National Geographic’s editor-in-chief, Nathan Lump, suggested the selections are also a response to a changing photography landscape, citing the value of documenting reality. “Together, these images remind us how much there is still to discover about our planet, and that the deeply human work of documenting what’s real is more valuable than ever in a time when fakes are everywhere,” he said.

Below are a few of our favorites from National Geographic’s Pictures of the Year 2026. All 25 images will appear in the December issue of National Geographic and can be seen now on the National Geographic website. [Editor’s note: National Geographic requires users to register for a free account to view the full set of images.]

A Greenland shark, the oldest vertebrate on Earth, swims underneath the meter-thick sea ice near the village of Kulusuk in East Greenland, as diver Philipp Oppermann watches. This shark came up from the depths into the shallows at night to follow the scent of a Greenlander’s bait, frozen ringed seal. This photograph was made March 17, 2026, in early spring, when the sea ice remains strong and the visibility of the water is spectacular, over 50m (165ft).

A crack of rifle fire marks the finale of a performance of tbourida, a Moroccan equestrian tradition in which a team of riders act out a cavalry charge. Women are gradually gaining a foothold in the centuries-old sport. At the festival pictured here, all-female brigades represented two of the 140 competing troupes.

Climber Chris Sharma dangles from a completely horizontal limestone face in the moments after August’s total solar eclipse in Spain.

Apparent path of the sun as seen from the western observation point at the Chankillo Solar Observatory in Casma (Ancash), Peru. The six-month-long continuous exposure (solarigraphy) taken between June 21 and December 21, 2025, accurately shows the sun’s path, with the winter and summer solstices located at the ends of the structure outlined by the silhouette of the towers.

Deep in Kenya’s Masai Mara, a reserve bordering the northern edge of the Serengeti, photographer Will Burrard-Lucas worked with a team of rangers to hide a camera trap high on a riverbank and waited for action. The images that came back revealed something extraordinary. The secluded crossing turned out to be a high-traffic wildlife thoroughfare. Among the passersby: a pair of slinking lions, unusual visitors here.

A pair of Abbott’s moray eels (Gymnothorax eurostus) reaching the pinnacle of their spawning run, three-tenths of a second after leaving the cover of coral. The male on the left is just releasing the jaw of the female, with both eels sending gametes into the water. Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan.

A curious troop of Gee’s golden langurs – named for a naturalist who documented them in the 1950s peer into a fisheye lens that Prakash Matada affixed to a telescoping pole. The endangered canopy dwellers here have formed a rare bond with humans and proved anything but camera-shy, gazing at their own reflections.

issues.title: Panasonic is working on the first power zoom for L-mount
issues.summary: Something for the videographers to look forward to.
issues.author: Mitchell Clark
issues.content_html:
Something for the videographers to look forward to.

Currently, there are no lenses that can make use of the zoom rocker on the SHX1’s grip. But that seems set to change.

Alongside its new cinema-focused SHX1 camera, Panasonic quietly announced that it’s working on something else for videographers: a power zoom lens. While there are pretty much no further details, it’s exciting to hear, as it’ll be the first full-frame power zoom option for L-mount.

The lack of any such options has been a bit of a notable omission for the mount, especially given how many video-focused cameras use it. There are, of course, Panasonic’s hybrid cameras like the S1II, S1RII and S5II series, which many videographers use, but BlackMagic Design sells pro-level studio cameras that use the mount as well.

The only mention of the lens is buried in the press release for the SHX1. In it, Panasonic says that it “is also developing a power zoom lens designed for the LUMIX SHX1 and for remote production.” To us, both the mention of remote production and the lens’s announcement being tied to a pro camera indicate that it’ll be a higher-end option, rather than a more consumer-oriented one like we’ve seen from Fujifilm, Canon and Sony. (Sorry, S9 vloggers hoping for a way to zoom in and out smoothly).

As for details like price, release date and focal range, we’ll just have to wait until Panasonic’s ready to share more. We combed through the SHX1’s announcement video to see if the company included any footage of it, but we couldn’t find any. Interestingly, one lens in the video looks an awful lot like a power zoom, but its design and the red ring near the flange strongly suggest a Canon model.

If you’re a videographer who shoots on L-mount, sound off in the comments below. Are you excited about finally getting a power zoom option, and, if so, what kind of option are you hoping for?

About the Author: Mitchell started taking pictures at 10 and hasn’t stopped since. It’s been a wide-ranging adventure, spanning a wide variety of genres and locales, and occasionally dipping into fascinations with video and filmmaking. They honed their technical knowledge doing documentation, programing and QA, writing for The Verge, and just generally messing around on the computer to see what breaks.
