We missed the launch of this one, but the pricing is GREAT right now, so thought we’d share for the guys at Freewell x Dunna Did It (and he certainly did, these look great!) A new locking filter system from Freewell and
issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Freewell and Dunna Did It launch ultra-slim modular filter system for photographers and filmmakers appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

We missed the launch of this one, but the pricing is GREAT right now, so thought we’d share for the guys at Freewell x Dunna Did It (and he certainly did, these look great!)

A new locking filter system from Freewell and photographer and filmmaker Dunna Did It combines magnetic attachment with a mechanical locking mechanism, allowing photographers to share filters across lenses with different thread sizes.

Freewell has teamed up with photographer, filmmaker and YouTube creator Dunna Did It to launch a new modular camera filter system designed to make switching filters between lenses quicker and easier.

The Dunna Did It × Freewell Ultra-Slim Locking Filter System uses a combination of magnetic attachment and a mechanical locking mechanism. Rather than needing a separate set of filters for every lens, photographers can use a single collection of filters across lenses with thread sizes ranging from 49mm to 95mm, simply by changing the base ring.

The system is available in two configurations: a Videography Kit aimed at filmmakers and hybrid creators, and a Photography Kit designed primarily for still photographers.

One filter system for multiple lenses

Anyone with a growing collection of lenses will know that filter sizes can quickly become a bit of a headache. Even when lenses have similar focal lengths, their filter thread sizes can vary, potentially leaving you with multiple versions of the same ND or polarising filter.

Freewell’s new system aims to address that problem by separating the filter itself from the lens mounting ring.

A dedicated base ring attaches to each lens, with the filters then transferred between compatible rings. Magnets help guide the filter into position, before a short clockwise turn engages the mechanical lock.

The system supports ten filter thread sizes: 49mm, 55mm, 58mm, 62mm, 67mm, 72mm, 77mm, 82mm, 86mm and 95mm.

There are a few other interesting details worth noting:

  • Ultra-slim design: The fixed ND filters measure just 2.95mm thick and weigh 18.4g, helping minimise additional bulk and weight, particularly useful for handheld and gimbal-based video work.
  • Magnetic attachment with mechanical locking: Magnets help position the filter, while a short clockwise twist locks it in place.
  • Colour accuracy: Freewell says the filters are designed to minimise colour shifts, helping maintain natural-looking skin tones, greens and skies.
  • Stackable filters: Compatible filters can be used individually or stacked to combine different effects, including exposure control, reflection reduction and diffusion.

Two kits for different creative needs

The system launches with two kits, each offering a different selection of filters.

Videography Kit

Designed with filmmakers and hybrid shooters in mind, the Videography Kit includes:

  • ND4 (2-stop)
  • ND8 (3-stop)
  • ND16 (4-stop)
  • ND32 (5-stop)
  • Glow Mist 1/4

The kit also includes a selected base ring, protective caps (including one with built-in reference targets) and a fitted carry case.

The range of ND filters provides exposure control across different lighting conditions, while the Glow Mist filter adds a diffusion option for video and still photography.

Photography Kit

The Photography Kit takes a slightly different approach, with a selection of filters aimed at everyday photography and longer exposures.

It includes:

  • UV filter
  • ND64 (6-stop)
  • ND1000 (10-stop)
  • CPL (circular polariser)
  • Glow Mist 1/8

As with the Videography Kit, it comes with a selected base ring, protective caps and a fitted carry case.

The combination covers lens protection, reflection control, long exposures and a touch of diffusion without requiring multiple filter systems.

Developed in collaboration with Dunna Did It

The system was developed over nearly a year in collaboration with Dunna Did It, a photographer, filmmaker and music producer based on Vancouver Island, British Columbia.

With an audience of more than 440,000 YouTube subscribers, Dunna regularly creates photography and video content, including gear reviews and tutorials.

The collaboration focused on refining the physical design and practical workflow of the system, including its locking mechanism, overall profile and ease of use when moving between lenses.

Pricing and availability

The Dunna Did It × Freewell Ultra-Slim Locking Filter System launched online on 26 August 2026.

Both the Photography Kit and Videography Kit have a launch price of US$299.99, reduced from the regular retail price of US$349.99.

Customers choose a base ring to suit their existing lens, with additional ring sizes available for use across the rest of their lens collection.

For more information, visit the Freewell product page or watch Dunna’s product introduction video on YouTube.

The post Is it still photography if you’re only using your phone? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

Yes.

That’s as simple as the answer need be, but that’s not the point of this article.

Another Godox press release (Those guys are busy!) and again, we’ve not had a chance to play with one of these so you’ll need to do your own research, but Godox have just announced the Smartphone Xenon Flash A2, and their tagline is “Your phone, now a pro camera” which isn’t exactly factual, but also, the definition of “pro camera” is very loose.

The thing to keep in mind with ANY small light source is that its going to be harsh – there’s stuff you can do about it, though. You can diffuse it, bounce it (though a small light like the A2 might not give quite enough output to do much there) but even things like bouncing it off a close wall or even a sheet of paper in a pinch – use what you have, experiment.

I love the idea of small portable lights, this one is certainly an interesting addition to your phone photography – maybe worth giving a try, it’s certainly a good starter to your photography lighting journey.

Here’s the Godox Press Release (With a little bit of my own ramble)

Smartphone Photography, Now With More Zap

Phone cameras keep getting better, but low light, backlighting and mixed lighting can still make them sweat. Enter the Godox A2: proper pro-style lighting for your phone, with more control over your light and a lot more room to play.

Its short, punchy burst of xenon light freezes motion in its tracks, which is great for action shots and stylized looks.

Xenon Flash: Bring Your Subject to Life

Go bold with direct flash, or add a subtle lift to a backlit portrait. With a guide number of roughly 15 (ISO 100, metres), the A2 has plenty of oomph for close-range shots. When flash is your main light, that quick burst also helps freeze movement. *For best results, keep the A2 within 2 m of your subject. Want more power or wider coverage? Pair Godox’s upcoming smartphone wireless flash trigger (sold separately) with Godox speedlights or outdoor flashes.

TTL and Manual Modes: Stay Spontaneous, Get Precise

Fast and flawless when the moment’s fleeting, or hands-on when you want to flex your creative muscles. TTL and Manual modes have you covered both ways.

High-Speed Sync: Find Your Balance

Why banish that bright background when it can star in the story? With high-speed sync up to 1/8000s, the A2 lets you control ambient exposure while lighting your subject. Balance a face against a sunlit scene, or go for a faster shutter speed to keep the action crisp.

Bi-Color LED: True Color for Everyday Stories

Truer colors and flattering skin tones make portrait videos look natural and beautifully textured. Low light or indoors, the results feel authentic and ready to share. Your content doesn’t just look good, it feels right, and it’s always social-media ready.

Godox Camera App: Your Look, at Your Fingertips

Find your look right on your screen. Built on Godox’s TTL know-how, the Godox Camera app keeps exposure simple in Auto (A) mode, with Natural, Even and Contrast flash effects to try out. Feeling fussy? Switch to Manual (M) mode and tweak shutter speed and flash output yourself. Bluetooth with NFC-assisted setup lets you adjust flash and LED settings wirelessly, on or off camera.

Dual-Side Magnetic Mounting: Snap On, Explore New Angles

The A2’s dual magnetic design isn’t just for the back of your phone. Snap it to any metal surface or pop it on a stand and you’re ready to roll. On the front, the magnetic ring lets you attach accessories to shape the light exactly how you like. Simple, flexible and always creative.

Magnetic Accessories: Change the Light, Set the Mood

Go moodier and more dramatic with optional extras like a honeycomb grid, barndoors or a snoot to aim your light and tame the spill. Add a touch of warmth with a full CTO magnetic filter. *For best results, use the A2 off-camera with light-shaping accessories.

Compact. Magnetic. More Ways to Light.

Pro flash power in a palm-sized body. Pocketable, portable and happy to go anywhere you do.

Four Colors, A Style of Your Own

The A2 brings pro lighting to your phone in four distinctive colors. Pick a finish that suits your everyday style, and make your kit as personal as the photos you take.

issues.content_html:
The post Do people still print their photographs? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

The guys at Godox sent across a press release (A few weeks back now I’m sorry as I’ve been a little ‘offline’) for their then new Godox Portable Colour Photo Printer, the P100. And it got me thinking, even at a simple, easy to use level of printing like this little guy, who is still printing out their photographs?

We celebrated my dad’s life recently, and at the wake my brother had printed out a couple hundred photographs that showed the life and times of dad and those he cared about. There’s something very real about having a print you can hold in your hand, nothing to log in to, no computers to boot up, just a square of paper and your memories.

Before we share this press release, here’s a challenge: In the next couple of months, aim to have one of your photographs printed, and to take that one step further, I was just listening to a clip from a podcast (You can see it here) Print Swap, what a great idea, print one of your images and send it to someone – to have and to hold.

Right, the Godox P100, it’s not an A3 Epson printing onto some beautiful Canson Rag, but it’s WITH YOU, you can print images and have them. (I’ve been grabbing frames with the beautiful FujiFilm Instax Mini 99 which prints a little 45x62mm photo)

On with our press release, please keep in mind we have not tested the P100 ourselves.

Godox Introduces P100 Portable Color Photo Printer

Godox has announced the P100 Portable Color Photo Printer, a compact dye-sublimation printer designed to turn digital images into physical prints wherever you are.

The P100 uses 300 dpi high-precision dye-sublimation printing, with 1,256 printhead heating elements and support for 16.7 million colours. According to Godox, the combination is designed to produce smooth colour gradations, fine detail and vivid colour reproduction.

Each print also receives an automatic protective overcoat, helping protect the finished photo from dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion.

Print and personalise from your phone

The P100 connects to the Godox Cam APP via Bluetooth, while NFC tap-to-connect provides another quick way to pair the printer.

From within the app, users can capture and print photos directly, or work with images already on their device. Creative options include filters, frames, stickers and templates, along with tools for creating ID photos and collages.

The app also allows users to check remaining paper and battery levels, making it easier to keep track of the printer’s status.

Designed to travel

With its compact design and lightweight construction, the P100 is intended to be easy to take along to parties, family gatherings, housewarmings and other everyday occasions.

Rather than leaving photos sitting on a phone or buried in a cloud library, the P100 gives users a simple way to turn them into physical prints that can be displayed, collected, added to a scrapbook or shared with friends and family.

Automatic protection

The P100’s automatic lamination process adds a protective overcoat to every finished print. Godox says this helps protect prints against dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion, as well as humid conditions.

The process happens automatically after printing, so there is no additional lamination step for the user.

All-in-one cartridge

The P100 uses an all-in-one photo paper cartridge, designed to make replacing the printing supplies quick and straightforward.

Combined with wireless connectivity and the Godox Cam APP, the system is designed to keep the process from capturing a photo to holding the finished print as simple as possible.

A physical home for digital memories

The P100 is ultimately aimed at something increasingly familiar in photography: we take plenty of photos, but relatively few ever make it off our phones.

By combining portable dye-sublimation printing with a range of simple editing and personalisation tools, Godox says the P100 is designed to make printing those images easier, whether you’re sharing them with friends at a gathering or simply putting a favourite photograph somewhere you’ll actually see it.

The Godox P100 Portable Color Photo Printer is now part of Godox’s expanding range of photography accessories.

You can get them online for around $200 Aussie, do a Google and see what you can find!

Don’t forget, PRINT YOUR WORK.

issues.title: Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in NYC Closet Sells for $4.9M
issues.summary: Calls to exclude Russia from Venice Architecture Biennale, Public Art Fund announces 2027 program, and more in today's art news.
issues.author: Phillip Pyle
issues.content_html:
Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic’s writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us .

Long-Lost Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in Closet Breaks Estimates

Georgia O’Keeffe’s “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” (1930), which was rediscovered in the back of an East Village closet where it was stored for four decades, fetched $4.9 million at Christie’s 20th-Century Evening Sale last night, November 18, surpassing its $2-3 estimate. Read Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar’s report detailing the fascinating backstory behind the painting, created just one year after the artist's first visit to New Mexico.

EU Countries Call to Exclude Russia From Architecture Biennale

Days before the close of this year’s Venice Biennale, 10 European Union countries are demanding that the European Commission exclude Russia from the 2027 architecture biennale. “In light of the current geopolitical realities … there should be no room for ‘normalisation’ of Russia’s participation in international sporting and cultural events, as long as there is no just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” reads a letter signed by representatives in Poland, Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden, according to Rapporteur.

Public Art Fund Announces 2027 Program

Ahead of its 50th anniversary next year, Public Art Fund has announced its 2027 exhibition program. The organization will continue its longstanding bus shelter series with I Happen to Like New York, which will transform 700 JCDecaux shelters across New York, Chicago, and Boston with the works of 19 artists, including Nicole Eisenman, Louis Fratino, and Toyin Ojih Odutola. New outdoor public sculptures from Ugo Rondinone, Lotus Kang, and Firelei Báez, a photo series from Catherine Opie, and a first-of-its-kind participatory performance by Jeremy Dweller round out Public Art Fund's 2027 offerings.

More in Today’s News:

  • Brooklyn artist Julia Jo's "One Fell Swoop" (2026) will be offered at Christie’s evening sale tomorrow, November 19, to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless. The New York-based nonprofit has supported unhoused individuals and families in the city through food, clothing, housing, job training, and youth programs since its founding in 1981. "One Fell Swoop" is estimated to fetch between $30,000 and $50,000, though a Christie’s spokesperson told Hyperallergic that “we think it will go for more.”
  • Two months before the closing of Ana Mendieta at London’s Tate Modern, the Museum of Modern Art has announced it will present the first retrospective on the late Cuban-American artist in the United States in over 20 years.
  • Leading feminist conceptual artist Eleanor Antin has sued her dealer Richard Saltoun , who operates galleries in New York, London, and Rome, over his alleged withholding of at least 179 works.
  • After this month’s “blue wave,” President Donald Trump will soon have to contend with a Democrat-majority Congress ready to investigate his culture war tirades against institutions including the National Portrait Gallery, the Smithsonian, and the Kennedy Center.
  • This week, the City of Sydney in Australia awarded 40 artists $25,000 “no strings attached” grants in a new initiative aimed at preventing the city from losing “its local storytellers and creative soul.”
  • Five works, including 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and 18th-20th century inscribed crosses, were repatriated to Ethiopia following a ceremony in London today, November 18, as part of a new partnership between the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio and the Ethiopian Heritage Authority.

issues.title: Is My Art Funny to You?
issues.summary: A sprawling exhibition across two New York campus galleries explores humor in contemporary art, imploring us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.
issues.author: Greta Rainbow
issues.content_html:
Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that it would behoove us socially. In a talk at the Aspen AIR Festival this year, poet and psychoanalyst Nuar Alsadir described eliciting Duchenne laughter as an attempt “to strip away the layers of socialization and the false self.” While laughter “flies under the radar because of our associations to it as being joyful,” when you dig deeper, it’s “usually coming from some kind of conflict in the unconscious.”

What to make of art that makes us laugh? (Or at least desperately wants to?) Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art, a sprawling exhibition across at Lehman College Art Gallery in the Bronx and The Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence in Bronxville, proposes comedy as a potent artistic device. Co-curators Melissa Brown, artist and professor of art at Lehman College, and John O’Connor, chair of the Visual and Studio Arts program at Sarah Lawrence, use humor’s various tones — absurd, cringe, slapstick, ironic — as organizing principles to present the work of 41 artists. From museum-collection heavy hitters like Ray Johnson and Cindy Sherman, to established cartoonists Roz Chast and Aline Kominsky-Crumb, to contemporary rising stars such as Ebecho Muslimova, Does This Taste Funny? implores us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.

Humor is “an emotional response that’s a little bit like a sneak attack,” Brown said in an interview with Hyperallergic. “It causes you to think about things in a way that is not led by a press release, not predetermined by art history. There’s something that’s very, very personal about it.” Indeed, humor tends to be anti-didactic. You either guffaw or giggle, or you don’t. Alsadir would say that what you find funny or not provides information about your psychic state — what does it say about me that I chuckled sympathetically at Jill Danenberg’s 2024 accordion book Underground Comic, detailing trials and tribulations between veganism and feminism, while my mouth refused to curl for Tony Matelli’s “Veg Man” (2008), a droopily vegetal bronze figure?

The participatory nature of humor means this show is uniquely invested in perception, and in provoking a certain response. As at an open mic, I felt the pressure of bearing witness, aware of my role as an audience member with the power to deem certain works successful or not by producing that ever-elusive involuntary laugh. This semester, O’Connor is teaching an undergraduate class on taking laughter seriously: He tasked his students with making small sculptures, their only instruction to try to be “the funniest in the class.” The winning piece, according to votes cast via smiley-face stickers on a table outside the gallery, is a realistic bust of Professor O’Connor with a No. 2 pencil stuck halfway up his nose. Second place was a reference to a meme O’Connor still doesn’t quite understand.

The oldest featured work in Does This Taste Funny? is Karl Wirsum’s drawing “Untitled (Study for Blue Tattoo)” (1964), featuring a classic Sailor Jerry star design on the tongue of a woman sporting a perfect mid-century housewife hairdo. Getting the reference is important to appreciating a good joke beyond the most base level of someone farting or slipping on a banana peel (which, to get psychoanalytic again, we laugh at to mask our own shame). Brown and O’Connor’s curation is never insidery or niche to the canon, but they are aware of the quality of funniness changing over time.

Some of O’Connor’s students recognized River Phoenix in Ray Johnson’s mail-art collage; more were taken by Jeremy Couillard’s “Escape from Lavender Island” (2023), an open-world video game simulation featuring deep-fried animation aesthetics and relatably tragic dialogue from the depths of neoliberal hell (“While he ate he would watch film classics on an overpriced streaming service and sometimes cry.”)

“Absurdism ends up being pretty timeless,” Brown said. “Using ridiculously absurd materials to make work that doesn’t connect necessarily to a political moment or a socioeconomic issue, it represents this irreverent attitude towards art-making.” And apparently that’s what appeals to Gen Z, who are inundated with visual content, yet perhaps still seeking a response to contemporary life that truly resonates.

Brown, who has been teaching at Lehman for 20 years, wants artists to find their idiosyncratic voice. If being funny comes naturally, maybe that’s the tack they should take.

“There’s such a tendency for imitation out there. You can easily become a version of something that exists, and that is no longer considered a bad thing,” she said. “I'm interested in trying to find, ‘What's your really weird way of approaching that?’”

Take Kristen Mills’s “It IS Cake” (2026), a filmic parody of the Netflix baking contest series Is It Cake? using entirely brown cardboard, displayed in the gallery on a screen within a faux kitchen made of the same plainly bland material. Installed nearby is puppet theater ephemera that does directly respond to a political moment: John Vasquez Mejias’s “The Puerto Rican War” (2026), which expands his novelette about revolutionaries fighting colonialism in 1950. The Puerto Ricans’ demands aren’t funny, but some of the depictions of American incompetence are.

Does This Taste Funny? reminds us of humor as a tool, as a way to frame whatever it is that we hope to communicate. Life is not always joyful, but it should at least be emotional. At Sarah Lawrence, I watched Robert DeJesus’s surreal video “The Survey” (2024), starring a talking Olmec head who speaks only when there are no corroborative witnesses. I didn’t laugh. Later in the day, turning a corner on the grounds of Lehman College, I was suddenly confronted with the stone statue, whose onscreen lips I’d just seen move. I audibly snorted.

issues.title: Arpita Singh, Indian Painter Who Never Stopped Innovating, Dies at 89
issues.summary: In this column honoring those we lost in the art world, we also remember a British painter of bewitching scenes and one of Japan’s greatest manga artists.
issues.author: Lisa Yin Zhang
issues.content_html:
In Memoriam honors those we recently lost in the art world.

Arpita Singh (1937–2026)
Indian painter who bridged fantasy and reality

One of the most high-profile contemporary Indian artists, Singh fused violent realism and fantasy imagery, constantly innovating across a six-decade career. In the 1970s and '80s, for instance, she explored abstraction, producing spare compositions filled with dots and dashes. She became more widely known in the West due to an exhibition at Serpentine Galleries just last year.

"Singh never settles into a mode or style," critic John Yau wrote in a 2017 review of her exhibition at New Delhi- and New York-based Talwar Gallery for this magazine. "This body of work, which is being shown for the first time in America, is a singular achievement."

issues.title: Led by Record-Breaking $190.4 M. van Gogh, Sotheby’s Impressionist and Modern Art Sales Rake in $777.8 M.
issues.summary: The 12-work Blaquier-Arrieta collection brought in $412 million, a record for a single-owner Impressionist-modern sale at the house.
issues.author: Alex Greenberger
issues.content_html:
It was an evening of superlatives at Sotheby’s, whose two auctions of Impressionist and modern art in New York tonight brought in a total of $777.8 million.

That total is the highest one for a single night at the auction house, edging past the $706 million achieved last November at the house’s inaugural evening double-header at the Breuer building. And while the 12 lots from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection came in at $412 million, just shy of their presale low estimate of $414.5 million, those dozen works still managed to set a record for a single-owner evening sale dedicated to Impressionist and modern art at Sotheby’s. (Unless otherwise noted, prices cited here are inclusive of fees.)

Two lots in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection were the most anticipated paintings of the season: Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890) and Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888–90).

They both achieved eye-popping prices—$190.4 million for the van Gogh, the artist’s highest price to date and the highest price for any work of art ever sold at Sotheby’s, and $111 million for the Cézanne, the second-highest price for Cézanne at auction. But the bidding was anticlimactic.

Both works hammered below their pre-sale estimates. There was just a smattering of bids on the van Gogh. The Cézanne inched along with four bids alternating between Sotheby’s specialists Lisa Dennison, Chairman Americas, and Helena Newman, chairman of Sotheby’s Europe. It hammered to Newman.

Asked after the sale whether the publicity surrounding the restitution claim against the van Gogh had affected bidding, Sotheby’s CEO Charles Stewart said he didn’t think so.

“First of all, it’s a record price for the artist,” he said, pointing out that it was also the fourth-highest price achieved by any artist at auction. “I think you have to separate auction heat from auction results,” he said.

The liveliest bidding came for the final two paintings, both of them with estimates on the lower side, for this sale. Edith Eustis and Simon Stark on the phones, as well as several bidders in the room, went for Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec’s Femme assise de profil vers la gauche (1890). It sold to a man in the second row for $3.8 million. Then, Wendy Lin, Serena Hildebrandt, and Alina Davey battled on the phones for the Camille Pissarro landscape, Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875). It came down to Lin and Davey, and went to Davey for $2 million. It was bought by the same bidder who bought Edgar Degas’s Avant la course (ca. 1893) for $18 million a few lots earlier, bidding with Sotheby’s Ben Doller.

Things picked up considerably during the 47-lot, multiple-owner sale that followed, which saw lively bidding in the room and no fewer than 33 Sotheby’s specialists fielding bids over the phones. All told, this sale made $365.8 million, with all but one of the lots sold. It helped that the highest-priced lots came early in the sale and generated heated bidding wars.

The top price from that sale was the $47.3 million for Edward Hopper’s 1944 seascape The Martha Mckeen of Wellfleet, from the collection of Baroness Carmen Thyssen-Bornemisza. It’s far from Hopper’s record—$91.8 million for Chop Suey from the Barney Ebsworth collection at Christie’s in November 2018—but it is his second-highest price at auction. As dealer Lock Kresler pointed out on the Nota Bene podcast, the closest comparison is another Hopper seascape, Blackwell’s Island, from 1928, which sold at Christie’s in 2013 for $19.1 million.

The Martha Mckeen sparked a bidding war between four Sotheby’s specialists on the phone bank, with Scott Niichel, vice chairman and head of middle market for modern and contemporary art, coming out the winner. Accounting for fees, the work made $47.8 million.

Close behind the Hopper was the $45 million achieved by Rene Magritte’s 1964 painting L’Ami de l’ordre, which stars the painter’s famous man in a bowler hat. It came from the collection of Sydell Miller, who bought it in 1998 for a mere $5.3 million. The previous record for a bowler hat paintingwas for the one sold at Christie’s London in March 2024 for £33.7 million (about $43.2 million), Magritte’s third-highest price. Several bidders in the room went up against two Sotheby’s specialists, Jackie Wachter and Bame Fierro March. A bidder in the room was the winner, but no one seemed to be able to identify him.

Also adding sparks early in the sale was Aaron Douglas’s 1931 painting of Harriet Tubman. Even if it had merely sold near its pre-sale estimate of $2.5 million–$3.5 million, the piece would have handily broken the record for Douglas: $600,000, for a piece sold at Swann Galleries auction house in 2008. But it more than quadrupled that estimate to make $14.1 million, all of which will go to Bennett College, a historically Black women’s college, that sold the piece.

Some eight bidders went after the painting, beginning with Jackie Wachter going up against her father, George Wachter, who serves as Sotheby’s chairman of North America and South America. Several bidders in the room popped in before Sotheby’s head of American art Stefany Morris entered the war. In the end, it was Morris versus the room, with Morris the winner.

“We knew it was going to make a big price,” Sotheby’s vice chairman and head of contemporary art David Galperin said after the sale. “That’s one of the most exciting auction moments—when you have something that is so categorically the very best” by an artist whose work rarely comes to auction.

Halfway through the sale came another big moment: a painting by Mary Cassatt, Summertime (1894–95), from the Armand Hammer collection, sold for $13.3 million, a new record that nearly doubles the previous one, $7.5 million. Here the evening’s depth of bidding was again on display: specialists David Galperin, Caroline Seabolt, Lin, and Simon Stock all went after it, but the winner was an online bidder.

On the lower end of the price spectrum, a landscape by Chaim Soutine, Place à Céret (1921–22), estimated at just $800,000–$1.2 million, made $3.9 million. Five Sotheby’s specialists on the phones wanted the picture; so did bidders in the room. Jen Hua, deputy chairman of Sotheby’s Asia, cast the final bid.

Over the course of the evening, Hua and Lin, the Sotheby’s Asia chairman, were especially busy. Asian collectors bought works by Signac, Maurice de Vlaminck, Cézanne, Claude Monet, Renoir, Soutine, Egon Schiele, and Degas (including the Degas in the Blaquier-Arrieta sale for $18 million). They bid on works by Monet (the Blaquier-Arrieta picture that sold for $20.2 million), Picasso, Magritte, Cassatt, and Degas.

The sale was not without hitches. A Remedios Varo drawing failed to sell, and three lots—pieces by Magritte, Cézanne, and Matisse—were apparently withdrawn while the sale was in progress, given that the withdrawals were not announced prior to the sale, as is customary. (Two of the withdrawn lots–Henri Matisse’s La Jetée à Collioure (estimate $5–$7 million), and Paul Cézanne’s L’Oncle Dominique (estimate $3–$5 million)–are among the 11 in the sale that come from the collection of George Weiss, the hedge fund founder now in bankruptcy, as ARTnewsrevealed earlier this month.)

Every one of the Blaquier lots was guaranteed. For Phillip Hoffman, founder and chairman of the Fine Art Group, that brought up a question about Sotheby’s strategy.

“The guarantees were just too high,” he told ARTnews immediately after the Blaquier-Arrieta sale. “I think these guarantees are just pushing the limit.”

He said Sotheby’s had left buyers very little room to compete, and had been too confident in its pricing, with the result a string of lots that attracted little meaningful competition.

Calling it “a little bit of overconfidence” on the house’s part, he speculated that they might have lost as much as $50 million on guarantees.

Stewart, the Sotheby’s CEO, defended the house’s approach to the evening.

“Our estimates weren’t shy,” he acknowledged. “You can read into that whatever you like. We were happy with the result of everything.”

issues.title: A Tiny Monet With a Wild Backstory Just Fetched More Than 20 Times its Estimate at a Christie’s Day Sale
issues.summary: The painting was commissioned by a French dealer, owned by a notorious Paris fraudster, and later acquired by major American collectors of Impressionism.
issues.author: Brian Boucher
issues.content_html:
The auction houses’ marquee evening sales get all the headlines, with high-eight-figure artworks and high-nine-figure totals, sometimes approaching the billion-dollar mark when the market is flush.

But the more modest daytime sales of lower-priced materials occasionally contain real treasures. When I wrote about them for Artnet Newsin 2015, experts told me that this is where the houses make a lot of their profits; dealers haunt these sales to stock up on inventory; they are far less stage-managed than the evening events; they may be more indicative of the actual health of the market; and you can find better deals.

And they can occasionally spark serious bidding wars. On Wednesday, a tiny artwork by a titan of French Impressionism became the latest example.

Claude Monet’s La Barque (ca. 1874), which came under the hammer at Christie’s Rockefeller Center saleroom at a day sale of Impressionist and modern art, was estimated at $300,000 to $500,000, but fetched just shy of $7 million. Its modest estimate matched its diminutive size: it measures only 2¾ by 3½ inches, so it sold for $722,285.71 per square inch.

More than 20 bidders fought for the tiny panel, some in the room and some bidding on the phone via Christie’s specialists, says the house; the contest went on for six minutes and 45 seconds, and Rachel White Young, head of the 20th-century evening sale, won the prize for her client.

Even before making a little auction history on Wednesday, the painting had an unusual backstory.

Paris art dealer Georges Petit, a collector and supporter of the Impressionists, commissioned it from the artist; the magazine L’Art Moderne wrote about it in June 1902, relating how the collector carried around small pieces of wood, cut to identical sizes, which he handed out to artists he admired. He would offer them 100 francs and ask if they would return the petite panel as a painting. He did the same with Camille Corot, Édouard Manet, Camille Pissarro, and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, all of whom obliged.

All five would come into the collection of Thérèse and Frédéric Humbert, notorious figures in French high society. She claimed to have been willed a fortune by an imaginary American millionaire, Robert Crawford, whose life she had supposedly saved. They borrowed against an imaginary fortune, buying a grand home and occupying the center of Parisian social life for two decades, until bank officials started asking questions and her creditors sued and the tissue of lies was shredded.

Funny enough, the resulting sale of their possessions would take place in 1902 at none other than Galerie Georges Petit. Galerie Bernheim-Jeune bought it and it remained with that family until 2013, when the ollectors Marlene and Spencer Hays got it at Paris auction house Hôtel Drouot, for the hammer price of €200,000. They began selling books door-to-door as a summer job for Southwestern Company and later went on to run the busines and start a clothing company.

According to their foundation, when asked what was the most fun part of their lives, they would say, “learning about art and building a collection that we treasure,” but would also quote Sir Richard Attenborough to the effect that art collectors are “simply its temporary, fortunate and delighted custodians.” Their collection included works by Pierre Bonnard, Edgar Degas, Henri Matisse, Amedeo Modigliani, and Édouard Vuillard.

They were as good as their word; they granted their collection to Paris’s Musée d’Orsay in 2016. It was the largest foreign collection donated since World War II, with some 600 masterworks from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He died the next year, survived by Marlene.

issues.title: Cézanne ‘Arlequin’ Sells for $111 M. at Sotheby’s, Becoming One of the Most Expensive Paintings by the Artist
issues.summary: The painting missed beating the artist's auction record, but its sale still received applause.
issues.author: Daniel Cassady
issues.content_html:
Paul Cézanne made his name painting apples and mountains. But on Wednesday night, the artist’s somewhat severe picture of a teenager in costume became one of the most expensive Cézannes ever sold at auction, after selling at Sotheby’s New York for $111 million with fees.

Arlequin (1888–90), a colorful painting of a young man in a red-and-black diamond-patterned costume, hit the block at Sotheby’s during its dedicated evening sale for the Blaquier-Arrieta collection. The painting hammered at $99 million.

It failed to beat the previous record of $137.8 million set by La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888–90), which sold at Christie’s in 2022 as part of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen’s collection. Still, once auctioneer Oliver Barker sold Arlequin tonight, a round of applause followed.

Sotheby’s didn’t publish an estimate for Arlequin prior to the sale, though the painting was expected to bring in around $120 million.

The figure in the painting is Cézanne’s son, Paul, dressed as Harlequin, the mischievous character from Italian commedia dell’arte theater. He wears a pointed hat and an elaborate white collar, and holds a slender baton as he walks across a sharply tilted floor. For someone dressed as a comic character, he looks surprisingly serious.

Cézanne painted the picture in Paris between 1888 and 1890, when he was experimenting with a series of theatrical subjects. There are only four paintings in the group, and Arlequin is the only one still in private hands. The others are in museums, including the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., the Pola Museum of Art in Japan, and the Pushkin Museum in Moscow.

The painting comes with quite a history. It passed through the hands of several of the great dealers of the early modern art market, including Ambroise Vollard and Paul Rosenberg, before become part of Lord Victor Rothschild’s collection during the 1930s. His son, Lord Jacob Rothschild, later inherited it, and in 1975 it was sold through London’s Lefevre Gallery to Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier.

Before leaving for Argentina, the painting appeared in major exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1929, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1952, and the Tate Gallery in London in 1954. After the Blaquiers bought it, it all but disappeared from public view for half a century.

Sotheby’s had guaranteed the painting before Wednesday’s auction, promising the sellers an undisclosed amount regardless of the outcome. It also secured an irrevocable bid, meaning at least one prospective buyer had committed to bidding before the auction began.

Such arrangements are increasingly common at the top of the art market. According to an analysis by the art-market data firm ARTDAI, just 19 guaranteed Cézanne lots make up 63 percent of the hammer-price value in its database of 640 Cézanne sales. In other words, a small number of exceptionally expensive pictures drive much of the artist’s auction business.

The record-setting Cézanne, La Montagne Sainte-Victoire, hammered at $120 million in 2022, more than twice the price achieved by the artist’s next most expensive auction result, a still life that fetched $60.5 million at Sotheby’s in 1999.

Of course, that auction record doesn’t tell the whole story. A version of Cézanne’s The Card Players was reportedly sold privately to Qatar for around $250 million in 2011, a reminder that some of the biggest deals in the art world never reach a public salesroom.

Arlequin was one of 12 paintings offered from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection on Wednesday, alongside Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), which had been expected to fetch around $180 million and ended up selling for $190.4 million.

issues.title: Van Gogh Slashes Auction Record at Sotheby’s, Selling for $190.4 M.
issues.summary: For much of the past week, there was some question whether the sale would happen at all.
issues.author: Daniel Cassady
issues.content_html:
After a week dominated by a Nazi-era restitution dispute, Sotheby’s finally got to sell a $180 million Vincent van Gogh painting on Wednesday night—for more than it bargained for.

Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), a picture of chestnut trees in bloom painted just weeks before the artist’s death, sold for $190.4 million (including fees), setting a new auction record for the Dutch painter. The painting, which carried an undisclosed guarantee, hammered at $165 million against an expectation of around $180 million (pre-sale estimates do not include buyer’s fees).

After the sale, Kelly Crow reported in the Wall Street Journal that dealer William Acquavella was the painting’s buyer, something that ARTnews also independently confirmed.

The fifth item and cover lot for the Blaquier-Arrieta collection sale, which the house had billed as “legendary,” hung behind the rostrum presided over by auctioneer Oliver Barker.

The artist’s previous record of $117.2 million was set at Christie’s in November 2022 when Verger avec cyprès (1888), a landscape from the collection of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen, sold, hammering for $102 million.

Wednesday’s result beats that by $73.2 million, a jump of 62.4 percent in just four years.

The record is certainly a victory for Sotheby’s, which almost wasn’t going to be able to sell Châtaigniers en fleurs. Last Thursday, descendants of Samuel Fischer, the German Jewish publisher who once owned the painting, challenged its sale, arguing that their family had been forced to part with it in Amsterdam in 1936 because of Nazi persecution. Sotheby’s disputed the claim, pointing to archival records showing the painting had sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, around $22,000 at the time, which it considered a fair market price. After several days of talks, the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the Fischer heirs reached an agreement this week, clearing the painting’s title before the sale. The terms weren’t disclosed, so it’s unclear whether the heirs will receive a share of the proceeds.

For a little perspective, van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr. Gachet (1890) fetched $82.5 million at Christie’s in 1990, then the highest price ever paid for a work of art at auction. That remained the artist’s auction record for 32 years, until the Allen sale. Now, just four years later, the ceiling has moved again.

Painted shortly after van Gogh arrived to Auvers-sur-Oise, Châtaigniers en fleurs is one of only roughly 50 landscapes the artist made during his two-month stay their before his death. Of those, the majority belong to museums, while only an estimated eight are still in private hands, according to research cited by the Art Newspaper.

This electric scene, with its thick brushwork, also hadn’t been seen in decades, last being exhibited at the Guggenheim in 1964. The consignors, Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, bought it in 1975 and kept it hidden for half a century. That kind of provenance and scarcity is exactly what fuels the trophy market for works of this caliber.

A record of this size for a Post-Impressionist painting might suggest that the market for this category is roaring back. While the market has certainly improved, the rise in sales of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art by 47 percent in 2025 to $1.8 billion, according to the Art Basel and UBS Art Market Report, is still nearly $1 billion short of its $2.6 billion peak in 2022.

issues.title: Hand-Marbled Papers Ground Sylvain Lefebvre’s Surreal Landscapes
issues.summary: 'Journeys Into the Unseen Forest' embraces the paradox of natural balance. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? The article Hand-Marbled Papers Ground Sylvain Lefebvre’s Surreal Landscapes appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
Enormous trees dominate dreamlike wooded landscapes in the mixed-media paintings of Sylvain Lefebvre. A spectral form with dense, gnarly branches shelters a lounging woman in “The Quercus Corallium,” and a table alive with conversation nests beneath the canopy in “A Debat at Tea Time.”

The French artist’s Journeys Into the Unseen Forest at Rebecca Hossack Art Gallery comprises a series of almost fairytale-like tableaux. Collaged, hand-marbled papers beneath the delicate layers of oil paint represent the barely visible or unknown. And trees group closely in the background darken in the distance, while diminutive figures climb around and relax at the base of monumental trunks.

Summer 2026 marked France’s hottest ever documented since records began, during which rainfall was low and unprecedented wildfires raged. Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, where the effects of the climate crisis are dramatic and impossible to ignore. In Journeys Into the Unseen Forest, Lefebvre delves into an imaginary realm where humans coexist harmoniously with flora and fauna, and old-growth sentinels harbor a wide range of life.

The artist says, “I wanted to put myself in the place of a forest and its trees by asking myself the following question: How is it that when we look at nature, whatever form it takes, it always appears balanced, while the trees that make it up can grow in such unbalanced ways… twisted, diagonally or horizontally, struggling to find their way towards the light?”

In “The Quercus Corallium,” a white tree glows like a sacred spirit, and in “The Polyphane Pachidermus,” one can imagine the canopy extending forever into the blue distance. “In the unseen forest, [Lefebvre] discovers species of trees that have never been seen before,” the gallery says. “They are completely plausible species that may exist somewhere in the few corners of the world that have not yet been discovered. Perhaps they are trees of the future.”

Journey Into the Unseen Forest continues through December 23 in London. See more on Lefebvre’s Instagram.

issues.summary: "2878" envelops a colonial-style building in silver thermal blankets typically used in emergencies. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Vhils and Marcelo Cidade Cloak a São Paulo Colonial Building in Silver Thermal Blankets appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Grace Ebert
issues.content_html:
“A construction can remain standing while losing its place in the everyday experience of the city. Its address remains, but its presence no longer draws attention. In this sense, disappearance can begin before demolition,” says a statement about a recent collaboration between Alexandre Farto (a.k.a. Vhils) and Marcelo Cidade.

The monumental project at Rua Cardeal Arcoverde, 2878 in Pinheiros, São Paulo, is a meditation on this sentiment as it considers how architecture and the seemingly mundane fixtures of city life shape our understanding of a place. Titled “2878,” the site-specific installation envelops a colonial-style building in silver thermal blankets typically used in emergencies. A cornstarch glue binds the utilitarian material to the structure’s facade, revealing the arched windows and ornate patterns in relief.

Both drawing attention to the building and masking its real condition, the metallic blankets prompt questions about how we care for places and spaces. As passersby walk past, the installation mirrors their silhouettes as faint reflections, while the surface’s color and light shift depending on the time of day.

The collaborative intervention also evokes Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s “Wrapped Reichstag” and the early years of Andy Warhol’s Factory, in which silver paint and tin foil covered the walls of the artist’s New York studio. Warhol was interested in transience and the attention that comes with fame, concerns we see echoed and translated into broader conversations about public space, collective memory, and urban life in “2878.”

Find more from Vhils and Cidade on their Instagrams.

issues.title: Meticulously Detailed Animal Portraits by Thomas Cian Pop from the Page
issues.summary: "It has a lot to do with a desire to reconnect with everything that exists independently of human beings," the artist says. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Meticulously Detailed Animal Portraits by Thomas Cian Pop from the Page appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
As if ready to swim right off of the page, Thomas Cian’s fish and other creatures are rendered in exquisite detail. Known for his realistic black-and-white portraits, the artist recently embarked on a series of hyperrealistic animal drawings in gouache and pencil. The new direction took him somewhat by surprise, as he realized one day he had been focusing much more on fauna than he had in years past.

“I think it has a lot to do with a desire to reconnect with everything that exists independently of human beings,” Cian tells Colossal. He felt compelled to get closer to what he describes as elemental raw matter, generated through eons of mysterious and fascinating evolutionary processes. “I think that’s what it comes down to: drawing something that hasn’t itself been designed by someone else.”

Cian’s technical aptitude is obvious, but for him, a work isn’t truly complete unless there’s another kind of investment. “For me, achieving a result I’m truly satisfied with is a considerable challenge because my approach is emotional long before it is descriptive,” he says. Truly understanding and sympathizing with a creature propels the process.

Light also plays an integral role in his deceptively simple monochrome approach: Cian highlights whatever the light touches and leaves everything else alone. A piece feels finished when “areas that remain black stop feeling black,” he says, balancing perception and technicality in equal measure.

The artist spends hours researching a subject before rendering it on paper, watching documentaries and browsing publications that give him a sense of their habitats and behaviors, but he resists working from printed images. Even the textures that, from a distance, may look realistic, are actually intuitive and imagined. “I never copy photographs,” Cian says. “I study the anatomy and then reconstruct it, sometimes exaggerating certain features, in a pose that allows me to feel as though I’m in the presence of that particular creature.”

See more on the artist’s Instagram.

The end of the year is quickly approaching, and you know what that means: gifting season is here.

Like clockwork, we’re back with a carefully curated, handy dandy gift guide to help you pick out the perfect presents for each name on your list. Organized by passions and personalities, our list has something special for everyone. So sit back, brew a cup of tea, and get scrolling! You’re about to have the breeziest holiday shopping yet.

As always, thank you for supporting Colossal.

For the Creative Professional

Visual thinkers understand the absolute joy of impeccably designed things. Treat the creative in your life to studio essentials that make the workday lighter and intriguing reads to keep the ideas flowing.

For the Maximalist

More is more! If bold colors, clashing patterns, and whimsical graphics are that special someone’s vibe, we’ve got the perfect accessories to complete their closet.

For the Nature Lover

We all know someone who feels the happiest among flora, fauna, and the great outdoors. Bring a bit of nature to them with a new pair of gardening gloves, fungi-inspired decor and puzzles, a guide to foraging for handmade inks, and plenty more.

For the Tasteful Host

Those with great taste often have a cozy home to match. Help your favorite host make their space even warmer with aesthetically-pleasing objects for cooking, gathering, and lingering just a bit longer.

For the Serial Hobbyist

Our exciting range of craft kits open up a world of possibilities for those who never seem to get tired of trying new hobbies. From hand loom weaving and embroidery to pressing flowers and growing herbs, there’s something new to try for everyone.

For the Budding Artist

What’s more important than encouraging those just beginning to explore their creative side? Surprise that little one with a big imagination with specially-crafted wooden toys, beautiful books, unique crayons, and beyond.

issues.title: Record-breaking $85.8 million Kandinsky leads Christie's November 2026 New York evening sale.
issues.summary: Russian painter Wassily Kandinsky ’s Betonte Ecken (Accentuated Corners) (1922–23), sold for $85.8 million with fees at Christie’s 20th-century evening sale in New York on November 17th, setting a new auction record for the artist. Bidding opened at $54 million, a price already about $10 million above Kandinsky's previous auction record of $44.8 million, set by Murnau mit Kirche II (1910) at Sothe
issues.author: Artsy Editorial
issues.content_html:
Russian painter Wassily Kandinsky’s Betonte Ecken(Accentuated Corners) (1922–23), sold for $85.8 million with fees at Christie’s 20th-century evening sale in New York on November 17th, setting a new auction record for the artist.

Bidding opened at $54 million, a price already about $10 million above Kandinsky's previous auction record of $44.8 million, set by Murnau mit Kirche II (1910) at Sotheby’s in 2023. Three bidders competed for the work, including art advisor Ralph DeLuca. Ultimately, Christie’s global president Alex Rotter won the painting for an anonymous client at a hammer price of $74 million.

The painting, estimated at $60 million to $80 million and backed by a third-party guarantee, was consigned by the Nahmad family, which purchased it at Sotheby's New York in 1986 for a hammer price of $1 million.

The nearly four-foot-square abstract composition, painted during Kandinsky’s early Bauhaus years, has a storied provenance. It was acquired in 1929 by Hilla Rebay, who became the Guggenheim Museum’s first director. She gave it to the museum in 1941. The Guggenheim deaccessioned it, along with dozens of other Kandinskys, at Sotheby’s in London in 1964. There it was sold to New York dealer Stephen Hahn before passing to Boston collectors Sandra and David Bakalar and then to the Nahmads.

The other star lot of auction night was Gustav Klimt’s Litzlbergkeller (1915–16), which sold for $82.3 million. It came into the sale as the highest-estimated lot of the evening. Together, the Kandinsky and the Klimt accounted for nearly 27 percent of the sale’s total of $626.6 million ($521 million at the hammer). The evening auction closed at the low end of its $511 million to $743 million estimate range. The sale itself was uneven and selective. Other lots included a group of seven small Jackson Pollock paintings, a 1915 Amedeo Modigliani portrait, and a Léger canvas, all of which went unsold. An 11-foot bronze horse by Fernando Botero, meanwhile, set an artist record at $5.2 million.

Kandinsky has had a strong year at auction. Born in Moscow in 1866, Kandinsky helped found the Blaue Reiter group, taught at the Bauhaus in Germany, and later had dozens of his works seized by the Nazis as “degenerate art” before he died in France in 1944. Earlier this October, Christie’s London sold the artist’s 1907 painting Das bunte Leben for £31,560,000 ($41.5 million).

issues.title: 5 Artworks We’d Gift Ourselves this Holiday Season
issues.summary: Shopping for an art lover is hard. Shopping for yourself is harder: Even if you’ve been saving and wishlisting all year, it’s easy to be overwhelmed. So we sorted our holiday gift list by collector type. Meet the Tiny Treasure Hunter , the Analog Enthusiast , the Dopamine Decorator , the Surrealist at Heart , and the Plant Parent : five collections for five art lover identities. Then we asked our
issues.author: Artsy Editorial
issues.content_html:
Shopping for an art lover is hard. Shopping for yourself is harder: Even if you’ve been saving and wishlisting all year, it’s easy to be overwhelmed.

So we sorted our holiday gift list by collector type. Meet the Tiny Treasure Hunter, the Analog Enthusiast, the Dopamine Decorator, the Surrealist at Heart, and the Plant Parent: five collections for five art lover identities. Then we asked our team to pick one work from each that they’d gladly give, or keep for themselves. Here’s what they chose.

Marlon de Azambuja, Mundo, 2025

Instituto de Visión

Price: $1,500

From: The Tiny Treasure Hunter

Mundo, 2025
Marlon de Azambuja
Instituto de Visión

I’ve always loved tiny things, from dollhouse furniture to small dogs, so The Tiny Treasure Hunter is very much a collecting identity that resonates (and full disclosure, I helped curate it). It’s full of gems, like a beach scene painted on a slice of toast and a little gold ceramic alien who looks like E.T. But at the top of my wish list is Mundo (2025), a thumbprint-sized snail shell by Spanish Brazilian artist Marlon de Azambuja.

It’s made of concrete, the pale gray stuff of smooth sidewalks, yet it looks delicate and organic. The sculpture was recently featured in “Light Field,” de Azambuja’s fall exhibition at Instituto de Visión in New York, which explored how small interventions can transform our perception of space. Mundo does just that: At just over an inch and a half tall, it hangs on the wall like a tiny talisman, as if resting before slithering off.

I love shells of all sorts but snails bring me back to childhood—they’d emerge after it rained and we’d go looking for them to collect them. “Mundo” of course means “world,” and so I’m also reminded that snails appear in creation myths across cultures, symbols of renewal and the cycle of life. I love how this tiny sculpture can hold an entire world of meaning and still it’s just such a delight.

—Casey Lesser, director of editorial and content


Herman Leonard, Louis Armstrong, Paris, 1960

Ellen Miller Gallery

Price: $5,000

From: The Analog Enthusiast

Louis Armstrong, Paris, 1960
Herman Leonard
Ellen Miller Gallery

There’s something quite wonderful about seeing Louis Armstrong like this. Not on stage, trumpet raised, nor posing with that signature warm smile, but sitting quietly, a hand resting on his instrument, seemingly lost in thought. I was actually listening to Armstrong’s 1957 album Under the Stars recently, and was reminded how his music can make even an ordinary evening feel magical.

Herman Leonard—who was to jazz photography what Mick Rock was to ’70s rock—took this photograph backstage at the Olympia Theatre in Paris in 1960. Armstrong was in the city performing and filming Paris Blues, which also starred Sidney Poitier, Paul Newman, and Duke Ellington (worth a watch!). I love that it captures a rare moment of pause in the life of someone whose music and energy brought so much joy to the world.

We see the man behind that magic. There’s a warmth to it, despite the black and white, and something deeply human about seeing him in this unguarded moment.

I’d hang it near a record player, or somewhere to unwind with a drink and some good music. For the music lover in your life, it makes a personal and timeless gift.

—Arun Kakar, senior art market editor


Patrick Hughes, Dancing, 2017

Flowers

Price: £600 ($789)

From: The Dopamine Decorator

Dancing, 2017
Patrick Hughes
Flowers

One of my most-played songs of 2025 was Robyn’s dancefloor banger named after the thrill hormone dopamine, so this collection really speaks to my need for a little visual joy. That also applies to the art that surrounds me. Whether it’s Sarah Morris’s massive neon print with a message or a cartoon-quoting aluminum wall sculpture by Andreas Stylianou, it’s hard not to be drawn to works that immediately lift you up and send you on a high.

Patrick Hughes’s “Rainbows” series is all about that high: in screenprints and paintings he rearranges the typical colorful arc from its spot on the horizon into unlikely scenarios. When a rainbow appears, after all, it brings an immediate hit of dopamine, both in the spontaneity of a one-off moment, and the optical pleasure of every color transitioning into a new one. In Dancing (2017), Hughes repurposes two rainbows as legs against a shocking blue sky, with a shiny red high-heel pump on the end of each. I love how they seem to saunter across the cloudless background, sassy and glamorous.

—Josie Thaddeus-Johns, editor in chief


Johanna Seidel, Sweetwater (II), 2026

Galerie Laetitia Gorsy

€3,900 ($4277)

From: The Surrealist at Heart

Sweetwater ( II ), 2026
Johanna Seidel
Galerie Laetitia Gorsy

The end of the year always takes on a strange dimension, with the days blending together into a blur and waves of the year’s memories flooding back to mind. During these long nights of winter, the magical possibilities of talking animals or women floating through the skies don’t seem so farfetched. This collection of Surrealist-inspired artworks taps into my end-of-year reverie in just the right way. From the chimerical, whimsical beasts of French artist Jacques Merle to a delightfully comical snake-like lady by Lebanese artist Annie Kurkdjian, there are more than a handful of works in the collection that I’ve been pining over.

But it’s German artist Johanna Seidel’s Sweetwater (II) (2026) that I kept returning to, with its uncanny depiction of a brown-haired girl submerged up to her neck in water, ringlets of hair haloing around her, and a swan swimming behind her. The sky is a wash of wild pinks and purples of dawn or dusk. The painting is in keeping with Seidel’s hazy, poetic imagery which draws from history, mythology, and dreams. Here, she references the myth of Leda and the Swan, as well as John Everett Millais’s famed painting Ophelia (1851–52), the tragic heroine of Shakespeare’s Hamlet. Sweetwater (II) is both beautiful and dreamy, but also a deeply uncertain image. Is the swan a friend or foe? In that sense, I think the painting captures some of my own amorphous hopes and anxieties as we head into a new year.

—Katie White, senior staff writer

Nourhan Tchelebi, Bouquet de tulipes jaunes, 2026

L’Original

Price: $445

From: The Plant Parent

Bouquet de tulipes jaunes, 2026
Nourhan Tchelebi
L'Original

During the pandemic, while many people were baking focaccia and sourdough, I picked up a different domestic hobby: raising plants. I’d buy them online and have them shipped across the country so I could nurse them back to health on my windowsill. That changed when I adopted my cat, Martini, who quickly decided he was also interested in gardening and began digging up all of my succulents. No more plant adoptions for me.

Now, to bring plants into my home, I have to get creative. This collection reminded me of all the ways I can add shades of green, bright botanicals, and dappled light back into my life. My favorite work from the bunch is Bouquet de tulipes jaunes (2026) by Nourhan Tchelebi. I love the shape of the work (no need to find a frame!), which is bold and clean, contrasting the hazy strokes and soft outlines of the tulips themselves. The colors also stand out—plants are never just green, and the blend of blues, greens, and yellows in the leaves and the backgrounds makes this bunch feel particularly alive. I’m also drawn to the happy, oversized heads of the tulips themselves, forever at full bloom. I’d put this piece by my windowsill (bright indirect light is best, I hear) to mark the start of a new collection of plants that never need to be watered (and can’t poison my cat).

—Sydney Gelman, copywriter

issues.author: Arun Kakar
issues.content_html:
The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (MFA Boston), will present “Taylor Swift: The Eras Collection” from April 10 through August 15, 2027, marking the institution’s first exhibition dedicated to a musician. Featuring more than 50 costumes, instruments, and objects from the pop star’s personal archive, the exhibition will trace two decades of Swift’s career through 12 vignettes, each dedicated to a different musical era. The MFA will be the only venue for this exhibition.

Highlights will include several costumes from Swift’s record-breaking Eras Tour of 2023–24, including a custom red Alberta Ferretti gown worn during the “Folklore” and “Evermore” sets, a bejeweled bodysuit designed by Zuhair Murad, and a tinsel fringe jacket worn during the tour’s “Karma” finale.

Other objects on view will include a Victorian-inspired dress and typewriter from the music video for “Fortnight,” displayed beneath an installation of swirling paper. Musical instruments will include a Deering banjo from the “Speak Now” world tour, a green Gibson acoustic guitar from the “Reputation” stadium tour, and a gilded pink-and-gold piano shell used during Swift’s performance at the 2019 American Music Awards.

“This is the first exhibition in the MFA’s history devoted to a musician, and we’re thrilled to invite visitors for an up-close look at the fashion and instruments of one of the most influential cultural figures of our time,” said Kristen Hoskins, the museum’s director of public programs.

The exhibition will explore Swift’s evolving approach to songwriting, performance, and visual storytelling, beginning with her 2006 debut single “Tim McGraw” and concluding with “The Fate of Ophelia” from her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl.

Tickets, priced at $40 including museum admission, will go on sale to the public on December 13th, Swift’s birthday, at 6 p.m. MFA members can reserve tickets ahead of the public sale.

issues.title: Artists Nieves González, Addie Wagenknecht, and Slawn behind Grammy-nominated album covers.
issues.summary: Artists Nieves González , Addie Wagenknecht , and Slawn are the creative forces behind three of the nominations for Best Album Cover at the 69th Grammy Awards. González is nominated alongside stylist Leith Clark for Lily Allen's West End Girl . Wagenknecht shares a nomination with musician Nick Steinhardt for Interpol's This Mirror Weighs a Ton . The cover of 21 Savage's WHAT HAPPENED TO THE STREE
issues.author: Katie White
issues.content_html:
Artists Nieves González, Addie Wagenknecht, and Slawn are the creative forces behind three of the nominations for Best Album Cover at the 69th Grammy Awards.

González is nominated alongside stylist Leith Clark for Lily Allen's West End Girl. Wagenknecht shares a nomination with musician Nick Steinhardt for Interpol's This Mirror Weighs a Ton. The cover of 21 Savage's WHAT HAPPENED TO THE STREETS?, credited to art director Tina Ibañez, also features a painted portrait by Slawn. The category’s other nominees include Rapsody’s God Gotta Afro and Gold Hoops and Mavis Staples’s Sad and Beautiful World.

González, a Spanish painter born in 1996 and based in Granada, works within the tradition of Spanish Baroque masters like Jusepe de Ribera and Francisco de Zurbarán, often depicting women in voluminous puffer jackets that she has described as treating “almost as if it were sculptural.” The West End Girl commission shows Allen in a periwinkle Miu Miu puffer and Valentino boots.

“It seems to me the portrait reflects so many facets of the album—strength, power, vulnerability, determination, and confusion,” Allen has said of the painting, which is now on view at London's National Portrait Gallery. González has since opened “Sacred Hair,” a solo show on Mary Magdalene at Rome's T293 gallery, and will mount her first institutional solo exhibition in November 2027 at Contemporary Gallery Kunming in China.

Wagenknecht, born in 1981 in Portland, Oregon, blends conceptual art, gestural abstraction, and computer hacking into her practice. She was an early adopter of drones as a painting tool in the 2000s. Her past work includes Believe me, a 2017 commission for the Whitney Museum of American Art's artport that layered cracked-screen imagery over political and internet-vernacular images. She has also collaborated with CERN, Chanel, Coinbase, and Google's Art Machine Intelligence group.

Slawn, born Olaolu Akeredolu-Ale in Lagos in 2000, moved to London in 2018 to study graphic design before turning to painting during lockdown. His style mixes graffiti and street art with influences from pop art and Abstract Expressionism. He designed the Britannia statuette for the 2023 BRIT Awards, becoming the youngest and first Nigerian-born artist to do so, and later designed the 2024 F.A. Cup Trophy. His album cover for WHAT HAPPENED TO THE STREETS? was inspired by artist Kerry James Marshall’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Shadow of His Former Self (1980) and included the addition of Slawn’s signature tattoos. It was issued with several numbered alternate covers also made by the artist. At Art Basel Miami Beach 2025, Slawn debuted a large-scale inflatable balloon, inspired by the album cover, in promotion of the album.

Slawn is represented by Saatchi Yates, where he opened his first major London solo show in 2024 and, this past July, his largest exhibition to date, a Nike- and Team Nigeria-themed pop-up in New York.

Winners will be announced at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards ceremony on Sunday, February 7, 2027.
