issues.title: They migrated to New York for work. Now they’re fighting to climate-proof it.
issues.summary: The worse the weather gets, the more delivery riders work. Can they teach the city how to adapt against climate-fueled disasters?
issues.author: Frida Garza
issues.content_html:
Earlier this year, riding his e-bike through New York City’s bustling streets on a sweltering July afternoon, José Yos began to smell smoke. It wasn’t coming from a nearby burning building or a beat-up yellow cab. Instead, the smell came from hundreds of miles away in Canada. Raging wildfires in Quebec had sent a cloud of thick, smoky air toward the city, blanketing it in a strange orange haze.

It wasn’t the first time Yos, a 40-year-old from Guatemala who delivers food and groceries on apps like DoorDash, had experienced this. In 2023, Canada had its worst wildfire season on record, with around 37 million acres (15 million hectares) of land going up in flames. Wildfire smoke traveled down from Quebec to New York, polluting the air and turning the skies a deep shade of orange. This summer, though, the city was also in the middle of a heat emergency — its second in as many weeks. The temperature was projected to reach close to 100 degrees Fahrenheit that day, and the heat index — the day’s real feel temperature — was supposed to be even higher.

In response to the extreme weather double whammy, the city had sent cooling vans around the city, opened additional cooling centers and urged New Yorkers to stay home, ideally in air conditioning. But Yos was on the clock. He couldn’t afford to go home or take a real break. He had reserved his hours on Uber Eats a week in advance and was worried that if he took longer than usual to fulfill orders, his in-app rating would go down, putting him at risk of being deactivated.

Before the enactment of the city’s deactivation protection bill in January 2026, a worker could be deactivated from an app without cause and with little recourse. Now, the apps are required to give 72 hours’ notice before deactivating a worker’s account, and workers have the right for the deactivation to be investigated. Still, workers don’t want to risk going through the hassle of a deactivation if they can avoid it. Even with the new law in place, dozens of workers visit the Brooklyn offices of Worker’s Justice Project, an advocacy group for low-wage immigrant workers, every day seeking help with reopening their accounts.

Too much was at stake. So, undeterred by the smoke, Yos pulled his balaclava over his nose and mouth and kept riding.

Yos is one of tens of thousands of app-based delivery workers in New York City, many of whom say that, regardless of the extreme weather conditions outside, they have no choice but to work.

“Everything that happens with the weather affects us in two ways,” said Yos in Spanish. “First, it puts our health and safety at risk. And second, it puts our livelihoods on the line.”

Most delivery workers in New York City ride two wheels — e-bikes or e-scooters — instead of cars, allowing them to mostly avoid traffic jams and cut down on delivery times. But working outside takes a physical toll on the body. Exposure to extreme heat, for example, can lead to dehydration, dizziness, nausea, heat stroke, and heart failure; heavy rainfall can lower visibility for both car drivers and cyclists, creating dangerous conditions on the road. The delivery apps don’t take any of this into consideration, said Yos.

“They don’t care, and they don’t give us extra time to pick up and drop off orders,” said Yos. “When it’s bad outside, we can’t hurry as well, and that in turn lowers our ratings.”

Resources for deliveristas

Do you work for a delivery app service in New York City? Read these guides by Documented that offer best practices for biking in dangerous conditions — from navigating icy roads to reckless drivers — and outline your legal rights and protections regardless of your immigration status.

Know Your Rights as an NYC Deliverista

How NYC Delivery Workers Can Stay Safe During Rain and Snow

Injured By a Car During a Bike Delivery? What NYC Immigrants Need to Know About Getting Help

1 of 1

Of the roughly 70,000 delivery workers across the five boroughs, many hail from Latin America, with a growing number being migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, all regions of the world facing the brunt of climate change. Many factors contributed to Yos’ decision to move from rural Guatemala to New York City, but part of it was that his family could no longer reliably depend on farming as a source of income due to unpredictable rainfall. In recent years, Guatemala has suffered from both droughts and flooding events, which have suppressed crop yields; researchers have linked this volatility to climate change in addition to El Niño weather patterns.

Now in New York City, Yos struggles with different extreme weather impacts. But as members of the so-called gig economy, Yos and other delivery workers are considered self-employed freelancers and lack adequate health and safety protections on the job.

Building on the recent successes of including gig workers in the broader labor movement, Los Deliveristas Unidos, a labor union representing delivery workers, is on a mission to make city officials aware of delivery workers’ needs on the road. As this is happening, the impacts of climate change are also making their work increasingly dangerous.

“During heat waves, snowstorms, floods, and wildfire smoke events, they continue delivering essential goods — including water, medication, and groceries — to help people stay safe,” said Ligia Guallpa, executive director of the Worker’s Justice Project, which helps run Los Deliveristas Unidos. “In many ways, delivery workers serve as essential responders during emergencies,” she added.

It’s one thing to acknowledge the critical role delivery workers play in the convenience economy of major cities like New York. It’s quite another to see delivery workers as experts with firsthand knowledge of how extreme weather collides with New York City’s infrastructure. Back home in Chimaltenango, Guatemala, Yos worked from a young age growing produce with his family to make ends meet. Now, at the other extreme of the food supply chain, he’s seen how extreme weather throws another wrench into how we eat today. The challenges Yos and his cohort face, like dangerous heat during the summer, flash flooding, and slippery roads with poor visibility during storms, will ultimately impact most New Yorkers, too.

Before the proliferation of app-based delivery companies in the mid-2010s, most delivery workers in New York City were employed directly by restaurants. Customers would place their food orders by phone, and the restaurant would dispatch a delivery worker straight to their door, assuming it was within a specific delivery range. But during the pandemic, delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats exploded in popularity, with spending via food delivery apps at quick-service restaurants tripling from about $400 million in December 2019 to $1.4 billion by 2022. Third-party delivery spending nearly quadrupled at full-service restaurants over that period, from about $100 million to about $400 million.

As New Yorkers endured the lockdowns, they grew reliant on food and grocery deliveries. Working the streets while most people hunkered down inside, delivery workers Gustavo Ajche and William Medin began to see how essential they were, and began to feel unappreciated by the delivery apps that provided no healthcare or workers’ compensation. That’s when they decided to organize.

In their early days, members of Los Deliveristas Unidos focused on protecting themselves from robbery rings targeting their e-bikes, which delivery workers often call their “tools” and cost around $2,000. Soon, the labor union’s work grew deeper in scope, focusing on a different kind of theft: the companies allegedly stealing their wages.

In 2018, the mobile delivery app industry was valued at $25.7 billion. Today, the market is worth $428.2 billion. With the expansion of the industry came a radical transformation in the city’s streetscape and labor force, which now includes some 20,000 more workers than before the pandemic. As app-based delivery companies disrupted the industry, seeing a surge in revenue, the immigrant workers who made up the backbone of the industry felt left behind.

All the while, Los Deliveristas grew into a formidable political force of nearly 15,000 active members, with reach in both City Hall and the state capital. In 2021, delivery workers won a historic, first-in-the-nation minimum wage law for app-based delivery workers. Before the law, delivery workers were paid well below the federal minimum wage rate of $5.39 per hour before tips. Now, workers often make at least $19.56 per hour before tips.

In 2021, Los Deliveristas also won the right to use restaurant bathrooms and to tiptransparency. In 2024, Mayor Eric Adams, who delivery workers once considered an ally, turned on them by proposing a law that would require them to be licensed by the city. Advocates like Worker’s Justice Project feared it would open the door to greater criminalization, and the union was able to push back. It was also able to win a slew of new labor protections that took effect this year.

Still, delivery work has been classified as one of the most dangerous jobs in the city, in part because workers report they cannot take breaks or slow down during bad weather conditions. The risks to their personal safety have grown as climate change drivesheavier rainfall and warmer days in the region. This summer was the wettest summer in five years, with a whopping 16.92 inches of precipitation recorded from June to August, according to the National Weather Service. Just under half — or about 40 percent — of the days in that period were wet. When it does pour, the city’s pain points become abundantly clear. Subways leak, storm drains get clogged with trash, and streets flood.

During the early days of the pandemic, Ajche said he and his fellow bikers had to search high and low for a place to take a break from the weather. He got the idea to convert unused newsstands throughout the city into rest areas.

Later in 2020, the idea became closer to a reality. On October 13, 2020, Senator Chuck Schumer biked through the empty streets of Manhattan alongside Ajche, who pitched him the idea. Schumer and Adams threw their weight behind the idea two years later, in 2022, announcing $1 million in city and federal funding for the project.

“Part of our goal is how the city of New York can bring in deliveristas as part of the conversation on city planning or emergency response,” said Guallpa.

By the time Adams’ term was up in 2025, the newsstand-to-delivery-worker-hub conversion had yet to begin. Upon taking office this year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani made it a goal to open the first deliverista hub within his first 100 days. Design and engineering teams got to work, condensing a process that would normally take two years into a couple of months. In April, the first delivery-worker hub officially opened, with much fanfare. But the results of the shortened construction timeline were obvious: The hub didn’t have electricity on opening day. Plans for a second hub in the Upper West Side also stalled after fierce community pushback.

Due to workers’ organizing efforts, the apps have taken steps to make delivery work safer. Although Uber Eats did not wish to comment for this story, they did point to their partnership with the Governors Highway Safety Association in developing a bike safety checklist for delivery workers, which provides tips on key safety issues such as helmet protection, following traffic laws, and staying visible. Uber Eats also now provides workers with safety gear like helmets and yellow safety vests. Uber is required by city law to provide safety equipment and educational materials to delivery workers.

GrubHub also declined to comment for this story, instead referring to its website for information regarding its worker safety policies.

Samantha Ramirez, Policy Communications Manager at DoorDash, says that the company has taken steps to protect its delivery workers from extreme weather by developing a Severe Weather Protocol. DoorDash closely monitors weather changes and issues proactive warnings and safety guidance to workers, merchants, and customers. In extreme weather conditions, the company will even temporarily suspend all operations if needed.

“We also send reminders to Dashers on how to stay safe in cases where it’s hotter or colder outside than normal, or if there’s exceptionally bad air quality,” Ramirez said in a statement. “We encourage anyone experiencing severe weather conditions to follow guidance from local authorities, take the right precautions, and prioritize their safety.”

Despite the mixed results, Guallpa and Los Deliveristas Unidos want the city to include the delivery workforce in its climate adaptation plans.

“We need policies that reflect the realities delivery workers face, including safe working conditions, hazard pay, and meaningful protections that allow them to prioritize their health and safety without risking their livelihoods,” she said. “Delivery workers must have a seat at the table as our cities prepare for and respond to the climate crisis.”

In response to a request for comment, Deputy Press Secretary for the Mayor’s Office Jeremy Edwards said, “Mayor Mamdani knows that delivery workers keep this city running,” and that City Hall knows “that these workers have no choice but to brave the elements.” He added that the administration is committed to protecting all New Yorkers — including delivery workers — from extreme weather, and would keep working with Worker’s Justice Project to do so.

One of the ways that Guallpa hopes the city can improve conditions for delivery workers is by holding the apps accountable for worker safety. Earlier this month, New York City Council Member Harvey Epstein introduced a bill that would force the delivery apps to provide workers with bathroom access, rest stops, e-bike charging stations, and bike storage facilities.

“I support delivery workers’ right to make deliveries in our neighborhood, and delivery app platforms must be held accountable for the hazardous working conditions that impact both deliveristas and our neighborhoods,” said Epstein in a statement.

Read Next New York City unveils its first rest stop for delivery workers Frida Garza

Both in their home countries and in New York City, climate change has quietly shaped the lives of workers like José Yos. But whether or not they should be classified as climate migrants is a complicated question. According to Erica Bower, who leads research on climate displacement at the international NGO Human Rights Watch, in order to be considered a climate migrant, individuals must have relocated as a direct response to environmental factors like a natural disaster — and those factors must have been made more likely or more intense because of climate change. But it’s often difficult to prove climate change is a driver of a particular extreme weather event — and it’s also tricky to pinpoint any one individual’s reasons for leaving home. As a result, Bower argues that the terms “climate migrant” and “climate refugee” should be used sparingly. Workers like Yos are more accurately described as labor migrants, Bower and others say, because they left their homes in search of better economic opportunities.

Migrants themselves may not even bring up climate volatility or natural disasters when asked about their reasons for leaving. There are likely many reasons for this: Researchers have hypothesized that environmental factors may reasonably be less front-of-mind as an immediate threat for someone seeking to escape poverty. But in an age of global warming, even migrants who are primarily searching for better economic conditions can have all sorts of stories regarding how a shifting climate uprooted their quality of life back home. Whether or not they share those accounts when asked about their reasons for moving often depends on how the question is phrased, said Lawrence Huang, a researcher focused on climate change and migration at the Migration Policy Institute.

For example, when the Mixed Migration Centre, a research hub under the Danish Refugee Council, asked West and Central African migrants to list the reasons why they moved away, fewer than 5 percent across regions and genders “spontaneously” mentioned environmental factors. But when prompted to think specifically about the role that natural disasters and other environmental challenges played in their journeys, respondents’ stories changed.

Roughly 30 to 40 percent then said environmental risks were related to the economic drivers of their migration. On average, another 14 percent said environmental factors directly impacted their living conditions at home, and 12 percent said environmental factors made them see how making a living there would be difficult in the long run.

Rather than standing alone as a motivation for migration, extreme weather conditions act as a “stress multiplier,” authors of the Mixed Migration Centre briefing paper wrote.

Speaking to delivery workers in New York City sheds light on how rising temperatures and other climate impacts add to the pressure to leave home.

Growing up in Nepal, Hari Sharan Tripathi worked on his family farm in Pokhara, tending orange trees. The groves had long been a steady source of income, but that changed when they started to yield less and less fruit.

“Those orange trees used to be grown by my grandfather and great-grandfather,” Tripathi said in Nepali. “We used to make money from selling those oranges, and our neighbors as well.”

Rising global temperatures are partly to blame.

As a child, Tripathi would stare at the snow-capped peak of Mount Machhapuchhre reflected in the clear waters of Phewa Lake. But before leaving his hometown, he looked back at the reflection once more.

“The snow started receding, and you could hardly see snow on the bases of mountains,” Tripathi, now 35, said. “Then there used to be some days where you couldn’t see snow in the mountains at all.”

Read Next This Sicilian community has endured for centuries. Can it survive a changing climate? Stefania D’Ignoti

Nepal is ranked fourth among the most vulnerable countries to the effects of global warming. In August, when thousands died and went missing because of catastrophic flash floods, scientists pointed to the glacier melt on mountains like Mount Machhapuchhre as a contributing factor. And climate impacts like unpredictable rainfall, which contribute to declines in agricultural productivity, have helped fuel an outward migration of people like Tripathi seeking better economic opportunities.

In the Big Apple, Tripathi, who is a member of another delivery worker advocacy organization called Justice for App Workers, continues to struggle with the effects of global climate change. With the city’s weather becoming more volatile due to climate change, as a delivery worker for Uber Eats, he routinely battles all manner of extreme weather, including heavy rainfall and flash flooding made worse by climate change. He’s also struggled to adapt to New York City’s cold winters, and particularly had issues on the road with snow and ice.

“I have fallen off my bike multiple times during snowy weather,” he said. “I didn’t know a bike could skid off the road because of black ice. I didn’t know anything about black ice.”

The city makes an effort to reach all New Yorkers with critical communication about extreme cold weather, sending alerts about snow, ice, and changing weather conditions in 14 languages, including English, Arabic, Chinese, Spanish, and Bengali. And this month, City Hall announced it would spend $25 million on upgrading its emergency weather protocol for freezing overnight temperatures known as Code Blue. The city’s Department of Transportation has also spent $2 million on new small snow-clearing equipment to help keep bike lanes clear of snow and ice.

The question of whether workers like Tripathi and Yos count as climate migrants carries with it real-life ramifications. For example, in recent years, New York City Council members have proposed creatinga climate migration services coordinator, or someone who helps the city both identify climate-displaced newcomers and connect them with social services. These bills haven’t gone anywhere, but they’re an example of how the city could do outreach to vulnerable populations on a warming planet.

Meanwhile, for the migrant delivery workers already here, the rain has become a particular problem.

Being a coastal city, New York is exposed to many types of flooding — but climate change has increased the risk of pluvial flooding, where rainfall exceeds what an area’s sewer or drainage system can handle. That can happen due to cloudbursts — large downpours of rain that start and stop abruptly, in a relatively short amount of time — and can result in flash flooding at the street level.

Earlier this year, City Hall and the New York City Department of Environmental Protection invested $108 million in upgrading the city’s sewer system — specifically catch basins, or the street-level storm drains that lead to the sewers. Making sure that rainwater can flow freely through the streets and into the sewer network — and not start to pool around a clogged catch basin — would greatly improve street safety, said Yos.

But heavy rainfall still presents other risks to cyclists on the road, such as low visibility.

Saliou Ndiaye, a 26-year-old Senegalese delivery worker, has also had to contend with the weather. In 2022, while making a delivery, Ndiaye was hit by a car during a rainstorm because the driver was unable to see him, he said.

“I tried to avoid it. I did everything I could, but he hit me,” he said. “I flew in the air and was rolling.”

He broke his leg and was unable to work for nearly a year until he recovered. “I was scared, you know,” he said. “When you see your leg broken, it’s scary. You freak out.”

Ndiaye said the weather also shaped his life in Thiès, Senegal’s third-largest city, his hometown. Senegal’s rainy season typically lasts between May and September, but with climate change affecting the seasonal pattern, storms are increasingly occurring during the dry season. Flooding in particular has gotten worse. The country’s most severe flood ever occurred in 2024, leaving thousands homeless.

“It’s worse because every time it rains, the whole day is raining, and there will be floods,” said Ndiaye. “You know, people’s homes are filled with water.”

Mansour Thioye, a 37-year-old Senegalese delivery worker, said in his hometown of Kaolack, flooding has become a routine part of life.

“When it’s raining, it’s very bad to live there,” said Thioye, who returns home regularly. He noted that sometimes families will take shelter in schools for months because of flood damage to their homes. “They use the classrooms to live because they don’t have anywhere to go.”

Thioye said that in New York, where he has now lived for 15 years and raised his family of four children, rain has also been a force to contend with as a delivery worker.

“When it’s raining, it’s so bad,” he said. “The drivers here, they don’t pay attention to when their car door is open, and we can crash into the door. That’s happened to me two times.”

How cities and states in the U.S. adapt to climate change — and prepare for any influx of climate migrants — is playing out in real time. Last year, Illinois passed a first-of-its-kind climate migration law, which was meant to kick off the creation of a task force that would study how incoming climate migrants might test the state’s infrastructure. But a year later, only one seat on the task force had been filled. (A second person was appointed to the task force after Grist reached out for comment earlier this year.)

It’s obvious that there is much that local and state governments around the country can do to anticipate what a warmer future might bring, even in terms of population changes. In New York City and elsewhere, elected officials could learn from listening directly to migrants themselves about what their needs are. Ask just about any delivery worker, and they’ll tell you the connection between the weather and their job is obvious: The worse the weather, the more people order food and groceries to their door.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline They migrated to New York for work. Now they’re fighting to climate-proof it. on Nov 18, 2026.

issues.title: What Congress’ bill to speed up energy projects would mean for you
issues.summary: The Senate’s permitting reform bill would make it easier to build renewables — but oil and gas infrastructure, too.
issues.author: Austin Corona
issues.content_html:
The largest renewable energy project ever built in the United States — the sprawling SunZia wind farm and power line in New Mexico — took two decades to build. Its transmission line, necessary to transport the wind power to cities in Arizona and California, faced opposition from birders, the military, and tribes. While some disputes were resolved, tribes’ concerns about the project’s impacts on historic sites have remained unsettled, leading to court battles that still haven’t been resolved even though the line was completed in June.

Such legal challenges commonly delay renewable energy projects and the transmission lines that carry their power to population centers. The threat of lawsuits and resistance from utilities have driven down long-distance power line construction in the United States, limiting the country’s ability to use cheap renewable energy.

The Senate is poised to pass a “permitting reform” bill that could make it much faster and easier to build transmission lines and renewable energy projects — but it casts a wide net, easing construction for almost all large infrastructure projects. Supporters of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA — including clean energy companies and prominent climate-conscious senators — argue the bill is necessary to clean up the power grid. Critics say it could disempower communities, tribes, and environmental groups while also speeding construction of fossil fuel infrastructure. Once through the Senate, the bill would still need to pass the House and receive the president’s signature before becoming law.

Here are the answers to some basic questions to help you understand the bill, why it’s such a big deal, and why it’s so controversial.

What would this bill do?

At its heart, the bill is an effort to streamline the federal government’s process for issuing permits for infrastructure projects, including many large-scale energy and transportation projects. Without these permits, developers can’t build infrastructure on federal land, across state lines, or with certain kinds of federal funding. But companies say getting a permit, and keeping it, is a time-consuming, unpredictable, and costly process, even when their project meets all necessary environmental standards.

That’s due in part to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, or NEPA, one of America’s bedrock environmental laws. NEPA requires federal agencies to study the environmental, economic, and social impacts of major government actions, including many infrastructure permits. They must consider alternatives to what’s been proposed, solicit input from the public, and publish their findings. A different law called the National Historic Preservation Act requires agencies to carry out similar reviews of projects’ repercussions for historic and archaeological sites.

While NEPA doesn’t explicitly hold projects to a higher environmental standard, it creates a formal process that can educate the public, inform government officials, and open pathways to better outcomes. Still, this process often becomes the source of delays. Opponents of a project can sue an agency, claiming it conducted an inadequate review, potentially forcing the government to redo parts of its analysis and halting construction in the meantime — even if the agency ultimately issues the same permit after redoing the analysis. The motivations for these lawsuits can range widely, from wealthy communities trying to protect their property values to tribes defending their sovereignty and religious freedom.

The Senate bill would speed up environmental and historic preservation reviews, narrow the potential impacts agencies must consider, restrict who can sue over them, and shorten the deadline for doing so. Supporters say that would prevent costly delays, which can be particularly consequential for land-intensive renewable energy projects. Critics say it would reduce public scrutiny and make it harder for communities and tribes to identify environmental harms, protect historic or sacred sites, and push developers toward better alternatives.

The bill would also make several changes aimed specifically at the power grid. It would give the federal government greater authority to override states that block interstate power lines and require regional grid operators to approve lines that improve reliability and affordability. Transmission construction in the United States has slowed over the last decade, even as its importance is expected to grow.

Controversially, the bill would also prevent states from using the Clean Water Act to block power lines or pipelines crossing waterways unless they directly discharge into the water. The bill would not affect the vast majority of projects built on private land within one state.

Would this bill change my community?

Tribes, states, and local groups would have less power to stop or delay some infrastructure projects, and projects could move forward with less time for public scrutiny. That could mean more power lines crossing landscapes and greater risk that communities’ concerns don’t get adequately considered.

But experts expect the bill to lower electricity costs slightly over the next 15 years by making it easier to move cheap power between regions, while helping states meet clean energy goals. Households and businesses would likely find it easier to sell electricity from rooftop solar and batteries onto the grid.

Most data centers wouldn’t see big changes because of the bill, as they are overwhelmingly constructed on private land whose development is overseen by local and state governments. (Proposals on federal lands exist, though they often involve significant legal issues that this bill would not necessarily change). The bill could accelerate the power and pipeline infrastructure that benefits data centers, but it would also require them to pay for grid upgrades they need and increase transparency around their electricity use. The bill could also make data centers’ power cleaner by making it easier for them to connect to grids with clean energy, rather than building polluting, off-grid gas turbines.

Would this bill be good for the climate?

The bill would enable energy infrastructure generally, meaning fossil fuel projects could grow alongside renewables. The advantage would likely tip toward renewable energy, according to projections from some organizations, though predicting future energy markets is tricky. Some experts believe the bill would make it harder for future administrations to limit fossil fuel projects, making emissions reductions more difficult.

Rhodium Group, an economic research firm, projects natural gas pipelines would continue advancing at roughly their current pace, while renewable energy deployment would accelerate due to faster permitting and greatly expanded transmission. Rhodium’s modeling finds a modest emissions reduction even if natural gas prices drop more than renewables, with larger reductions if renewable energy becomes much cheaper than natural gas.

But arguably the bill’s biggest climate effect would be strengthening future clean energy initiatives: States pursuing clean electricity or electrification would have an easier time building the infrastructure they need, and future federal clean energy incentives could produce better results.

The reverse is also possible. Republicans could take advantage of faster permitting processes to speed up fossil fuel infrastructure while suppressing renewables. The bill attempts to limit presidents’ ability to discriminate among energy sources, although recent amendments slightly weakened those provisions. Some opponents worry these provisions wouldn’t keep President Donald Trump from continuing to suppress wind power, while others worry they will be too successful and prevent Democratic presidents from phasing out fossil fuels.

Who supports the bill, and who opposes it?

Supporters include labor unions, clean and fossil energy companies, a few tribes and tribal energy advocates, centrist policy organizations, and some climate advocacy groups. Clean energy companies have been especially enthusiastic, arguing that permitting and transmission constraints have become some of the biggest obstacles to expanding renewable power.

Opponents include environmental nonprofits, dozens of tribes, rural landowners, civil rights groups, and other climate activists. Some opponents support the bill’s transmission provisions but argue its changes to environmental review would excessively weaken the ability of communities and tribes to scrutinize projects and seek alternatives.

That disagreement has split Democrats and the climate movement. Climate-focused Democratic senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich co-wrote the bill, while Green New Deal sponsors Ed Markey and Mazie Hirono opposed it. Climate movement veterans Al Gore and Genevieve Guenther have also opposed the current legislation, while climate scientist Zeke Hausfather and utility watchdog David Pomerantz support it.

Neither camp is monolithic, and advocates on both sides offer nuanced explanations of the trade-offs they are or aren’t willing to accept. Many opponents say they support permitting reform but believe Democrats should wait until January, when they will have majorities in both houses of Congress, to negotiate stronger protections for clean energy, communities, and tribes. Some supporters counter that the country needs new clean energy infrastructure now and that there is no guarantee a better political opportunity will arrive.

Will this bill become law?

The bill is likely to pass the Republican-controlled Senate, where nearly every Republican and half of Democrats have voted to advance it for consideration. If struggles over new amendments don’t derail it, the bill could leave that chamber before Thanksgiving. Afterward, however, BAAJA faces a more uncertain future in the House of Representatives.

The bill was crafted with limited input from members of the House, so the lower chamber might have less motivation to pass it quickly. The chamber is also controlled by Republicans, but some — including House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie of Kentucky — have signaled concern over transmission provisions. Many lawmakers in the House of Representatives come from rural districts, and they might be hesitant to sacrifice local influence over infrastructure projects.

House Democrats, including top Democrat Hakeem Jeffries of New York, have also expressed concerns about the bill. If a large group of Democrats can convince a handful of Republicans to vote against it, they might be able to defeat it.

Trump has said he supports the permitting reform effort, meaning it should become law if it makes it out of Congress. If BAAJA doesn’t get signed before the new year, however, it will die, and lawmakers will have to start over if they want to pass permitting reform in the next session.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline What Congress’ bill to speed up energy projects would mean for you on Nov 18, 2026.

issues.title: In Utah, a ‘hydrocarbon highway’ could run right through this petroglyph-filled canyon
issues.summary: The Trump administration revived a plan to blast a 5-mile road for trucks carrying crude from oil fields. A new lawsuit aims to block it.
issues.author: Leia Larsen
issues.content_html:
Federal land managers call it “the world’s longest art gallery,” a Utah red-rock canyon full of ancient petroglyphs, Native American panels, and pioneer-era inscriptions written in axle grease. Earlier this year, the Trump administration approved plans to blast a “hydrocarbon highway” connecting nearby oil fields to rail-loading facilities through Nine Mile Canyon’s cultural and archaeological-rich sites. Last month environmental and historic preservation groups sued to stop them.

“It’s like constructing a highway through the Louvre Museum,” said J. Michael Hansen, president of the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, in a statement.

The Trump administration resurrected the project in eastern Utah after it stalled out during President Joe Biden’s term. Plaintiffs in the lawsuit say approvals for the highway bypassed the normal public comment and ecological review processes. The Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, and the Center for Biological Diversity filed their complaint in Utah’s U.S. District Court against the Department of Interior and Bureau of Land Management.

Nine Mile Canyon runs about 46 miles. Plans call for dynamiting, paving, and widening a road through Gate Canyon, a tributary to Nine Mile, which has 47 historic sites of its own with 43 eligible for the National Register of Historic Places, according to BLM documentation from 2015.

The proposed highway would cut through 5.3 miles of land owned by both the Bureau of Land Management and Utah’s Trust Lands Administration, although most of the switchbacks the highway project would straighten sit on state land. (A BLM spokesperson declined to comment on the lawsuit.)

The federal agency began considering plans to realign Gate Canyon’s winding dirt Wells Draw Road in 2015, after Duchesne County sought a more direct route from the oil fields in the Uinta Basin to the rail-loading facilities of Carbon County. The project could bring up to 500 heavy trucks through Nine Mile Canyon per day. Duchesne County, which needs the federal government’s approval for the project since part of Gate Canyon lies on BLM land, has also said straightening the old county road would provide for safer travel.

In 2016, the BLM received nearly 700 public comments sharing concerns about potential impacts to Nine Mile Canyon from the increased traffic, the agency noted in its latest assessment.

The BLM paused its earlier environmental assessment of the project, the lawsuit claims, but it solicited public comments again in 2023 after reviewing an amended right-of-way that covers 2.8 miles running through federal lands. The highway proposal was again hit by a round of opposition. The plan was scrapped, with the BLM citing the need for further cultural surveys and reports.

But a Duchesne County special service district submitted a new development plan in September 2025, which it finalized on April 13 of this year. The BLM approved it on April 28 after determining the highway “will not significantly affect” the environment, recreation, wildlife, or quality of life.

In their lawsuit, the environmental groups disagreed with that assessment.

“The road construction will facilitate increased traffic through Gate Canyon and the adjoining Nine Mile Canyon, threatening some of the state’s most important cultural and scenic values in the larger Nine Mile Canyon region,” the lawsuit said.

Although the BLM issued a final environmental assessment in April, the environmental groups said the agency violated several federal laws, including the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, the Federal Land Policy and Management Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act. The Gate Canyon project area potentially includes habitat for the threatened Mexican spotted owl, according to the agency’s own 2015 draft environmental assessment, environmental groups argued.

And despite that previous draft assessment identifying dozens of sites within Gate Canyon that are eligible for the National Register, including 11 “within feet” of the existing dirt road, the plaintiffs say the BLM signed off on the project without identifying any historical or archaeological resources. The lawsuit says they asked for public comment periods and to participate in the National Environmental Policy Act process after learning of the highway’s new development plan in March, but that the BLM either did not respond or denied those requests.

“This lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s disgraceful plan to transform a quiet backcountry road into a highway clogged with speeding oil tanker trucks,” said Deeda Seed, senior Utah campaigner at the Center for Biological Diversity. “We’re going to court to protect this irreplaceable cultural treasure and the animals calling it home.”

The federal government has not yet filed a response with the Utah District Court.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline In Utah, a ‘hydrocarbon highway’ could run right through this petroglyph-filled canyon on Nov 18, 2026.

issues.title: Tribes push back as Congress moves to fast-track energy projects
issues.summary: A bipartisan “permitting reform” bill would help expand the grid, but tribal nations fear it would mean “the demolition of our heritage.”
issues.author: Jake Bittle
issues.content_html:
After years of negotiation, Congress is on the cusp of passing a bipartisan “permitting reform” bill that would make it far easier to build power plants and electric transmission lines in the United States. The bill was negotiated by a bipartisan group of senators including Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse, a noted climate hawk, and Republican Mike Lee, an opponent of environmental regulation. It has picked up support from cleanenergyadvocates because it would promote more transmission lines to carry renewable power to cities, speed up review for solar and wind projects, and stop presidents from cancelling offshore wind farms. It has also been endorsed by many conservative, business, and fossil fuel groups, who say it would cut down on environmental red tape and speed up natural gas pipelines.

The bill has divided the climate movement, separating groups focused on decarbonization from those focused on endangered species protection and environmental justice, but the most influential opposition has come from tribal nations. The bill would weaken a historic preservation law that tribes often use to protect cultural and religious sites from development, and numerous prominent Indigenous nations and organizations have said it harms tribal sovereignty.

While the bill cleared a procedural hurdle in the Senate last week, it remains unclear whether it will pass there or in the House. The negotiators who framed the bill say they believe they have the votes, but a number of Democrats in both chambers have opposed the bill. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next Speaker of the House, has criticized what he called the bill’s “failure to adequately protect tribal sovereignty.” Nevada senator Catherine Cortez Masto, who voted to advance the bill, has said she won’t ultimately vote to pass it, saying she “cannot ignore the concerns” of tribes in her state.

“Projects affecting tribal governments before were already fast-tracked, but now this allows for a super fast track,” said John Bathke, a member of the Navajo Nation, a former historic preservation officer for the Quechan Tribe of the Fort Yuma Reservation, and now a professor of Indigenous studies at San Diego City College.

The 1966 National Historic Preservation Act, passed in the wake of nationwide urban renewal efforts that demolished many old buildings, requires the federal government to consider the effect of construction projects on historic and cultural properties. (Most intact objects or properties that are more than 50 years old and have some kind of historical, cultural, or religious significance qualify under the law.) When you’re building a solar farm or a transmission line, that is a big undertaking: The area of review can extend for as much as 5 miles away from the project itself, and major transmission lines can be hundreds of miles long. Even if a project is visible a few miles away when you’re standing in a historic area, that still counts as a potential effect.

While tribal nations have control over infrastructure projects on their reservations, many tribes have cultural, religious, and political claims over areas that are outside their reservation boundaries. The historic preservation law is one of the only tools they have to stop or alter construction projects that might desecrate sacred territories or religious sites.

“Even though a lot of these projects aren’t on reservation land, it’s part of their traditional homeland, it’s part of their spiritual landscape,” said Bathke. “That land still belongs to them and they belong to that land.”

Tribal nations have used this law to limit energy projects that they say would harm their sacred territories. In perhaps the best-known example, the Quechan Tribe of the Fort Yuma Indian Reservation sued the federal government in 2010 over its approval of a 6,000-acre solar farm on federal land in California, one of the first such projects in the United States. The tribe argued that the project would destroy religious sites and buried remains and that the government had rubber-stamped it after just a few meetings. A court sided with the tribe and the solar developer nixed the project, moving to build on private farmland instead. (Bathke was the tribe’s historic preservation officer — the tribal official who helps with historic reviews — during the solar dispute.)

Supporters of clean energy development have long sought to reform the law. They argue that historic preservation review has become a far more sweeping and burdensome process than the authors of the law intended, and that clean energy projects are affected more than any other type of construction. The onus is heaviest for transmission lines — in some cases, the area under review can extend to hundreds of square miles, and entire rivers or valleys can be considered historic sites. Since transmission wires can be seen from miles away, it’s hard to eliminate all visual impacts associated with building them.

“As written, [the historic preservation law] is a modest procedural check on hasty decisionmaking. … In practice, it has grown into a substantive burden on building infrastructure of all kinds,” write Ben Schifman and Aiden Mackenzie, two research analysts at the Institute for Progress, in a report on how the law affects energy development. The Institute for Progress has been a leading advocate for reforming the law and for the bipartisan permitting bill.

To illustrate their argument, Schifman and Mackenzie cite the example of SunZia, an $11 billion transmission line that carries wind energy west from New Mexico to California. The project took two decades to complete. The line had to secure permits from multiple state power regulators, but it also had to undergo a historic review process that covered an area twice the size of Delaware. Among many other things, the government had to consider whether being able to see the transmission line in the distance would harm the historic characteristics of thousands of different sites across multiple states.

While the government undertook this review, a coalition of tribes in the area protested the process. One of their main arguments centered on the San Pedro River Valley, a landform in Arizona that is sacred to the Apache, O’odham, Hopi, and Zuni peoples. The tribes wanted the government to declare the entire valley a historic zone, which could have required SunZia to reroute its wires. The government declined to give the valley that designation, arguing that the tribes had not identified the issue early enough in the review process. The Tohono O’odham and the San Carlos Apache tribes along with a group of environmental nonprofits then sued to stop the line. They failed to halt construction before the wires joined the grid, but the case is still ongoing, and a court could still force the developer to alter the project if the tribes win.

The initial version of the permitting bill limited the scope of the historic review process in several ways in an apparent attempt to avoid future SunZias. It made consultation with tribes effectively optional, allowing the federal government to move ahead with projects in cases where a tribe’s designated historic preservation official took too long to identify important sites. It outlined a definition for “traditional religious or cultural importance,” which had previously been open-ended under federal law. It narrowed the definition of a “visual” impact, requiring that such impacts “direct[ly]” and “significantly diminish” the historic value of a place; this standard is subjective, but it would likely exclude things like being able to see a wind turbine on the horizon. It also prohibited judges from halting construction work on projects if they find a flaw in a historic preservation analysis, as happened in the Quechan Tribe wind farm case; instead, judges could only order the federal government to redo its analysis as construction continued.

These provisions provoked an immediate outcry from several tribal nations and Indigenous groups, who said it would threaten tribal sovereignty. A coalition of several major tribal groups, including the National Congress of American Indians, said that the bill was in “deep conflict with federal trust and treaty obligations” and that Senate negotiators were “proposing to facilitate the demolition of our heritage.”

Some lawmakers who support the bill expressed regret about their failure to incorporate Native interests.

“We didn’t bring the tribes along on this … we could have done better on it in retrospect,” said Republican senator Alan Armstrong, who represents Oklahoma, in an interview with Punchbowl News.

Negotiators amended the bill earlier this month to address these concerns. The bill now makes tribal consultation mandatory throughout the historic review process, which isn’t the case under current law. It also prevents the government from taking over the historic review process when tribal officials are slow to respond. These changes are significant given that the Trump administration is already trying to weaken the historic review process through executive action. The administration’s rulemaking could limit the historic review process even if the permitting bill doesn’t pass.

The tribes and tribal organizations that opposed the first version of the bill say these changes are nowhere near enough. Their primary areas of concern, including the limited definition of visual effects and the ban on injunctions, are still in the new version.

“While this amendment addresses select concerns, the authors ask Indian Country to be grateful Washington chose to take away fewer of our rights in the name of ‘progress,’” said Ira Matt, the head of the the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers and a member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes. He also said the bill erodes “protections we have spent decades fighting to secure” and that those supporting it had demonstrated a “fundamental failure to understand and respect Tribal sovereignty.”

It’s unlikely that lawmakers will strip the historic preservation section altogether. Many of the most suitable areas for clean energy development are on federal land in the West. In order to build enough clean energy to replace fossil fuels, developers will likely have to build projects that pass near tribal cultural sites. In that light, the bill’s historic preservation reform represents the biggest win for clean energy companies since the passage of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, which subsidized wind and solar construction and has since been largely repealed.

Some tribal nations believe they themselves will benefit from the bill’s effort to speed up energy permitting. A few tribes have endorsed the bill, most of them tribes that have significant coal and oil resources. The Apsáalooke (Crow) tribe, whose reservation covers 2 million acres in Montana, told Senate negotiators last month that the bill could deliver “a predictable regulatory environment” and greater investment certainty” for “energy-producing tribes.” The tribe has significant coal reserves and has historically been a large coal producer, but its production has declined in recent years. The National Tribal Energy Association, which represents a number of fossil-fuel producing tribes, has also endorsed the bill.

The bill will also strengthen the investment case for solar and wind on tribal lands, said Anthony Walters, a member of the Cherokee Nation and the vice president for government relations at the Alliance for Tribal Clean Energy, which helps tribes develop renewable energy. Walters says the main constraint that many tribes face is getting access to capital, and speedy environmental reviews and more transmission lines would make it easier for tribes to attract the money they need.

Even so, he said the economic benefits of that development could never outweigh the potential destruction of sites that tribes hold sacred.

“The bill would help clean energy development projects across the board, so tribes would see the benefit of that,” he said. “But on the whole, right, we can’t do that at the expense of all the processes that tribes use to protect their interests. It’s a big trade-off.”

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline Tribes push back as Congress moves to fast-track energy projects on Nov 17, 2026.

issues.author: David Brown
issues.content_html: World Anteater Day falls on Nov. 19, in recognition of the tube-nosed, ant- and termite-eating animals living across Central and South America. Closely related to sloths, anteaters generally live in trees. The largest species, the giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla), lives on the ground, though, where it rips open anthills and termite nests with its razor-sharp claws and slurps up the insects with its long, sticky tongue. The species is listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Giant anteaters have disappeared from parts of their range due to habitat destruction and hunting, but habitat restoration and rewilding efforts are helping their return in some of their former range. A giant anteater’s return in Argentina offers a case for letting nature restore itself In 2025, a giant anteater returned to the Alma Guaraní reserve in Argentina’s Gran Chaco region for the first known time since 1986, reported Mongabay contributor Sean Mowbray. Habitat degradation in the Gran Chaco due to agricultural expansion and forest loss had reduced ant abundance by 30-50% compared to well-preserved areas, directly affecting the giant anteater. Alma Guaraní Natural Reserve, which covers approximately 6,400 hectares (about 15,800 acres), has been the site of volunteer-led restoration work for more than a decade. In some areas, volunteers actively planted native trees; in others, they used fences to allow the land to regenerate naturally, free from incursions by livestock, dogs, and hunting and fishing activity. Placing the Ba Besanan Memorial Stone in the forest was partly a celebration by the […]
issues.author: Danielle Keeton-Olsen
issues.content_html: Indigenous communities in Malaysian Borneo gathered on Nov. 4 to place a memorial stone in commemoration of their three-year battle with an oil palm plantation that threatened their native customary land rights and also endangered a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Placing the Ba Besanan Memorial Stone in the forest was partly a celebration by the Berawan, Penan, and Tering peoples, but also a warning to current and future generations about the outside interests seeking to make money off their native customary land, one leader said. “I remind the people that we can’t overstate [the victory],” Willie Kajan, an Indigenous Tering member who represents the Berawan and Tering in Mulu, in the state of Sarawak, told Mongabay by phone. “We don’t know their next tactic.” Ukau Lupung, the representative of the Penan community at Bateu Bungan, places a stone on top of the Ba Besanan Memorial Stone as a symbolic gesture to mark its inauguration on Nov. 4, 2026 in the Mulu area of Malaysia’s Sarawak state. Image courtesy of Keruan. A surprise victory The Berawan, Penan and Tering peoples live both within and around the nearly 53,000-hectare (131,000-acre) Gunung Mulu National Park, and they rely on the land for their livelihoods and cultural preservation. Indigenous residents first detected logging there in 2018, when employees of Malaysian firm Radiant Lagoon Sdn. Bhd. began clearing land for development. The firm held rights to a 4,400-hectare (nearly 11,000-acre) oil palm concession, which also overlapped with Gunung Mulu National Park — declared a UNESCO…This article was originally published on Mongabay

issues.title: Greenpeace drops ‘Attenboulder’ to deter UK bottom trawlers in a marine protected area
issues.summary: Greenpeace activists recently dropped several enormous boulders in the U.K.’s Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area to discourage destructive bottom trawling currently permitted in the area. The nearly 37,000 square kilometer (about 14,000 square miles) MPA is part of the U.K.’s network of marine protected areas, which contribute to its commitment to the global conservation […]
issues.author: Bobby Bascomb
issues.content_html: Greenpeace activists recently dropped several enormous boulders in the U.K.’s Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area to discourage destructive bottom trawling currently permitted in the area. The nearly 37,000 square kilometer (about 14,000 square miles) MPA is part of the U.K.’s network of marine protected areas, which contribute to its commitment to the global conservation target of protecting 30% of the Earth’s land and sea by 2030. However, the MPA currently allows bottom trawl fishing, a commercial fishing practice in which a large, weighted net is dragged along the seafloor and scoops up marine life in its path. Greenpeace U.K.’s head of oceans, Elena Polisano, said the MPA amounts to little more than a paper park — a protected area in name only. “In a way it’s false advertising because the marine life isn’t protected in these areas,” Polisano told Mongabay in a video call. “They kind of bulldoze the seabed taking everything in their path,” Polisano said. Bottom trawling is “pulverizing marine life, stripping the ocean of fish and killing porpoises, sharks, dolphins, seabirds,” she added. To create barriers for bottom trawlers, Greenpeace placed 10 boulders, each about 2 tonnes (4,400 pounds), on the seafloor. One was carved in the likeness of naturalist David Attenborough and dubbed “Attenboulder.” Greenpeace shared coordinates for the boulders with authorities and fishers. Polsano said they won’t necessarily stop bottom trawlers, but they will create new obstacles for their operations. The European Bottom Fisheries Alliance decried Greenpeace’s actions saying environmental protection “cannot be achieved…This article was originally published on Mongabay

The famous El Tovar Hotel along with several other lodges will reopen Friday now that the park has reached […]
issues.author: Associated Press
issues.content_html: GRAND CANYON NATIONAL PARK, Ariz. (AP) — Officials at Grand Canyon National Park announced Wednesday that they are easing water restrictions, meaning hotels on the South Rim will once again be able to accommodate overnight guests. The famous El Tovar Hotel along with several other lodges will reopen Friday now that the park has reached a milestone in restoration of water service following severe flooding earlier this year. Flooding in late August caused three deaths, prompted rescues and damaged key infrastructure, including a water intake pump and a significant stretch of a decades-old pipeline that supplied water for millions of visitors to the South Rim and about 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village. At the time, officials said they were just over a month away from completing a more than $200 million upgrade to the 12.5-mile-long (20-kilometer) Transcanyon Waterline. More flooding in September damaged temporary repairs. Although lodging is reopening, park officials urge visitors to conserve as restoration of the water system continues. “Simple actions, including taking shorter showers, turning off faucets when not in use and avoiding unnecessary water use, help support the park’s water system as operations resume,” the park said in its announcement. Food and beverage services will resume gradually, according to park officials. By Associated Press Banner image: The Grand Canyon. Image courtesy of Amy Martin via National Park Service. issues.title: How can more girls be encouraged to take up sport?
issues.summary: Moves are being considered to encourage girls to stay active as they move into secondary school.
issues.content_html:
Work is being done to encourage girls to stay active as they move into secondary school, after a survey found fewer playing sport after leaving primary school.

The 2026 Active Healthy Kids Report Card led by the Health Improvement Commission found 60% of girls in primary met global recommendations on physical activity, which dropped to 51% in secondary.

For boys it went up from 66% to 68%. The World Health Organization's recommendation for children and adolescents is at least 60 min of moderate to vigorous physical activity - such as running, cycling or swimming - per day on average.

Jane, 15, and Bella, 16, are members of The Youth Commission's Youth Forum and think there are a variety of reasons why girls may not continue sports - including exam pressures and social media.

Jane said: "When it starts getting closer to exam season, it is kind of a wake-up call to start thinking of priorities so they think 'where can I save time' so that's when they kind of drop sports.

"Sometimes there are more social pressures - especially in teenage years for girls."

Bella said: "As a teenager, your body is changing but you also get into social media and there are a lot of views on how someone should look and act - I find you find more sporting content for boys rather than girls."

Bella added she thought more low pressure sports clubs may encourage more girls to take part.

The report is Guernsey's contribution to the Global Matrix 5.0, which is being launched next month and involves 67 countries around the world.

It was compiled from a variety of available data including the 2022 Guernsey Young People's Survey 2022, which involved more than 1,300 pupils from school years 6, 8 and 10 answer questions on health, wellbeing, and school experiences.

Molly, 11, dances and plays netball, she said: "I enjoy playing sports, it is exciting and gives you a lot of energy and adrenaline to do it again."

Isabella, 10, said: "I feel like the girls need more opportunities - I went to an open day and more boys than girls were playing sports."

  • More news stories for Guernsey
  • Listen to the latest news for Guernsey

Local sport projects target inequalities in sport, including The Guernsey Sports Commission's Sports Voucher scheme - a voucher will cover the cost of subscription for one full season of the chosen sport.

The scheme is available for any child or young person in full-time education between the ages of four and 18 who is eligible to claim uniform allowance or whose family is on income support.

Organized sport participation is higher amongst boys than girls, particularly in team sports with 52% of boys report taking part in team sports compared to 34% of girls.

However, there are a range of sports clubs with dedicated girls teams - such as Guernsey Hockey.

Rosie, 12, who plays a range of sports including hockey, said: "Sometimes I have to leave some sports five minutes early so I can be at the next one.

"I think it's sad more girls do not continue, because that means more boys may go pro."

Alex Costen, the commission's be active lead, said: "Earlier on the differences of activity between boys and girls are less marked, but as the girls go up through secondary school you see a drop off.

"There are numerous reasons why this happens and we at the commission want to speak to girls and find out what they are.

"I think it needs to be a really collaborative approach looking at how girls may be more active, because what might encourage one girl may not work for another.

"Our first stages, we are pulling together a steering group with individuals and teachers to talk about what we can do going forward to encourage girls.

"There are so many things to think about like sports kit, periods and even simple things like having a hairdryer available after swimming."

issues.title: Luka Doncic calls his play 'unacceptable' as Lakers' 9-game winning streak ends
issues.summary: LOS ANGELES (AP) — Luka Doncic wants the blame placed on him after the Los Angeles Lakers' nine-game winning streak ended with a shocking loss to the previously struggling Utah Jazz on Wednesday night.Doncic wasn't great despite his 29 points in the Lakers' 109-97 defeat, missing 10 of his 12 3-point attempts and committing nine turnovers.
issues.author: GREG BEACHAM
issues.content_html:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Luka Doncic wants the blame placed on him after the Los Angeles Lakers' nine-game winning streak ended with a shocking loss to the previously struggling Utah Jazz on Wednesday night.

Doncic wasn't great despite his 29 points in the Lakers' 109-97 defeat, missing 10 of his 12 3-point attempts and committing nine turnovers. His streak of 11 straight 30-point games also ended.

Although the ugly game was the culmination of a punishing stretch played mostly at less than full strength by Los Angeles, the Slovenian superstar still feels a personal responsibility when he can't will the Lakers to victory.

“Honestly, I've just got to do way better than this,” Doncic said. “This is unacceptable for my part. I've got to lead the team in better ways. Got to look at this game, got to move on and learn from this.”

The Lakers are still 13-3 and atop the Western Conference after their first loss of November was handed to them by a two-win opponent that only ended a 12-game losing streak one night earlier.

Playing without injured second-leading scorer Austin Reaves, the Lakers made only 38.2% of their shots and 27.3% of their 3-point attempts against the Jazz, both season lows. LA managed only nine 3-pointers, tying its season low.

Doncic claimed the blame, but his teammates and coaches weren’t having it.

“Of course he’s going to say that,” Jake LaRavia said. “It’s obviously not on him. It’s a team game. He’s been carrying the offensive load, so if there’s ever bad shooting nights, it’s on the rest of the team to help be better.”

All of the Lakers had an off night, but they rely heavily on Doncic, the league's top scorer during one of the best starts to a season in NBA history.

Doncic's usage rate — a statistic that estimates a player's involvement on offense — is at 40.6%, the highest in the league and the highest of his career. Doncic took 28 shots against the Jazz, and that was only tied for his fourth-highest total this season.

Lakers coach JJ Redick says he's confident Doncic's current preeminence to the Lakers' offense won't prove to be unsustainable.

“The shot creation that is required from him, I think it takes its toll,” Redick said. “That's part of it when Austin is out, for sure.”

Fatigue isn’t allowed to be a factor, Doncic said.

“All NBA teams play 82 games, so that can’t be an excuse,” Doncic said. “I’ve got to do way better, I know that. I feel like we had some open shots we didn’t make. But it’s one game. We’ve got to move on.”

Yet the culprit in this stinker against Utah was most likely the game accumulation that drags down every NBA team at times.

The loss came on the back half of a back-to-back set after the Lakers had to rally from an 18-point deficit late in the third quarter to beat Charlotte on Tuesday night. Doncic scored 37 points, but Quentin Grimes dramatically stepped up with a career-high 47, even forcing overtime with his 10th 3-pointer.

The loss to Utah was the Lakers' third game in four days without the high-scoring Reaves, who has a bruised heel, and it was their 10th game already in November. No team has played more games this season than the Lakers' 16 in the first 29 days, and their top three scorers have all missed games due to injury already.

“Frankly, if you’re playing 82 games, you’re going to have some horrible shooting nights,” Redick said. “My belief in the group and who we are, I’m not going to overreact to a bad offensive night for us.”

The Lakers host Sacramento (1-13) on Friday.

___

issues.title: Verstappen 'trusts' F1 over Middle East decision
issues.summary: Max Verstappen says he trusts in Formula 1 after their decision to end the season in the Middle East, despite the ongoing conflicts in the area.
issues.content_html:
Max Verstappen says he "trusts" Formula 1 has made the right decision in pressing ahead with the final two races of the season in the Middle East.

Last week, F1 stood down preparations for a substitute race at Imola in Italy if the events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi could not be held because of ongoing conflicts in the area.

The sport will now conclude the season in the Middle East, unless the situation deteriorates before the Qatar event on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December.

Verstappen said: "I trust F1 and FIA to make the right call on that, right?

"I don't have all the intel. I'm not an officer. I just hope that they make the right call on that. And that's all that you can rely on, really.

"They also send over their findings and understanding. So I trust them."

  • How sporting events are being affected by Middle East conflict
  • Yamaha will not travel to Qatar for MotoGP race

Verstappen had previously voiced his opposition to ending the season in the Middle East.

"Normally I am happy to go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but you know, when there is a war nearby, and if some of the countries are in conflict with each other, then I think we shouldn't go," Verstappen said in September.

The Red Bull driver's fresh remarks reflect a uniform public stance in F1 on the situation, even though there are widespread misgivings among personnel about travelling to the Middle East in the context of the two conflicts in the area.

Last Sunday Iran targeted a US military base in Bahrain with a drone attack for the second time in three days, the latest salvo in the war launched against the country by the US and Israel in February.

And Houthi rebels in Yemen are advancing in their war against the Saudi-backed government of the country.

Missile attacks from the Houthis into Saudi Arabia are threatening that country's chances of hosting the second grand prix of next season, which is scheduled for 19-21 March.

McLaren's Lando Norris said that while he is "fine" with the decision to race, he is concerned about the "big team" behind him.

"I have my friend's wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there and then going on to Qatar and then Abu Dhabi," he added.

"But it's not about me. It's a lot more people. It's the fans, it's the team personnel, so the question is for them, more than I would say it is for myself."

Mercedes driver George Russell said he has "no hesitation" in racing and that while he's "sure some people have their reservations" he doesn't "know of anyone who's concerned".

"I know people who live in the region and they said it quite bluntly, if they didn't feel comfortable they wouldn't be there with their families," he said.

"When you look around the world there are a lot of terrible things going on.

"You've just got to trust in the people. If they say it's safe, then you trust in them. F1 aren't stupid and I'm sure there's plans A, B, C, D, etc. So fingers crossed it'll all be fine."

MotoGP, which is owned by the same US group as F1, held a race in Qatar last weekend without problems.

F1, which has significant commercial links with the Middle East, has been closely monitoring the situation and has been advised by security officials and government figures in the Gulf and Europe that the races can go ahead, and there is no official advice against travelling to Qatar or Abu Dhabi.

F1 said in a statement last week that it was still prepared to cancel the two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi if the situation deteriorated.

"If the situation develops negatively in the coming weeks before the events in the Middle East, we will not hesitate to do the right thing and the safety of everyone will always be the priority," an F1 spokesperson said on Tuesday.

issues.title: UW Film Study: Michigan State Spartans
issues.summary: The Washington Huskies took down the Michigan State Spartans 21-14, notching their third straight road win.
