Nonetheless UW was able […]
issues.content_html:
The Washington Huskies took down the Michigan State Spartans 21-14, notching their third straight road win. It was not the prettiest game (which is on par for the season), as it was 14-14 for most of the second half, despite the Spartans going down to their 2nd and 3rd string QBs. Nonetheless UW was able to come up on top, lead by Chris Lawson who continued his breakout season, notching 124 yards and 2 touchdowns.

The Dawgs become bowl eligible as they head into their toughest 2 weeks of the season, hosting #8 Indiana then heading down to Eugene to play #13 0regon, hoping to playing upset and crush CFP dreams for their B1G counterparts.

To the film.

Offense: Going Deep

Against Michigan State, we saw a version of the offense that looked much more like the pre/early-Demond 2024 scheme than the 2025 or 2026 scheme, and while the offense was still anemic for long stretches of the game, there was proof that the skill talent and the scheme can be explosive when properly executed. What does that mean? Well, instead of the screen and drop back-heavy passing offense that’s been stagnant all season, Fisch called more of the over-the-middle shot concepts that he leaned on heavily back in 2024. Concepts like Mills and Yankee came back into the fold, and so did some of the half-roll and sprint out backfield/protection concepts. The offense couldn’t connect on very many of these shot plays, but they ended up being the difference in the game.

Hypothetically, this added vertical dimension that’s largely been missing this season could be something that opens up more opportunities underneath. To a certain extent, it’s a little too late in the season for the offense to be finding a formula that works and it make a huge difference, but I guess we wanted to feature these plays here to point out that the talent and the scheme are sufficient to give us a viable and dynamic passing game.

1st Quarter – 1:38 – 1st & 10

First up we have a Yankee concept paired with a half roll backfield action/protection. I apologize for only having the replay angle, but this was the only one available on the game recording that was half decent.

As some of the long-time readers might remember, the Yankee concept is a vertical concept that attacks the safeties with a Post-Dig route combination. Normally a concept that’s called against 1-high safety coverages, the Post-Dig combination creates a high-low stretch on the deep safety. If the safety comes up to help on the Dig, the Post route can run into open grass behind the defense. Alternatively, if the deep safety stays back to help with the Post, then the Dig route has space behind the linebackers to get open. Typically, Yankee is paired with play action and heavy protection to buy the QB time to allow the routes to develop, as well as to suck the LBs up to the line to further open the space behind the second level for the Dig to work into.

Those are the basics of the Yankee concept, but there are many variations of the core concept that offer answers to 2-high coverages, like we’re facing on this play. On this play, we have Roebuck (WR, #2) and Rashid Williams (WR, #3) running double Posts to the right side of the formation and Chris Lawson (WR, #8) running the Dig from the left. On a conventional Yankee play design facing 2-high safeties, one safety would be able to assist with the Dig and the other could help with the Post. However, with the double Posts, we’re able to attack the deep defender on the right side of the formation with multiple routes. Even if the defense is in Cover 4, we’d still have the double Posts in 1v1 coverage. That Post from Williams is what gave this play a shot.

At the snap, you can see MSU’s #24 bail deep as if he has deep half field coverage with eyes to the inside. If Rashid didn’t have a vertical route, #24 could’ve honed in on Roebuck and provided over the top support on a solo Post. Williams does a good job of selling the vertical outside release, drawing the CB’s eyes towards the sideline, forced him to flip his hips to protect the sideline, and kept Roebuck open deep downfield.

To be honest, I’m not sure what Michigan State has called here in coverage. It’s either some form of inverted coverage or a totally blown assignment because there’s no way that they wanted a LB matched up deep against Roebuck. It ended up as a missed opportunity, but the play was there to be made for a nearly 60-yard TD.

1st Quarter – 0:40 – 3rd & 11

Next up we have a Mills concept for the first UW TD. Much like the Yankee concept, this is a vertical shot play concept that features a Post-Dig route combo. Mills, popularized by Fisch’s coaching idol Steve Spurrier, was a staple of the offense over the last couple of seasons. Really, the only big picture difference between the Yankee and Mills concepts is that on Yankee the Post and Dig are run from opposite sides of the formation, whereas on Mills the Post and Dig are run from the same side. Mills is also primarily a 1-high coverage beater that attacks the deep safety, but variations of the concept can be effective against 2-high coverages as well.

On this play, we’re getting a pre-snap 1-high coverage look from MSU, but post-snap they are dropping into a version of Cover 2. This version of Mills, like the Yankee concept in the last play, has an answer for 2-high. Prior to the snap, we’re motioning Rashid across the formation to set up a Double Dig Mills concept. Lawson is running the Post here that goes for the TD, but it’s the other two routes from the right side that set his route up. Mason James (WR, #6) starts on the right and runs the first of the two Dig routes (the second coming from Rashid). His Dig route draws the initial attention from the deep safety to the left side of the formation. Rashid’s Dig draws the attention of the rotated shallow safety. By keeping the shallow safety low with the second Dig route, he isn’t able to drop and provide any over the middle help to the CB #24 who’s trying to keep up with Lawson who has inside leverage.

Shout out to the OL for providing ample time for Demond to scan the field and let the routes develop.

2nd Quarter – 8:15 – 1st & 10

Last up for offense we have a half roll concept for a big gain. Early in Demond’s career we used this half roll backfield action a lot, but for some reason we haven’t seen it as much this year. This season we’ve seen a lot of naked bootleg concepts from under center, and I think it’s because of Fisch’s preference to emulate the Shanahan/McVay offenses from his NFL days. On naked bootlegs, the QB is entirely reliant on the play action fake to preoccupy the roll out side edge defender. As we all know, our run game hasn’t been good enough to really preoccupy the edge defenders, so they often times are just fixated on Demond running around with no protection help. The difference with these half roll backfield looks and those naked bootlegs is that we’re actually designing the protection scheme to account for the play side edge defender, thus allowing Demond to actually look downfield instead of running for his life.

As you can see here on the replay, with this half roll action, we still have play action going to the right with Demond looking to move out of the pocket to his left. However, between being able to start in shotgun, thus allowing him to keep his eyes on the defense the whole time, and Rashid staying in as a personal protector against the edge defender, Demond actually has enough time to scan the field and get to his second read. That second read, Decker DeGraaf (TE, #86), is coming wide open on a crossing route behind the LBs.

The beauty of this type of half roll action is that we’re able to unlock the best traits of Demond while simultaneously mitigating his, and the offense’s, weaknesses. Like the naked bootlegs, we’re able to get Demond out of the pocket, which forces the defense to react and make decisions about sticking with their coverage assignments or playing contain. This leverages Demond’s mobility as a threat that the defense has to account for despite it being a pass play. We’re also able to get him a better view of the defense and better passing lanes outside of the pocket. Finally, it takes the edge off of the opponent’s pass rush.

Defense: Mismatch Trends

For defense this week, instead of focusing on a game-specific trend or wrinkle, we wanted to take a look at a trend that we’ve noticed over the course of conference play. The Spartans aren’t a great offense this season, but they were able to get some big plays on us using heavier personnel packages and play action. This was the same formula that Minnesota, Iowa, and Penn State all used in some form to beat us. In each instance, multiple TE personnel groupings allowed them to attack our base nickel personnel using the run game, get our defense to press, and then play off of our aggressive run fits using play action. It wasn’t always the TEs themselves who were getting big plays on us in the air. Instead it’s the oft-forgotten blocking matchups with TEs on EDGEs or LBs that set everything up.

MSU didn’t rack up a huge day on the ground, but it was effective enough when using these heavier personnel packages that the play action threat was effective. Let us show you what we mean.

1st Quarter – 13:32 – 1st & 10

First up, we have MSU in a 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 TE) condensed formation running a play action bootleg concept. This should look familiar to UW fans since this is a type of play that we’ve tried time and time again this season when we’re on offense. Against this, we’re playing a 1-high coverage look with our 5×1 Penny front that’s bolstered by Alex McLaughlin playing as the box safety.

When facing these heavy condensed formations with the offense, where the TEs and WRs are lined up tight to the OL, the WRs and TEs become real blocking threats who could factor into a potential run play blocking scheme. This creates extra gaps that the defense has to account for in their run fits. Keep in mind, the TEs and WRs who are now blocking threats are being covered by DBs, who are now also factoring into the expanded run fits. Our defense likes to play base nickel personnel against 12 personnel packages. From a coverage match up perspective, we typically like to match Jacob Manu (LB, #9) on the RB, then play our safeties on the TEs. When I’m talking about safeties, I’m including Rashawn Clark (nickel/safety, #2). The problem is that our coverages don’t always work out where our most capable run support safeties (McLaughlin and RDA) are playing in the box where they can cover the TEs and factor into the run fit effectively. We try to account for this, or try to give ourselves the flexibility to play different safeties deep, by using our Penny front with ZRS picking up more run responsibilities for Clark and having McLaughlin pull double duty as a super aggressive box defender. However, this can get picked on.

As you can see here, we’ve got RDA playing deep 1-high safety with McLaughlin and Clark in the box over the two TEs. on the left side of the offensive formation. Clark, knowing that that his primary responsibility is the inside TE, either soaking up the block or sticking to him in coverage, is plastered to the TE #82. However, McLaughlin, likely feeling the responsibility of having to make a play against a potential run, plays the run aggressively and loses track of the TE #12. This leaves a wide open man for their QB to dump the ball off to down field for a chunk gain.

I’m not sure if we would’ve been better off playing base 4-3/3-4 personnel against their 12 personnel where an LB would’ve been matched up on one of the TEs. At the end of the day, McLaughlin’s guy is who got open, and I wouldn’t want to sub out McLaughlin for the LB. Maybe he wouldn’t have played the run so aggressively if there were another LB on the field, but that aggression is also what makes him such a playmaker for our defense. Again, MSU’s offense isn’t a juggernaut, and their run game wasn’t having a field day like Iowa or Penn State’s was, so that could be the reason why we stuck with base nickel personnel. Regardless, the fact that we’re seemingly splitting run/pass responsibilities to account for some of our personnel mismatches does seem to indicate a recognition that we’re struggling with the 12 personnel runs when playing nickel.

Awgs’ Bonus Play(s) of the Week

Jacob Manu takes this week’s honors with an incredible, athletic heads up INT, making an already bad play for the Spartans even worse.

issues.title: 24 teams come together to form Collective Cycling Group, the latest venture aiming to 'unlock the value' of pro cycling
issues.summary: Collective Cycling Group rises from the ashes of One Cycling with official announcement
issues.author: Laura Weislo
issues.content_html:
Following the collapse of the One Cycling project that aimed to reform professional cycling into a more lucrative business model, a new group has officially made its presence known with similar aims but stronger support. The Collective Cycling Group (CCG) issued a press release on Wednesday announcing the new movement.

It was stated that 24 teams from the men’s and women’s WorldTour and ProTeam ranks have already signed up, and that there are ongoing discussions with additional teams. Several teams have shared news of the announcement, indicating that they are part of the movement, but not all have.

The CCG aims to "develop and market selected commercial rights and activities to strengthen the economic model of professional cycling", according to the announcement.

It also wants to "unlock the value potential of professional cycling, elevate the product to better serve a global fan base, and address the need for a more sustainable economic model in professional road cycling and the broadening of its global reach".

The company is registered in the UK and is essentially the same entity as One Cycling, with government files showing the name was changed to Collective Cycling Group on June 2, 2026.

Soon after, ownership of the project changed hands, with Visma-Lease a Bike team boss Richard Plugge standing down both as a 'director' and 'a person with significant control', and replaced in both cases by Oliver Ciesla, a sports marketing executive who previously worked in motorsport.

"This broad and inclusive initiative by so many teams represents a significant milestone in the long and proud history of the sport," Ciesla said.

"Teams carry much of the sporting and financial risk in professional cycling, while many of the sport’s commercial opportunities remain fragmented. The UCI reform process creates a first opportunity to address these challenges together.

"Through a closer cooperation with organisers, the UCI and other stakeholders, teams can create products that none could offer alone, enhancing the experience of fans worldwide, increasing the sport’s visibility, and contributing to a sustainable economic model."

Which teams are on board?

It was not stated in the launch announcement which 24 teams have signed up to form the Collective Cycling Group.

Some teams have since publicly shared the announcement, indicating they are on board. Those teams include EF Education, which has men’s and women’s WorldTour squads, Canyon-SRAM, and Pinarello-Q36.5.

Given Richard Plugge’s prominent role in One Cycling and the push for reform more generally, it can reasonably be assumed that Visma-Lease a Bike are part of the project.

According to Escape Collective, 13 of the 18 men’s WorldTour teams have signed up. The five absentees were said to be UAE Team Emirates-XRG, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, Netcompany-Ineos, Jayco-AlUla, and Groupama-FDJ United.

As for the Women’s WorldTour, 10 of the 14 teams are reportedly signed up, with UAE Team l’IMAD, FDJ United-Suez, Liv AlUla Jayco, and Human Powered Health declining.

Why now?

Revamping pro cycling's business model has been a decades-long ambition for many of the stakeholders of a sport

Tour de France owners Amaury Sport Organisation (ASO) are one of the few to be profiting off the sport.

The UCI's formation of the ProTour (now WorldTour) under Hein Verbruggen could be considered to be one of the first attempts at modernizing pro cycling, although the effort was met with extreme resistance from the ASO.

The WorldTour promised to bring more stability to teams, with three-year guaranteed entry into the biggest races, but the sponsorship model of professional cycling remains on shaky ground.

Teams with billionaire backers and generous budgets dominate the sport, while smaller outfits such as TotalEnergies have had to fight for their lives after sponsors pull out.

Even One Cycling wasn't the first try at a new model: In 2011, the Rothschild financial group were backers of what was then called a 'breakaway league' - the World Series Cycling (WSC), with 14 teams on board.

The Velon group came in 2014, with a more modest ambition to add on-board footage and real-time rider stats to their marketing campaigns. How teams really benefited from being a part of Velon is less concrete, and mainly helps with fan engagement and commercialization.

How the CCG will differ from the previous attempts remain to be seen.

One Cycling failed to obtain support from the UCI, who deemed the project as "incompatible with the governance and regulatory framework of the UCI as well as lacking sporting coherence" last June.

How the new CCG project will be received by the UCI should become more clear after the WorldTour seminar, which runs from December 9-10, 2026.

The UCI has its own reforms in the early stages, too, with the results of a massive stakeholder consultation released during the Road World Championships in Montreal.

The topics included calendar and participation, the economic model, fan engagement, safety and integrity.

Some of the ideas floated in the document include shortening Grand Tours to 16 days, budget caps, and joint broadcast rights.

issues.title: Primož Roglič will continue racing into 2027 as new team for 'final chapter' is finally revealed
issues.summary: Multiple-time Grand Tour winner and current European TT champion to lead NSN Cycling on one-year contract
issues.author: James Moultrie
issues.content_html:
After months of speculation, Primož Roglič will continue his career into 2027, having signed with NSN Cycling Team on a one-year contract.

The 37-year-old looked to be heading for retirement after his time with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe came to an end – despite being the reigning European time trial champion and having finished second at the Vuelta a España in September – but with NSN, he has found a place for the final chapter of his storied career.

A five-time Grand Tour winner, Roglič will make up part of the Swiss WorldTour team’s general classification ambitions, alongside fellow new signings for 2027, Richard Carapaz and Lennert Van Eetvelt.

"I always like challenges. That's why I'm here, to take these on together and see what the future brings us," said Roglič on the team's website.

"It took me some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never. It feels like the perfect connection.

"I still believe I have some work to do – in both racing and with myself. I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things."

10 years after his first WorldTour season with LottoNL-Jumbo, former ski jumper Roglič will arrive at NSN as the rider with the most victories among active men's pros at 93, only trailing Slovenian compatriot Tadej Pogačar.

Now into his late 30s, he's raced limited calendars in recent seasons, but can still ramp up his performance for the big occasion at Grand Tours, finishing second at the most recent Vuelta, eighth at last year's Tour de France, and winning his fourth Vuelta title as recently as 2024.

Delighted by bringing in the talents of one of the modern era's best GC riders, NSN revealed their new star signing with a social media post of Roglič following NSN on Instagram.

"Welcoming Primož Roglič to NSN Cycling Team is a hugely exciting moment for our organization. From the first moment we spoke, it was evident that Primož still has a lot of passion for the sport and a drive to be the best he can. It was an easy decision to make," said NSN General Manager Kjell Carlström.

"Primož is one of the outstanding riders of his generation. His achievements speak for themselves, and the opportunity to bring someone with his experience, quality and winning mentality into our team is something we are incredibly proud of.

"This signing reflects the ambition we have for the future. We want to compete at the highest level, challenge for major results and continue building a team capable of achieving great things. We are confident that Primož can play an important role in that journey, and we look forward to seeing him race in NSN colours."

issues.title: Broken frame no problem for Lukas Malezsewski, who wins UCI Gravel race after being hit by a driver
issues.summary: Malezsewski was struck during The Gravel of Marathon in Greece
issues.author: Owen Rogers
issues.content_html:
A broken chainstay proved no problem for Belgian gravel racer Lukas Malezsewski, who won the Greek round of the UCI Gravel World Series last weekend.

Riding for Greg van Avermaet’s GVA Gold team, Malezsewski was just 17km into The Gravel of Marathon race when the incident happened: a driver hit him, breaking the chainstay on the drive side of his Basso bike frame.

But rather than give up, the 25-year-old remounted and raced on, eventually winning the Elite Men’s race more than three minutes ahead of second-placed Kasper Enstad.

In its first edition, The Gravel of Marathon is the first UCI round of the UCI Gravel World Series to be staged in Greece, starting and finishing in the ancient city of Marathon. The Elite men raced over a 95km course, which, though relatively short, comprised more than 1,300m of vertical ascent, with 71% of the course off-road.

Malezsewski was hit by the vehicle after the day’s first climb, and not long after emerging from the route’s second gravel sector. "Got hit by a car after 17km and broke my frame. Still made it to the finish line in first place," Malezsewski wrote in an Instagram post.

Rather than treading the well-worn path to gravel from road racing, Malezsewski is an accomplished mountain bike rider, winning the European junior title in 2019 and the Belgian under-23 title in 2022, though he’s not raced at UCI level since 2024.

While he’s raced occasionally at national and UCI .2 level on the road since then, he’s concentrated on gravel.

And to great effect, winning two UCI races last year and repeating the feat this season, when he won Tartu Rattmaraton in Estonia in mid-September, before finishing in the top six of every other race he started before last weekend’s Greek event.

issues.title: 'Tour de France Femmes goal for 2029' – There’s a new US team on the scene, and they have big ambitions
issues.summary: Andrea Cyr and Aline Seitz to lead Austin-based Orange Seal p/b Autowurks for inaugural season in 2027 at Continental level
issues.author: Jackie Tyson
issues.content_html:
The paperwork has been submitted to the UCI and Dr. Andrea Cyr expects to lead the next US-based Continental women's team, Orange Seal presented by Autowurks, in 2027.

The team will be based in Austin, Texas with a "clear ambition" to become a top-25 team in the world with a majority of riders from the United States, and to earn a place in the Tour de France Femmes by 2029.

"We have high aspirations, but the first step is we're going to be a Continental team for 2027. We want to be a ProTeam in 2028, that's where you start to get a lot of the invites like the Classics and bigger UCI stage racing. Then we have a Tour to France Femmes goal of 2029," Cyr told Cyclingnews.

"A lot of this is sparked by my own ambition too. There's some development programmes to get people interested in the sport and then there's WorldTour, but there's nothing in between. I'm in a unique position, with resources and networking to actually put things together. A year ago this was not the plan."

For her 14th season racing bikes, Cyr, who is also a sports medicine doctor, launched a six-rider domestic elite women's squad in 2026 to continue her career and provide earning opportunities for other female athletes. A total of 10 supported riders meshed well and went on to land 70 podiums across North American events, mainly one-day races, with Cyr scoring a win and second overall at the 2026 Chicago GRIT series and Aline Seitz of Switzerland second overall in the American Criterium Cup.

The new team merges Cyr's HigherDOSE-Renova criterium-based programme with the former ROXO Continental women's squad, which last competed in 2024 as Boneshaker Project presented by Orange Seal.

"We didn't want this to just be a one-year adventure. We wanted to do something a little bit more sustainable," Cyr said about the next step after HigherDOSE. "So we started conversations with a management group from Texas. All three of these guys have different roles, they've known each other for like 20 years. I think they have found new vigor and motivation through this too."

Leadership at Orange Seal p/b Autowurks includes former WorldTour rider Chann McRae as head sports director, Austin attorney Todd Reed as team manager, and real estate executive Charlie Tames as co-owner. The trio had most recently been involved in supporting French women's ProTeam Mayenne Monbana My Pie. Justin Kirk will split time as a sports director with the women's team and the Texas Roadhouse elite masters team. This quartet of management, along with Cyr, form the ownership group for the team.

"Our goal is to build a top-25 team in the world with a majority of riders from the United States and the resources to compete in the biggest races. Bringing these programs together gives us an established foundation to build on," Tames said in a team statement after a formal launch party in Austin on November 15.

"The 2027 season is the first step toward our top-25 ambition and our goal of reaching the Tour de France Femmes by 2029."

More than half of the roster will come from HigherDOSE, including Cyr and Seitz, with Marjie Bemis, Elizabeth Dixon and Odette Lynch preserving the foundation created in 2026. The ROXO connection brings Femenina a Guatemala stage winner Kira Payer, as well as additional leadership and resources to support the next stage of growth.

Other new riders include Canadian Jenna Nestman, former Fount Cycling rider Alia Shafi, and Nicole Steinmetz, who previously raced for Cynisca and Virginia's Blue Ridge TWENTY24. According to Cyr, two more riders have been offered contracts and the full roster will be confirmed in the coming weeks.

"American racers are struggling, and it's really struggling on the women's side. I personally started shifting my own goals and my own thinking, and I had a really good result at Pro Road Nationals, a top 10 in the road race, fourth in the crit, and then had a really good result at Philly. I got to thinking, maybe I'm more than just a crit racer," Cyr described to Cyclingnews her inspiration to form a new team.

"It was really awesome to have Philly back, and I finished that race [top 15 - Ed.], and I was like, 'That was the best day ever! Like that was my favorite ever.'

"We need more of this, like hard racing with strong teams and strong riders from all over the world. This is what I'm craving, and I know I'm not alone in that. I know a lot of other female racers are probably looking for the same thing."

Once Continental status is confirmed, the team plans to firm the 2027 calendar with UCI races in South America and Europe for the spring, and a return block of racing to Europe in July and August. Key US races will include Redlands Bicycle Classic, Tour of the Gila, USPro Road Nationals and Philadelphia Cycling Classic p/b AmeriGas, as well as a selection of criteriums.

"We want a well-rounded race calendar, but also aware of our short and long-term goals. To achieve our long-term goals, we need to get points and really establish quickly as a strong, confident team," Cyr said.

"It's important to stay engaged with the racing we have here in the U.S., which is a lot of criterium racing. It's good for sponsors."

Orange Seal joins as title sponsor, with Autowurks as presenting sponsor. The team is also supported by bike sponsor Winspace with equipment and apparel partners ABUS, Tifosi, MUMU and Schwalbe.

issues.content_html:
It may have been a different era, but the 1970s contain salutary lessons for a club in serious decline once again

In many ways, there are striking parallels between the Manchester United relegated in 1974 and the Manchester United sitting in the relegation zone at this stage of the season for the first time in 40 years. A legendary manager leaves, his shadow remains; with boardroom dithering and uncertainty, his replacements churn and burn as the club slide over several years.

Sir Matt Busby stepped aside as manager of the 1968 European Cup-winning side, but stayed on as a director, just as Sir Alex Ferguson did, watching from the Old Trafford directors’ box as successors tried and failed.

issues.summary: The time for formal measures has passed but all involved have betrayed the trust of a country whose Test team is sacred Cry havoc. But Cameron Bancroft did not let anything slip, not after close to a decade of keeping his mouth firmly shut. It was a deliberate, considered and lengthy deed of revelation that the former Test opening bat chose to publish in the West Australian newspaper on Wednesday,
issues.author: Geoff Lemon
issues.content_html:
The time for formal measures has passed but all involved have betrayed the trust of a country whose Test team is sacred

Cry havoc. But Cameron Bancroft did not let anything slip, not after close to a decade of keeping his mouth firmly shut. It was a deliberate, considered and lengthy deed of revelation that the former Test opening bat chose to publish in the West Australian newspaper on Wednesday, claiming to finally fill in a wealth of detail around Australian cricket’s 2018 cheating scandal that so many others seem to have gone to such lengths to keep concealed.

It was also a devastating repudiation of Pat Cummins, a teammate of equivalent juniority to Bancroft during their few months playing together, but now the Test captain, who had delivered his own manifesto in spoken form at a press conference last week. That version of events, in which Cummins was adamant that he had never been aware of any kind of ball-tampering in Australian colours, was what pushed Bancroft from silence to speech. “It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone,” Bancroft wrote. “What I saw, experienced and lived with not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously.”

The latest legal case against the men’s world No 1 brought by the mother of the former couple’s daughter alleges that Zverev violated the terms of an out-of-court settlement between the pair after the woman accused him of assaulting her.
