  • Audit connections: HubSpot’s audit logs show who has connected it and when.
  • Restrict accounts: Claude Enterprise admins can block HubSpot connections from Claude accounts outside their Enterprise organization.

Measure efficiency and pipeline contribution.

  • Time savings: Time one recurring task, like the weekly campaign readout, for a few cycles before and after rollout.
  • Adoption: Team and Enterprise owners can see who uses Claude and which features stick in its usage analytics. On Enterprise, the dashboard also splits usage and cost by group and lists the skills and connectors each group used beside its spend.
  • Follow-up speed: Track the days between event registration and first personalized outreach, plus how quickly stalled deals get a next step.
  • Revenue: HubSpot Marketing Hub supports automation and reporting, including campaign Revenue reports (Professional) and model-based Revenue Attribution (Enterprise). Treat gaps between Claude-assisted and manual campaigns as leads to investigate, since timing, budget, and audience also move revenue.

When to Use Dashboards Instead of Claude AI for Marketing

Dashboards support recurring KPI monitoring better than ad hoc AI analysis. Questions that repeat on a fixed cadence, like weekly lead volume against goal or monthly pipeline created, deserve a saved report that answers them without anyone typing a prompt.

HubSpot dashboards group related reports on one screen for a specific audience or goal. Owners control access by keeping a dashboard private, opening it to the whole account, or limiting it to chosen users and teams. Report emails can run on a daily, weekly, or monthly schedule, and dashboard emails can recur as well, though only HubSpot users can receive the recurring versions. Each recipient gets the same report configuration every cycle, with no prompt involved.

Claude covers the questions nobody has built a report for. Saved reports and dashboards don’t appear among the objects the HubSpot connector for Claude can read, so Claude works from records such as contacts, deals, campaigns, and marketing emails instead. That suits one-off, multi-condition questions, like which contacts opened a launch email in the past two weeks, have an open deal, and haven’t heard from sales since. Claude also handles the conversation and help desk summaries mentioned earlier, where the answer is a pattern in written text.

The Claude Cowork scheduling from the follow-up section still fits here: It can draft commentary on recurring numbers while the numbers themselves stay on a dashboard.

Teams get the most from running the two in sequence:

  1. Spot the change: A dashboard shows landing page conversions dropped last week.
  2. Diagnose it: Claude reviews that page’s campaign results alongside recent customer conversations and email clicks to suggest likely causes.
  3. Act on it: Claude drafts revised copy and, once you approve the edit, updates the landing page in HubSpot.

Frequently Asked Questions About Claude AI for Marketing

How can I connect Claude to HubSpot without developer support?

The HubSpot connector for Claude installs without code. You need a paid Claude subscription plus an active HubSpot user account at any edition, even free. Open Claude’s Settings > Connectors, click Browse, find HubSpot, click Connect, and sign in to grant permissions. Unless you’re a Super Admin or have App Marketplace Access, a Super Admin approves it first.

What are the best Claude prompts for email and ads in HubSpot?

Strong prompts give Claude a job title, the HubSpot records to check, and an output shape. For email, have Claude write a follow-up for contacts who opened a send without clicking, saved as a HubSpot marketing email. Ads differ: Since the connector can’t create them, Claude drafts headline variants from help desk objections for your ad platform.

How do I keep Claude on-brand and compliant?

For brand voice, convert your style guide into a skill that Team and Enterprise owners can provision org-wide. For compliance, set Write tools to Needs Approval so every edit waits for your Yes.

When should I rely on dashboards instead of Claude?

Rely on dashboards for metrics your team revisits every week or month, since HubSpot can email those reports automatically. Turn to Claude for unplanned questions that combine several filters and for themes hidden in support conversations. Dashboards aren’t on the connector’s readable object list, so Claude pulls numbers straight from deals, campaigns, and other records.

How should I measure ROI from Claude inside HubSpot?

Measure time and money separately. Clock a repeat task, like a campaign recap, now and again once Claude handles it. Team and Enterprise owners can see connector users, read and write action counts, and estimated time saved in Claude’s analytics. For money, Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise include a campaign ROI report weighing revenue against spend.

issues.title: AI influencers: What consumer sentiment data tells brands
issues.summary: As you scroll through your TikTok or Instagram feed, you’ll no doubt come across at least a handful of influencers trying to sell you something by wearing the latest viral lip gloss, hopping into luxury cars, and taste-testing popular treats. But what if I told you that while these content creators may look like real people, they’re actually AI influencers?
issues.author: esantiago@hubspot.com (Erica Santiago)
issues.content_html:
As you scroll through your TikTok or Instagram feed, you’ll no doubt come across at least a handful of influencers trying to sell you something by wearing the latest viral lip gloss, hopping into luxury cars, and taste-testing popular treats. But what if I told you that while these content creators may look like real people, they’re actually AI influencers?

If you’re a marketer or business owner who is already fully using AI in your digital marketing strategy, then you’re likely already familiar with the concept. You may even be curious about leveraging AI influencers in your influencer marketing strategy.

But how will your target consumers feel about the use of AI influencers? Will they be receptive, or can AI influencers erode the trust you’ve built with your audience? Can AI influencers really save you money compared to working with human influencers? And are all virtual influencers AI? Keep reading for answers to these questions and more.

Table of Contents

  • What are AI influencers, and why are brands considering them?
  • What do consumers think about AI influencers and AI models?
  • Do AI influencers build or erode brand trust?
  • Notable Virtual Influencers + Brand Examples to Learn From
  • Do AI influencers save brands money?
  • How to Use AI-Assisted Content Workflows Without Losing Authenticity
  • Common Pitfalls With AI Influencers and How to Avoid Backlash
  • What’s Next for AI Influencers
  • Frequently Asked Questions About AI Influencers

What are AI influencers, and why are brands considering them?

AI influencers are virtual personas whose appearance, voice, behaviors, or content are created or assisted by generative AI. An example of an AI influencer is Aitana Lopez, who has over 400,000 followers on Instagram. She’s marketed as a virtual fitness and lifestyle influencer and has promoted brands such as Amazon, Victoria’s Secret, Olaplex, and Razer.

Her work as an influencer has reportedly earned her and The Clueless, the Barcelona-based tech company that created her, over $11,000 per month.

          View this post on Instagram                      

A post shared by Aitana Lopez (@fit_aitana)

AI influencers fall under the umbrella of “virtual influencers,” but make no mistake — while every AI influencer is a virtual influencer, not all virtual influencers are AI-generated. For example, the virtual influencer, singer, and model Miquela Sousa (formerly known as Lil Miquela) was created in 2016 using artist-driven CGI, and her music is created by a collective of singers, songwriters, and instrumentalists—not generative AI.

Over the last decade, Miquela Sousa has worked with brands like Gucci, Prada, and Calvin Klein. She’s also the first virtual avatar to sign with a model agency, having signed to CAA in 2020 and previously being represented by WME.

          View this post on Instagram                      

A post shared by Miquela (@lilmiquela)

Why are brands interested in AI Influencers?

Brands are dabbling with using AI influencers and virtual models like Aitana Lopez and Miquela Sousa for three reasons — creative control, reduced costs, and scalable content.

Creative Control

Ruben Cruz, founder of The Clueless, says Aitana Lopez was created so the company could make a “better living and not be dependent on other people who have egos” or “who just want to make a lot of money by posing.”

In other words, Cruz wanted to avoid working with influencers whose personalities, creative processes, and work styles clash with his company’s creative vision—a sentiment brands wanting to leverage AI influencers can relate to.

AI and virtual creators will recite a script, deliver a video, or conform to a brand’s aesthetic exactly as agreed upon. Companies never have to worry about unwanted input or script changes that could slow production.

Reduced Costs

The initial creation of an AI influencer or virtual internet personality can cost anywhere from a few hundred dollars to a few hundred thousand. However, once out of the initial setup phase, AI influencers can save companies money on lighting, production, and paid partnerships.

Scalable Content

Human influencers need to sleep, eat, take breaks, pick up their kids from school, or walk the dog — they can’t make content 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. But AI influencers can. Though AI influencers like Aitana Lopez may look super busy doing their makeup, traveling, and hopping into luxury cars, it’s all fake— so they always have time to make content.

What do consumers think about AI influencers and AI models?

Many consumers feel that AI influencers corrode trust, with one Reddit user saying, “If I see something that is AI but tries to appear real, it’s an instant turn-off and trust killer. It’s enough for me to see it once for a brand, and the trust is gone forever.”

The skepticism toward AI influencers shows up in surveys, too. According to a study published via ResearchGate, 45.3% of consumers would view an ad with an AI influencer without taking action, 28.3% would ignore the ad completely, and only 26.4% would actively engage with the ad, such as by clicking or searching.

Do AI influencers build or erode brand trust?

AI influencers pose a high risk of eroding trust between brands and consumers because using a fake person to promote a brand’s goods or services doesn’t read as authentic. The appeal of human influencers and content creators is that they’re real people who cultivated a consistent following by being their genuine selves.

Influencers and content creators bond with their followers over shared interests, hobbies, and beliefs, and they often get their audience interested in a product or service by using it themselves.

In fact, a survey by Clutch shows that if a human influencer is found to use AI-generated content, 71% of consumers say they would question the recommendation, and 53% are less likely to buy from a brand known for using AI in social content.

An AI or virtual influencer can’t use a product or service, can’t have a genuine interest, nor a human experience to connect with human followers.

That said, the trust risk is not equal in every situation. It concentrates where audiences are skeptical, where safeguards are missing, where disclosure is weak, and where nobody is measuring the effect. Score each area below before you decide to leverage AI influencers.

How to score it:

  • Any No-go: Don’t launch. Fix the issue or choose a different approach.
  • All Go: Proceed to a limited pilot.
  • Mix of Go and Conditional: Launch only if each Conditional item has an owner and a fix date before the first post.

Why these four areas matter: Consumers aren’t rejecting AI across the board. That same Clutch survey also found that 42% view AI positively when it’s used for educational content, but 64% would trust a brand or creator less if AI were used to misrepresent products. Nearly 90% say it’s important to disclose AI-generated content.

Disclosure is also becoming a legal matter. For example, as of June 9, 2026, New York requires certain ads featuring AI-generated human performers to include a disclosure, and the EU’s Article 50 transparency obligations have applied since August 2, 2026. Always double-check to confirm what applies to your markets.

Notable Virtual Influencers + Brand Examples to Learn From

Virtual influencers have been working with brands for years, so their campaigns show what works and what doesn’t. Each example below is broken down by what it teaches about creativity, community, transparency, representation, and governance.

1. Miquela x PAC SUN Back-To-School Campaign

PacSun teamed up with Miquela for its back-to-school and holiday 2022 campaigns, and said the deal marked the start of a broader push into virtual influencers. The two collaborated on social content to amplify those seasonal campaigns after both had taken part in the ComplexLand digital event.

Source

Creative

The partnership was built around a persona who already lived online, with roughly 3 million Instagram followers at the time. Choosing a virtual star with an existing audience meant the brand didn’t have to build one from scratch.

Community

The fit rested on shared audience territory. PacSun framed the move as a way to strengthen its connection with a core demographic exploring the digital space. Takeaway: pick a persona whose community already overlaps with yours.

Transparency

Miquela is open about being a virtual influencer, describing herself as a “Robot living in LA,” so there was no deception to manage. The audience was in on it from the start.

Representation

PacSun’s president pointed to Miquela’s involvement in the Black Lives Matter movement and the Rally the Vote campaign as aligned with the brand’s values. That raises a fair question for any brand: a persona’s advocacy is authored by its creators, so scrutinize whose voice is really speaking.

Governance

A virtual star never ages, clothes always fit perfectly, and she does what you ask, but that control is also a responsibility. Set clear approval processes for any social or political messaging attached to a persona, since you are effectively the speaker.

2. Samsung and Sam

Sam is Samsung’s own virtual influencer, created in collaboration with Cheil and the Brazilian design firm Lightfarm. She is used mainly in Latin America, and in July 2023, she connected to the regional launch events from Seoul, where she covered the global Galaxy Unpacked event.

In January 2024, she was named Samsung’s AI ambassador ahead of Galaxy Unpacked 2024, where she was set to present products and interview five live influencers from Latin America.

Source

Creative

Sam works because she’s integrated into real brand moments rather than confined to social posts. She has blogged, made tutorials, released a music video promoting the Galaxy Z Flip 5, and helped sell devices at Unpacked events.

Giving a persona several jobs, from host to educator to performer, builds her into the brand’s story rather than treating her as a one-off stunt.

Community

Samsung paired Sam with real people. At Unpacked 2024, she interviewed Latin American creators live, bridging the virtual and human sides of the community. Her role was also regionally focused, which suggests a persona can work better as a local community figure than as a global one.

Transparency

Sam is openly presented as a virtual influencer, and Samsung’s own newsroom calls her one. Her role is also clear (host, guide, ambassador), so audiences aren’t asked to believe she personally uses Samsung products.

Representation

As a brand-owned character, Sam’s look, voice, and personality are entirely Samsung’s choices. Treat that as a casting decision: involve regional teams and creators in shaping a persona who will speak to their audience, rather than designing her centrally and exporting her.

Governance

Samsung reported that Sam helped boost early sales of its new devices in Latin America, including a 30% increase in sales on its Mexico live-shopping portal.

Set measurable goals and a content plan before launch, attribute any performance claims to their sources, and decide in advance who will maintain the persona, since a neglected virtual influencer can quickly feel stale.

3. Amazon Prime, boAt & Kyra

Kyra was launched by FUTR Studios in January 2022 as a virtual influencer that is both CGI and AI-powered. Her first brand partner was boAt for the #FutureOfAudio campaign, which launched its Rockerz 330 and 333 ANC neckbands.

Amazon Prime Video followed, integrating Kyra into the promotion for its sci-fi series “The Peripheral,” with her creator noting that the team recreated the show’s VR headset and transported her to its setting.

Source

Creative

Both campaigns leaned into science fiction, which is where a virtual persona excels. boAt said the collaboration enabled a sci-fi-like audio-visual experience that wouldn’t be possible with any other influencer. Choose briefs a human can’t easily deliver.

Community

The boAt launch reached beyond social posts. Kyra appeared at an in-person boAt party through a 3D projection installation, alongside human creators. Bridging virtual and live moments helps a persona feel part of a scene rather than an ad.

Transparency

The pairing with Prime Video worked partly because it was an obvious fiction-meets-fiction match. When the story is openly synthetic, disclosure becomes part of the creative rather than a caveat.

Representation

Kyra was positioned as India’s first virtual influencer, and her creators said they planned a new model with a South Indian focus. That’s a useful prompt for brands: local relevance matters, and a single persona rarely represents an entire market.

Governance

Early results were strong, but they come from launch-novelty periods. Judge a persona on sustained performance, not a debut.

4. Dior & Noonoouri

In 2018, Dior’s beauty team had Noonoouri recreate its Rouge Dior Ultra Rouge launch film. The original starred Natalie Portman; the tribute was nearly a shot-for-shot reenactment, down to the Dior ring. Noonoouri also took over the Maison’s Instagram during the Dior Cruise show.

Source

Creative

Rebuilding a famous campaign with a stylized animated character created instant buzz. The contrast between the original and the tribute did most of the work.

Community

Dior used the persona to reach younger Instagram audiences interested in high-end beauty. The takeaway is to match a persona to an audience you’re trying to grow, not just one you already have.

Transparency

Noonoouri’s doll-like proportions make her unmistakably an animation, so nobody is misled about what they’re seeing. A clearly stylized persona carries less deception risk than a photorealistic one.

Representation

Her exaggerated features reflect a stylized ideal, not a real body. Brands should consider what beauty standard a digital character promotes, especially in cosmetics.

Governance

Stepping into a role originally played by a real actress raises questions about likeness, permission, and optics. Clear agreements around any reference to a real person’s work are essential.

Do AI influencers save brands money?

AI can save brands money, but it depends on what you count. AI influencers can cut the most visible line item, production, while adding costs elsewhere: oversight, disclosure, rework, reputation, and measurement. A fair comparison looks at the total cost of the program, rather than the cost of a single post.

You can look up costs online but be aware that cost claims are mostly published by vendors and agencies that sell AI content, and they vary widely. Some guides puts AI influencer creation at $15,000 to $100,000+ upfront, with monthly costs of $500 to $15,000+. But other sources claim 80-95% savings on large volumes of video. Treat all of these numbers as starting points for your own testing, not benchmarks.

Taking a Total-Cost View

1. Production. This is where savings are most credible. Once a persona exists, the marginal cost of producing one more piece of content approaches zero, and there are no talent fees, travel, or scheduling.

The catch is the upfront build and the ongoing work of generating, editing, and approving content. A persona that looks effortless usually still has a team behind it.

2. Risk management. Brands often cite reduced risk of scandal as a draw. In a World Federation of Advertisers finding reported by Favikon, 58% of brands interested in AI influencers named reduced risk of influencer scandals as a top draw. But the risk doesn’t disappear completely; it only changes shape.

You swap the risk of a creator’s behavior for the risk of your own content errors, off-brand outputs, or a backlash against the concept itself. Budget for review and an escalation plan.

3. Disclosure compliance. This cost is growing. Platforms like Instagram and TikTok have their own AI labeling rules and protocols. And other countries and regions have legal requirements regarding AI disclosure. In the EU, for example, transparency obligations for AI-generated content began to apply in August 2026.

The direct cost is modest, covering labels, templates, and legal review. The hidden cost is audience trust: consumer distrust is a recognized downside when disclosure is unclear.

4. Rework. Generated content needs corrections: anatomical glitches, inconsistent facial expressions, misreading cultural cues, tone issues. Rework hours rarely appear in a vendor’s cost comparison, so track them in your own use case.

5. PR and reputation. As I said earlier, public perception of AI influencers or synthetic personas ranges from curiosity to hostility, and it varies by category and audience. Set aside time and budget for a communications plan, including how you’ll respond if people accuse you of replacing real creators.

6. Community impact. Human creators bring a ready audience and a relationship with it. A new AI persona has to build both. The savings can also be offset on the other side: some AI adopters found that when creators use AI to cut their own costs, those savings haven’t led to lower fees, because brands pay for influence and credibility.

And partnerships with AI accounts aren’t a sure thing; Data shows that brand deals with AI social accounts fell by about 30% in the first eight months of 2025 compared with the same period in 2024.

7. Measurement. Fairly comparing AI and human influencers takes planning. You need matched campaigns, consistent metrics, and enough time to see past the novelty effect. Some of this has a real cost in analyst hours and tooling, and without it, you’re making decisions based on anecdotes.

As one analysis puts it, the honest comparison isn’t a cost debate but a question of what a campaign asks the influencer to do.

Where AI Influencers Tend to Save Money (and Where They Don’t)

They tend to help when you need high volumes of content, many variations to test, a tightly controlled brand look, or multilingual output. They tend to be a poor fit when the sale depends on lived experience or personal credibility, such as skincare results, health claims, parenting, or financial advice.

There, the cheaper post can cost you in conversion and trust.

A Qualitative Worksheet to Complete Before You Model Any Finances

Before you build a spreadsheet, answer these in plain language. If your team can’t answer them, then you’ll already know you need to reevaluate your strategy.

Then add two summary questions: What is the strongest reason this would save us money, and what is the strongest reason it wouldn’t? Count the “High” ratings. A cluster of them in risk, disclosure, or community impact is a signal to slow down, no matter how good the production savings look.

Then, build the model.

Once you’ve done the worksheet, a simple model has four parts: one-time setup costs, recurring monthly costs, the hidden costs from your worksheet (rework hours, legal review, monitoring, crisis reserve), and the performance side (conversions, engagement, or sales per dollar spent). Run it against a human-creator pilot of similar scope, and revisit it after a quarter, not a week.

The Bottom Line

AI influencers can lower the cost of making content. Whether they lower the cost of the program depends on your category, your audience, your compliance exposure, and how honestly you count what’s outside the production line. The brands most likely to come out ahead are the ones that measure the whole picture and start small.

How to Use AI-Assisted Content Workflows Without Losing Authenticity

Audiences forgive AI-assisted content that’s honest and consistent. They don’t forgive content that feels off-brand, evasive, or unreviewed. Build the workflow around human judgment, and aim for consistency over perfection.

Codify your brand voice.

Write the voice down in a form both people and AI tools can use.

  • Voice guide: Tone, vocabulary, phrases to use and avoid, and a few on-brand and off-brand examples.
  • Persona sheet (if you use a virtual influencer): Backstory, values, topics they will and won’t discuss, and visual style.
  • Standing prompts: Turn the guide into reusable instructions so every draft starts from the same baseline.

Set clear approvals.

Not every asset needs the same scrutiny. Tier them by risk:

  • Low risk (routine posts, repurposed content): Social lead approves.
  • Medium risk (sponsored content, product claims): Brand and social approve.
  • High risk (health, finance, political or social topics, anything involving a real person’s likeness): Brand, legal, and social all approve.

Name one person who can pull a post immediately.

Standardize disclosure.

Create templates in advance so disclosure is never improvised. Cover three cases: AI-generated persona, AI-assisted content from a human creator, and paid partnerships. Each should state who made it and whether it’s an ad, in plain language. Have legal review the templates once, then reuse them.

Check requirements for each platform and market, since they differ and are changing.

Govern your assets.

Keep one source of truth for approved content.

  • Store approved images, prompts, character references, and disclosure templates in a single library with version history.
  • Log which tool and prompt produced each asset.
  • Record usage rights, especially for any real person’s likeness or voice.
  • Retire outdated assets so they can’t be reused by accident.

A content management system, such as HubSpot Content Hub, can serve as a shared home for assets and approval steps, but the process matters more than the tool.

Run review loops.

  • Before publishing: Check voice, accuracy, cultural fit, and disclosure. Reject anything that looks polished but feels hollow.
  • After publishing: Review comments and sentiment weekly in the early weeks.
  • Monthly: Compare a sample of recent posts against the voice guide to catch drift, and update the guide with what you learn.

Establish who owns what.

Escalate questions on tone to brand, questions on claims or rights to legal, and questions on audience reaction to social. One person should own the overall workflow so nothing falls between teams.

Favor consistency over realism.

Hyper-realistic output isn’t the goal. A persona that stays recognizable, sounds like your brand, and is clearly labeled will earn more trust than one that’s flawlessly lifelike but inconsistent. When in doubt, a human decides.

Common Pitfalls With AI Influencers and How to Avoid Backlash

Most backlash comes from a few repeatable mistakes, but each one is avoidable.

Weak Disclosure

The problem: Audiences feel tricked when they discover a persona is AI after the fact, and regulators and platforms increasingly expect clear labeling.

How to avoid it: Say it upfront. Put the AI label in the bio and on sponsored posts, and use plain language rather than burying it in hashtags.

Uncanny Visuals

The problem: Almost-human faces, odd hands, and inconsistent features break trust fast and invite mockery.

How to avoid it: Choose a stylization you can execute well and keep it consistent. A clearly stylized character often lands better than a flawed attempt at photorealism. Have a human review every image before it goes live.

Values Misalignment

The problem: A persona that comments on social issues or endorses products it can’t plausibly use will seem opportunistic, because a company is writing every word.

How to avoid it: Define what the persona will and won’t talk about. Skip causes you aren’t prepared to support with real action, and avoid testimonials that depend on personal experience.

Poor Representation

The problem: Using AI to depict diverse identities without involving those communities can read as tokenism, and generative models can reproduce stereotypes.

How to avoid it: Involve people from the communities being portrayed in development and review. Use AI personas alongside human creators rather than as a replacement for them.

Over-Automation

The problem: Fully automated posting and replies produce tone-deaf responses, repeated phrasing, and errors nobody catches in time.

How to avoid it: Keep a human in the approval loop for anything public, especially replies, sensitive topics, and sponsored content. Automate drafting and scheduling, not judgment.

Unclear Ownership

The problem: If it’s unclear who owns the persona, the underlying model outputs, or any real person’s likeness or voice involved, disputes can surface at the worst moment.

How to avoid it: Document ownership and usage rights in contracts from the start, including agency and vendor agreements. Record which tools and training materials were used.

Mitigation Checklist

Disclosure

  • AI label appears in the bio and on every relevant post
  • Sponsored content is marked as an ad
  • Disclosure wording is approved by legal and checked for each platform and market.

Visual Authenticity

  • Style is consistent and deliberate, not a half-realistic compromise
  • A human has checked every asset for glitches and artifacts
  • A reference sheet defines the persona’s look

Voice Consistency

  • A written voice guide and persona sheet exist
  • Off-limits topics are defined
  • Posts are sampled monthly against the guide

Cultural Review

  • Content is reviewed by people familiar with the target market
  • Imagery and language are checked for stereotypes
  • Community members are consulted where the persona represents them

Consent

  • Written consent covers any real person’s likeness or voice
  • Contracts specify permitted uses, duration, and compensation
  • Rights to the persona and its assets are documented

Privacy

  • Follower data and DMs are handled under your privacy policy
  • No personal data is entered into AI tools without approval
  • Data practices comply with the rules in each market you serve

Crisis Response

  • One person has authority to pause or remove content immediately
  • A holding statement is drafted in advance
  • Roles for brand, legal, and social are assigned
  • A plan exists for retiring or pausing the persona if trust breaks down

What’s Next for AI Influencers

I can absolutely see both virtual and AI influencers becoming more common as businesses further integrate AI into their digital marketing strategy, but three shifts are worth planning around: more interactivity, more personalization, and tighter regulation. The regulatory evidence is much stronger than the evidence on the other two, so plan accordingly.

Near-term Shifts

Interactivity: expect more, with thin evidence so far. Industry commentary points to AI influencers paired with chatbots to offer 24/7 personalized engagement. Marketers also describe tracking conversation depth and return engagement as AI-driven interactions grow. Most of this is vendor and agency commentary rather than measured results, so treat it as direction, rather than proof. One practical point is firm, though: if a persona chats with people, EU rules now require that they be told they’re interacting with AI (see below).

Personalization: promised, not yet proven. Brands can use AI personas to give customers more personalized attention without expanding costly support teams. I found no independent data showing this works better than human-led engagement, so test it before building a strategy on it.

Regulation: the clearest shift. Governments are starting to set rules for AI-generated content in advertising, particularly around disclosure. For example, the EU’s AI Act includes transparency requirements for AI-generated content and for AI systems that interact with people.

In the US, New York has passed a law requiring disclosure of AI-generated “synthetic performers” in ads, and the FTC has indicated that its endorsement guidance applies to virtual endorsers as well as human ones. Other jurisdictions are considering similar measures.

Now, I’m not a lawyer and this isn’t legal advice, but I can tell you these rules differ by region and platform, and they change frequently. So, before running a campaign with an AI persona, check the current requirements for each market you’re targeting with qualified counsel.

Review quarterly.

Rules, platforms, and tools are changing quickly enough that annual reviews will lag. Each quarter, review four things:

  • Policies: Check disclosure language and templates against current EU, US federal, and state requirements. Update anything that changed.
  • Voice standards: Compare a sample of recent posts against your voice guide and persona sheet. Fix drift and add new examples of on-brand and off-brand content.
  • Vendors: Reconfirm contracts, usage rights, data handling, and AI-labeling features. Ask what changed in their tools and terms.
  • Pilot results: Review performance against your human-creator benchmark, plus sentiment, rework time, and incidents. Decide to continue, adjust, or stop.

Assign one owner to run the review, with brand, legal, and social each contributing.

Start with a phased pilot.

The timeframes below are suggestions, so adjust them to your campaign cycle.

Phase 1: Limit channels (weeks 1-4). Launch on one or two channels and in a limited set of markets. Start with the markets where disclosure rules are clearest. Write starter creative guardrails before the first post, covering topics to avoid, tone, and approval steps.

Phase 2: Test messages (weeks 4-8). Run small A/B tests comparing AI-persona content with a human-creator benchmark on the same message. Change one variable at a time and measure conversion, not only engagement.

Phase 3: Monitor sentiment (ongoing from launch). Review comments, mentions, and shares weekly. Track whether audience reaction is curious, neutral, or hostile, and flag any confusion about whether the persona is AI. Set a threshold in advance for when you pause.

Phase 4: Codify guardrails and decide (weeks 8-12). Turn what you learned into written rules for visuals, voice, topics, disclosure, and escalation. Then make an explicit scale, hold, or stop decision based on results and sentiment, not momentum.

Expand only after a pilot passes your own criteria. Keeping it small is what lets you change course cheaply.

Frequently Asked Questions About AI Influencers

Do AI influencers need to disclose that they are AI?

In practice, yes, and the rules are tightening. Platforms like Meta, TikTok, and YouTube have their own AI labeling requirements. On the legal side, the EU’s AI Act transparency obligations (Article 50) began to apply from 2 August 2026, and they cover content generated or modified with AI.

In the US, the FTC still expects a clear “this is paid” disclosure on sponsored posts. Some sources also report that the FTC treats presenting an AI-generated persona as a real human without disclosure as potentially deceptive, and that several states are moving toward requiring a synthetic-performer disclosure.

Treat the legal details as a moving target and have counsel review any paid campaign, especially if it reaches EU audiences. Beyond compliance, disclosure is also good brand hygiene: audiences tend to react worse to a reveal than to an upfront label.

How should brands measure AI influencer success?

Use the same core metrics you’d apply to any creator: reach, engagement rate, click-through, conversions, and cost per acquisition. Then add a few that are specific to synthetic personas.

Track audience sentiment (are comments curious, indifferent, or hostile?), brand-lift or recall in the persona’s target segment, and content production efficiency, since one of the main advantages is speed and cost.

Be cautious with headline numbers. Some analyses suggest AI personas can be cheaper than human creators. In contrast, others find human influencers drive higher engagement, so run your own test against a human-creator benchmark rather than trusting industry averages.

When should brands avoid AI influencers?

Avoid them wherever personal credibility is the product. That includes skincare or supplement claims that rely on real results, health and wellness advice, parenting, financial guidance, and any category where followers expect lived experience.

An AI persona can’t truthfully say “I tried this and it worked for me.” They tend to fit better into visual, aspirational, or entertainment-led categories such as fashion, gaming, and lifestyle.

Also steer clear if your audience is hostile to synthetic content, if you can’t commit to clear disclosure, or if your team lacks the capacity to manage the persona consistently over time. Public backlash against AI-generated models in fashion advertising shows the reputational risk is real.

Can AI influencers fit DEI and representation priorities?

They can broaden the range of faces and identities a brand shows, but they come with real trade-offs. A brand can create personas across ages, body types, ethnicities, and abilities without a casting budget.

The risk is that this substitutes for hiring and paying real people from those communities, and it can read as tokenism or “representation without the representatives.” Generative models also carry biases from their training data, so outputs often skew toward narrow beauty standards unless you actively guide them.

A sensible approach is to use AI personas alongside human creators rather than instead of them, involve people from the communities being depicted in the creative process, and review outputs for stereotypes before publishing.

How do we keep brand voice consistent with AI-assisted content?

Start with a documented voice guide: tone, vocabulary, words to avoid, and example posts that are on-brand and off-brand.

Feed that guide into your prompts or tooling as a standing reference, and keep a fixed character sheet for the persona (backstory, values, visual style) so the look and personality don’t drift between posts. Keep a human editor in the approval loop, especially for anything customer-facing or sponsored.

Finally, audit regularly by comparing a sample of recent posts against your guide, since drift tends to creep in gradually.

issues.title: AEO benchmarking: What market data reveals about AI search
issues.summary: AEO benchmarking measures your brand’s AI search visibility against competitors and market trends. It tells you whether a change in your visibility comes from the market or from your own brand, so you can prove performance to leadership before you change tactics.
issues.author: ttaylor@hubspot.com (Tristen Taylor)
issues.content_html:
AEO benchmarking measures your brand’s AI search visibility against competitors and market trends. It tells you whether a change in your visibility comes from the market or from your own brand, so you can prove performance to leadership before you change tactics.

Here’s the problem it solves.

Your AI visibility drops this week, and you can’t tell whether ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity changed how they answer or your content slipped. Without a benchmark, every dip looks like your fault — and every spike looks like your win.

Table of Contents

  • What is AEO benchmarking, and why does it matter now?
  • AEO Benchmarking With a Two-Tier Model: Market Benchmarks Plus Brand Performance
  • What to Measure in AEO Benchmarking: Citations, Share of Voice, and Sentiment
  • How AEO Benchmarking Datasets Work: Prompt Cohorts, Cadence, and Coverage
  • AEO Benchmarking Tools You Can Try Now with AI Search Sensor
  • AEO Benchmarking to Diagnose Market Shifts vs. Brand Issues
  • Turn AEO benchmarking into an action plan.
  • Best AEO Benchmarking Practices for Teams
  • Frequently Asked Questions About AEO Benchmarking

What is AEO benchmarking, and why does it matter now?

AEO benchmarking is the practice of comparing your brand’s visibility in answer engines against a reference point: competitors, an industry baseline, or your own history. If you’ve done competitive benchmarking in other channels, the logic is the same. You measure against peers on consistent metrics so a number like “38% visibility” carries meaning. The channel is what changes. Instead of rankings and clicks, you measure how often ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity mention and cite your brand.

It matters now for two reasons.

  • Buyers research in AI search.HubSpot’s 2026 survey of more than 3,000 CRM purchase decision-makers worldwide found that 42% used AI search during their evaluation, and those buyers were 36% more likely to purchase than those who didn’t.
  • Clicks are shrinking. Pew Research Center tracked 900 U.S. adults’ browsing in March 2025. Users clicked a traditional result in 8% of visits when a Google AI summary appeared, versus 15% when it didn’t, and clicked a link inside the summary in 1% of visits (Pew, July 22, 2025).

Together, these create an accountability gap. Organic traffic can fall while rankings hold, because the answer appears above the links. Leadership asks what changed, and without a benchmark you can’t separate a market shift from a brand-specific issue.

Pro tip: Treat every unexplained change as two questions. What happened to the market? What happened to us? Benchmarking answers the first so you can focus on the second.

AEO Benchmarking With a Two-Tier Model: Market Benchmarks Plus Brand Performance

The two-tier model pairs market-wide benchmarks with brand-level performance data. It’s how you benchmark your AI search performance against your industry: read the external trend first, then your internal KPIs.

AI Search Sensor provides market-wide AEO benchmarks. It’s a free dashboard (currently in beta) covering ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. HubSpot AEO measures brand-level AI visibility performance, and teams on Marketing Hub Pro or Enterprise get AEO included. AI Search Sensor pairs with HubSpot AEO for two-tier AEO measurement.

A single tier misleads in both directions. Brand-only data can’t show whether a drop is yours or everyone’s. Market-only data can’t show whether you’re keeping pace. Comparing the two before you change tactics prevents the most expensive AEO mistake: fixing a problem that isn’t yours.

HubSpot’s AEO case study shows benchmarking first in practice. Benchmark data revealed significant Reddit citation growth in German and French markets with zero HubSpot mentions. After a localized campaign, HubSpot’s mention rate rose from 0% to 33.5% in France and 17.1% in Germany within one month.

What to Measure in AEO Benchmarking: Citations, Share of Voice, and Sentiment

AEO benchmarking measures four things across AI engines: citation rate, share of voice, sentiment, and citation/source attribution. Each answers a different diagnostic question.

The citation rate formula comes from Stackmatix’s September 2026 measurement guide. AI Search Sensor reports two related market benchmarks: visibility score (how often a brand is mentioned relative to other tracked brands, 0 to 100%) and citation share (how often a brand’s domain appears among all citations analyzed).

Share of Voice vs. Competitors

Share of voice shows how prominent you are relative to competitors. If 100 brand mentions appear across you and your competitors and 25 are yours, your share of voice is 25%. It’s the metric most likely to explain why a competitor gets named in buying conversations, and you don’t.

Sentiment

Sentiment shows whether engines describe your brand favorably, and it connects directly to your brand health. If sentiment falls while visibility holds, you have a perception problem rather than a discovery problem, and the fix differs.

Citation and Source Attribution

Source attribution shows where engines get their information about you, and it often points off your own site. In AI Search Sensor’s Top Citation Domain Analysis, NerdWallet and Bankrate out-cite Bank of America and JPMorgan combined in Financial Services (HubSpot, updated October 2026, based on 50 representative HubSpot AEO portals). When third parties shape your category’s answers, your own blog can’t move the number alone.

Brand-Level Companions: Topic Coverage and Entity Alignment

Topic coverage is the share of your priority topics where your brand appears at all. Entity alignment is whether engines describe your brand, products, and pricing accurately, which Stackmatix tracks as brand mention accuracy. Market benchmarks don’t show either one, so they belong in your internal tier.

How AEO Benchmarking Datasets Work: Prompt Cohorts, Cadence, and Coverage

A reliable AEO benchmark depends on three design choices: which prompts you track, how often you run them, and which engines you cover.

Prompt Cohorts

A prompt cohort is a fixed set of prompts that you run the same way over time. Prompt cohorts improve benchmark reliability through consistent coverage. An ad hoc query set, where you test whatever question comes to mind, can’t show trends because week-to-week results aren’t comparable.

Build the cohort around intent. Stackmatix recommends 50 to 100 prompts organized by topic cluster and intent type, covering category, brand-adjacent, and direct brand questions.

Pro tip: Check out more market research tools and resources that can help you source category questions and competitive context.

Cadence and Consistent Sampling

Run the same cohort on the same schedule. Weekly is a practical default and matches the weekly rhythm of AI Search Sensor’s traffic and citation data. Keep engines, prompt wording, and settings fixed, and label any change so a method shift doesn’t look like a market shift.

Confidence and Limitations

AI answers vary from run to run, so one sample can mislead. A 2026 paper by Ronald Sielinski sampled Perplexity, OpenAI’s SearchGPT, and Google Gemini repeatedly. It found unstable citation rankings and many apparent domain differences inside the noise floor, and it recommends reporting uncertainty estimates.

If you’re new to the concept, this guide to statistical significance explains why small gaps often mean nothing. Stackmatix reaches a similar conclusion and recommends 30 to 60 day trend windows over point-in-time snapshots.

AEO Benchmarking Tools You Can Try Now With AI Search Sensor

AI Search Sensor is a free tool that benchmarks AI visibility, citations, and traffic by industry, and you can test it below. Paid options exist too. Stackmatix’s guide compares platforms such as Scrunch AI, Otterly AI, Semrush’s AI Toolkit, and Ahrefs Brand Radar. For market context, start with the widget.

How to Test Category Questions in the Widget

Work through the dashboard in this order:

  1. Answer Engine Volatility Tracker. The daily 0 to 100 score reads Calm (0 to 29), Moderate (30 to 59), Elevated (60 to 89), or Extreme (90+). It shows whether engines changed recently.
  2. AI Visibility Benchmarks by Industry. Toggle between visibility score and citation share, and note where recognizable brands in your industry sit.
  3. Citation Share Trends. See which content types and source channels engines favor right now.
  4. Your own numbers. Check these last.

That order applies the two-tier model: external market signal first, then internal brand performance.

What we like: AI Search Sensor publishes its methodology. Industry benchmarks use four representative companies per industry, built from public information. Traffic, citation, and volatility charts use anonymized HubSpot customer data.

To see your brand’s numbers, use HubSpot AEO.

AEO Benchmarking to Diagnose Market Shifts vs. Brand Issues

To tell whether answer engine behavior is shifting across the market right now, check the volatility score, then compare it with your own metrics. The AI Search Sensor compares daily mention rate, citation rate, citation type, and AI-referred traffic against rolling averages. A spike means the engines changed. Market-wide benchmark changes help diagnose external AI shifts versus brand-specific performance issues.

Two hypothetical scenarios show the logic.

In the first, your visibility falls during a week when volatility reads Elevated. Wait a week, gather more data, and report it as a market event.

In the second, your visibility falls during a Calm week while a competitor’s share of voice climbs. That points to your brand, and a content audit is justified.

Both scenarios prevent the same false alarm: rewriting content to fix a change that content didn’t cause.

Turn AEO benchmarking into an action plan.

An AEO benchmarking action plan sorts findings into two buckets: actions the evidence supports and hypotheses that need testing.

Actions Supported by Evidence

  • Answer-first content updates. If citation share shows engines favoring a content type you under-publish, such as comparison pages or guides, prioritize it. HubSpot’s case study reports a 56% increase in AI citations after it updated product pages with FAQs, question-based headlines, tables, and structured data.
  • Structured data and entity checks. If accuracy or sentiment data shows engines misdescribing you, audit schema markup and the pages engines pull from.
  • Off-site gaps. If review sites, earned media, or forums gain share, add off-site work to the plan.
  • Competitor gaps. Pull prompts where a competitor is named and you aren’t. A competitive analysis kit gives you a structure for comparing positioning and content side by side.

Hypotheses That Need Testing

Conclusions from a single week of data, and explanations for why an engine favors a format, are hypotheses. Test them on a limited set of pages, then watch your cohort for several weeks before scaling.

Reporting to Stakeholders

Lead with the two-tier comparison: what the market did, what you did, and the gap. Label which conclusions are evidence and which are hypotheses. Leadership trusts a team that states its uncertainty.

Best AEO Benchmarking Practices for Teams

Comparable AEO benchmarks require governance. The practical version is a short checklist:

  • Assign cohort ownership. One person owns the prompt list and approves changes.
  • Version the cohort. Keep a dated log of added, removed, or reworded prompts.
  • Fix engine coverage. Start with ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, and add engines deliberately.
  • Label everything. Every chart carries its window, engine set, cohort version, and sample size.
  • QA before reporting. Spot-check raw answers against your tool’s scores.
  • Set a reporting cadence. Weekly for the team, monthly for leadership.
  • Baseline before targets. Collect four to six weeks of data before setting goals.

Frequently Asked Questions About AEO Benchmarking

How many prompts should I include in an AEO benchmarking cohort?

Start with 50 to 100 prompts organized by topic cluster and intent. That range, recommended by Stackmatix, covers category, comparison, and brand questions. Smaller cohorts work for pilots but produce noisier results, so keep the set stable and trend it over several weeks.

Which AI engines should I track first for AEO benchmarking?

Track ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity first. AI Search Sensor and HubSpot AEO both cover these three, so your brand data and market data line up on the same engines. Add Google AI Overviews and others once your core workflow is steady.

How often should I run my benchmark tracking?

Run it weekly. Weekly cadence matches the rhythm of AI Search Sensor’s market data and gives you enough points to see a trend. Review monthly for strategy, and judge change over 30 to 60 day windows rather than single days.

How do I connect AEO benchmarking to my content roadmap?

Map each finding to a content decision. Citation share by content type shows which formats to publish, competitor prompt gaps show which topics to cover, and channel data shows where off-site work belongs. Rank the list by evidence strength and put hypotheses behind a test.

How do I report AEO benchmark changes to leadership without over-attributing the cause?

Show the market trend and your trend side by side, then state what you know and what you’re testing. If volatility was Elevated or Extreme when your numbers moved, say so, and hold off on claiming credit or blame until you have several weeks of data.

Ready to see where the market stands? Get the data behind these benchmarks in the State of AEO report.

issues.title: If AI works from anywhere, why are we commuting to watch it?
issues.summary: The collaboration they promised, in practice. Companies say it’s about collaboration. That’s garbage. The reality is a room full of people in headphones, doing alone what they could’ve done at home. The recent post from Alexa von Tobel on LinkedIn. Alexa von Tobel, who runs an early-stage fund and has backed a long list of founders, posted a small, honest question. She hadn’t been pitched a single
issues.author: Dan Maccarone
issues.content_html:
Companies say it’s about collaboration. That’s garbage. The reality is a room full of people in headphones, doing alone what they could’ve done at home.

Alexa von Tobel, who runs an early-stage fund and has backed a long list of founders, posted a small, honest question. She hadn’t been pitched a single remote-only company in six months, and she wanted to know if anyone else was seeing it.

The replies were a mix. A few pushed back. One said she had landed a remote role just fine and that nobody had to pitch her anything. Another figured the remote crowd was mostly off building their own companies now.

The reply that stuck with me came from a CEO, who said being fully remote would be harder, and less fun. It resonated because he is half right. Something real does get lost when everyone is scattered. He is just wrong about what fixes it.

What I haven’t seen is anyone ask what should be the obvious question. If the office is winning, what exactly is it “winning” people back to do?

This matters more than it used to, because the thing we always said the office was for has left the building (pun intended). We told ourselves we showed up every day to get the work done together. The making, the producing, the actual output. You went to the office because that was where the work physically got made, and it got made faster with everyone in one place.

Thomas Allen measured the reason decades ago at MIT. The closer two people sit, the more they actually talk, and past about fifty feet the conversation falls off a cliff.

Proximity was the whole point. The commute bought you that.

The work doesn’t live there anymore. It runs on its own now, in the cloud, whether you are at your desk or asleep. Gartner expects forty percent of business software to have agents built into it by the end of 2026, up from under five percent a year earlier.

Offices may still exist, but perhaps we lost the reason for them.

My position is simple, even if the fight over it refuses to be. The office isn’t dead, but it shouldn’t be mandatory. It’s worth protecting for the handful of things people can only do well together, the ones AI can’t touch. Instead it’s being forced on everyone for the work that no longer needs a building at all.

The work left the building

The founders von Tobel is funding are increasingly building agents that do the production themselves. Y Combinator’s recent cohorts are full of companies whose entire pitch is autonomous software that writes, tests, and ships code with a human barely touching it, and the firm’s own partners say AI has collapsed the cost of producing software by a factor of ten to a hundred.

This is not a forecast. It already shows up in who has a job. Erik Brynjolfsson and his colleagues at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab tracked real payroll data and found that employment for workers aged twenty-two to twenty-five in the most AI-exposed jobs sits about nineteen percent below where it should be, while their older colleagues are fine.

The gap is coming from companies not hiring junior team members, because AI is doing the checkable, process-heavy tasks that used to justify an entry-level seat. You know, the production work, the stuff we all started our careers doing.

It is not only software. Anthropic, looking at how its own models actually get used, found that coding is the single biggest category, and that while most use still has AI working alongside a person, a large and growing share, more than four in ten interactions, is now the model doing the task outright rather than assisting.

The line between the two is blurry, but it is clearly moving in one direction.

Designers feel it and say so. Francisco Barrera Aros points out that AI has swallowed the how of building an interface and is coming for the what, which is why job boards have started sprouting roles like AI Product Designer that nobody could have described two years ago.

AI took over the task of doing the work. The deciding, however, is still yours, and the deciding is where the money is.

Let’s look at what that leaves for the purpose of an office. For a century it was where the production happened, because production needed people in one spot with the files, the tools, and each other. Take that out, hand it to the agents, and the physical building becomes a very expensive room you commute to in order to do work that could happen anywhere.

Which should, by any reasonable prediction, empty the place out.

We all remember 2020, right? The pandemic sent nearly everyone home at once. Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom, and Steven Davis called it a mass social experiment in working from home, with Americans doing roughly half of all paid hours from home through most of 2020, up from about five percent before.

The floors we were told could never go dark went dark, and the striking part, in their data, is how many people were surprised they could do the job from home at all. The mandates coming down treat remote work as an unproven indulgence, when we have years of evidence that most of the job travels. The question should be which parts don’t work and why not?

So everyone scattered, right?

Obviously, work is more portable than it has ever been, but the freer people are to work anywhere, the more they actually want to be together.

Y Combinator, which has funded a good chunk of the companies building these agents, spent years running its batches remotely, and in those years its founders were scattered all over the map. Then it brought the program back in person, in San Francisco, and the founders came right back with it. The trend is easy to see in YC’s own public directory, which one analysis tracked batch by batch.

When the program went remote, barely a quarter of companies listed San Francisco as home. Once it came back in person, that climbed past three quarters, and a chunk of those founders kept choosing the city even after the three months ended and nothing required them to stay. The same batches are stuffed with startups whose product is autonomous software.

The people automating the production hardest are also the people most determined to sit in the same zip code while they do it.

This is one contender to define whole AI era, at least for the workforce. Gensler’s global survey found that the workers most embedded in AI are also the most collaborative and the most drawn to the office, which is the reverse of the lonely-robot future everyone predicted.

As AI takes more of the solo production, the human collaboration it can’t do becomes a scarce, valuable thing, and the people who live in these tools feel the pull toward the room where that still happens.

If the office were really about the work, this is backwards. These founders have built, and are selling, the exact tools that make location irrelevant. They could run these companies from anywhere, and they tell you so with a straight face in the pitch deck. Then they sign a lease three blocks from each other.

The clustering is telling you something that a pitch deck won’t. Whatever they are gathering for, it is not the production, because they already shipped the production to the cloud. It is the other thing.

There is real research on what that other thing is. Daniel Carmody, Martina Mazzarello, Paolo Santi and their colleagues at MIT’s Senseable City Lab studied what happened to people’s networks when everyone went remote, and found that distance measurably starved the weak ties, the loose connections that only form when people share a space. Weak ties are the people you don’t work with closely, the person two teams over, the one you only ever talk to because you both happened to be refilling coffee.

Mark Granovetter named their importance decades ago, in the work that gave us the phrase. The loose connections, not the close ones, are where new information and unlikely ideas actually travel. They are also the first thing to die when everyone is a tile on a screen, because nobody schedules a video call with the person two teams over for no reason.

That is what the founders are re-clustering to get back. Not the work. The accidental stuff around the work. The collisions you cannot put on a calendar, which turn out to be the one thing the agents can’t do for you and the screen can’t give you either.

The office we actually built

Stroll into a lot of these offices and look at what is actually happening.

Rows of people who commuted in to sit at a desk and type into a chatbot. Four people at four screens running four separate conversations with four separate AIs, in the same room, not speaking to each other. The agents are collaborating with nobody. The humans are collaborating with nobody.

Everyone is doing, in a shared space, the exact solo work they could have done at home, now with an uncomfortable chair and a commute attached.

I know this office because I have been there. I’ve worked as a fractional CPO at a variety of startups over the past few years and some of them required everyone in office for collaboration and culture purposes, and what was actually happening was a floor of people at open desks and shared tables, everyone heads-down in their own tasks, earbuds in, which is not collaborative in any way whatsoever.

The only real interaction occurred when somebody took a call out in the open and derailed the eight people near them, who were now straining to hear their own thoughts over somebody else’s pitch meeting. The in-person mandate had not created the intended collaboration. All it did was take solo work that people were doing fine at home and made it harder.

This is the part of “Office Space” that could have been a documentary. Peter Gibbons didn’t hate his job because the work was hard. He hated the commute, the eight bosses who each wanted the same TPS report, and the open floor where a man could lean over the partition at any moment to ask why he hadn’t used the new cover sheet.

The building added nothing to the work and did create a great deal of misery. The movie played it as absurd, but, frankly, a lot of return-to-office plans have adopted that as an operating model.

This is not an anecdote the research argues with. Ethan Bernstein and Stephen Turban put sensors on employees before and after a company tore out its walls for an open floor plan, the layout that is supposed to spark all that spontaneous mingling. Face-to-face interaction dropped by about seventy percent.

People responded to being shoved together by putting their headphones on and retreating into email and chat. This is the equivalent of throwing a party, forcing everyone to come, and watching them text each other from opposite corners of the room.

So if being in office isn’t producing collaboration, what is the mandate for? Yuye Ding and Mark Ma looked at the S&P 500 companies that ordered everyone back and found no improvement in firm value and a measurable drop in how people felt about the job. Their read was blunt. The mandates lined up with managers using the office to reassert control and to have someone to blame, not to get better work.

Forget the productivity numbers. The real cost is the people you lose, and you lose the best ones first.

Nicholas Bloom and his colleagues ran a real randomized trial, published in Nature, with more than sixteen hundred employees split between five days in and a hybrid schedule. The hybrid group quit about a third less often, with no hit to performance or promotions.

Forcing everyone back five days a week does not buy more output. It buys more resignations, and the first ones gone are the people with somewhere else to go.

That a pretty big cost for the privilege of watching your agents do the work in a room full of other people watching theirs.

The thing is, the people deepest into AI are the ones who most want to be together, and not to sit in silence. Janet Pogue McLaurin and her team at Gensler surveyed more than sixteen thousand workers and found that the heaviest AI users, about a third of everyone, are also the most collaborative, the most connected to their teams, and the most likely to come into the office. They are coming in for each other.

These five-day in-office mandates are coming almost entirely from the biggest companies, and, to be fair, that is the one place the evidence says in-person helps. Arpit Gupta, Abhinav Gupta, and Elena Simintzi tracked remote work across thousands of firms and found it cut productivity at established companies by about nine percent, while raising it at startups by about twelve.

Big, old organizations genuinely struggle to coordinate when scattered. Small teams thrive, because remote lets them hire the best people anywhere instead of the nearest people around. So the companies swinging the hardest mandates are the ones with a real coordination problem, and they are solving it by forcing the fix on everyone, including the small teams it only slows down.

What the room is actually for

Full disclosure. I have run my company fully remote since 2019, before the pandemic made it “cool.” For most of our work, I still think remote is the right answer. It’s not my favorite thing to admit that I have found that the office turns out to be very good at a few specific things, and that those few things are suddenly the only ones that really matter.

Once the agents take the production work, the part of the human’s job that remains relevant is to decide what’s worth making, to catch the thing that’s wrong and to teach the person above and below you on the ladder how to see it too.

That happens to be the work the research ties to being in a physical place together.

Melanie Brucks and Jonathan Levav ran a study putting pairs together either in person or over video and asking them to generate ideas. The in-person pairs came up with meaningfully more, and more creative, ideas. The video pairs were just as good at the next step, picking which idea to run with.

Basically, generating creative ideas is helped by sharing a space, and choosing the ones to implement isn’t. This lines up exactly with the split the agents just created. The machine is a fine partner for narrowing and deciding against known options. It is a worse one for the wide-open, slightly stupid, what-if-we-tried part, and that part goes better with a human across the table.

There is one finding that gives me pause, because it’s the real cost of how I’ve chosen to work, and it is definitely one AI has made worse.

Someone has to learn to do the actual jobs. People learn skills by sitting near other people who already know how, absorbing the small corrections, asking the dumb question out loud instead of filing a formal ticket for it. Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais measured this and found that junior engineers got dramatically more feedback when they sat near senior ones, and lost about a fifth of it when they went remote.

Proximity is how the craft gets handed down. Distance quietly starves it.

I feel this one personally, because it is the hardest part of running a company the way I do. One of my own designers, still growing in her career, put it this way. “Constructive feedback is how I know I’m improving, and that’s hard to get when you can’t just walk into your boss’s office and ask them to look at something with you. I’m lucky I’m on a small enough team that I feel comfortable reaching out. If I were part of anything larger, I think it would be much harder. Even on bigger client teams, the feedback I get from people outside my everyday group is thin, when I get it at all.”

She is right. The ambient coaching that used to just happen in a room, the over-the-shoulder correction, the pulled-aside-after-a-meeting, does not happen on its own when everyone is remote. We made it happen on purpose.

We hold a standing thirty-minute check-in every week, time that exists for nothing but the feedback and questions they’d otherwise have had to catch me in a hallway to ask. It is a deliberate, scheduled replacement for a thing that used to happen a bit more naturally. Remote turns the mentoring into something you have to build on purpose, instead of something you can assume.

This isn’t just happening at my company, of course. The KPMG American Worker Survey found AI adoption and office mandates rising together, and concluded that managers are now the linchpin for turning in-person time into real mentorship for the people earliest in their careers, the exact thing a crowded floor of people in headphones does not deliver on its own.

Now put that next to what the agents are doing. Remember the Stanford finding, that the entry-level jobs are the ones vanishing, because AI is doing the checkable, process-heavy tasks that used to be a junior’s whole first year. Those tasks were how you learned, by doing the boring version a hundred times until you could feel when it was wrong.

Anyone who watched Richie spend a week at that fine-dining restaurant on The Bear understands this. They hand him a mountain of forks to polish and nothing else, and he spends days furious about it, a grown man doing the most menial job in the building. Then somewhere in the repetition it clicks, and he comes out the other side understanding the whole craft in a way no shortcut could have taught him.

That was the art of apprenticeship. In our world, the agents are polishing the forks now, and the mentor who would have stood over you while you learned lives on a screen, if they’re there at all.

The on-ramp to every one of these careers is being pulled up from both ends at once, by the agents from below and by the distance from above, and almost nobody is talking about the two as the same problem. They are the same problem.

This is where the office earns its keep now, if it earns it anywhere. It’s not necessarily a place to produce deliverables, the agents clearly have that, but as the one place a person can still learn the judgment the agents can’t, from another person.

You cannot apprentice over a screen share nearly as well as you can over a shoulder.

Designers have already championed this work-style. Patrick Neeman has written that the next decade of design work is about owning the systems and the trade-offs underneath the screens, the part you can’t hand to a model. Vlad Derdeicea pointed out that most of a design lead’s day was never mired in pixels in the first place, but rather focusing on aligning, deciding, and convincing. Pushing pixels was a small piece of the day that a machine can now take, which gives leaders more time to do the teaching, which was always the actual job.

None of this adds up to an argument for the five-day in-office mandate. It adds up to something narrower. The office matters now for exactly the things it was never really designed to optimize, the idea you’d never have had alone, the greener team member who evolves by watching you work, the trust that only seems to set when people share a space. It matters more than ever, and for less than ever.

So what is the commute for

Every one of these mandates comes with the same justification. Andy Jassy wrote in his Amazon memo that collaborating, brainstorming, and inventing are simpler and more effective in person, and that teaching and learning from one another are more seamless. Jamie Dimon called the benefits of being together substantial and irreplaceable.

The reality is, these leaders are not wrong that those things matter, but it’s worth considering whether they are wrong that a mandate delivers them.

Chris Wardman describes this contradiction pretty bluntly, saying companies deploy AI that strips out the everyday interactions where knowledge actually transfers, then mandate attendance to protect the very thing they are automating away.

The Flex Index, which tracks the policies of roughly nine thousand companies, now puts about a third of American firms on full-time in-office, and the biggest companies are leading the charge. What that mostly creates, though, is a building full of people doing exactly the work that no longer needs a building. In the meantime, the collaboration they said they wanted is just sitting right there on the mandate, impossible to order up.

You cannot schedule serendipity for 9 a.m. Nobody mentors the new kid on command.

A good idea has never once shown up because a policy required it. Drag everyone in and chain them to the desks, and all you have manufactured is a more expensive version of the thing they were already doing at home, plus traffic.

A move that actually fits the current environment is narrower and a little strange. Treat the office the way you’d treat any specialized tool. You don’t run your whole life out of the one drawer with the good scissors, you open that drawer when you need the thing that’s in there.

Nicholas Bloom’s data keeps pointing at the same sweet spot, a couple of deliberate days together, the rest wherever the work actually gets done, which buys the retention and the output without the resentment.

Yuan Yuan and his colleagues found the same thing when looking at badge data from forty-three thousand people across a global company’s offices. Left alone, people coordinate their own in-person days around the work and the teammates that actually need to be there.

Any mandate that just counts heads on a Tuesday misses the point of being together. Come in for the ideation, the teaching, the arguing, the trust that only seems to set face to face. Then go home and let the agents run the production from a server farm that never needed to see your face anyway.

While the office technically never died, it shouldn’t be roaring back to what it was. AI merely changed what it’s for. For a hundred years it was where the work happened and now the work happens in the cloud, and the building is left holding the handful of human things we were always a little embarrassed to admit were the actual point.

Ryan Anderson, writing in Forbes about Atlassian’s internal findings, argues that as AI absorbs the routine work, value creation migrates toward the things that require human insight and collaboration, which makes the physical workplace more important, not less. Sure, AI doesn’t need an office, but the people using it do, mainly for the handful of things this quickly moving technology cannot do for them.

This brings us back to Alexa’s question. People are coming back to the office, but that was never really the question. The question is what they think they’re coming back to do. If the answer is to sit at a desk and quietly prompt a machine that works fine without them, next to other people doing the same, then they didn’t come back for the right reasons.

If people are merely driving in to be alone together, then, that, you really can do from home.

References and further reading

The work left the building

  • Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen, “Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts About the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence” (Stanford Digital Economy Lab, 2026). On the widening employment gap for young workers in AI-exposed jobs, as AI takes the entry-level tasks that once justified a first job.
  • Anthropic, “The Anthropic Economic Index.” Anthropic’s own analysis of how its models are used, with coding as the largest category and a large, growing share of use that automates tasks rather than assists.
  • Francisco Barrera Aros, “The crisis of the what” (UX Collective, 2026). A designer on AI taking over the how of building interfaces and coming for the what, leaving judgment as the differentiator.
  • Thomas Allen, “Managing the Flow of Technology” (MIT Press, 1977). The origin of the Allen Curve, the finding that communication between coworkers drops off sharply with physical distance.
  • Gartner, “Gartner Predicts 40% of Enterprise Apps Will Feature Task-Specific AI Agents by 2026” (2025). The forecast that agents built into software will jump from under five percent of enterprise apps to forty percent in a year.
  • Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom and Steven J. Davis, “Why Working From Home Will Stick” (NBER, 2021). On the pandemic as a mass forced experiment in remote work, and how surprised workers were that they could do the job from home.

So everyone scattered, right?

  • Y Combinator, Frequently Asked Questions. YC’s own statement that the batch runs in person in San Francisco, having moved back after a brief remote stretch, because it works better that way.
  • Daniel Carmody, Martina Mazzarello, Paolo Santi and colleagues, “The effect of co-location on human communication networks” (MIT Senseable City Lab). On how remote work impedes the weak ties that form through physical proximity.
  • Mark Granovetter, “The Strength of Weak Ties” (American Journal of Sociology, 1973). The foundational work on why loose connections, not close ones, carry new information and ideas.
  • Janet Pogue McLaurin, Anita Grabowska and Katherine Engel, “Will AI Make the Workplace More Human?” (Gensler Global Workplace Survey 2026). A survey of more than sixteen thousand workers finding that the heaviest AI users are also the most collaborative, the most connected to their teams, and the most drawn to the office.

The office we actually built

  • Ethan Bernstein and Stephen Turban, “The impact of the ‘open’ workspace on human collaboration” (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 2018). Sensor data showing face-to-face interaction fell about seventy percent after a move to open-plan.
