issues.title: Anthropic Will Get to $100B in Revenue with ~7% of the Headcount Google and Meta Needed
issues.summary: Jon Ma posted Brad Gerstner’s Anthropic thesis from TomorrowX this morning. Google needed about 100,000 people to get to $100B in revenue. Anthropic will get there with about 5,000. The money Google spent on people, Anthropic spends on compute. Brad $ANT Thesis: – Google had 105k people to get to $100B revenue– Anthropic needs 5k... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Jon Ma posted Brad Gerstner’s Anthropic thesis from TomorrowX this morning. Google needed about 100,000 people to get to $100B in revenue. Anthropic will get there with about 5,000. The money Google spent on people, Anthropic spends on compute.

Brad $ANT Thesis:
– Google had 105k people to get to $100B revenue
– Anthropic needs 5k people to get to $100B revenue
– the 100K people Google had, Anthropic can allocate the human cost to compute

cc @altcap@AltimeterCap@TomorrowXSummit

— Jon Ma (@jonbma) November 17, 2026

The exact figures in the post are a bit off. Anthropic’s S-1 supports the thesis anyway, and Meta’s numbers back it up too.

Google Had 80,110 Employees at $100B. Meta Had 71,970.

Alphabet did $110.9B in revenue in 2017, the first year it passed $100B. It ended that year with 80,110 employees.

Meta passed $100B four years later. It did $117.9B in 2021 and ended the year with 71,970 employees.

Those were two of the most efficient large companies ever built, and each still needed 70,000 to 80,000 people to get to $100B.

Anthropic Has 5,300 Employees and an $81B Run-Rate

Anthropic’s S-1/A shows about 5,300 employees as of September 30, 2026, and an $81B run-rate as of October 31. It added $10B of run-rate in October alone.

At that pace, Anthropic passes a $100B run-rate around the end of the year with fewer than 6,000 people. That’s about 7% of Google’s headcount and about 7% of Meta’s at the same milestone.

$15M in Revenue per Employee vs. $1.4M at Google and $1.6M at Meta

Google did about $1.4M in revenue per employee in 2017. Meta did about $1.6M in 2021.

Anthropic does about $15M per employee on a run-rate basis, roughly 10x either company at the same scale. On trailing twelve months, the S-1 says $6.6M per employee, up from $1.4M a year earlier. Over that year, revenue grew about 1,200% and headcount grew about 170%.

Q3 2026: Compute Was 58% of Revenue, People Were 10%

Anthropic’s Q3 2026 numbers:

  • Revenue: $16.96B
  • Compute and infrastructure: $9.86B, or 58% of revenue, up from 48% in Q2
  • Personnel: $1.71B, about 10% of revenue

Anthropic spent almost 6x as much on compute as on people. Year over year in Q3, personnel costs grew about 3.5x, from $489M to $1.71B. Quarterly revenue grew more than 12x.

Google Had a 23.5% Operating Margin and Meta Had 40%. Anthropic Lost $567M in Q3.

Google earned $26.1B in operating income in 2017. Meta earned $46.8B in 2021. Anthropic posted a $567M operating loss in Q3 2026.

Anthropic didn’t eliminate the cost of 75,000 people. That money now goes to Google, Amazon, Broadcom and the other compute providers. On Q3’s numbers, it costs more than the people did. That could change as inference gets cheaper per token and pricing matures. For now, the small headcount is driving growth, not profit.

What Changes for B2B Founders

The operating plan used to be built around headcount. Revenue per rep, ramp time and quota capacity set how fast you could grow, and the hiring plan sat in the middle of the board deck.

Now the plan gets built around how much work your agents can do and what that work costs. Three things follow:

  • Revenue per employee tells you less than it used to. Anthropic does $15M per employee and still lost money in Q3. Gross margin after inference and cost per unit of output tell you more.
  • Compute spend grows with usage. A hiring freeze does nothing to it, so it needs the same monthly review headcount used to get.
  • Customers are moving payroll money into AI spend. B2B AI companies that charge 2x what pre-AI competitors charge are being paid out of salary budgets.

SaaStr Runs on 3 Humans and 20+ Agents

We see the same thing at SaaStr on a much smaller scale. We run the company with 3 humans and 20+ AI agents in production, and our fastest-growing cost is the AI tools those agents run on.

Google needed 80,000 people to get to $100B, and Meta needed 72,000. Anthropic will get there with about 5,300 people, and in Q3 it spent $9.86B on compute.

issues.title: 5 Interesting Learnings from the Databricks AI Index: Open-Weight Jumps to 31% of Enterprise Tokens, 72% of Companies Now Use Multiple Model Providers, and a 281x Gap Between Median and Power Users
issues.summary: Most model share data we get comes from consumer apps, developer routers, or surveys. The Databricks AI Index uses a different source: actual token traffic from more than 10,000 companies that route their AI through Databricks’ Unity Gateway. That includes Fortune 500 and Global 2000 companies, plus traffic Databricks sends out to Anthropic and OpenAI.... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Most model share data we get comes from consumer apps, developer routers, or surveys. The Databricks AI Index uses a different source: actual token traffic from more than 10,000 companies that route their AI through Databricks’ Unity Gateway. That includes Fortune 500 and Global 2000 companies, plus traffic Databricks sends out to Anthropic and OpenAI.

One caveat before the data. Databricks hosts open-weight models and has a commercial interest in companies using them, so its customers probably lean further toward open-weight than the average enterprise. Even with that discount, the speed of what changed here is hard to ignore.

1. Open-Weight Went From 7.3% to 30.9% of Enterprise Tokens in About Four Months

Open-weight share of enterprise token traffic: 7.3% in July, 30.9% in November.

Patrick Wendell, a Databricks co-founder, said why in his launch thread. Anecdotally, companies use them mostly to cut costs on high-volume work. Enterprises are not swapping open-weight in for Claude on their hardest problems. They’re moving the bulk work there: classification, extraction, summarization, the stuff that runs a million times a day.

Two details stand out:

  • The open-weight leaders are mostly Chinese labs. The index lists Zhipu (GLM), DeepSeek, and Moonshot (Kimi) as the open-weight providers. These are large enterprises running Chinese-origin weights on US infrastructure, at volume. A year ago most enterprise security teams would have said no.
  • One model release can move the whole category. GLM 5.2 accounts for about 40% of open-weight tokens on the gateway, one month after its mid-July availability.

What this means if you’re building: If your product makes a model call on every record, every ticket, or every email, a third of your enterprise buyers’ traffic now runs on models that cost a fraction of frontier pricing. Your competitors will rebuild their COGS on open-weight. If you still route everything to a frontier model, you’ll lose on gross margin before you lose on product.

2. Single-Provider Companies Fell From 64% to 28%

Enterprises on Unity Gateway relying on one model provider: about 64% in July, falling to 28% by November 2. That happened in one quarter.

Databricks’ earlier data shows the same trend at the model level. Average unique models per customer rose from 4.2 to 7.1 since January. Roughly 40% of those models were open-weight.

Enterprises now treat models the way they treat cloud regions: several in use, routed by workload, swapped out when something better ships. It matters for two reasons:

  • “We’re built on GPT” or “we’re built on Claude” isn’t a moat, and enterprise buyers don’t want to hear it. They want to know you can use whichever model they’ve already approved, including the open-weight ones running inside their own perimeter.
  • The release pace makes lock-in impossible anyway. Since May 2026, a new flagship model launched roughly every week, or every 3.7 days when regional labs are included.

3. Anthropic Still Owns the Proprietary Side, and Opus 5.5 Took Over in Six Weeks

Open-weight is growing, but Anthropic’s lead within proprietary models grew too. Anthropic’s overall share rose from 57.6% to 68.8% over the period covered, which the article ties to Opus 5.5’s launch.

How fast it happened is the real point. Claude Opus 5.5 went from 7.2% to 37.9% of proprietary-model tokens in six weeks. Enterprises are supposed to be slow. These ones moved a third of their proprietary traffic to a new model in a month and a half, because a gateway turns switching into a config change.

The flip side matters just as much. The best model on Databricks’ coding benchmark is Claude Fable 5.1, yet Fable 5.1’s share of proprietary tokens fell from 5.5% to 0.6% over six weeks. The most capable model is not the most used. Once a model is good enough at a lower price, enterprises move to it.

Databricks did the same thing internally. They kept Opus 4.8 rather than upgrading to Opus 5, because the upgrade wasn’t worth the added cost for its workloads.

4. Gemini 3.8 Flash Had a Low Token Price and Cost $11.97 Per Task

This is the most useful section for anyone pricing an AI product. Databricks built a coding benchmark from real merged pull requests in its multi-million-line codebase and measured cost per task, not cost per token.

  • Best quality: Claude Fable 5.1 at 96.0% task success, $7.47 per task. Muse Wonder: 94.9% at $1.53 per task. That extra 1.1 points costs almost 5x as much.
  • GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5 both hit 89.1%. Luna averaged $0.05 per task versus $1.62 for Opus 5.5, about 32x less.
  • Gemini 3.8 Flash averaged 140 turns per task and $11.97 per task, one of the most expensive in the benchmark despite a low token price.
  • On open-weight, DeepSeek V4.1 and GLM 5.3 are both third, with a 93.1% pass rate, which is ahead of Opus 5.5 on this benchmark.

The harness matters almost as much as the model. In a separate test, the same model scored 61.7% in one harness, 48.1% in another, and 38.4% bare.

The decision for founders: Stop judging models by price per million tokens. A cheap model that takes 140 turns to finish costs more than an expensive one that finishes in 10. Measure cost per completed task on your own workload. Same score, 32x cost difference. That’s your gross margin.

5. The Median User Spends $2.49 a Week. The P99 User Spends $699.74.

This is the number I’d put in front of every B2B CEO still pricing AI per seat.

Median: $2.49. It more than doubled from $1.10 over six weeks. P90: no value given. The article says it stayed “relatively flat.” P99: $699.74, about 281x the median.

$700 a week works out to about $36,000 a year in list-price tokens for one person. That’s more than most companies pay per seat for any software they own. And the median user doubled their spend in six weeks.

It means three things:

  • Flat per-seat pricing breaks at the top of the distribution. Your heaviest 1% of users can wipe out the margin from everyone else. You need usage caps, credits, or tiers that track consumption.
  • The budget is real, and it isn’t software budget. I’ve said I won’t invest in an agentic B2B company unless it unlocks budget beyond software budget. Paying $36K a year for one power user’s tokens is the clearest sign yet that this budget exists. It’s being spent on headcount-level output, not on seats.
  • CFOs are about to notice. Databricks titled one of its own posts “The AI Bill is coming.” Expect enterprise buyers to ask you for per-user budgets, routing, and visibility into spend before they’ll sign.

A Few More Interesting Learnings

  • Better models can cost less. Inside Databricks, Opus 5.5 delivered improved quality at 29% lower cost per session than its predecessor. Upgrading isn’t always a price increase.
  • Frontier guardrails are pushing some work to open-weight. Hosted frontier models refused Hugging Face responders’ analysis of attack logs and exploit payloads. The team used GLM 5.2 instead. Security and other edge-case workloads will move to models you can run yourself.
  • Data retention is now a selling point. Databricks says frontier providers have departed from zero-data-retention, including a 30-day minimum retention tied to Anthropic’s frontier tier. If you sell to regulated industries, expect retention terms to become part of model selection.
  • The #1 model keeps changing. The top intelligence ranking has changed hands 20+ times since May 2023. Build the routing layer now, because the model you depend on today won’t be the leader next quarter.
  • Wasted agent tokens are a large, hidden cost. One Databricks post describes cutting $1 million a year of wasted agent spend in one hour by fixing bugs in MCP tool servers. If you run agents in production and nobody is tracing tool calls, you’re probably paying for loops.

Sources:

  • Databricks AI Index
  • Introducing the Databricks AI Index (Databricks blog)
  • The Enterprise Case for Open-Weight Models (Databricks blog)
  • FourWeekMBA on Wendell’s launch thread

issues.title: Dear SaaStr: What Was the Toughest Rejection You Ever Had in Sales?
issues.summary: Dear SaaStr: What Was the Toughest Rejection You Ever Had in Sales? The hardest rejection I’ve had in sales was around renewals. Especially ones I thought we really had earned. But still lost. In particular, in the early days of EchoSign / Adobe Sign, we had a particular manager at a strategic partner where I... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Dear SaaStr: What Was the Toughest Rejection You Ever Had in Sales?

The hardest rejection I’ve had in sales was around renewals. Especially ones I thought we really had earned. But still lost.

In particular, in the early days of EchoSign / Adobe Sign, we had a particular manager at a strategic partner where I did everything I could to help him. We made nothing off this partner — zilch — but I did everything I could to help him succeed. I built an integration when no one else would. I even flew to an event to help him, again for $0. He also had been to our home personally. A coincidence, but someone who I’d broken bread with on several levels and in several states.

He then joined one of our top logo customers as a manager. The next week, he called to tell us he was canceling the contract. We’d just done an NPS survey and found the team he had just inherited loved us. 100% support. Zero complaints. It was a game-changer for them. And no one there was asking for change management to learn a new vendor.

But … our competition was smart. They’d essentially bribed him. They’d already wined and dined him before he even started. They’d offered to do case studies with him and invited him already to their VIP Customer Conference. They’d also already invited him to a retreat in Napa. They’d offered to make him a hero. And he really didn’t care about the costs to switch vendors, or which one was better for his new team.

We lost this top logo customer, despite making everyone there insanely happy.

It hurt.

Champion change is tough. It’s risky. And when it comes, you gotta jump on it. If you don’t — the competition will.

And remember, go long. More times that not, you’ll get another chance if you treat a happy customer that churns well. It just may be years down the road.

More here: Champion Change: You Gotta Jump On It | SaaStr

issues.title: DD415 / MBA: school of profit
issues.summary: Issue 415: MBA: school of profit – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
When I finished high school and started exploring my study options back in Germany, I came across the then-new MBA (Master of Business Administration) and found it a bit baffling. I thought you first had to master a craft, then turn it into a business. The MBA seemed to suggest that the craft was not important and you could just learn how to run any business. The course description was thick with English jargon, which didn’t help. I vaguely remember someone describing it as learning how to make more money without producing anything.

That description came back to me while reading a recent opinion piece by Christopher Marquis, who has spent more than 20 years teaching at famous business schools. His verdict on his own industry: business schools can’t be repaired; it’s time to shut them down.

“I’ve come to realize that business schools don’t just reflect our economic system – they actively manufacture its priorities and normalize its harms, training the future leaders who will design and defend the structures driving our overlapping global crises. Tinkering at the margins with a class on corporate responsibility or ethics is not going to help. We don’t need to ‘fix’ business schools. We need to abolish them.”

Marquis points to research showing that managers with business degrees cut wages, yet didn’t become any more productive. He concludes:

“What registers as managerial acumen turns out to be wealth transfer – value moved away from workers and toward profits, shareholders and executives.”

He also puts into words what I couldn’t as an adolescent:

“A medical school’s core justification is health, and a law school’s is justice – undisputed public goods. Business schools are organized explicitly around a private good: the pursuit of profit. The American sociologist Thorstein Veblen identified this tension a century ago, criticizing university schools focused on commerce because they ‘need imply nothing in the way of serviceability to the common good.’”

The tension is usually glossed over with the comforting ‘win-win’ story:

“These aspirations are built on the delusional but widely accepted idea of ‘stakeholder capitalism’: that companies can produce climate stability, fair wages, healthy communities and functioning democracies while also delivering profits. Executives promise that technology will solve our environmental problems; voluntary measurement systems are offered as appropriate alternatives to public accountability; ethics is rebranded as competitive advantage rather than moral obligation.”

So what should we teach instead? Marquis points to the idea of “schools for organizing” rather than schools for business:

“Students would study co-ops, unions and social movements alongside the shareholder corporation. The central question would shift from ‘How do we maximize shareholder value?’ to ‘How do different forms of organization distribute power, risk and reward – and which should we strengthen?’”

“The goal is not to write off the students as aspiring selfish capitalists; it is to stop funneling them through a machine that narrows their sense of possibility. Many of my students arrive on campus wanting to work on the crises that our economic system has created. What they lack is an institution that is worthy of their better impulses.”

To me, this is what rethinking our economic system could look like at its most basic level. An ethics elective won’t do it. The work starts with how we teach people to think about power and capital: how currently both tend to accumulate at the top, while the ecological and social mess gets filed under ‘externalities’ and left for future generations to sort out.

We need people who can read a balance sheet and run a payroll, of course. But we could also teach them to build co-operatives, strengthen communities and organise around shared interests. Extracting value for personal gain is one model of doing business, with a long track record of consequences, but certainly not the only one.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD414 / Organising the discontent
issues.summary: Issue 414: Organising the discontent – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
I can still feel it – the collective exhale. Ann Friedman calls it ‘the great unclenching’, and Rebecca Solnit writes that a win for democracy of this size deserves a proper celebration. Fair enough.

But while the rest of us were glued to swing-state maps, something remarkable was unfolding in a corner of Europe that rarely makes our news feeds.

In Serbia, a movement led by students forced snap elections and then won them outright, ending more than a decade of autocratic rule. It started in 2024, when a train station canopy collapsed and killed 16 people. To many Serbians, it was corruption made visible. Students blockaded their universities and demanded accountability. Within months, farmers, actors, judges and pensioners had joined them, filling city squares in some of the largest protests the country has ever seen.

What’s amazing is that this ideologically mixed movement hasn’t splintered into rival factions. Instead, it has built a shared identity without a single face on the poster. Its electoral list had no leader. The 250 candidates on the ballot papers were nominated, grilled and voted on by student plenums – open assemblies at each university. This produced something that represents a decent slice of the country: a cardiologist, a grammar school teacher, a coal miner, a social worker, a former central bank governor and, for good measure, a retired basketball star.

I’ve been a fan of citizens’ assemblies for years (see DD220). There is lots of evidence that ordinary people, given time, reliable information and a genuine stake in the outcome, can make remarkably good and fair decisions. Serbia’s plenums aren’t a textbook citizens’ assembly – nobody was picked by lottery – but they share the spirit. The power to choose sat with big, messy rooms full of people. And few people have a bigger stake in the outcome than students, who’ll be living with the results long after today’s power brokers have retired to their holiday homes.

It’s hard not to see echoes of Serbia in the Gen Z protests spreading across the world. Of course, some protests turn ugly, and the looting and vandalism deserve condemnation. But the media is often far more interested in pictures of ghouls smashing shop windows than in understanding why so many people took to the streets in the first place, why so many young people can’t see a future worth studying for. Serbia shows what that frustration can build once it gets organised.

The proof is in the pudding, of course. Leaderless movements can be great at opposing and clumsy at governing. Decision-making by committee isn’t pretty. Consensus takes time, patience and a healthy tolerance for disagreement. But there’s something very inspiring about a political movement that started by asking who should represent it, not who should lead it.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD413 / The lost art of having people over
issues.summary: Issue 413: The lost art of having people over – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
As a kid, I loved our big lunch and dinner parties. There are photos of 30-odd people – friends, family, neighbours – squeezed into our apartment on borrowed chairs around tables that didn’t match. It was chaotic, loud and a lot of fun. They didn’t happen nearly often enough, and I sometimes wonder why something we all enjoyed so much was saved for birthdays and other rare occasions.

Over the years, we’ve actually made them rarer still. Derek Thompson has the numbers to prove it:

“In the last 30 years, Americans have seen double-digit declines in practically every measure of socializing. ... The share of Americans who say they host friends or family at their home at least monthly has fallen from 42 percent in 1975 to 12 percent in 2026 – a 70 percent collapse in a half-century.”

These days, the convenience economy has made staying in so easy that inviting people over feels like a self-inflicted chore.

Elizabeth Oldfield went the other way. For more than a decade, she and her husband have hosted shared dinners every other week, first squeezing eight people around a table in a tiny London flat, now feeding up to 16 at a time in their community house. By her count, around 1,500 people have come through the door. The trick, she says, is putting it in the calendar and refusing to renegotiate:

“This bizarre culture of possessive individualism will always give us reasons not to be together, so sometimes it takes a strong container to push back. ... Always keeping our options open and autonomy over our time sounds good but leaves us lonely and disoriented. Make a commitment and your future self will thank you.”

I love how unbothered she is about the state of the house. As her husband puts it, hospitality is ”not the same as entertaining”:

“To be invited into someone else’s imperfect house is, it turns out, a blessing. I do not tend to find very primped, spotless, Instagram-ready homes especially relaxing to be in. If we are going to move towards each other and build real community we have to let go of the desire to impress people.”

I wrote about the radical act of regular open-door dinners a while back (DD331), and Oldfield’s dinners are about the most practical version of that idea I’ve come across. (Do check out her list of tips in the essay.)

So why don’t more of us do it? Thompson has a pretty good theory:

“Everybody might prefer, in the abstract, a world of dinner parties, neighborhood friendships, and spontaneous gatherings. But on any given Wednesday at 7:45pm., it is easier to look at a screen than to host a party; easier to listen to a podcast while doing yoga than to plan a gathering. This is not so much an individual failure as a coordination failure. ... Compared to TikTok, a dinner party is a terrible leisure technology. It requires matching schedules, cleaning the house, buying food, accommodating children and allergies, tolerating awkwardness, and taking the risk that the evening is mediocre. By contrast, what does television ask of us? Nothing. TikTok? Even less.”

When I look at those old photos and my mum’s kitchen, I notice who’s doing the cooking. Those parties ran on a lot of unpaid labour, mostly by women, and Thompson points out that the social calendar frayed when they took on paid work and the men didn’t pick up the slack. Today’s cost-of-living pressures and two exhausted working parents make the couch and screens combo look very appealing.

Oldfield offers us a way back that doesn’t require a kitchen full of women doing all the work and stressing about being a perfect host. Her dinners run on cheap dahl and wine from Lidl. Guests chop, set the table and stay for the clean-up. Nobody performs, nobody keeps score, and somehow everyone leaves a little less alone.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

issues.title: DD412 / Breaking up with Gmail
issues.summary: Issue 412: Breaking up with Gmail – Read the full issue in the archive.
issues.author: Kai Brach
issues.content_html:
On a visit to Google’s HQ in Mountain View in 2007, I watched people run almost their entire working lives out of a browser. Gmail was still new-ish, and the Googlers I met were doing clever things with labels, aliases and filters that made my Outlook setup look like an old filing cabinet.

When Google started offering a paid Gmail version with custom domains, I made the move and Gmail slowly became the app I spent most of my days in. Docs, Sheets and Google Maps followed.

By the time I started feeling uneasy about Google, I was thoroughly entangled. The thought of dragging hundreds of thousands of emails somewhere else, and giving up some of Gmail’s then-unique features, sat in the too-hard basket for almost a decade.

But earlier this month, a friend reminded me of the EFF’s Opt Out October, and that finally gave me the nudge. I know plenty of you are in the same boat, so here’s a quick rundown of how it went.

My emails turned out to be the easy part, which is annoying given how long I spent dreading it. My shortlist came down to Proton, Fastmail* and iCloud. I liked Proton a lot when I trialled it, but its (admirable) emphasis on security means calendars and contacts won’t sync with the native apps on my iPhone. iCloud now supports custom domains, and since I’m already deep inside Apple’s walled garden, it would have been the path of least resistance. It would also have meant handing more money to a different Big Tech company.

So I went with Fastmail, a small Melbourne company (represent!) with a solid reputation. Its migration tool pulled everything across via IMAP in a few hours and mirrored my Gmail labels. On my laptop I use the web interface and don’t miss a single feature. On my iPhone, I can still use the native Calendar and Contacts apps, and Fastmail’s own app for email (it’s good). When I made a mistake during my custom domain setup, an actual human replied to my support request within a day with an answer that helped. I’d forgotten that was possible.

Google itself isn’t disappearing from my life any time soon, though. Too many clients and collaborators live in Docs and Sheets. But, I learned that once you remove your custom domain from Google Workspace, it takes Google about 20 days to ‘release’ it, after which you can sign up for a free Google account with that same custom email address.

What you can’t do is bring your other stuff with you. Ugh. Drive files have to be exported and re-uploaded into the new account. Maps and YouTube have no migration path at all, so I’m rebuilding those from scratch, one saved café at a time. Google Maps’ reviews are hard to beat, sorry Apple.

So yeah, Google does remain a fixture for a handful of ‘free’ apps. But the elephant in the room – my big fat inbox – walked out the door far more willingly than I’d expected. All up, it took a few hours over a couple of weekends. Years of dread, overcome by two weekends of mild admin. Shoulda done it ages ago. (And yet, I was just in time.)

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

* This is a referral link that gets you 10% off your first year.

issues.title: Is Dominica Worth Visiting? (Don’t make the mistakes I made!)
issues.summary: Is Dominica worth visiting? After six challenging days on the island, my honest answer is: only for a certain kind of traveler. My husband Charlie and I visited Dominica in December 2025, and it was the toughest stop by far on our four-week trip across the Caribbean. We dealt with some of the worst roads I’ve […] The post Is Dominica Worth Visiting? (Don’t make the mistakes I made!) appeared first
issues.author: Adventurous Kate
issues.content_html:
Is Dominica worth visiting? After six challenging days on the island, my honest answer is: only for a certain kind of traveler.

My husband Charlie and I visited Dominica in December 2025, and it was the toughest stop by far on our four-week trip across the Caribbean.

We dealt with some of the worst roads I’ve ever experienced, nearly constant rain, and a horrible last night spent searching for food near the airport.

Part of the problem was our expectations. Almost everything I’d read about Dominica in travel media, from “the nature island” tagline to the gorgeous waterfall roundups, made it sound like an unspoiled paradise, the ultimate gem, the place that would be everyone’s favorite island if only they knew it existed.

I knew not to expect great beaches. What I didn’t know was how much effort it would take just to get from one place to another, or how stressful those drives would be.

Planning your trip to Dominica soon?

Dominica’s tourism is growing every year, and many small guesthouses and tours fill up quickly. Book ahead to avoid disappointment!

Top Experiences and Tours in Dominica:

  1. VIP Tour: Trafalgar Falls, Sulfur Spa, and Beach (Includes my favorite hot spring!)
  2. Waterfalls, Titou Gorge, and Spa (Cool gorge swimming and my fave hot spring)
  3. Waitukubuli Volcano Snorkeling (Unique snorkel adventure)

Top-Rated Hotels in Dominica:

  1. Secret Bay (THE best small luxury hotel on the island)
  2. Kootney Resorts (I stayed here — nice midrange cottages in Portsmouth)
  3. Fort Young Hotel (Small hotel with infinity pool in Roseau)
  4. Ti Kwen Glo Cho (Spend one night at these hot springs!)

Best Dominica eSIM:I recommend an Holafly eSIM to stay connected in Dominica. Get 5% off with code HOLAKATE.

Renting a car in Dominica?Find deals on car rental rates here (but make sure you read about the reality of driving here first).

I’ve wondered for so long if I should even write this post. Not because I struggle to tell the truth — the number-one thing I hear from my readers is “You’re so honest!” — but because I don’t want to hurt a struggling island.

Dominica is still rebuilding after Hurricane Maria, and Dominicans are working hard to grow their tourism industry the right way. The last thing I want to do is punch down.

I’ve realized the most useful thing I can do is be honest but fair about the mistakes we made and what you should do differently on your trip, dear readers.

So grab yourself a cup of tea and sit back to read about one of the most lush and vibrant places I’ve ever visited: an island that is spectacularly beautiful, often deeply frustrating, and full of wonderful people who deserve a break.

This post was published in November 2026.

Is Dominica underrated, or unpopular for a reason?

Dominica occupies a unique position in travel media. Most people don’t know this island even exists, or they mix it up with the Dominican Republic.

It’s easy to see why. Dominica has no big, sandy beaches and very few large beach resorts, which keeps away mass-market tourism. Its small airport can’t handle large jets, so getting here usually means connecting through another island.

Most visitors arrive on cruise ships, spend a few hours on an excursion, and leave by dinnertime. Even some Caribbean aficionados haven’t heard of Dominica.

Dominicans are well aware of this. Thea Lafond-Gadson won Dominica’s first-ever Olympic medal, a gold, in the triple jump at the 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris, and I remember her press conference immediately after:

Okay, we’ll start with the basics. My country’s name is Dominica. We are not Dominican Republic, so it’s pronounced differently. We are about roughly 70,000 people, not 7 million, not 70 million, 70,000. And it is a gorgeous, gorgeous gem in the Caribbean.

And among the travel writers who DO know Dominica, the coverage is almost universally glowing.

Dominica is “the nature island.” Dominica is the greenest island. Dominica is the “most authentic” Caribbean island (if there were a measure for authenticity, but I digress…) Dominica is the island of 365 rivers. Dominica is the Caribbean the way it used to be.

What you rarely read is what it’s actually like to get around, where to find food, or how much it rains. And it was in this context that I planned our trip.

Dominica has been through a lot.

The most important thing to know before visiting is that Dominica has gone through some very difficult times.

In 2015, Tropical Storm Erika caused deadly flooding and landslides. Two years later, Hurricane Maria destroyed homes and infrastructure across the island, with damage and losses estimated at 1.37 billion USD. Thirty people were confirmed dead; a similar number were reported missing.

The damage was more than twice the size of Dominica’s GDP. Imagine a single storm wiping out more than two years of everything your country produces.

Dominica is still rebuilding today, and a lot of what frustrated me as a visitor, especially the roads, traces back to the damage of those storms. It’s important to keep this context in mind as you read this post.

Our Itinerary

After doing some research, we decided we would fly in and out of Dominica, rent a car for the duration of our trip, and spend six nights based in Portsmouth, Dominica’s second city, in the northwest.

For accommodation, we booked Kootney Resorts, with cottage-style accommodation.

In terms of activities, this is what we chose to prioritize:

  • Taking a boat ride on the Indian River
  • Visiting Cabrits National Park
  • Exploring Morne Trois Pitons National Park, the island’s sole UNESCO World Heritage Site
  • Hiking to Middleham Falls
  • Soaking in the hot springs in Wotten Waven

There is one prominent activity in Dominica we chose not to do: the Boiling Lake Hike.

Dominica is home to one of only two boiling lakes in the world (the other is in New Zealand), and that’s normally the type of activity I’d be keen to experience.

But the hike is very challenging, with lots of vertical climbs, and takes around 6-8 hours, and Charlie and I didn’t want to commit to a hike that was both long and difficult.

Another special activity in Dominica is swimming with sperm whales, but these are done as weeklong trips, not a day activity.

Arrival in Dominica

We arrived at Douglas-Charles Airportin Dominica via direct flight from Barbados and picked up our rental SUV.

In Dominica, they drive on the left side of the road. As Charlie is a Brit and I haven’t driven on the left in anything bigger than a Thai motorbike, we decided he would do the driving.

Dominica’s airport is located in Marigot, in the less-developed northeast of the island. This is far from Roseau, Dominica’s capital, largest city, ferry hub, and cruise port, which is in the southwest.

We set out for our accommodation in the town of Portsmouth, on the northwest corner of the island.

And so began one of the most terrifying drives of my life.

The roads between the airport and Portsmouth were in horrible condition — narrow, full of potholes, lots of switchbacks, and with deep trenches dug on each side. Not ordinary trenches. These were so wide that if you drove onto them, your car would flip over, and much of the time they were obscured by unkempt vegetation.

And that’s not all. Our flight had been delayed a few hours, so the sun set in the middle of our drive. We drove through the darkness as trucks, often with no lights on, passed us while beeping.

Charlie is a skilled driver — I trust him. But this drive was so frightening, I could barely move, my heart thudding the whole time. Google Maps said the drive would take around an hour; it took closer to two.

Once we arrived at our cottage, I collapsed in relief, my hands still shaking. And all I could think about was, We’ll need to drive BACK to the airport, too.

Settling In, and a River Journey

The owner of our cottage at Kootney Resorts, Trish, had told us not to worry about checking in that night and to just get some sleep and come by in the morning. So we walked to a Chinese restaurant down the street for a quick dinner of lo mein and fried rice.

A Chinese place? Yes.

Once you start noticing Chinese construction in Dominica, you see it everywhere: signs on building sites, Chinese crews, Chinese restaurants, and the massive new Chinese-built international airport under construction on the northeast coast.

This isn’t an accident. It goes back to 2004, when Dominica cut diplomatic ties with Taiwan in favor of Beijing. This triggered a wave of Chinese grant-financed infrastructure projects in Dominica.

China initially committed $112 million USD to Dominica in 2004; the projects have only increased since then. China also helped fund rebuilding after Hurricane Maria in 2017, including six new schools.

But why is China spending all this money? The Chinese government wants more nations to side with China and no longer recognize Taiwan. Dominica is one of many Caribbean nations where China is doing this. As always, China is playing the long game.

(This is a very interesting story, and The People’s Map: Dominica has a great read on it.)

That next morning, we headed out for a riverboat trip with Indian River Tours at 8:00 AM. I had WhatsApped the company the night before, and our guide, Dexter, encouraged us to come for an early tour to enjoy the river before the cruise ship day-trippers showed up.

Together with a French couple, we glided down the peaceful Indian River, tall palm trees poking into the stormy sky. Dominica claims to have 365 rivers — though let’s just say they have a generous definition of “river” — and they give the landscape life.

Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man’s Chest was shot in part here, and we got to see a piece of the remaining set: Tia Dalma’s shack!

We arrived at our eventual destination, a bar set in the woods, where Dexter took us on a short walk. Charlie and I played with a little brown tabby cat we named Domingo (it was Sunday, after all!).

Our tour cost $25 USD each, or 68 East Caribbean Dollars (XCD). (Many places in Dominica quote prices in USD, but XCD is more widely accepted than USD and you will almost certainly get change in XCD.)

Dexter told us we had to buy a national park pass, and we got one at a nearby gas station. National park passes are either $5 USD for one site or $12 USD for one week.

After the river trip, we went for breakfast at a cafe called Water’s Edge, a lovely little spot in Portsmouth with hearty Dominican dishes and drool-worthy baked goods. Praise music blared on the radio as we devoured an enormous pair of cookies.

Next, we hit up a local grocery store for provisions, buying a little can of jerk Vienna sausages out of curiosity. A woman walked down the aisles, her phone on speakerphone, blasting a sermon.

If you somehow ended up in Dominica on a Sunday and had no idea which day of the week it was, I think you’d figure it out pretty quickly.

Back at Kootney Resorts, we checked in with the owner, Trish. A longtime expat living in Dominica, Trish welcomed us with big hugs, gave us travel tips, and encouraged us to swim or even bathe in the creek behind her house.

Overall, we liked our cottage — it had decent internet, good cooking equipment, the AC worked well, and the covered porch was nice, even when it rained. Restaurants and the grocery store were a quick drive or a 10-minute walk away.

I highly recommend this place if you want to stay in Portsmouth, and Trish is a lovely person.

That afternoon, we made the short drive to Cabrits National Park. Located on the edge of Portsmouth, it’s the smallest of the three national parks on the island. Here we explored Fort Shirley, a British garrison edged with cannons.

That day, a Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection ship was docked just off the park. (While most cruise ships dock in Roseau, some smaller ships dock here in Portsmouth.) And I won’t lie — it looked like a VERY NICE place to spend a vacation!

Cabrits National Park is also home to some short and easy hiking trails. We walked down a few of them.

To be honest, Cabrits National Park is nothing special — I don’t think it’s necessary to visit, and it’s definitely not worth paying for an additional national park pass unless you already have a weekly pass.

After the park, we drove up the coastline to the towns of Savanne Paille and Toucari, and once again I held my breath as Charlie drove those twisted, hilly, rugged roads.

But the journey was worth it. While the conventional wisdom is that Dominica is not a place you come to for beaches, there were actually a few nice ones up here.

The beaches themselves were narrow, with not much room to spread out, but they were pretty, with calm water and gorgeous sunset views.

We grabbed some sodas at a beach bar called Keepin It Real and enjoyed shrimp and macaroni pie at Roots Rock Bar & Grill. The sunset that night was purple and lovely.

Also on this part of the island? The InterContinental Resort, with a long driveway leading up to the luxurious grounds. Charlie and I wondered if they offered day passes.

Oh, and they did. But something else came up first.

So Much Rain

By the time we arrived in Dominica, Charlie and I had been in the Caribbean for three weeks spanning late November and early December. We had a little bit of rain in Curaçao, Barbados, Grenada, and Martinique, but the showers were always brief and gentle.

That wasn’t the case in Dominica. Here, the rain came down in sheets and lasted for hours.

On our second full day, it was pouring so hard that we only left our cottage to eat and get more groceries, and spent the rest of the time doing laundry and catching up on our inboxes.

The day wasn’t a loss, though — we got some delicious shawarmas for lunch at a place called Kenan Shawarma King, and spent our meal cuddling a tiny calico kitten. After lunch, we bought a big bag of kitten food for the owner, who was delighted.

As it continued to rain over the next few days, I realized that our clothes weren’t drying. We were hanging them on a drying rack inside, and they were still damp days later.

And it’s not like I was washing jeans — I brought a wardrobe almost entirely made of thin performance merino wool, which usually dries in less than half a day. How do people even dry their clothes here?!

Dry season in Dominica is technically from December to May, but rain can happen anytime. We soon learned that it would pour throughout our trip.

Exploring the Rainforests of Dominica

On our third full day, we decided to explore the interior of Dominica and spend thenight in Wotten Waven, a town known for its geothermal activity.

Even though Wotten Waven was only an hour and 15 minutes from Portsmouth according to Google Maps, we figured it would be safer to stay over, rather than rushing to get back before dark.

As we drove southward toward Roseau, the road changed. The closer we got to the city, the wider and smoother the roads became.

Of course, it wasn’t without its challenges. Google Maps sent us down a few dead ends until we finally made it to the Emerald Pool in UNESCO World Heritage-listed Morne Trois Pitons National Park.

We parked nearby, spent about 15 minutes walking through the forest, and made our way down a staircase to the pool.

This is the kind of place that makes you appreciate Dominica — the lush, thick vegetation, rivers, and waterfalls. It feels like the jungle setting was turned up to eleven.

It was a beautiful place to visit — but not a place where you necessarily need to linger, unless you want to swim. We took our photos, enjoyed the atmosphere, and climbed back up.

The good thing is that we set out early and were able to beat the cruise ship excursions. Had we gone in mid-afternoon, our photos would have been full of bobbing heads.

Hiking to Middleham Falls

After grabbing lunch at another roadside restaurant (with yet another cat, of course), Charlie and I drove to the trailhead for Middleham Falls. While the Emerald Pool and Middleham Falls look close on a map, you actually have to drive all the way back to the west coast, then down another inland road.

We chose Middleham Falls for our hike in Dominica because we wanted a hike that was around medium difficulty and not more than a few hours, with a great visual payoff. It was also fairly close to our final destination of the day, Wotten Waven.

The road to the trailhead was the single worst road we experienced in Dominica. This was a dirt road so badly torn up that you had to creep along at a snail’s pace or risk popping your tires.

But it wasn’t a very long drive to the trailhead, and soon we were in the parking lot, looking at the wreckage of a half-built eco-resort with grass roofs that had been abandoned mid-construction.

The hike to Middleham Falls is an out-and-back hike that is 5.3 km or 3.3 miles total and takes about 1.5-2 hours.

The hike started nicely, and soon the rain began to fall again. We didn’t mind it that much; we could handle it. Even when we passed a shaded gazebo that marked the halfway point, we didn’t feel the need to stop.

As we continued along dirt paths in the forest, climbing stairs into the hills, and stepping around giant tree roots, we breathed in that delicious forest air. The rain fell harder and harder, but the scent of the forest made me feel alive.

And there we were, probably a five-minute walk from the gorgeous waterfall, so close that we could hear the rush of water, and the trail…turned into a pile of rocks.

We would need to scramble on our hands and knees and climb down the boulders in order to get to the waterfall.

What the hell?!

The hike had been perfectly moderate until then, and nothing I’d read had mentioned scrambling.

We stood there, underneath our umbrellas, wondering if it was worth the risk. We would probably be fine. Or it could go very, very badly. And I did NOT want to risk hitting my head or breaking a bone in Dominica.

So we made the decision to call it. Five minutes from the waterfall. Oh well.

We hiked back to the gazebo at the halfway point to wait out the rain. The rain did not change whatsoever, and so we continued in the downpour.

Back at the car, I peeled off my soaked merino socks and squeezed out my hair. It was time to head to the hot springs.

Overall, Charlie and I thought this was a lovely hike until the end, and if it hadn’t been raining so hard, we would have tackled the scramble. But boulders plus sheets of rain was just too much.

Wotten Waven Hot Springs and Ti Kwen Glo Cho

There are lots of “hot springs resorts” in the town of Wotten Waven, but Ti Kwen Glo Cho is one that came highly recommended to me. It’s a popular spot for cruise ship excursions during the day, but if you stay overnight, you can enjoy the pools without the crowds.

Wotten Waven is perched on a hill in the interior of the island, with lots of colorful houses and churches. We found Ti Kwen Glo Cho easily, checked in, and were given a simple, rustic room with bunk beds that could have accommodated a family with kids.

The grounds at the resort are beautiful, filled with flowers, fruit trees, and nicely manicured paths. From the check-in area, you walk down staircases built into the hills until you reach the pools.

There are two pools — a “warm pool” and a “mud pool,” though to be honest they looked and felt the same — as well as a bathtub with a stream of water falling into it. A river flows behind the pools, and there’s a shaded changing area.

And while it was still raining, it felt absolutely divine slipping into that velvety warm water, surrounded by flowers as little cold raindrops dotted my cheeks. What a treat for sore muscles. By the late afternoon, we were two of only five people at the pools.

We did have one snafu — we went to the restaurant for dinner and the staff were annoyed that we hadn’t told them we wanted dinner when we checked in. That was our mistake.

If you want dinner, tell them when you check in. (They still fed us, and we had some delicious quesadillas.)

Something to keep in mind is that the walls are thin here. Staying in the room next to us was a family with two rambunctious kids, and just down the street was a Pentecostal church blasting its service.

Earplugs are always a smart thing to pack, wherever you travel, and that’s especially true for Ti Kwen Glo Cho.

A day visit at Ti Kwen Glo Cho costs $10 USD as of 2026, and double rooms with spa access start at $80 USD per night. Breakfast is $15 USD extra.

One thing I especially enjoyed is that Ti Kwen Glo Cho is owned by a local Dominican family. If you want to keep your money in local hands, this is a great place to do so.

A Day at the InterContinental

The next morning, Charlie and I took a final soak in the hot pools, had a tasty breakfast of eggs, beans, and plantains, and drove back to Portsmouth without incident.

And we decided to splurge.

By this time, we were tired of white-knuckling the terrible roads. Tired of being wet all the time. Tired of climbing stairs to get anywhere.

So we called the InterContinental and ordered day passes for the next day, at $37 USD each.

As we drove up that long driveway, I felt a bit embarrassed. Did I really travel to one of the least touristy places in the Caribbean, just to escape to a luxury resort? I roll my eyes at that kind of traveler.

And let’s talk about the most important part: it’s not like most Dominicans can pick up and spend the day at a luxury hotel when they need a break from their island. It’s not like they can decamp to a resort after a hurricane destroys their home.

That being said — luxury resorts, especially large resorts run by international chains like the InterContinental, are instrumental in growing Dominica’s tourism industry.

Yes, they employ locals, but they are also training locals in international hospitality standards. That training is critical to growing locally owned tourism in developing parts of the world.

I believe that many Dominican InterContinental employees will go on to open their own hotels and tourism businesses, and they’ll be better, more sustainable businesses as a result.

The InterContinental is perched on the coast, but there are no beaches. Instead, the pools feel a bit like the sea — you walk in and they deepen gradually.

And after the last several days, it was SO nice to sit on a lounger, read my Kindle, drink a coffee frappe, swim, and dry myself with a towel that was fluffy and not crispy, while enjoying the T-Pain-filled 2000s R&B playlist the resort was playing.

As usual, it rained hard for about 90 minutes. We spent that time in the restaurant. But this time, the sun actually came out afterward.

And those few hours of relaxation were exactly what we needed for the journey ahead.

Advance registration is required for day passes at the InterContinental Dominica Cabrits Resort & Spa. You can email info.dominica@ihg.com or call +1 767-445-1000. Passes are $37 USD on weekdays and $60 USD on weekends.

The Departure from Hell

Shortly before arriving in Dominica, we were notified that our WinAir flight from Dominica to St. Maarten had been rescheduled from 11:55 AM to 7:15 AM.

That threw a wrench into things — in order to make our flight, we would either need to leave Portsmouth in the middle of the night, or spend our final night by the airport.

I immediately vetoed driving on those roads after dark again, so we decided to shorten our stay at Kootney Resorts and drive to the town of Marigot while it was still light out the day before our departure.

At first I assumed we’d just stay at the airport hotel, but no, there was no airport hotel. There were actually no hotels near the airport. Just guesthouses.

No problem. We’d stay at a guesthouse. We booked the Golden Inn.

The drive back from Portsmouth to Marigot was terrifying once again, but I concentrated on breathing deeply through my fear, and I even managed to get a few photos.

We pulled up to the Golden Inn and nobody was home except a little boy around 10 years old, who showed us to a room reeking of old shrimp with a dirty unmade bed.

“Is your mom going to be home soon?” I asked him. He shrugged.

“Okay. We’ll get some food and come back and talk to your mom, okay?”

“Okay.”

And off we set to find some dinner in the town of Marigot. Google Maps had a handful of restaurants on the map.

We headed to the first one, La Petite Bistro. It had been shuttered for a long time.

We headed to the next one, JU-C FRU-T SMOOTH-E HUT. Also shuttered.

We drove to the Last Flight Bar & Grill. It had an airplane sitting next to it, but the restaurant was just a shell.

“Let’s just find a minimart or something,” I told Charlie. “We can eat chips and cookies for dinner if we have to.”

There were no minimarts, no grocery stores, no convenience stores. We started pulling over and asking locals if there was a restaurant, a store, anywhere we could buy food. And each time, they would say, “Not here,” and shrug.

Desperate, I hopped back into the car after my latest fruitless inquiry with a shop owner. “Let’s just go to the airport,” I told Charlie. “There HAS to be something there.”

We drove to the airport — and THERE WAS AN OPEN RESTAURANT! It was 5:50 PM, they were closing in ten minutes, and all they had left were sandwiches and fries.

We returned to the Golden Inn, where the owner was now home and had made up a clean bed for us. The shrimp smell was still terrible, but by that point, we weren’t going anywhere else.

And by then, we were expecting to just get out of Dominica with no further issues, but no, there was one more surprise planned to send us off! Our luggage was too heavy, the WinAir worker told us, and we would need to pay more.

“Fine,” I said. “I don’t care. We’ll pay.”

“And the machine isn’t working,” she said. “We can only take cash.”

“FINE,” I said through gritted teeth. “I will go to the ATM.” I would have paid whatever they asked.

As our flight took off, cresting over the hills of Dominica, I squeezed Charlie’s hand and sighed with relief. I have never been so relieved to leave an island.

What I Would Have Done Differently

So, if you’re reading this and you’d be interested in visiting Dominica, but doing it in a much better way than I did, that’s great!

Let me tell you what I would have done differently.

I would not have rented a car. I would have hired drivers. Even though Charlie drove well in Dominica, the scary drives turned me into a basket case, which is not how anyone should spend their vacation.

I would have stayed in the Roseau area for at least some of the time. Roseau is the most developed part of the island, with much better roads, the greatest variety of accommodation and restaurants, and most tours depart from here (though they’re primarily designed for cruise ship excursions).

While I enjoyed Portsmouth and especially staying at Kootney Resorts, I think it would be better suited for a shorter duration.

When I found out about the flight being rescheduled to early in the morning, I would have hired a driver to take us VERY early in the morning. It was absolutely not worth spending a night in Marigot.

I would have visited during the driest months of the year. While the dry season in Dominica technically runs from December to May, the driest months are February, March, and April.

I would not have trusted Google Maps, especially for restaurants. So many of the restaurants listed as active and open on Google Maps had been closed for months. I don’t know if this would have helped, but it would have kept my expectations in check.

I would have considered taking the ferry to Roseau rather than flying in. There is a passenger ferry called the FRS Express des Îles that runs from Guadeloupe to Dominica to Martinique to St. Lucia. While that didn’t work for our particular trip, this is a great way to avoid the airport altogether.

I would have packed backup protein bars. I always pack protein bars when traveling solo, and eat them when I arrive late or don’t feel like going out, but I don’t when traveling with Charlie, as he would NOT be happy eating a protein bar for dinner. But they would have saved us on the final night.

Is Dominica worth visiting?

Overall, I feel like Dominica is worth visiting if you’re a certain kind of traveler — the kind of traveler who genuinely enjoys visiting less developed places and relishes the challenges of travel.

(And no, I’m not talking about the people who THINK they should enjoy visiting less developed places — I mean people who genuinely prefer them.)

Dominica is also a nice choice for people interested in outdoor exploration and hiking, especially hardcore hiking, but not beaches.

But you need to be both of these things: an outdoorsy person AND a person who enjoys the challenges of less developed countries. If I were traveling for outdoor exploration and hiking, I’d visit Costa Rica or Guatemala in a heartbeat before returning to Dominica, because they have much better travel infrastructure.

Additionally, if you’re visiting Dominica, you need to be okay with a LOT of rain, including rain while hiking, swimming, and hot spring-basking.

My friend’s parents owned a house in Dominica for many years, until Hurricane Maria destroyed it. Her dad is the kind of person who enjoys being on a tropical island, far away from everyone, ESPECIALLY tourists.

Back in 2022, Charlie and I happened to be in Puerto Vallarta when our friend’s dad passed through for one night after a vacation on the Oaxaca coast. We met up, and Charlie asked him how he liked Vallarta.

“I’M NEVER COMING HERE AGAIN!” he yelled.

For him, Dominica was perfect. (“He would still be there if he weren’t 78 years old,” my friend told me.)

Would I go back to Dominica? To be completely honest, I don’t see the need to return. But not in a “I would NEVER go back!” way.

There are so many Caribbean islands I would rather return to than Dominica (Bequia, Curaçao, Martinique, and St. Lucia, among others). Not to mention the Caribbean islands I haven’t visited yet (Anguilla is hopefully next).

Our time on this planet is limited. I’d rather spend my time exploring places I want to see, not returning to a place I didn’t love just to make a point.

I feel like I’ve given Dominica a chance, and even though the trip was challenging, I still had some moments of joy, like the Indian River trip, most of the hike to Middleham Falls, and our time at Wotten Waven.

Dominica is not the place for me. But it might be the place for you.

Does Dominica sound like your kind of place?

The post Is Dominica Worth Visiting? (Don’t make the mistakes I made!) appeared first on Adventurous Kate.

issues.content_html:
Yes, you need an eSIM for Croatia — even though it seems like everywhere has wifi! From cafes in Split to apartments in the hills of Dubrovnik, it seems like the wifi card is just about everywhere.

But that only gets you so far. You will likely also need data in Croatia when road-tripping along the coast (did I mention that Croatia is one of the best countries in Europe for a road trip?), exploring natural wonders like canyons and lakes, and in city squares when the public wifi happens to be on the fritz.

And believe me — when it comes to Croatia travel, I know what I’m talking about!

I visit Croatia often; have covered all the nation’s corners, from Istria to Slavonia to Dalmatia; and I even threw my 40th birthday party in Croatia, inviting friends from around the world to celebrate on my beloved island of Korčula.

In 2022, I was awarded the Golden Pen Grand Prix, Croatia’s top travel writing award for foreigners, and I received one of my favorite compliments ever — “You understand Croatia like Croatians do.”

And I would never dream of visiting Croatia without an eSIM in my phone. Having internet on my phone makes my Croatia trips easy and so much better. Here’s exactly which one to get, and why.

This post is published in partnership withHolafly. All opinions and stories are most definitely my own!

Best eSIM for Croatia

  • Best eSIM for Croatia Overall: Holafly
  • Best Budget eSIM for Croatia: Airalo
  • Best eSIM App Experience in Croatia: Saily
  • Best eSIM for Calls and Texts in Croatia: SimLocal
  • Best eSIM for Short, Simple Trips to Croatia: Breeze

Do you really need an eSIM for Croatia?

If you live in a country outside the EU, you almost certainly need an eSIM for Croatia. (If you live in the UK, double-check that, as some UK phone plans still cover EU roaming — but if you’re from the US, Canada, Australia, etc., you will most likely need one.)

And even relying on wifi alone isn’t enough in Croatia. Here are some things to keep in mind when traveling in Croatia:

Stone walls can block signal. And Croatia has a LOT of stone walls and buildings, from Dubrovnik’s walled Old Town to Diocletian’s Palace in Split to the tangled lanes of Korčula and Hvar Town. These centuries-old limestone buildings were designed to be thick enough to hold off an attack from seafaring marauders. They’re also very good at blocking signal indoors.

Ferries and catamarans are dead-zone roulette. If you’re taking a ferry a short distance, like the 50-minute car ferry from Split to Brač, you’ll usually be fine.

But on longer crossings to further-out islands like Vis, you’ll hit stretches of open water where your signal disappears. Know that if you’re planning to message your apartment host as you pull into the harbor.

National parks are in canyons and forests. Plitvice Lakes National Park is so beautiful because it’s a series of lakes and waterfalls tucked deep in a forested gorge, and that terrain isn’t kind to mobile signal. Same with the rocky national park of Paklenica and parts of Krka.

The drive inland is empty. Driving from Zagreb to the coast through Lika, or crossing the Velebit mountains, you’ll go long stretches with nothing but forest, rock, and the occasional roadside peka (lamb cooked under the bell). Offline maps are your friend here, but a solid eSIM can make a big difference.

Apartment wifi is a gamble. Accommodation in Croatia, like many Balkan countries, is primarily private rented apartments (sobe and apartmani), and wifi quality can vary wildly from host to host. (Don’t ask me about the time in Montenegro when “in-apartment wifi” meant “lean out the window and get on the signal from the restaurant across the street.”)

None of this means eSIMs don’t work in Croatia — they do, and well, in the places tourists actually spend most of their time. It just means the eSIM you pick, and how you use it, matters more here than in a place with uniformly excellent coverage.

Which Croatian Networks Do eSIMs Use?

Croatia is simpler than most countries: there are only three mobile networks. Most eSIM providers connect to one or more of these rather than running their own local network, so which carrier(s) your eSIM uses affects your real-world coverage.

Hrvatski Telekom (HT) is the biggest, owned by Deutsche Telekom, and generally has the widest coverage, including on islands and in rural areas. If you’re heading somewhere remote, you want an eSIM that can use HT.

A1 Croatia is the second-largest network, with coverage that’s close to HT’s in most of the places tourists go.

Telemach is the smallest of the three. It’s solid in cities and along the coast but thinner in remote spots.

Holafly connects across Croatia’s major carrier infrastructure, which is part of why it’s my top pick for the country specifically — you’re not locked to a single network’s blind spots.

Why can’t I just use my home phone plan in Croatia?

Please, please, please don’t do this. It’s almost always an expensive mistake.

International roaming — especially on US plans — is often absurdly expensive, and Croatia is no exception. I’ve had friends come home from a week in Europe to a $200+ phone bill because they didn’t think a few social media uploads would cost THAT much.

An eSIM for Croatia typically runs a small fraction of that cost of international roaming, and you can install it from your couch before you ever board the flight.

What Matters When Choosing an eSIM for Croatia

Are you visiting any countries besides Croatia? This is the big one.

Croatia only? Get a Croatia eSIM.

Croatia plus Slovenia or Italy, or maybe somewhere else in the EU, like France or Greece? A Europe eSIM makes sense.

But are you planning to visit Bosnia or Montenegro, too? Most Europe eSIMs do not include these non-EU countries. You may need a different eSIM covering these countries.

(Traveling in several Balkan countries besides Croatia and Slovenia? Holafly has a Balkans eSIM that covers Bosnia, Montenegro, Serbia, North Macedonia, and Albania.)

Now, do you actually need an eSIM if all you’re doing is day-tripping to Mostar or Kotor? Personally, if it’s just one day, I think I’d go without and lean on wifi. But both Mostar and Kotor are much better if you stay overnight, and if you stay for multiple days, definitely get an eSIM.

Are you sailing? Croatia is home to some of the clearest turquoise waters you’ve ever seen, and I highly recommend some time on a boat, whether it’s a day trip to the Blue Cave, a chartered sailboat, or even the Yacht Week.

On a boat, your phone is often your only internet connection, and if you’ve got signal when nobody else does, trust me, EVERYONE will want to hotspot off you. Unlimited data is worth its weight in gold here.

Will you be taking a lot of photos and videos with your phone? I mean, I almost feel dumb asking that, because Croatia is one of the most beautiful countries in Europe, if not the world. You WILL take a ton of photos and videos.

But keep in mind that if your photos automatically sync to the cloud, that will eat up your data SO fast. Once again, it’s wise to get unlimited data for this reason alone.

Will you need to make calls? Most Croatian apartment hosts and tour guides use WhatsApp for communication, so you probably won’t need a local number. But if you’re booking a boat captain in a small harbor or calling a konoba for a table, a plan with voice can come in handy.

Best eSIM for Croatia Overall: Holafly

Holafly is the eSIM I use on every international trip, and it’s what I recommend for Croatia.

Holafly offers unlimited data with no throttling, and connects across Croatia’s major carrier network rather than relying on just one — which matters a lot, given how much coverage varies between Dubrovnik’s old town, the remote island of Vis, and Zagreb’s city center.

The big reason for Holafly is because it offers unlimited data. On a Croatia trip, especially one involving the gorgeous coastline, I don’t want to be rationing gigabytes. I want my photos to back up without it costing me a fortune.

Every Holafly eSIM also includes Always On, a 1GB-per-month backup data allowance. That’s a real safety net if your main plan runs out while you’re stuck at an airport, trying to figure out how to navigate flight delays.

Holafly offers a Croatia-specific eSIM as well as a Europe eSIM, which is handy if you’re combining Croatia with Slovenia, Italy, or anywhere else in the EU.

(Keep in mind that the Europe eSIM does not cover Bosnia or Montenegro, but their Balkans eSIM covers Bosnia, Montenegro, Serbia, North Macedonia, and Albania.)

You can get 5% off your Holafly eSIM with the code HOLAKATE. This code also gives you 10% off subscription plans.

Best Budget eSIM for Croatia: Airalo

If you mainly need maps, WhatsApp, and email in Croatia, without dealing with many photo or video uploads, Airalo is hard to beat on price.

Airalo’s Croatia eSIM connects across multiple Croatian networks and you can find the cheapest plans for prices as low as just a few dollars.

The tradeoff: I would double-check that your photos don’t automatically upload to the cloud, because if they do that, you will need to top up constantly throughout your trip and the low price goes out the window.

Best eSIM App Experience for Croatia: Saily

Saily — the eSIM from NordVPN — bundles in an ad blocker, web protection, and a virtual location tool.

Coverage across Croatia is solid, and entry pricing is competitive, with short plans for just a few dollars.

Just know that even Saily’s “unlimited” plans give you a set amount of high-speed data per day before slowing down, which is worth checking against how heavily you’ll be using data on your journeys.

Best eSIM for Calls and Texts in Croatia: SimLocal

SimLocal is worth a look specifically for people who need to make phone calls.

You may need to call guesthouses, restaurants, or apartment rental hosts who don’t always respond on WhatsApp, especially outside the major cities. A phone number will solve these problems.

SimLocal plans run 7 to 90 days with a no-questions-asked refund policy on unused plans, though pricing isn’t always the cheapest and network quality can vary by region.

Best eSIM for Short, Simple Trips to Croatia: Breeze

Breeze is a good fit for a quick long-weekend trip to Zadar or Dubrovnik or Split — no app required, plans valid for 12 months from purchase. Simple and easy.

Just note their “Unlimited” plans throttle hard after 1GB/day, which is on the low side if you’re going to be uploading video.

How to Install an eSIM for Croatia

If you go with Holafly:

Buy your Holafly eSIM at Holafly.com before you leave — don’t forget code HOLAKATE for 5% off. Choose Croatia (or the Europe eSIM if you’re visiting multiple countries), and select your trip length.

You’ll get install details by email and WhatsApp within about a minute.

Install via QR code, manual entry, or one-tap install if you’re on iOS 17.4+.

Once you land — in Dubrovnik, Split, or wherever — turn on your eSIM and set data to roaming.

(I always do this before I even board the flight, so I land already connected instead of hunting for airport wifi.)

If you run into any issues, Holafly has 24/7 customer support via chat and WhatsApp.

Frequently Asked Questions About eSIMs for Croatia

Do I need an eSIM for Croatia, or is wifi enough?

Wifi alone isn’t enough. You’ll want data for navigating historic centers, catching buses and ferries, translating menus, and booking last-minute reservations, all of which often happen when you’re away from working wifi.

Do Croatian eSIMs work in Bosnia and Montenegro?

Usually Croatian eSIMs do not work in Bosnia and Montenegro, as these countries are outside the EU. But double-check with your eSIM provider.

Do eSIMs work on Croatian buses?

Generally yes, in populated areas, but expect drops on rural stretches between cities and towns. Coverage tends to be strongest in and around major stations.

Do eSIMs work on Croatian ferries and islands like Hvar and Korčula?

For the most part, yes! Coverage is decent near shore and in port towns, but can be spotty on longer ferry crossings to further-out islands like Vis. Many Croatian islands are home to decent-sized cities, and they have good coverage.

Is an eSIM cheaper than a tourist SIM at the airport?

Usually, yes, once you factor in the time saved and the ability to set it up before you even land — plus, you skip the line and the passport paperwork, which to me is always worth it.

Which Croatian network does my eSIM use — Hrvatski Telekom (HT), A1, or Telemach?

It depends on the provider.Holafly connects across Croatia’s major carrier infrastructure; other eSIMs can vary. Check before you buy if you’re headed somewhere rural.

Are eSIMs safe?

Absolutely. They’re held to the same telecom security standards as physical SIM cards, and they can’t be physically removed or stolen the way a plastic SIM can.

Does an eSIM drain my phone’s battery?

No, this is a common misconception. eSIMs don’t drain your battery any more than a regular SIM card.

Can I keep my regular number while using a Croatia eSIM?

In almost all cases, yes — most phones support two active SIMs at once. Just check with your home carrier about text charges while abroad. And turn off data roaming for your home SIM card or eSIM!

What if my phone isn’t eSIM compatible?

If you’ve got an iPhone XS or later, a Samsung Galaxy S20 or later, or a Google Pixel 3 or later, you’re set. Older phones and a lot of budget Android models don’t support eSIM, so double-check your specific model before you buy anything.

If your phone isn’t eSIM compatible, you’ll need to get a physical SIM card on the ground.

Which eSIM Should You Choose for Croatia?

For most Croatia trips, Holafly is still my pick. Unlimited data means I have the freedom to take as many photos and videos as I want, knowing that they’ll be saved to the cloud at no extra cost to me.

I’m not doing math every time I want to upload a video from Zadar or Mljet. That’s no way to spend a vacation.

Airalo is the better call if you’re on a tight budget and traveling light on data. Saily adds security extras. SimLocal is worth it if you need to make phone calls. Breeze is fine for a quick weekend in one or two cities.
